E3.justification: The principal segmentation experiments move from PSPNet to SegFormer-b0. v1 permits early stopping and uses recommended configurations for individual baselines; v5 specifies matched configurations, fixed 160k-iteration training, and best-mIoU checkpoint selection. Reported validation and sensitivity-update schedules also change. New protocols include foundation-model fine-tuning, 20k-iteration ACDC Snow adaptation, and training-size sweeps from 1,000 to 5,000 samples.

E4.justification: v5 adds a clean-warmup ablation, training-data-size analysis, runtime/storage comparison, and dedicated windshield-wiper occlusion cases. The uniform control changes its question: v1 Table 5 removes sensitivity guidance, whereas v5 Table 6 samples uniformly among sensitivity-selected levels. Existing KID/FID, level-count, and training-curve analyses are retained in reorganized locations.

E5.justification: v5 Table 1 newly reports mean and standard deviation across four timing runs, and Section 4 states that experimental random seeds are fixed. v1 provides neither disclosure. This is a limited extension of statistical reporting: segmentation performance tables still provide point estimates without run-to-run uncertainty, and no increase in accuracy-evaluation runs is established.

E6.justification: The robustness and ablation tables contain substantially replaced results under changed experimental settings, alongside new fine-tuning, adaptation, classification, and efficiency results. Even the retained clean-backbone comparison changes entries: PSPNet RandAugment mIoU is 45.245 in v1 Table 1 and 69.360 in v5 Table 11, while Ours remains 71.840. These are reported-result changes, not evidence of same-setting performance gains across versions.

M1.justification: The KID-based sensitivity estimator, equal-spacing objective, PCHIP approximation, and online augmentation framework remain. However, v1 Equations 10–11 specify accuracy-squared sampling weights within augmentation types and uniform type probabilities, whereas v5 Algorithm 1 and Section 4.6 specify accuracy-ranked Beta-Binomial sampling with parameters 0.75 and 1.0. This changes the sampling component within the retained framework.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and existing methodology exposition are substantially rewritten. The basis-augmentation background moves from the main text to Appendix J.1, the experimental narrative is reorganized, and the appendices are extensively rearranged. These changes affect the presentation of retained material as well as accommodating new experiments.

P2.justification: v5 redraws the overview diagram, adds data-size plots and occlusion examples, replaces qualitative comparisons, and restructures major tables by changing comparator rows and reducing displayed metric columns. Existing augmentation illustrations and the clean-backbone table move to the appendix, while the training sensitivity curves move into the main text. Typography and page layout also change throughout.

R1.justification: v5 expands discussion of adversarial augmentation and segmentation-specific Superpixel-Mix, and adds references supporting VIPAug, IDBH, and foundation-model experiments. It removes the Kamann–Rother and Alomar-based motivation used in v1. The central positioning relative to AdvSteer, random augmentation, and learned augmentation policies remains.

T1.justification: v5 Appendix A adds an explicit proof of the existing equal-spacing solution, establishing the bound Gmax/L and its attainability under continuity assumptions. It also clarifies the clean-data endpoint and accuracy normalization. v1 already presents the telescoping identity and equal-spacing solution, so this is a focused formalization rather than a new theoretical framework.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens empirical support by replacing loosely specified SOTA comparisons with named, more consistently controlled baselines and directly measuring the central efficiency claim in Table 1. Detailed configurations and new transfer, adaptation, and ablation experiments make the work more reproducible and its applicability better tested. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: the explicit no-sensitivity-analysis control is lost, accuracy uncertainty remains unreported, and some prose overstates the evidence—for example, Figure 3 does not show Ours leading at every training size, and Table 7's caption incorrectly identifies IDBH as the next-best ACDC comparator.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sensitivity-guided augmentation work despite different titles and substantial revision. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v5 reports original segmentation, fine-tuning, domain-adaptation, classification, ablation, and runtime results in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation experiments, corruption evaluations, component ablations, and sensitivity-analysis studies in Section 5 and the appendices.

results.title: Adaptive Sensitivity Analysis for Robust Augmentation against Natural Corruptions in Image Segmentation

C1.justification: The central TOPF contribution, benchmark novelty, and clustering-performance claims remain. v2 foregrounds robustness to heterogeneous sampling and adds an explicit conclusion about performance on very sparse datasets. The introduction also removes v1's blanket assertion that graph models cannot capture higher-order topological information.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for projection-ablation exceptions on thin manifolds, downsampling failures on Ellipses and Spaceship, sampling-density robustness, and Python–Julia runtime overhead. It interprets pretrained neural comparisons through training-data requirements and qualifies VAE applications by the presence of meaningful topology. The original general limitations are largely retained.

D1.justification: v2 documents downstream spectral clustering, benchmark-label construction, WSDesc implementation and keypoint settings, VAE feature-selection settings, and automatic landmark/random subsampling. Existing package access and hardware disclosures remain. Some new details conflict: Section 4 reports 518 image patches, while Figure 12 reports 578; reported raw-image dimensions are also inconsistent.

E1.justification: The seven TCBS datasets and protein/Lorenz examples remain; Spheres+Grid becoming 4Circles+Grid does not establish new data. v2 adds cyclooctane conformation data and image-patch experiments in VAE latent spaces and raw image space. Neural comparisons also introduce ShapeNetPart and 3DMatch pretraining.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds PointNet and WSDesc and removes the Agglomerative Clustering column, although that comparator remains in the new sampling studies. Those studies additionally evaluate OPTICS and Mean Shift. The retained TPCC, spectral clustering, DBSCAN, ToMATo, geometric-feature, and node2vec comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces random downsampling with a reported minimum of 16 points, asymmetric half-cloud downsampling by factors up to 100, parameter sweeps, and density-scaling runtime tests comparing automatic sparsification with sparsification disabled. These are new evaluation designs; the retained benchmark's ARI metric and default TOPF parameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained noise/outlier tests and weighting illustration, v2 adds a harmonic-projection ablation (Table 2), interpolation/threshold/feature-selection and clustering sensitivity analyses (Figure 10), sampling robustness studies (Figures 5, 15–16), and runtime scaling analysis (Figure 11). These directly test component necessity, parameter dependence, and practical robustness.

E5.justification: Both versions report 20 runs with means and standard deviations in Table 1 and 95% confidence intervals for noise/outlier results. v2 specifies 100 repetitions for the new sampling studies, with standard deviations explicitly reported in Figure 15. This does not establish increased repetitions for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Retained TOPF benchmark ARIs remain unchanged, including the 0.86 mean, while reported mean runtime changes from 17.5 to 15.1 seconds. v2 adds PointNet and WSDesc mean ARIs of 0.44 and 0.39. Table 2 reports 0.47 mean ARI without harmonic projection versus 0.86 with it, alongside substantial new sampling, sensitivity, runtime, and application results.

M1.justification: The four-step TOPF pipeline remains. v2 adds an integer-program repair for generators whose Z/3Z-to-real lift is not a cycle, skipping features when repair is infeasible (Appendix B.3). Appendix G also introduces an alternative fixed-count feature-selection rule. These are localized procedural extensions.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition remains. Editorial changes include the Point-Level title, localized shortening and rewording, moving the main theorem from Section 4 to Appendix C, and repartitioning appendix material. New scientific sections expand the document without a wholesale rewrite of the retained narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds an ablation table and numerous application, sensitivity, sampling, and runtime figures, and changes Table 1's comparator columns. Earlier Figures 2–3 are combined, the qualitative overview gains a VAE panel, and noise/outlier panels are enlarged and reversed. Some captions deteriorate: Figure 3 retains an editing note, and Figure 6 misidentifies its left/right panels.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to local topological signatures, multiparameter representations, Mapper, topological autoencoders, topological node2vec, and adversarial graph representations. Appendix A explicitly positions TOPF's localization of global topology against methods that preserve topology during embedding or compute local and global summaries separately.

T1.justification: v1's alpha-filtration sphere theorem becomes Theorem C.1 primarily for alpha*, with additional circumsphere conditions for the implemented alpha filtration and an added contractible-subcomplex case. Definitions distinguish alpha*, Gabriel simplices, and alpha complexes, and the proof is extended. Appendix B also adds a continuous differential-form construction and mathematical treatment of failed real lifts.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation that was missing in v1: Table 2 tests harmonic projection, Figure 10 tests parameter sensitivity, and sampling studies and high-dimensional applications probe practical scope. The revised theorem states additional conditions for the implemented filtration, and the lifting repair addresses an overlooked procedural case. These gains outweigh the conflicting VAE details and caption errors, although those defects limit reproducibility and polish.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TOPF research by the same authors, despite the title changing from Node-Level to Point-Level. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds harmonic-projection ablations, sampling and parameter studies, runtime analyses, and cyclooctane and image-patch experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original clustering accuracies and runtimes in Table 1, noise/outlier experiments in Figure 5, and qualitative feature extraction on synthetic and protein data.

results.title: Point-Level Topological Representation Learning on Point Clouds

C1.justification: The central post-hoc linearization, function-valued GP and scalability claims remain. V2 reframes the Laplace-centered presentation as the broader LUNO framework and explicitly accommodates non-Gaussian random processes. Compatibility with alternative Gaussian inference schemes was already acknowledged in v1.

C2.justification: V1 discusses modest empirical gains and future interpolation-error investigations. V2 adds explanations of ensemble covariance rank deficiencies and rollout error accumulation, qualifies rank claims for numerical singularities, and identifies weight-space covariance modeling as the main limitation. It also distinguishes ensemble advantages in next-step prediction from their rollout uncertainty weaknesses.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds substantial reproducibility information absent from v1: APEBench and custom PDE-generation procedures, solver and grid details, training epochs, AdamW and scheduling, JAX/Flax/Optax, padding, rank-500 GGN approximation, and a 500-point calibration grid. These are documented details, not evidence that every underlying implementation choice changed.

E1.justification: Burgers and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky remain, while KdV is removed and Hyper-Diffusion is added. V2 also evaluates two-dimensional advection-diffusion-reaction problems with velocity reversals and heat sources/sinks, plus autoregressive scenarios with accumulating prediction errors.

E2.justification: V1 compares NOLA against input and weight perturbations. V2 retains these comparator types, with weight perturbations corresponding to Sample-Iso, and adds deep ensembles, Sample-LA and the LUNO-Iso variant. Tables 1 and 4–6 establish these additions despite inconsistent labels in Tables 7 and 11.

E3.justification: The low-data protocol changes from 32/64/128 training trajectories to 25, twenty-input/twenty-output prediction to ten-input/one-output prediction, and 16 modes/32 hidden channels to 12/18. Evaluation increases from 100 to 250 test samples, and v2 adds 50-trajectory rollout evaluations. The Q statistic is retained under the chi-squared terminology.

E4.justification: V2 removes the training-size sweep but adds matched sampling-versus-linearization comparisons, covariance and eigenfunction visualizations, ensemble null-space error analysis, distribution-shift and rollout robustness tests, and runtime comparisons. Figures 2–4 and 6–7 substantially extend v1's single KdV prediction illustration.

E5.justification: Sampling-based uncertainty estimation uses 200 predictions instead of 100, and v2 specifies ten differently seeded ensemble members. Table 12 introduces runtime values with ± terms, without defining those terms or the repetition count. Main performance tables still lack uncertainty across repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: V1's three-training-size results are replaced by results under revised settings, with additional OOD, rollout and timing outcomes. V2 Table 1 reports Burgers NLL of -2.0787 for LUNO-LA versus -0.8145 for ensembles; Table 2 instead favors ensembles on Pos-Neg-Flip (-1.014 versus 1.164). These are new comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The core Gaussian linearization and last-Fourier-block construction are retained under the name LUNO. Appendix A.4 adds an abstract-Banach adaptation using separating linear functionals instead of point evaluations, including a bidual fallback when the output process cannot be constructed in the original space.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and conclusion are substantially rewritten, with NOLA renamed LUNO and Gaussian currying reframed as probabilistic currying. Laplace background moves from Section 2.3 to Appendix B, the detailed FNO derivation moves to Appendix C, and experimental documentation is reorganized into Appendix D.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one column to two. The overview diagram is relocated and relabeled, while experimental displays are extensively redesigned with covariance/eigenfunction panels, spatial residual maps, rollout curves, and new dataset, OOD and runtime tables.

R1.justification: Literature coverage expands across FNO theory and applications, active learning, Bayesian optimization, probabilistic numerics, ensembles and operator-GP methods. V1 distinguishes its Banach setting from earlier Hilbert-space work; v2 develops an explicit embedding relationship with the Owhadi/Batlle frameworks in Appendix A.5.

T1.justification: V1's Banach-valued Gaussian currying theory is substantially generalized to random processes on vector spaces, including non-Gaussian cases and new measurability/separation results. Appendix A adds weak Gâteaux differentiability, bidual constructions, and propositions and proofs connecting the framework to Hilbert-space operator-valued Gaussian processes.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's explicitly acknowledged need for more diverse, multidimensional tests and substantially strengthens comparisons through ensembles and matched sampling-versus-linearization controls. OOD, covariance and rollout analyses make benefits and failure modes more assessable, while detailed experimental appendices improve reproducibility. Losing the training-size sweep and introducing some table-label and timing-reporting ambiguities are limited drawbacks relative to these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renaming and relocation.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original PDE experiments, including low-data evaluations, distribution shifts, autoregressive rollouts and runtime measurements.

before.justification: Section 5, Figure 2 and Table 1 report original uncertainty-quantification experiments with Fourier neural operators on KdV, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and Burgers equations.

results.title:
Linearization Turns Neural Operators into Function-Valued Gaussian
  Processes

C1.justification: The central positive convex-LCQP and qualified MI-LCQP expressivity claims remain. v2 makes convexity and mixed-integer nonuniversality explicit in the abstract, adds nonconvex failure to the stated contributions, emphasizes efficiently checkable favorable subclasses, and mentions its QCQP extension in the introduction.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 and Appendix D add substantial interpretation of symmetry, practical subclass frequency, diagnostic checks, and possible remedies using additional features or stronger GNNs. New benchmark discussion acknowledges fitting difficulties. Section 5 also introduces a broad runtime-superiority interpretation, although Table 1 shows slower GNN times at batch sizes 1 and 10.

D1.justification: v2 adds a link to the work's own code, detailed portfolio and SVM generation recipes, and Maros-Meszaros scaling, PIQP labeling, and instance-selection information. Existing Python/TensorFlow versions, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, GPU, loss, and parameter counts are retained.

E1.justification: v2 retains generic synthetic LCQP and MI-LCQP experiments and adds portfolio optimization, SVM optimization, the Maros-Meszaros convex-QP collection, and QPLIB mixed-integer instances. It also studies quantized QPLIB inputs. The QCQP extension is theoretical, without corresponding experiments.

E2.justification: v2 adds OSQP as a direct runtime comparator in Table 1; v1 uses solvers for labels without this comparison. PIQP supplies benchmark labels in Appendix G.5 and is not an evaluated competing predictor.

E3.justification: New protocols include application-specific instance generation, scaling and selecting 136 successfully solved Maros-Meszaros instances, fitting 73 QPLIB instances, and quantization at steps 0.1, 0.5, and 1. The runtime experiment uses 1,000 synthetic problems, four GNN batch sizes, and an OSQP relative-error target of 0.001. Original synthetic sampling and generalization splits are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix D.2 adds a structural sensitivity analysis testing how quantization changes WL-defined solvability and analyzability on QPLIB. Table 1 adds batch-size sensitivity of inference time. The original embedding-size, sample-size, and generalization analyses remain; moving generalization to Appendix G is not a new analysis.

E5.justification: v2 adds shaded bands to Figure 3, error bars to Figure 4, and explicitly reported timing standard deviations in Table 1. Neither version specifies seeds or repeated-run counts, and v2 does not define the plotted bands or bars, so additional runs cannot be established.

E6.justification: Figure 4's numerical curves change, and v2 adds application, benchmark, timing, and quantization results. Table 2 reports 19 of 96 original instances classified as GNN-insolvable, increasing to 63 after integer rounding. Table 1 reports OSQP at 4.48 ms versus GNN at 53.62 ms for batch size 1 and 0.089 ms for batch size 1,000. These are new comparisons, not improvements over v1 results.

M1.justification: Section 2 changes LCQP messages from edge-weighted node functions to functions receiving both node features and edge weights, a formulation already used for MI-LCQPs in v1. New Appendix E introduces a substantive QCQP adaptation with hyperedges, learned constraint-variable edge states, and additional update equations.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, Section 4 reorganizes and renames its central concepts, and a new practical discussion subsection is introduced. Generalization discussion moves to the appendix, the former Appendices C and D exchange roles, and implementation material moves from Appendix E to G.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, and Figure 2 repurposes an earlier appendix example for the continuous-case discussion. v2 adds application and benchmark plots plus timing and quantization tables, introduces uncertainty graphics, and revises Figure 4's axes and display. The generalization plots and parameter-count table are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through an explicit comparison with Wu et al.'s concurrent QCQP work, distinguishing graph representations and mixed-integer coverage. It also introduces substantive connections to higher-order and k-hop GNNs, random features, and algorithm unrolling, alongside references supporting the new benchmarks and solvers.

T1.justification: v2 broadens graph domains beyond positive-semidefinite Q, localizes convexity assumptions, and adds an explicit nonconvex counterexample. Appendix E introduces QCQP definitions, an associated WL algorithm, approximation theorems, and separation proofs. Existing approximation proofs become substantially more explicit. GNN-analyzability and GNN-solvability retain the earlier MP-tractability and unfoldability conditions under new names.

improvement.justification: The real-benchmark fits and QPLIB quantization analysis make practical limitations assessable beyond v1's generic synthetic experiments. More explicit proofs, implementation recipes, and a code link substantially improve verifiability. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses: undefined uncertainty graphics, Figure 2 retaining integer constraints in an example discussed as continuous, and runtime claims broader than Table 1 supports.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GNN expressivity study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching renamed concepts and relocated material.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices D and G report original synthetic and benchmark experiments, runtime measurements, and analysis of QPLIB instances under coefficient quantization.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E report original experiments on synthetic LCQP and MI-LCQP instances, including fitting errors, model-capacity studies, and generalization results.

results.title: Expressive Power of Graph Neural Networks for (Mixed-Integer) Quadratic Programs

C1.justification: The original contribution of deriving equivariant kernel recursions remains. v2 adds a central claim about matching augmentation-based and equivariant mean training predictions at infinite width, including off-manifold inputs, with approximate finite-width evidence. Its claimed practical contributions also expand from planar medical-image prediction to SO(3) kernels and molecular-energy prediction.

C2.justification: v2 develops substantive interpretations of augmentation-equivalence, explicitly distinguishing equal ensemble means from unequal distributions of individual networks (Section 5.4). It states quadratic-loss and infinite-width conditions, with the augmentation proof restricted to finite groups, and explains the SO(3) implementation's global-filter restriction. These substantially expand applicability boundaries beyond v1's general research outlook.

D1.justification: Appendix F and Tables 1–3 add extensive reproducibility information: histology filter sizes and a 1000-image test set, molecular features, grids, bandlimits, smoothing parameter and a 100-molecule test set, and finite-width ensemble architectures. s2fft and escnn are newly identified dependencies. Details newly disclosed for the retained histology experiment do not establish that those settings changed.

E1.justification: v1's empirical application coverage is histological-image classification. v2 adds QM9 molecular-energy regression and MNIST/CIFAR10 training with artificial out-of-distribution inputs for ensemble comparisons. This substantially expands tasks, domains, and test conditions, including continuous 3D rotational symmetry.

E2.justification: The CNN-kernel comparator for histology is retained. v2 additionally evaluates an MLP-kernel comparator against the SO(3) molecular predictor and data-augmented finite-width CNN ensembles against GCNN ensembles (Figures 2, 4, and 6). These introduce substantive comparison methods beyond extending the original comparator pair to another dataset.

E3.justification: The histology training-set range expands from 200 to 1000 images. Added protocols include QM9 energy prediction evaluated by MAE and 20-epoch comparisons of out-of-distribution logit distances across ensemble sizes 1, 3, 8, and 100. Table 2 specifies different nonlinearities for the new molecular comparison: ReLU for the MLP and Erf for the GCNN.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses testing whether augmentation-equivalence persists at finite width, varying ensemble size and tracking prediction discrepancies throughout training on out-of-distribution inputs (Figures 2 and 6, Appendix F.4). These address a new robustness and sensitivity question. The original width-convergence analysis remains, with its NNGP panel relocated.

E5.justification: The retained kernel-convergence experiment still averages 1000 initializations and reports bands of one standard deviation. The new application and ensemble-comparison plots introduce no confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. Ensemble size is varied as an experimental configuration rather than reported as repeated evaluation trials.

E6.justification: v2 adds molecular-energy results favoring the SO(3) kernel over the MLP and ensemble results showing generally smaller prediction discrepancies for larger ensembles. The expanded histology curve reports approximately 74% GCNN versus 57% CNN accuracy at 1000 training images, beyond v1's 200-image range. These are additional results, not evidence of a same-setting improvement over v1; the kernel-convergence findings are retained.

M1.justification: Beyond the retained general recursions and planar implementation, v2 adds Fourier-domain SO(3) kernel computation and a molecular pipeline using spherical per-atom inputs and aggregation (Section 4.3, Appendix D, Table 2). Fourier computation was future work in v1. The main pooling definition also changes from inverse-square-root-volume normalization to inverse-volume normalization, although Appendix C retains the earlier convention.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around augmentation-equivalence. Background material is condensed or moved to Appendix A, planar formulas and proofs are consolidated in Appendix C, and the CNN warm-up derivation is removed. A new central theory section replaces much of the earlier narrative emphasis, and the extended research outlook becomes a short conclusion.

P2.justification: v1's paired convergence panels become separate v2 Figures 1 and 5, and the medical learning curve is redrawn with an expanded axis. v2 adds molecular and ensemble-comparison plots, out-of-distribution example images, and three architecture tables. These substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 reframes the motivation around the equivariance-versus-augmentation debate, introducing AlphaFold 3, Does equivariance matter at scale?, and Swallowing the Bitter Pill. It adds spherical-computation and ensemble-equivariance literature while removing several references supporting v1's future-work discussion. This materially changes research positioning beyond bibliography maintenance.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorems 5–7 and Appendix E proofs connecting full augmentation, group-averaged kernels, and GCNN ensemble means, plus SO(3) Fourier-recursion lemmas and proofs in Appendix D. It also makes kernel right-invariance conditional on invariant filter supports, whereas v1's Remark 2 stated it unconditionally. Existing group and planar recursions are largely retained or relocated.

improvement.justification: The augmentation-equivalence results give the kernel framework a substantive explanatory application that v1 lacked, supported by finite-width checks. The SO(3) construction also realizes Fourier computation left as future work in v1, while Appendix F substantially improves experimental documentation. Different QM9 nonlinearities complicate attribution, and the pooling conventions are not fully reconciled between the main text and Appendix C, but these issues do not outweigh the substantial theoretical and practical gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Equivariant Neural Tangent Kernels by the same authors. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix F report kernel convergence, histological-image classification, QM9 molecular-energy regression, and MNIST/CIFAR10 ensemble experiments.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figures 1–2 report original Monte Carlo kernel-convergence experiments and histological-image classification results.

results.title: Equivariant Neural Tangent Kernels

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion broaden demonstrated applicability and performance claims from 2D/ViZDoom navigation to continuous control and rover navigation. The central 5000-layer contribution remains. The conclusion also drops v1's claim of 'exponentially' longer-term and larger-scale planning, retaining the narrower scaling claim.

C2.justification: v1 explicitly lists knowing the shortest-path length as a limitation; v2 instead discusses usable non-expert and heuristic estimates with measured penalties (Appendix F.2). v2 adds explanations involving compounded transition errors, disruption from intermediate skip connections, and interpretations of model/data scaling and computational costs (Section 4.4 and Appendix G).

D1.justification: v2 supplies continuous-control and rover architectures, hyperparameters, dataset identities, pretraining instructions and terrain-label construction. It newly documents maze-layout separation between training and testing, the maze policy head and ViZDoom spatial units. GPU-hour accounting supplements wall-clock measurements. These disclosures substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the retained maze splits.

E1.justification: v2 extends the maze/ViZDoom evaluation to Point Maze and Ant Maze continuous control and Apollo 17 terrain-image navigation. It also adds differential-drive, eight-neighbor movement and controlled noisy-observation scenarios. Although detailed 25×25 comparison plots disappear, that maze size remains represented in scaling experiments.

E2.justification: VIN, GPPN and Highway VIN remain the principal comparators. v2 adds an evaluated CNN+A* baseline for rover navigation (Table 3), combining learned obstacle classification with classical search. Newly discussed methods such as MuZero and implicit differentiable planners are not additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include continuous-control training on 9×12 layouts followed by evaluation on unseen 35×35 and 100×100 mazes, terrain preprocessing and elevation-based labels, and data/depth sweeps. GPPN is now reported at 5000 layers, previously excluded. Section 4 also revises SPL and optimality definitions toward expert-path lengths and relative optimality; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 separates state-dependent and observation-dependent kernel ablations, adds obstacle-count and loss analyses, learned-kernel visualizations, gradient measurements and additional highway variants (Figures 6–7). Appendices C, F and G add noise and movement robustness, approximate-path-length tests, highway-spacing sensitivity, reduced-data experiments and computational/sample/depth scaling analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three random seeds and mean/standard-deviation reporting. However, v2 Figure 3 omits the DT-VIN uncertainty bands visible in v1's 100×100 success-rate and optimality-rate panels. The corresponding success-rate table retains standard deviations. No change in run count or statistical testing is reported.

E6.justification: Many results are added, including 93.26±3.14% success for DT-VIN versus 61.78±6.12% for GPPN on 100×100 Ant Maze (v2 Table 2). The original maze success table is preserved as Table 7, while detailed 25×25 comparison curves are removed. For the stated 600-layer, 35×35, 30-epoch configuration, DT-VIN memory changes from 53.3 to 7.2 GB and training time from 12.1 to 12.3 hours, without explaining the revision.

M1.justification: The core dynamic transition, softmax and adaptive highway mechanism remain. v2 adds task-specific adaptations, including continuous-control pretraining and a state-conditioned action head, plus shared CNN encoders for rover imagery (Appendices D–E). The written loss also changes from 1/K to 1/(K|D|) with the same K definition; whether this reflects an implementation change is unexplained.

P1.justification: The introduction and preliminaries are rewritten to emphasize imitation learning and distinguish planning scale from horizon. The method explanation separates two kinds of kernel dependence. Ablations become a separate subsection, ViZDoom and limitations move into appendices, and supplementary material is extensively reorganized into method, task, ablation and scaling sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 3 is rearranged and loses its 25×25 panels; ablations expand into Figures 6–7 with new diagnostics. Numerous task illustrations and tables are added. The original success table and ViZDoom figure move to appendix Table 7 and Figure 11.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning relative to classical search, explicit learned world models and Zhao et al.'s implicit differentiable planners, plus diffusion planners as a future integration direction. Imitation-learning and new dataset references are added, while CNN-background references are removed. The central relationship to VIN, GPPN and Highway VIN remains.

T1.justification: Section 4 replaces globally minimum-length optimality with minimum length among expert and compared-model solutions, a substantive definition change. Appendix B.2 newly argues that CNN-generated dynamic kernels preserve translation equivariance. These are limited mathematical additions rather than a new theorem or substantial proof development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's narrow evaluation and limited component diagnosis through continuous-control and terrain tasks, separated kernel ablations, gradient measurements, and tests of approximate path lengths and scaling. These additions provide stronger evidence about generality, mechanisms and applicability limits. Unexplained loss/resource revisions and omitted uncertainty bands remain reporting weaknesses, but the broader diagnostic evidence and implementation documentation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DT-VIN research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and retained methods, experiments, tables and figures can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds continuous-control, terrain-image navigation, robustness, ablation and scaling results.

before.justification: v1 reports original maze and ViZDoom experiments, component ablations, depth comparisons and computational measurements.

results.title: Scaling Value Iteration Networks to 5000 Layers for Extreme Long-Term Planning

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a differentiable decoder-derived regularizer for valid LSO. v2 drops the 'exact' characterization, qualifies comparative improvements as occurring 'in most cases,' and adds single-hyperparameter and 'always' improved-quality claims. The latter overstates Table 12, where pretrained Zaleplon validity is 0.65 for LES versus 0.66 for unregularized gradient ascent.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands discussion of bijectivity, CPA approximation, and dependence on decoder quality, including advice against using LES with poorly trained decoders. It interprets valid-versus-unfiltered results as an optimization/validity tradeoff. v1's explanation attributing UC's validity advantage largely to early stopping is removed, and the computational limitation discussion is revised.

D1.justification: v2 provides an explicit VAE training recipe, including 300 epochs, Adam, learning rate 0.001, and batch size 256, alongside corpus sizes, deep-kernel dimensionality, and optimizer-specific settings. The printed code pointer changes from scales to les. v1's finite-difference epsilon, sequence-truncation details, and supporting software-link list are not retained.

E1.justification: The five optimization objectives and three validity notions remain. v2 additionally trains SELFIES models on approximately 200,000 quality-filtered ZINC250k molecules, alongside the retained pretrained SELFIES model. The much larger architecture and beta sweep mainly expands configurations within existing tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds Likelihood and TuRBO to optimization comparisons, and Likelihood and Train distances to validity-classification comparisons. Polarity remains in Appendix Table 10 despite its omission from the main AUROC table. The ScaLES early-stopping comparator reported in v1 is removed.

E3.justification: v2 adds architecture/beta configurations and substantially revises evaluation settings. Query batches increase from 5 to 20; SELFIES initialization increases from 1,000 to 1,500 points while its evaluation budget decreases from 1,250 to 500. Top-10 reporting becomes top-20, and the stated expression objective changes from negative RMSE to -log(1+MSE). AUROC sampling, step sizes, regularization settings, and the UC threshold also change.

E4.justification: v2 systematically examines architecture/beta robustness, adds TuRBO parameter sensitivity tests, expands existing L-BFGS sensitivity experiments, and contrasts valid versus unfiltered optimization outcomes. Lambda sensitivity is retained but reworked. Conversely, v1's early-stopping control and comparison of reconstruction losses for valid versus invalid molecules are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report optimization over 10 independent runs; no increase in repetitions is established. v2 adds counts of results within one standard deviation of the best method. However, its validity tables omit the uncertainty values provided for validity rates in v1 Tables 2-3 and Appendix B.

E6.justification: The three-row AUROC evaluation and five optimization cases in v1 are replaced and expanded by 22-model AUROC and 30-case optimization results, alongside new baseline, timing, and sensitivity outcomes. v2 reports mean LES AUROC 0.93 and average optimization ranks 2.15 for the best solution and 1.9 for top-20 performance. Changed models, budgets, and metrics prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: Beyond renaming, v2 Equation (12) removes the prior-density term and rho weighting from v1 Equation (13). It redefines the augmented decoder using reciprocal softmax normalizers and introduces a Jacobian determinant computation avoiding pseudoinversion. The penalized acquisition function and normalized-gradient framework remain, but the score and its computation materially change.

P1.justification: v2 renames the method and title, substantially rewrites the experimental narrative, and replaces task-specific result subsections with a unified comparison. Method and computational explanations are reorganized and expanded. The appendices are restructured into proofs, ablations, and additional results, removing standalone resources and broader-impact sections.

P2.justification: v2 adds the derivation diagram in Figure 2, rebuilds tables around architecture/beta configurations and comparator columns, and splits Guacamol trajectories into large best-solution and top-20 figures with valid/unfiltered line styles. v1's expression/logP trajectory plots are removed. Title, typography, and page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning relative to GFlowNet, diffusion-based molecular generation, and trust-region optimization, with supporting citations on matrix-volume transformations and sample efficiency. The original ZINC and L-BFGS references are removed. The principal positioning against decoder-uncertainty regularization remains.

T1.justification: v2 revises Theorem 3.1 and Lemma A.1 around reciprocal normalizers and modified Jacobian expressions. It adds Lemma A.2 and a proof intended to relax injectivity through a measure-zero collision condition, plus new mathematical reasoning about closed-form gradients and avoiding pseudoinversion. These extend and revise the formal argument beyond notation changes.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for applicability across decoders: architecture/beta comparisons and Likelihood/TuRBO baselines with sensitivity checks address v1's narrow model and comparator evaluation. Explicit training details and valid-versus-unfiltered analyses improve reproducibility and interpretation. Lost validity-rate uncertainty, inconsistent win-count captions in Tables 8-9, and overstated universal validity wording are weaknesses, but the broader controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same decoder-based latent-space optimization work, renamed from ScaLES to LES. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: Sections 3.2 and 4 and Appendices B-C report original classification and optimization results across multiple VAEs, timing measurements, and sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: Sections 3.3 and 4 and Appendices B-C report original validity-classification, Bayesian optimization, and computational timing results.

results.title: Mitigating over-exploration in latent space optimization using LES

C1.justification: Both versions claim that faster-learned examples resist forgetting, stronger memory capacity extends retention toward slower-learned examples, and speed-based replay selection improves diverse continual-learning methods. V2 emphasizes behavioral observation and reorganizes the contributions, but retains the central scientific claims and state-of-the-art performance claim.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies v1's broadly shared buffer preferences by explaining that class-incremental learning slightly favors faster-learned examples because task inference is harder. It adds that short training schedules remain useful when the network converges, despite noisier speed estimates, and explains the preference for learning speed over alternative scores. The single-epoch streaming limitation remains.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies 50 epochs per task for the multi-method comparison, baseline random/reservoir buffer handling, a q = s = 20% default, and optimizer-specific settings for the added sensitivity experiments. RotNet tuning and runtime guidance are expanded. The existing ResNet-18, SGD and TITAN X configuration is largely relocated to Appendix A.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet, including task-incremental and class-incremental classification, rotation classification and random-label scenarios. CIFAR-100-20 introduces a finer partition of existing classes; this changes the evaluation protocol rather than the represented dataset or task domain.

E2.justification: V2 adds LARS to the replay-sampling comparisons, including the retained two-task experiments in Table 3. Random sampling, maximum entropy, IPM, GSS and Herding remain. Figure 25 additionally compares learning speed with uncertainty, final loss and c-score as example-scoring functions.

E3.justification: V2 adds CIFAR-100-20 partitions, 5k-buffer multi-task sweeps, and controlled variations in optimizers, architectures, training epochs, learning rates, regularization and class splits. Reported settings also change: Figure 4c specifies a 20k TinyImageNet buffer instead of v1's 10k, although v2 Figure 22c inconsistently says 1k. These are documented protocol additions and revisions, not proof that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing dataset, architecture and subsequent-task analyses, v2 adds systematic training-setting sensitivity tests (Appendix D), fixed-versus-tuned sampling, alternative scoring functions (Appendix G), and multi-task forgetting/composition analyses. Class-incremental forgetting dynamics receive additional direct analysis. V1's separate class-incremental GEM composition grid is no longer presented.

E5.justification: Both versions retain ten-network/repetition means and standard-error reporting, without an explicit increase in runs or new inferential procedures. However, v1 Figure 16's separate GEM heatmap standard errors are omitted while the corresponding mean-results analysis remains in v2 Figure 14c. Changed error magnitudes alone do not establish a new estimation procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for sampling comparisons, class-incremental evaluation, robustness sweeps and alternative scores. For the retained CIFAR-100-2/1k comparison, Goldilocks/SBS changes from 71.53 ± 7.31 in v1 Table 2 to 71.71 with standard error 0.22 in v2 Tables 3–4. Section 2.4 also corrects the buffer-size correlation from +0.966 to -0.966. Results under newly introduced settings are additional evidence, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Goldilocks is renamed Speed-Based Sampling (SBS). Equation 1 and Algorithm 1 retain the same procedure: average epoch-wise correctness, remove the quickest and slowest fractions, and sample uniformly from the remainder. SBS-fix assigns constants to existing parameters rather than introducing a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: V2 changes the title, renames Goldilocks to SBS, and substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction and contribution list. Buffer-composition observations move into Section 2, while Section 3 separately develops SBS, its evaluation and limitations. The appendices are reorganized and explanations of tuning and practical use are expanded.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column layout to two columns. Classification matrices receive new colors and ordering, and composition heatmaps display accuracy differences from uniform sampling instead of absolute accuracy. Benchmark plots are consolidated, tables are expanded and reorganized, and numerous new analysis panels are added.

R1.justification: Section 1.2 adds distinctions from curriculum and self-paced learning and connections to active, semi-supervised and transfer learning, with corresponding citations. Appendix G introduces the uncertainty-score and c-score references. The central positioning as a data-centric study of forgetting and a general replay-sampling strategy remains.

T1.justification: The continual-learning setup, learning-speed definition in Equation 1, classification matrix and remembered-example definition remain substantively unchanged. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs; the expanded behavioral explanations and empirical score comparisons do not introduce new mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for v1's broad robustness claims through controlled sensitivity tests, fuller class-incremental analyses, alternative-score comparisons and fixed-versus-tuned sampling results. These address dependence on training choices, the scoring proxy and parameter tuning, while the reorganized presentation improves usability. Conflicting buffer-size captions and unexplained standard-error revisions remain, but the added evidence provides a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same learning-speed and catastrophic-forgetting study, despite the changed title and method name. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent matching the work.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds robustness sweeps, scoring-function comparisons, fixed-parameter sampling results and further class-incremental analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original neural-network experiments measuring forgetting, replay-buffer composition and classification accuracy, including repeated-run results and appendix analyses.

results.title: Predicting the Susceptibility of Examples to Catastrophic Forgetting

C1.justification: v2 expands the introductory claims to cross-source robustness and mitigation of LLM-judge biases. Its headline changes from 89.1% agreement at $25 to 98.6% correlation/agreement at $20, and from threefold tighter confidence intervals to threefold higher separation. These revise the claimed evaluation capabilities and quantitative guarantees, although the central automated-curation contribution remains.

C2.justification: v1 primarily treats verbosity and self-bias as limitations. v2 interprets new experiments as evidence of separating substance from style, resistance to length/markdown gaming, and reduced self-bias through ensembles. It adds reasons for excluding multilingual and multi-turn evaluation, while removing the calibration caveat accompanying v1 Figure 5. The anti-gaming interpretation is broader than the tested manipulations establish.

D1.justification: v2 documents style features, normalization, and new markdown-manipulation system prompts. It specifies sampling two prompts from each selected cluster and adds annotation-cost estimates of approximately $500 with GPT-4-Turbo or $45 with Llama-3-70B, including token-price assumptions. These substantially extend technical and resource information; the original annotation and judging prompt templates are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation using WildChat user–ChatGPT conversations, extending beyond Chatbot Arena evaluation traffic. It processes 150,000 queries and constructs the 250-prompt Wild-Hard-Auto benchmark, evaluated against a random WildChat subset. This materially broadens evidence across data sources; the English, single-turn scope remains.

E2.justification: The main MT-Bench/AlpacaEval comparisons and four individual judges plus ensemble are retained. Supplementary comparisons change: v2 Table 12 adds a length-only judging policy, while the GPT-versus-Claude length-bias comparison in v1 Table 7 is replaced by comparisons between uncontrolled and style-controlled GPT-4 judging.

E3.justification: v2 introduces style-controlled human reference rankings, Kendall tau reporting, a 250-prompt WildChat evaluation, and a 10-model alternative-annotator experiment. Section 4.2 also revises the reported filtering recipe and thresholds, without establishing that the original benchmark was regenerated. Both versions retain 500 Arena-Hard prompts and 1,000 judgments; the table's 1,000-to-500 prompt-count correction does not establish a reduced evaluation budget.

E4.justification: v2 tests dependence on the prompt annotator, expands verbosity experiments to three models and markdown manipulations, and adds style-control and model-family self-bias analyses. Conversely, v1's calibration plots, three-run stability table, and second music judgment example disappear. The quality-score sensitivity plots and original Arena random-subset comparison are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 95% confidence intervals from 100 bootstrap rounds. v2 removes v1 Table 8's explicit reporting of three separate GPT-3.5 evaluation runs. Appendix A.1 expands the bootstrap explanation, but does not establish additional repeated evaluations or an increased run count.

E6.justification: In the general English comparison, Arena-Hard confidence agreement changes from 89.1% to 90.9%, while Spearman correlation changes from 94.1% to 93.2% (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 1). Hard-prompt agreement changes from 92.0% to 98.6%. v2 adds WildChat, annotator, style-control, and self-bias results and revises the leaderboard. Its headline 98.6% figure comes from different comparison conditions than v1's headline 89.1%.

M1.justification: Section 6.5 and Appendix A.2 introduce style-controlled scoring: the Bradley-Terry model gains covariates for response length and markdown features, changing how model strengths are estimated. This is a substantive new evaluation component. The underlying seven-quality curation approach and GPT-4/Gemini judge ensemble already appear in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. Sections 4–6 are reorganized around pipeline costs, generalizability, and bias mitigation; limitations are rewritten; Brier-score background and prompt examples move into dedicated appendices. The benchmark name drops 'v0.1', and references change from numbered to author-year citations.

P2.justification: v2 adds a benchmark-classification figure and multiple robustness and style-control tables, removes the calibration figure and repeated-run table, and substantially expands the leaderboard. Existing plots are rearranged, benchmark-table columns are reordered with a Kendall tau row added, and several main-text tables move to the appendix. These substantially change the presentation beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: Related work adds WildBench, LiveBench, MixEval, BigCodeBench, WildChat, and Chatbot Arena style control. The introduction and new classification figure sharpen the existing positioning around automated, configurable, open-ended curation. The reference to Verga et al.'s ensemble-judge work is removed despite retaining ensemble judging. These are targeted changes within the established research framing.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds a formal style-augmented Bradley-Terry objective, covariate definitions, and proportional feature normalization. Appendix A.1 also qualifies the existing Gaussian approximation and describes empirical probability estimation when normality fails. The original three benchmark metrics remain; the substantial mathematical addition concerns style-controlled estimation, not new theorems.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens two important weaknesses in v1: limited validation beyond the original data/annotator and acknowledged judging biases without a tested style-control remedy. WildChat and alternative-annotator experiments broaden validation, while Sections 6.5 and A.2 provide an implemented, documented mitigation supported by controlled experiments. Removing calibration and repeated-run evidence reduces transparency, and the broad anti-gaming and 98.6% headline claims need qualification. Nevertheless, the added validation and actionable bias treatment provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BenchBuilder/Arena-Hard research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds WildChat experiments, alternative-annotator tests, style-control experiments, and self-bias analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark comparisons, prompt-quality experiments, judge comparisons, random-subset evaluations, and appendix analyses of verbosity and repeated runs.

results.title:
From Crowdsourced Data to High-Quality Benchmarks: Arena-Hard and

C1.justification: The central claim favoring Gaussian-based flows with a final tail transformation remains. However, the conclusion changes materially: v1 identifies TTFfix as best overall and generally favors two-stage methods, whereas v2 recommends joint tail learning for density estimation while retaining the benefit of fixed parameters for VI. This changes the principal practical recommendation.

C2.justification: V2 explains learned tail parameters as compensating for preceding flow layers, links joint learning's benefits to flexibility such as tail asymmetry, and identifies substantial preliminary tail-estimation costs. It revises the CDF transformation's applicability and develops a mechanism-based proposal for differential-equation generative models. The explicit warning about dependence on arbitrary coordinate parameterization is removed from the limitations.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies spline bounds [-2.5, 2.5] with five bins, full-batch synthetic training, real-data batch size 512, and additional optimization and dataset information (Appendices G and I). Much of the expanded implementation appendix relocates existing initialization, sampling and numerical-stability details. These disclosures do not establish changed settings for retained experiments, and code-access information is effectively unchanged.

E1.justification: Real-data evaluation expands from S&P 500 returns to include Insurance medical claims, Fama 5 financial returns and CLIMDEX meteorological data (v2 Section 4.2 and Appendix I). V2 also adds the heavier-than-Cauchy ν = 0.5 VI scenario, which v1 explicitly excluded. The original regression and synthetic density-estimation tasks remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds normal and COMET comparators to the retained S&P 500 experiment, includes COMET at synthetic dimension d = 50 where v1 omitted it, and adds TTF_tBase to the synthetic comparisons. These extend the existing comparator suite; the VI comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: The added CLIMDEX evaluation uses five RQS layers alternating with LU layers and a different optimization schedule, including cosine annealing and more steps. The new ν = 0.5 VI experiment uses gradient-norm clipping at 5. S&P evaluation contracts from 100/200/300 dimensions to 300 and reports total rather than per-dimension NLL. Synthetic-table failure markers change from Inf/NaN outcomes to final loss above 1e5. These are distinct from newly disclosed settings for retained experiments.

E4.justification: Appendix J adds an architectural ablation combining heavy-tailed inputs with TTF and a learned-tail-parameter analysis comparing fitted parameters against fixed theoretical values. Appendix D adds a qualitative exploratory comparison with the CDF transformation, and VI receives a stronger tail-severity test. The sigmoid/ReLU regression analysis is retained in Appendix F, while the S&P dimensionality comparison is removed.

E5.justification: Real-data uncertainty reporting changes from ten-repeat boxplots in v1 Figure 2 to means and standard deviations, with within-one-standard-deviation highlighting, in v2 Table 2. Synthetic density-estimation standard errors and the stated ten density-estimation/five VI repeats remain unchanged; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: V2 adds results for three real datasets, ν = 0.5 VI, TTF_tBase and higher-dimensional COMET comparisons. CLIMDEX NLL is -2214.28 for TTF versus -2090.91 for TTFfix. S&P results are replaced: gTAF now scores 321.81 versus mTAF's 322.98, reversing their earlier ranking. The 100/200-stock results disappear. Shared synthetic density-estimation and ν ≥ 1 VI table entries are retained, so the additions do not establish improvements in those unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The main TTF transformation in Equation (3) and the TTF/TTFfix procedures remain unchanged. V2 adds the experimental TTF_tBase architecture, combining TTF with a Student's T base whose degrees of freedom are trained. Appendix D also describes a two-stage application of the previously discussed Student's T CDF transformation.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: regression moves to Appendix F, initialization to Appendix G, and dataset descriptions to Appendix I. Theory receives separate subsections, references move before the appendices, and experimental summaries and conclusions are rewritten. These changes reorganize existing material as well as accommodating additions.

P2.justification: The S&P boxplots are replaced by a broader real-data table, and a new Figure 2 displays learned tail parameters. The synthetic table becomes a main-text subset plus an expanded appendix table; the regression table moves to the appendix, VI gains columns, and hyperparameter and dataset tables are added. The document also adopts a denser layout without the earlier running headers.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused positioning around universality, citing Huang, Jaini, Draxler, Teshima and Van der Vaart, and connects future applications to Lipman's flow-matching work. The established positioning relative to TAF, COMET and extreme-value methods remains. Publication updates for existing references are bibliographic changes rather than newly cited research.

T1.justification: V2 adds a proof that finite Gaussian mixtures are light tailed (Appendix A), a formal weak-convergence definition of universality, and a continuous-mapping proof that adding TTF preserves a universal flow family's universality (Appendix E). The proposed extension to coupling-flow results is explicitly left incomplete. Existing TTF and COMET asymptotic results are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence that was limited to one real dataset and lacked high-dimensional COMET comparisons. The expanded evaluation reveals where TTFfix performs poorly, producing better-supported guidance on learning versus fixing tail parameters. New ablations, parameter analysis and the universality proof improve understanding of the method. Although removing the smaller S&P comparisons loses one sensitivity analysis, the gains in empirical support and theoretical characterization outweigh that loss.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Flexible Tails for Normalizing Flows by the same authors. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds real-data evaluations, experimental variants and parameter analyses. Some CLIMDEX baseline scores are explicitly attributed to prior work, but the paper also reports its own results.

before.justification: V1 reports original neural-network regression experiments, synthetic density estimation, S&P 500 density estimation and synthetic variational-inference results.

results.title: Flexible Tails for Normalizing Flows

C1.justification: The central claims about succinct predictions, near-optimal consistency–robustness and fractional-to-integral conversion remain. v2 narrows the trade-off lower-bound statement to deterministic algorithms and explicitly qualifies the integral conversion guarantee. Interval optimality receives greater prominence in the contribution summary.

C2.justification: v2 more explicitly distinguishes assumptions needed for trusted fractional algorithms, robust MIX and integral conversion, and states that learning the predictor is outside scope. It adds interpretations of the synthetic error parameter and suggests that workload-value distributions explain Sentinel's poorer Google-trace performance.

D1.justification: Appendix A.7.1 newly documents uniformly generated prediction intervals for MIX and IPA. It also specifies Google instance construction through duration scaling, resource factors, item counts and weights. The code-access information is unchanged, and neither version supplies hardware or seed details.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on Google cluster traces, introducing workload-derived inputs beyond synthetic and financial data. Its reported Bitcoin coverage also expands from 2017–2018 to 2017–2019 (Appendix A.7.1).

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain their comparator sets: the Sentinel synthetic comparison includes PP-a, Fr2Int-PP-a, Sentinel and ZCL; Bitcoin includes the first three. Google extends that existing three-method comparison without introducing a new baseline.

E3.justification: For 10,000 Bitcoin items, the reported item weight changes from 0.0001 to 0.001, increasing total offered weight from 1 to 10 against unit capacity. v2 also introduces a Google-trace instance-construction protocol. These materially change evaluation conditions, although the PDFs do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The new Google experiment tests sensitivity to prediction error across several delta values (Figure A4), extending robustness evidence to workload-derived inputs. Existing studies of value range, critical-item weight, interval width, prediction correctness and trust parameter are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions use CDFs and notched boxplots. v2 introduces no seed reporting, repeated-run counts, significance tests or new uncertainty-estimation procedure; changed boxplot values retain the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: New Google results show plotted median competitive ratios around 1.15–1.19 for PP-a and Fr2Int-PP-a versus approximately 1.53–1.62 for Sentinel at delta values 0.5–2 (Figure A4). Synthetic and Bitcoin boxplot distributions also change between v1 Figures 3–4 and v2 Figures A2–A3. Bitcoin results use revised conditions, so they do not establish same-setting gains.

M1.justification: PP-b, PP-a, IPA, MIX and Fr2Int retain their decision rules. Indexed state notation in PP-a, expanded explanations and relocation of IPA pseudocode do not change the algorithms.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten around near-optimal trade-offs. Assumptions receive dedicated discussion, proofs are reorganized and rewritten, and most Sentinel and real-data experimental discussion moves from Section 6 into Appendix A.7.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, adds a contribution-summary table, and moves IPA pseudocode into the main text. Existing Sentinel comparisons move to the appendix and are redrawn alongside a new Google plot. Retained supplementary plots are redistributed and regrouped, rather than constituting entirely new figures.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially expands positioning against frequency predictions, advice complexity and Pareto-optimal algorithms for simplified knapsack variants, explaining why their guarantees do not transfer. Appendix A.1 adds stochastic and unit-profit knapsack coverage, with new references including Vondrak and Zenklusen and Boyar et al.

T1.justification: v2 adds the matching interval-prediction lower bound (Theorem 3.6) and integral-knapsack impossibility results (Theorems A.1–A.2). It corrects the point lower-bound proof to use min{1, omega}, substantially rewrites PP-a and Fr2Int proofs, and explicitly conditions Theorem 5.2 on maximum item weight. It also specifies an adaptive adversary and restricts Theorem 4.2 to deterministic algorithms.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses concrete weaknesses in the theoretical account: capped critical-weight reasoning is corrected, PP-a receives explicit feasibility and profit invariants, and Fr2Int's weight condition becomes precise. Added interval and integral lower-bound analyses substantially improve completeness, while Google-trace experiments broaden validation. These gains support a substantial improvement independently of higher reported performance; the changed Bitcoin setup limits direct score comparisons.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same knapsack algorithms, predictions and theoretical framework despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic, Bitcoin and Google-cluster-trace experiments, including comparative performance and sensitivity results in Section 6 and Appendix A.7.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on synthetic instances and Bitcoin prices, including algorithm comparisons and prediction-sensitivity studies in Section 6 and Appendix A.6.

results.title: Near-Optimal Consistency-Robustness Trade-Offs for Learning-Augmented Online Knapsack Problems

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: confidence-aware pose guidance, confidence-based hand enhancement and progressive latent fusion for long, temporally smooth videos. Condensed wording and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Appendix D newly attributes cross-domain generalization to a possible shared pose-feature subspace and limb-length mapping to reference characters. Section 4.3 adds interpretation of fusion's selective improvement in FVD despite other metrics not improving. The original explanations of pose robustness and hand enhancement remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds PoseNet's layerwise architecture, 576-by-1024 training resolution, 16-frame clips, noise-distribution parameters, 10:1 hand-loss weighting, six-frame overlap for the illustrated fusion comparison, and user-interface randomization details. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing retraining. Conversely, v1's explicit SVD 1.1 checkpoint designation, 40GB GPU specification and executable Merge listing are omitted.

E1.justification: Appendix D adds evaluation on four cartoon and four animal dancing videos, extending coverage beyond human subjects to different visual styles and body proportions. The human training collection and TikTok evaluation remain unchanged. This substantially broadens demonstrated domain coverage, although the added evidence is qualitative.

E2.justification: v2 adds MagicAnimate, printed as 'MagicAnymate' and identified by the Xu et al. reference, to Table 1's quantitative TikTok comparison. MagicPose, Moore and MuseV remain. The qualitative comparisons and preference chart retain their original comparator membership.

E3.justification: v2 adds SSIM and PSNR alongside FID-VID/FVD and introduces four quantitative component configurations in Table 2. The TikTok 335-340 split, central cropping, training budget and user-study size remain consistent. Newly stated clip lengths, noise parameters and display randomization document settings rather than establish changes to existing experiments.

E4.justification: v1 supports its three components with qualitative ablations. v2 retains those examples and adds Table 2, measuring configurations that progressively enable fusion, confidence guidance and hand enhancement across four metrics. Appendix D also adds cross-domain transfer cases. These substantially strengthen component analysis and generalization evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. Point-estimate reporting and the 36-participant, six-pairs-per-baseline user study are retained. Pose-confidence scores are method inputs, not experimental uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Existing FID-VID/FVD scores, including MimicMotion's 9.3/594, and user-preference percentages remain unchanged. v2 adds SSIM/PSNR results, including 0.795/20.1 for MimicMotion, the additional baseline's results, quantitative ablation outcomes and cartoon/animal outputs. Table 2 newly shows fusion alone improving FVD from 776 to 678 while slightly worsening the other metrics. These are additional findings, not performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The written output-assembly rule changes: v1's Listing 1 retains the complete first segment and skips the initial C frames of subsequent segments, whereas v2's Algorithm 1 returns each segment's first N-C frames. This is a limited revision to the specified procedure; an implementation change is not established. The backbone, confidence guidance and hand-loss mechanism remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and numerous paragraphs across the introduction, preliminaries, architecture description and experiments are substantially condensed or rewritten. v2 adds organized Appendices A-D and an Impact Statement, and changes citation style. This is extensive editorial restructuring despite retention of the main scientific narrative.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference main text, with widespread resizing and relocation of figures. v1's confidence/occlusion illustration is removed; retained ablation figures are renumbered. Table 1 gains a comparator and metric columns, while Tables 2-3 and Figures 10-12 add ablations, architecture details, the study interface and cross-domain examples.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including StableAnimator, ControlNeXt, DisPose, VividPose, DiT and noise-schedule research, plus sources supporting newly documented settings and metrics. DreamPose is removed. The central positioning relative to SVD, MultiDiffusion and Lumiere remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The diffusion preliminaries and denoising-loss mathematics are retained, with equations condensed or renumbered. No new theorem, proof or substantive theoretical derivation appears. Appendix A's noise-distribution formula documents a training setting.

improvement.justification: v1 relies on selected visual examples for component ablations and describes PoseNet only broadly. v2's quantitative controls in Table 2 and detailed training/architecture specifications in Appendices A-B substantially improve the central contributions' evidential support and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of some checkpoint and merge details. Cross-domain evidence remains qualitative, and statistical uncertainty reporting remains absent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MimicMotion and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. All pages were inspected, including v2's Appendices A-D; v1 ends with references and has no appendices. Renumbered and reformatted material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds quantitative component ablations, additional comparison metrics and cartoon/animal generation examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original TikTok benchmark results, qualitative component ablations and a 36-participant preference study.

results.title: MimicMotion: High-Quality Human Motion Video Generation with Confidence-aware Pose Guidance

C1.justification: V2 expands the main contribution from a customizable RL environment framework to an efficient platform for single-agent, multi-agent, embodied and continual-learning research. It adds quantitative efficiency claims and claims novelty in combining vast 3D open worlds with multi-agent support. The original five environments, presented partly as benchmarks in v1, are explicitly reframed as illustrative examples.

C2.justification: V2 adds proposed explanations for throughput differences, interprets selected continual-learning gains as forward transfer, and discusses richness–efficiency tradeoffs. It newly states that agent count is limited by CPU-core count and qualifies the learning demonstrations as untuned examples whose performance may improve with longer training (Appendices E and G).

D1.justification: Beyond v1's basic mod and Gymnasium examples, v2 documents engine modifications, action mappings, API functions and PettingZoo usage (Appendices A–D). It adds benchmark hardware, CleanRL implementation and commit references, preprocessing, budgets, prompts, generator parameters and an environment-creation tutorial (Appendices E, G and I). The project repository link is retained.

E1.justification: The five original single-agent task types are retained. V2 additionally evaluates one-versus-one combat, an open world with resource-gathering, hunting and defense objectives, and a ten-task continual-learning dungeon sequence (Section 3.5 and Appendix G). These substantially expand the evaluated task requirements and interaction settings.

E2.justification: V1 discusses alternatives without evaluating comparators. V2 benchmarks Craftium against MineDojo and VizDoom for single-environment throughput and against VizDoom for parallel throughput. Its demonstrations also compare PPO+LSTM with LLaVa-Agent and from-scratch PPO (FS) with continual fine-tuning using L2 regularization (FT-L2).

E3.justification: Reported episode limits change substantially: ChopTree and Room increase from 500 to 2,000 steps, SmallRoom from 200 to 1,000, Speleo from 500 to 3,000, and SpidersAttack from 2,000 to 4,000 (v1 Section 3.4; v2 Appendix G.1). V2 also introduces throughput-testing and learning protocols, including million-step PPO training and open-world comparisons with different observation formats and time/step budgets.

E4.justification: V1 contains no corresponding analyses. V2 tests throughput sensitivity to parallel environment count, frame skipping, observation resolution, world complexity and agent count (Appendix E, Figure 13). It also compares four LLaVa-Agent prompts to select the demonstration prompt (Appendix G.3, Figure 17).

E5.justification: V2 introduces repeated-run and uncertainty reporting absent from v1: five-run throughput measurements with means and standard deviations in Table 4, five-run learning curves with standard errors in Figures 8 and 15, ten random seeds for the open-world comparison, and five repetitions per prompt. These are newly reported experiments, not increased repetitions of v1 results.

E6.justification: V1 reports no measured performance. V2 adds throughput means of 2,746.69, 2,091.91 and 71.87 steps/s for Craftium, VizDoom and MineDojo respectively (Table 4), plus over 12,000 steps/s in a parallel configuration (Figure 13a). It also adds learning curves, open-world achievements and task-dependent FS/FT-L2 results. These are new findings, not same-setting improvements over v1 measurements.

M1.justification: V1 leaves multi-agent interaction and PettingZoo integration as future work.
