LoRA-GA ranks below LoRA on both datasets in v1 Table 3 but above it in v2 Table 5. V2 also adds substantial LLM, generation, robustness, efficiency and appendix results. Table 2's image-classification values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The Bayesian expected-loss objective, filter-scaled Gaussian perturbations and seed-based reconstruction remain unchanged. Appendix C introduces an all-layer variant that additionally perturbs normalization parameters, biases and embeddings using absolute-weight-based noise. This extends the procedure without replacing the core method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and method explanations undergo extensive rewriting. Related work gains numbered subsections, integration comparisons and ablations receive separate experimental sections, and Appendices A–E are introduced. Terminology and front matter are also revised, including correcting 'Adaption' to 'Adaptation'.

P2.justification: V2 switches to a two-column conference layout, relocates existing displays and redraws the rank plots with shaded bands. It adds a method schematic, generated-image comparisons, corruption charts, landscape surfaces, diagnostic curves and multiple experimental tables. These substantially change the visual presentation beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against random-perturbation methods and LoRA variants, including Gaussian model perturbation, NoisyTune, LoRASC and BAR. It adds references supporting smoothing theory, new benchmarks and GaLore/CorDA comparisons, while dropping some earlier references. These changes extend beyond publication-status updates to retained citations.

T1.justification: V2 adds the LoRA-SAM full-weight perturbation expansion and approximation in Equations 3–4 and the attributed smoothing Lemma 3.1. It also revises the forward-variance derivation to include nonzero input means and states Proposition 3.2. These substantially extend v1's short mathematical justification without changing the core noise rule.

improvement.justification: V1 supports its central flatness and efficiency arguments mainly indirectly. V2 adds direct SAM-space comparisons, landscape and generalization-gap diagnostics, and measured resource costs, substantially strengthening those arguments while testing larger models and distribution shifts. Reporting inconsistencies remain: Section 4.5 claims gains of 0.71 and 1.83 points, whereas Table 4 implies 0.92 and 2.23. These issues temper confidence in individual statements but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Flat-LoRA and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. Corresponding methods and experiments can be matched. V1 has no appendix; v2's Appendices A–E are included in this comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original fine-tuning experiments and adds LLM, image-generation, distribution-shift, efficiency and appendix results.

before.justification: V1 reports original T5-base and CLIP fine-tuning results, comparisons with LoRA variants, and rank-sensitivity experiments in Tables 1–3 and Figure 2.

results.title: Flat-LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation over a Flat Loss Landscape

C1.justification: The central claims of simulation-free GP-stream training, variance reduction and integration of correlated observations persist. v5 adds explicit claims about smoother fields, computationally efficient generation, irregularly spaced observations and complementarity with endpoint coupling. The Bayesian perspective ceases to be a headline contribution but remains part of the paper.

C2.justification: v5 expands the mechanism account to suppression of spurious intermediate modes and easier numerical integration. It interprets CIFAR-10 results as suggesting limitations of high-dimensional minibatch OT and acknowledges that combining OT with GP streams need not improve performance. Conversely, v1's explicit complete-observation requirement and proposed latent-space remedy disappear, without a demonstrated missing-data solution. Appendix I adds a biological interpretation of the generated LFP trajectories.

D1.justification: v5 supplies hardware specifications and training timings for retained applications, plus CIFAR-10 optimizer, clipping, EMA, noise, solver and clean-fid details. It also documents LFP selection, temporal subsampling, rescaling and runtime. These substantially expand implementation and reproducibility information; the code-access link remains the same.

E1.justification: v5 adds unconditional CIFAR-10 natural-image generation and multiregion mouse-brain time-series generation using one LFP recording session. Appendix F also introduces a two-Gaussian-to-three-Gaussian transformation scenario. The original MNIST, HWD+ and toy-data coverage remains.

E2.justification: The existing standard-Gaussian-to-two-Gaussian comparison expands from I-CFM and GP-I-CFM in v1 Figure 1B to include OT-CFM and GP-OT-CFM in v5 Table 1. These methods already participated in the MNIST comparison, whose comparator membership remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce substantial protocols: CIFAR-10 uses a 128-channel U-Net, batch size 128, specified noise controls, DOPRI5 sampling, FID from 50,000 generated images and timed ten-image batches. The LFP application uses 214 trials, seven regions and five selected time points from 50, with rescaled time. These are new experimental settings; the retained MNIST/HWD+ architectures and HWD+ split remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix F and Figure 7 add a focused comparison of intermediate distributions, testing whether GP streams suppress spurious modes during a two-to-three-Gaussian transformation. Appendix I also reports LFP runtime with five versus 50 time points. The existing variance-schedule and crossing-stream/covariate analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The existing 100-run experiments retain mean and standard-error reporting. v5 Table 4 adds a distinct repeated-evaluation procedure: each trained CIFAR-10 model undergoes 20 FID evaluations and 20 generation-timing measurements, summarized by means and standard errors. These are repeated evaluations of trained models, not 20 independent training runs.

E6.justification: For the retained Gaussian-mixture setting, I-CFM/GP-I-CFM Wasserstein means change from 1.51/1.27 in v1 Figure 1B to 1.54/1.51 in v5 Table 1. New CIFAR-10 FIDs are 3.75, 3.74, 3.62 and 3.75 for I-CFM, OT-CFM, GP-I-CFM and GP-OT-CFM, respectively, alongside timing results. Intermediate-mode and LFP findings are added, while MNIST means and variance-schedule scores are retained.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains joint GP sampling of positions and velocities, the squared-error stream objective, endpoint coupling and optional starting-point conditioning. Revised notation, covariate terminology and additional applications do not introduce a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are substantially recast. Section 2 becomes Background and Notation, much of the Bayesian argument moves to Appendix A, applications are organized by purpose, and proofs are consolidated under Appendix J. Stream notation and related/labeled terminology are revised throughout.

P2.justification: Numerical panels embedded in v1 Figures 1, 2, 5 and 7 become standalone tables in v5. Plots are resized or rearranged, HWD+ image traces move to Appendix Figure 9B, and the MNIST sample-image panel is removed. New displays show intermediate modes, CIFAR-10 results and samples, and LFP trajectories.

R1.justification: v5 explicitly positions GP-CFM as extending stochastic interpolants and acknowledges multimarginal work by Albergo and colleagues, qualifying v1's assertion that existing FM methods only accommodate endpoints. It also credits earlier covariate/guided-flow methods by Isobe and Zheng and removes several diffusion/latent-model references. This revises the novelty context beyond a bibliographic update.

T1.justification: The Bayesian squared-error justification, GP conditioning and derivative formulas, linear-kernel reduction, and three continuity/gradient-equivalence proofs remain substantively the same. The Bayesian argument moves to Appendix A, and v1 Theorems 1–3 become v5 Propositions 1–3 in Appendix J. Notation and regularity-condition wording change without a substantive new derivation or result.

improvement.justification: v1 supports its practical claims mainly through toy problems and handwritten digits, with little measured computational-cost evidence. v5 substantially strengthens that foundation through the CIFAR-10 quality/timing comparison, smoothing analysis, real time-series application and implementation disclosures. Clearer positioning against stochastic-interpolant and multimarginal research also improves the contribution's assessment. The LFP evidence remains descriptive, and removing the complete-observation caveat weakens limitation reporting, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the gains in empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GP-CFM research despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: The retained experiments are supplemented by original CIFAR-10 quality and timing results, intermediate-distribution analyses and an application to mouse-brain LFP recordings.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and Appendix E report original Gaussian-mixture simulations and MNIST/HWD+ experiments, including repeated-run Wasserstein, KID and FID results.

results.title: Stream-level flow matching with Gaussian processes

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions add computationally efficient semi-adaptivity, a dimension-independent sample bound under a high-precision condition, and empirical claims of practicality and improved sample efficiency. v1's contributions were theoretical and left the computational expense of fully adaptive estimation unresolved.

C2.justification: v2 interprets convergence gains as overcoming initial estimation overhead by concentrating sampling on high-risk groups, and interprets disproportionate sampling of a small Adult subgroup as evidence of GDRO's robustness objective. It also explains the new method's high-precision restriction and explicitly qualifies suppression of log-log factors in Appendix B. The existing last-iterate-convergence limitation remains.

D1.justification: New Appendix F supplies substantial experimental reproduction information: synthetic loss scaling and parameters, Adult features and group composition, normalization by a common maximum feature norm, absence of batching, and the full-information reference-optimization procedure. These details accompany newly introduced experiments rather than disclose changed settings for an existing study.

E1.justification: v1 has no evaluated datasets or simulation scenarios. v2 adds actual simulation of the lower-bound construction and Adult income classification across ten race-by-gender groups. The theoretical construction already existed, but its empirical use is new.

E2.justification: v2 introduces an empirical baseline comparison against Zhang et al.'s Stochastic Mirror Descent for GDRO (SMD-GDRO), visibly reported against SB-GDRO-SA on Adult in Figure 3. v1 discusses prior algorithms theoretically but reports no evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: The new experiments introduce protocols with 10^6 rounds, delta = 0.01, and target gaps of 0.005 for the synthetic instance and 0.001 for Adult. Section 5 and Appendix F specify normalized losses, single-sample updates, and a 10^7-round full-information procedure for estimating Adult's reference optimum.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses testing whether small dominant sets emerge during learning and how sampling concentrates across demographic groups. Figure 2 tracks dominant-set sizes and their running averages; Figure 4 examines Adult group-selection frequencies. v1 has no corresponding empirical diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports aggregation across five independent runs with seeds 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. v1 has no empirical run information. The added reporting does not include confidence intervals, quantified dispersion, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds the first empirical findings. Figure 3 reports SB-GDRO-SA reaching an Adult optimality gap below 4 × 10^-5 before 400,000 samples, while SMD-GDRO remains near that gap around one million samples. Figures 2 and 4 additionally report small dominant sets and concentrated group sampling; these are new results, not improvements over measurements in v1.

M1.justification: v2 introduces SB-GDRO-SA (Algorithm 9), which estimates the sparsity gap during optimization, halves lambda when dominant sets exceed a threshold, and refreshes samples subject to a lower cutoff. This is distinct from the retained SB-GDRO-Full, renamed SB-GDRO-A, and the existing dimension-free method moved to Appendix C.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: the generic optimization discussion moves into Appendix B.1, Section 4 is recast around full and semi-adaptivity, and the former dimension-free Section 5 moves to Appendix C. The introduction and explanations are rewritten, algorithms are renamed, and experimental discussion becomes a main section.

P2.justification: v2 adds three empirical figures showing dominant-set trajectories, convergence with a zoomed inset, and group-selection counts. Table 1 gains the semi-adaptive bound, a new algorithm display is added, and MaxP moves into the main text. The original lower-bound illustration is retained as Figure 5.

R1.justification: The bibliography retains the same 29 works. v2 makes limited positioning refinements, including distinguishing bounded-loss assumptions in prior work, revising its description of prior sleeping-bandit tuning requirements, and explaining the suitability of SMD-GDRO as an empirical baseline.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix B.3 add the semi-adaptive sample-complexity theorem, its more general formulation, and supporting proofs. Appendix D also changes the regret term from K^(1-alpha)/(eta_T(1-alpha)) to (K^(1-alpha)-1)/(eta_T(1-alpha)), repairing the stated alpha-to-one limit used to obtain the Shannon-entropy bound.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper by partly addressing v1's explicit computational-practicality limitation through SB-GDRO-SA, correcting the entropy-limit proof step, and adding the first empirical tests with documented settings. The new guarantee is conditional on high precision, and empirical support remains limited to two instances without uncertainty intervals. Nevertheless, the gains in theoretical support and demonstrated applicability are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GDRO research, with matching authors, foundational definitions, algorithms, and proofs. The main text and all appendices are readable, and renamed or relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 Section 5 reports original experiments on a synthetic lower-bound environment and Adult income classification, including dominant-set trajectories, convergence comparisons, and group-sampling counts. Appendix F documents the experiments.

before.justification: v1 contains theoretical results, proofs, and schematic illustrations, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes, including in its appendices.

results.title:
Beyond Minimax Rates in Group Distributionally Robust Optimization via a
  Novel Notion of Sparsity

C1.justification: The central claims about inaccurate PPO critics and effective Monte Carlo credit assignment remain. v2 extends superiority claims to RLOO/GRPO and newly claims to be the first RL post-training algorithm that scales generalization slope through additional compute. Higher test accuracy at comparable training accuracy was already claimed in v1 Appendix C.7; its promotion to the abstract is not an entirely new finding.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new critic diagnostics as evidence against undertraining and argues that already-capable LLMs justify spending more compute on accurate updates. Appendix E.27 adds a useful qualification: nonzero advantages need not correspond to logically incorrect or insightful steps. The earlier explanations concerning KL efficiency, temperature sensitivity, and errors later in reasoning chains remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds RLOO/GRPO hyperparameters and implementation information, identifies RhoMath across both datasets as the basis for PPO hyperparameter selection, and explains checkpoint loading and separate vLLM engines per GPU rank. Existing hardware, timing tables, software choices, and code/container access statements are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use MATH and GSM8K for mathematical reasoning. The added diagnostics and examples remain within this coverage; no additional dataset, domain, or distinct task scenario is evaluated.

E2.justification: RLOO and GRPO, previously discussed but not experimentally compared, become evaluated baselines across both datasets and model sizes. v2 includes them in performance, generalization, and runtime comparisons in Figures 4–6, while retaining PPO, DPO+, and RestEM.

E3.justification: v2 adds explained variance as a critic diagnostic and specifies protocols for the new RLOO/GRPO experiments, including KL-coefficient tuning and a selected coefficient of 3e-3. Existing dataset splits, model sizes, Pass@1 evaluation settings, and PPO/VinePPO hyperparameters remain unchanged. Expanded descriptions of existing sampling budgets do not establish that those experiments changed.

E4.justification: v2 adds an analysis addressing critic undertraining through explained-variance and MAE trajectories (Appendix D.2), extends the existing rollout-count ablation to wall-clock efficiency (Figure 7b), and adds three credit-assignment case studies (Appendix E). Existing generalization, KL, temperature, and value-ranking analyses are retained or expanded rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Section 7 newly quantifies uncertainty in the 256-rollout reference values: their Bernoulli sample-mean variance is at most approximately 0.001. The reference sample count is unchanged, and both versions average accuracy over 16 evaluation rounds with different random seeds; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial comparator and diagnostic results. For DeepSeekMath on MATH, Figure 4 newly reports RLOO at 36.8% and GRPO at 36.4%, alongside unchanged PPO and VinePPO scores of 42.8% and 46.0%. It also adds rollout-count timing and case-study outcomes. Figure 5 revises the RhoMath/MATH train-versus-test trace from v1 Figure C.4 without explaining the revision; this should not be interpreted as a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: Both versions replace PPO's critic with Monte Carlo value estimates, compute stepwise advantages, and assign each reasoning step's advantage to its tokens. Auxiliary rollouts remain excluded from direct policy training. Section 4 is clarified and rewritten without changing the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method explanation, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Results are reorganized around performance, efficiency, generalization, and rollout count; KL and temperature discussions move to the appendix, while the existing generalization analysis moves into the main text. An impact statement is added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 2 is substantially redrawn, comparison plots gain additional methods, diagnostic panels are split or recombined, and numerous existing figures move between the main text and appendices. New diagnostic plots, a baseline hyperparameter table, and illustrated case studies further change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Chang et al., Chu et al., DeepSeek-R1, and Agent Q, while removing several earlier introductory and discussion references. It more explicitly positions the work against methods without stepwise credit assignment and adds the generalization-scaling novelty claim. The established relationships to Vine-TRPO, MCTS, and process supervision remain.

T1.justification: Appendix C.5 adds mathematical definitions of GRPO and RLOO advantages and reasoning about baseline dependence and gradient bias. Section 7 adds the Bernoulli variance calculation. The original MDP formulation, PPO/GAE equations, VinePPO estimator, and unbiasedness claim remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 discussed critic-free RL alternatives without testing them, leaving an important comparative gap. v2 directly evaluates RLOO and GRPO and adds critic-training diagnostics and rollout-count efficiency analysis, substantially strengthening the evidence for VinePPO's practical advantages. Additional implementation details improve reproducibility. The stronger claim about scaling generalization slope is less directly demonstrated than the accuracy and runtime findings, but the improved comparative evidence provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VinePPO research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial rewriting and relocation of material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and reports additional RLOO/GRPO comparisons, critic diagnostics, rollout-count timing results, and credit-assignment examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original MATH and GSM8K experiments with RhoMath 1.1B and DeepSeekMath 7B, including benchmark results, ablations, timing measurements, and value-prediction analyses.

results.title: VinePPO: Refining Credit Assignment in RL Training of LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction refocus broad logical-consistency and overall-robustness claims on logical preference consistency and judgment robustness. The four principal contributions, alignment-preservation claim and downstream-performance claim remain; the conclusion still uses broader reliability language.

C2.justification: Appendices H, M and N add substantive guidance on choosing K, attribute alignment losses after downsampling to information loss, and discuss aggregation limitations involving indirect comparisons, ordering and ties. Section 3.3 also changes the interpretation of transitivity from a proxy for global reliability to one for local robustness.

D1.justification: Appendix G supplies previously missing NovelEval, CaTeRS and instruction-tuning prompt templates, plus explicit metric-computation instructions. Appendix B documents MS MARCO preparation and label provenance. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the existing LoRA settings, hardware description and ANONYMOUS code/data placeholder remain.

E1.justification: Appendices B and L add MS MARCO query–passage data for REPAIR training and evaluation, extending the intervention beyond summarization. Document reranking was already represented by NovelEval, and all original datasets and tasks remain.

E2.justification: v1 mentions Elo and Bradley-Terry as possible alternatives; v3 actually compares both against win-loss aggregation in Table 7. The original LLM comparator roster remains; Deepseek-chat-v2 clarifies the model already associated with the DeepSeek-v2 citation.

E3.justification: v3 adds training-data-size controls, a subgraph-size sweep and an MS MARCO protocol using 800 training and 200 test examples with ten retrieved candidates and GPT-3.5-derived rankings. Figure 7 also revises the existing SummEval prompt to require only A or B; the PDFs do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to subgraph size K (Appendix H), whether consistency gains persist after matching training-set sizes (Appendix M), and dependence on the ranking estimator (Appendix N). These address methodological questions absent from v1.

E5.justification: Appendix I adds a binomial/normal-approximation sample-size argument at 95% confidence for the existing M=1000 sampling cap, although the numerical error margin is unspecified. The existing ten CoT samples, 100 PairS runs and correlation significance reporting remain unchanged; no new empirical uncertainty estimates are provided.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 and Figures 4–5 retain their values. v3 adds substantial results in Tables 5–7 and Figure 9: for example, Table 5 reports MS MARCO transitivity of 86.7 versus 91.3 and PairS scores of 58.1 versus 61.0 for perturbed versus REPAIR training. v1's reported correlations below 0.05 between transitivity and human accuracy are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, conclusion and several main-text passages are substantially condensed or rewritten, with revised preference-consistency terminology and REPAIR naming throughout. The original Section 4 motivation moves to Appendix K, the downstream subsection is consolidated, and the appendix organization expands considerably.

P2.justification: The main text and bibliography change from single-column to two-column layout, with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. Figure 7 expands into a three-task prompt grid, and v3 adds Figures 8–9 and Tables 5–7.

R1.justification: Appendix E adds a focused distinction from social-network clustering, triad census and E-I measures with supporting citations. Additional references support sampling theory, Elo and MS MARCO, while some instruction-tuning background references disappear. The main positioning against factual-knowledge and NLI consistency research remains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same consistency metrics and ranking-based data refinement framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite the changed title and formatting.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds MS MARCO experiments, size-matched training comparisons, ranking-estimator comparisons and a subgraph-size sensitivity analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM evaluations, instruction-tuning experiments and downstream ranking results in Tables 1–4 and Figures 4–5.

results.title:
Aligning with Logic: Measuring, Evaluating and Improving Logical
  Preference Consistency in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central claim of inexpensive, transferable adaptive evasion remains. v2's contribution statement qualifies broad superiority as Pareto optimality above 90% evasion, explicitly acknowledging GPT-4o's quality advantage on some Pareto fronts. It also emphasizes success under the more restrictive no-box threat model and adds public paraphraser release as a contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving token-sequence avoidance, lexical substitutions, and learned edit distance, plus an interpretation of shorter outputs as a consequence of not penalizing brevity. It explicitly acknowledges imperfect alignment between LLM judges and human judgment and discusses restrictions of closed-model attacks. These substantially expand v1's mechanism discussion and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the 296-prompt evaluation set and its non-overlap with the retained 1,000-prompt training set, the MarkLLM implementation, and the GPT-4o version used. It changes a promised code/model release to a reported paraphraser release at a new repository location. The original hardware, prompting, optimizer, and LoRA details remain.

KGW corresponds to the retained Dist-Shift scheme. The underlying task remains text generation and paraphrasing.

The original DIPPER, translation, word-perturbation, and open-model baseline families remain, so this is a limited extension of the comparator set.

Appendix A.7 additionally evaluates n-gram overlap and normalized token edit distance. These are new evaluation protocols, not demonstrated changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: Appendices A.5–A.7 add distributions of text lengths, quality scores, and watermark scores, top-50-token comparisons, and n-gram/edit-distance analyses investigating attack behavior. The original model-size, adaptivity, FPR, watermark-bias, and example-based analyses remain; moving the FPR and bias studies into the appendix does not remove them.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 2 identifies its shaded bands as one standard deviation; v2 retains the bands but removes that explanation. The 95% confidence-interval description remains for the Qwen repetition experiment, moved from Figure 7 to Figure 6. No new repeated-run counts, seed reporting, or significance-testing procedures are documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results in Figures 7 and 9–15, including watermark-specific GPT-4o trade-offs and lower n-gram overlap after optimization. Figure 7 retains GPT-4o on the SIR and KGW Pareto fronts. Original results such as Figure 3 and the quality table remain numerically unchanged. However, v2 Table 4 retains v1 Table 3's values while reversing their quality/evasion labels, creating inconsistent metric assignments.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains surrogate-key generation, repeated paraphrasing, quality-and-detection filtering, preference pairing, and DPO optimization. The revised pseudocode is equivalent. Training a Qwen2.5-3b paraphraser against Unigram applies the existing procedure to another watermark without introducing a method component.

Related Work moves before the method, contributions become integrated introductory prose, and the FPR and bias discussions move into a substantially reorganized appendix. The title is shortened and terminology is standardized throughout.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column proceedings layout. v2 adds a workflow schematic and multiple analytical figures, resizes and relocates retained plots, changes Table 2 from stacked examples to three columns, and splits the bias table's paired values into labeled subcolumns. These are substantial visual and display changes.

R1.justification: v2 substantively positions the work against Jovanovic and Pang's sample-dependent attacks and Zhang's impossibility/random-walk setting, emphasizing inexpensive no-box optimization. It also adds references for SynthID, Unigram, SIR, MarkLLM, and AutoPrompt, while removing Nicks and Uchida citations. The revised distinctions materially expand the account of how this work differs from prior research.

Appendix A.7 introduces mathematical definitions for the newly evaluated overlap and edit-distance ratios. The original robustness inequality and optimization objective retain their substance, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence beyond v1's four-watermark evaluation through three additional watermark schemes, GPT-4o comparisons, a different quality judge, and direct textual analyses in Appendices A.4–A.7. Clearer training/evaluation documentation and explicit judge limitations also improve assessability. New reporting defects, including reversed Table 4 headings, conflicting overlap definitions in Equation 3 and Figure 15, and Figure 13's caption/legend mismatch, weaken specific details. Nevertheless, the broader comparative evidence and deeper analysis provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same preference-optimized watermark-evasion study. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison, and the original algorithm and experiments can be matched across the restructuring.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds watermark evaluations, GPT-4o comparisons, and analyses of paraphrased text in Appendices A.4–A.7.

results.title: Optimizing Adaptive Attacks against Watermarks for Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: single-reference event customization, the training-free FreeEvent framework, compatibility with subject customization, two benchmarks and strong comparative performance. C2.justification: Appendix F newly explains how large reference-to-target shape differences create a trade-off between event fidelity and entity appearance, with a tuning remedy. Appendix E qualifies event-subject customization as a secondary capability and acknowledges differing comparison settings. The original limitations concerning small or numerous entities and Stable Diffusion capabilities are retained in Appendix G.

E1.justification: Both versions retain SWiG-Event with 5,000 samples and Real-Event with 30 reference images. v2 modestly extends generation requirements through explicit attribute-control tests, including color and material, and subject-customization examples using personalized background concepts. Appendix E and Figure 9 introduce evaluated comparisons against AnyDoor, PhotoSwap and MS-Diffusion for event-subject customization, substantially broadening the comparison methods. The original six Real-Event baselines remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 expands retrieval evaluation with GSRTR verb-detection accuracy, CLIP-I, DreamSim, DINO, CLIP-T and FID. The user study changes from 30 trials requiring three selections to 50 trials allowing one to three selections. The subject-customization demonstration switches from DreamBooth to Break-A-Scene, and Appendix F introduces a separate experiment with altered guidance and injection schedules.

E4.justification: The original qualitative path and prompt ablations remain. v2 adds quantitative component-removal ablations on Real-Event in Table 3, attribute-control examples in Figure 8, expanded subject-customization investigations, and a shape-mismatch case study comparing guidance and injection schedules in Figure 10. These substantially broaden the analysis of component effectiveness and practical behavior.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Both present point scores and human-judgment counts; the revised number of user-study trials changes evaluation design rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 retrieval values are retained, including FreeEvent's 41.12/63.02/72.74. v2 adds MIGC results and additional metrics, including FreeEvent's 34.10 top-1 verb accuracy and 29.05 FID, plus quantitative ablations and new qualitative outcomes. Table 2 replaces the human-judgment counts under the revised protocol, including FreeEvent's 30 becoming 50; these counts have different trial denominators.

M1.justification: The core two-path FreeEvent procedure and Equations (1)–(6) remain unchanged. Appendix D adds a limited attribute-control adaptation: cross-attention guidance and regulation are applied to attribute words using the masks of their corresponding entities.

P1.justification: v2 shortens the abstract, revises the evaluation narrative and expands the appendix organization. Limitations move from the conclusion to Appendix G, the societal-impact paragraph becomes an Impact Statement, and acknowledgements are added. Much of the introduction, related work and method prose remains closely matched, so this is a limited editorial reorganization.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column layout to a two-column conference format, with substantially rearranged figures and tables. Figure 3 is repacked, Figure 6 is redesigned, Table 1 gains grouped metric columns, and Table 3 and new analysis figures are added. Qualitative grids are expanded and reorganized, retaining many earlier examples.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the new experiments, including MIGC, Break-A-Scene, GSRTR, DreamSim, FID, PhotoSwap and MS-Diffusion, and discusses the relationship to subject-swapping methods. The main related-work narrative and novelty positioning remain largely unchanged. Publication-year and venue updates to existing references do not constitute new cited works.

T1.justification: The task definition, diffusion formulation, attention guidance, regulation and feature-injection mathematics in Section 3 are substantively unchanged. No new theorem, proof, derivation or formal assumption is introduced in the appendices.

improvement.justification: v1's automatic evaluation relied on retrieval, while its component ablations were qualitative. v2 substantially strengthens validation through event-specific verb detection, complementary similarity and quality metrics, MIGC comparisons and numerical component ablations in Table 3. Appendix F also provides concrete guidance about a meaningful failure condition. The subject-customization comparisons remain limited by acknowledged setting differences, and uncertainty reporting is still absent, but the core empirical support and applicability analysis are substantially stronger.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FreeEvent research, with matching authors, task, core method and benchmarks. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and reports additional evaluation metrics, quantitative ablations, subject-customization comparisons and a hyperparameter case study.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval results on SWiG-Event, qualitative comparisons and ablations, and a Real-Event user study in Tables 1–2 and Figures 4–6.

results.title: Event-Customized Image Generation

C1.justification: v1 frames its contributions around Red-Green watermark schemes; v2's introduction additionally claims generalization to all schemes vulnerable to learning-based spoofing, with AAR/KTH demonstrations. The abstract and conclusion also explicitly qualify the previously broader 'all current spoofing methods' language as learning-based attacks.

C2.justification: Appendices D–F add substantive interpretations of reference-data mismatch, attacker data scaling, and why reprompting is preferable to fixed calibration. v2 also acknowledges AAR false-positive inflation, explicitly identifies short input length as a limitation, and expands discussion of edited text, piggyback spoofing, and watermark security trade-offs.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link and specifies previously unstated attacker training-data sizes: 30,000 samples of 800 tokens for Stealing and 640,000 samples of 256 tokens for Distillation. New appendices document additional experimental parameters. The training-size disclosures do not establish changes to the retained experiments.

Edited-text experiments specify insertion proportions and separate sample counts for mixing and paraphrasing (Appendices A.5, D–H).

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to reference-corpus mismatch and attacker training size, the effect of estimating prompts, and the necessity of reprompting versus fixed calibration. Additional robustness experiments examine another model pair and false positives after text insertion or paraphrasing. The original concatenation and context-dependence analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 5.1 and Figure 2 supplement v1's visual normality assessment with Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Pearson normality tests, reporting p-values and rejection decisions. Figure 9 adds distributional boxplots with explicitly defined whiskers. Neither version reports repeated-seed uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in v1 Tables 1–5 are retained in v2 Tables 1, 5, 2, 3, and 4, respectively. Substantial new results appear in Figures 6 and 9–15. For example, Appendix G reports about 90% AAR detection with 500 tokens at nominal 1% rejection, accompanied by approximately 2% empirical false positives. These results concern newly evaluated conditions.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix G extend the detector beyond binary Red-Green colors. AAR uses negative-log watermark scores; KTH introduces Levenshtein alignment costs and a surrogate context of h = 5. These are substantive scheme-specific scoring adaptations, while the original Standard and Reprompting procedures remain.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title, rewrites substantial introductory material, combines background and related work in Section 2, and moves the spoofer-model study from Section 5.3 to Appendix A.4. The appendices are extensively reorganized, and impact and acknowledgment sections replace the earlier document's closing structure.

P2.justification: The main paper changes to a two-column layout with resized and relocated displays. The spoofer-model table and figure move to Appendix A, eight new figures are added, and Figure 2 gains p-values and colored normality-test indicators. The five original tables remain, with renumbering and layout adjustments.

R1.justification: Sections 2 and Appendix J substantially expand research positioning around learning-based, piggyback, and step-by-step spoofing, deployed watermarks, and cryptographic defenses. New citations include Aaronson, Dathathri et al., Christ and Gunn, and recent watermark-identification work. Existing publication-year and venue updates are separate from these substantive additions.

T1.justification: v2 adds a general mathematical representation of watermark transformations and nonbinary score definitions for AAR/KTH. Lemma 4.1, its assumptions, and its proof remain unchanged, moving from Appendix D to Appendix I. No corresponding generalized proof accompanies the new extensions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical validation by testing assumptions that v1 left largely unchecked: reference-corpus mismatch, prompt estimation, fixed calibration, and modifications to genuine text. These experiments clarify when the detector works and expose a failing calibration alternative; added code-access information also helps reproducibility. The broader generalization claim remains limited by AAR false-positive inflation and the absence of an extended proof, but these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and applicability assessment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, despite the changed title and publication format. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds experiments on reference-corpus mismatch, attacker training size, reprompting alternatives, additional watermark schemes, and modified watermarked text.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on generated and spoofed text, including false-positive rates, detection power, model comparisons, and validation analyses in Sections 5 and Appendices A–C.

results.title: Discovering Spoofing Attempts on Language Model Watermarks

C1.justification: The central claim that algorithm selection for OOD generalization is learnable remains. v2 broadens the stated empirical applicability from synthetic and image tasks to language tasks, presents multi-label classification as the principal solution, and promotes the dataset-construction workflow to a released research tool. These extend the contribution statements without replacing the central thesis.

C2.justification: v2 derives concrete algorithm-choice recommendations from decision trees and adds cost-amortization reasoning. It explicitly discusses support-limited generalization, information potentially missed by handcrafted descriptors, binary-class/binary-attribute restrictions, and unaddressed forms of covariate shift. v1's explanation of PPL's advantages disappears. These substantially revise both interpretation and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and tool-release statement, specifies the fixed suitability threshold and highest-logit inference rule, and reports hidden width 100 for the real-data MLP. It also documents new dataset-construction procedures and the depth-three decision-tree and distillation recipes. These materially expand reproducibility information; the PDFs alone do not verify the linked resource's contents.

COCO evaluation is removed, while MetaShift supplies a different image population for the retained cat/dog and indoor/outdoor task. v2 additionally evaluates OfficeHome object/domain pairs, Colored-MNIST digit/color tasks, CivilComments toxicity classification, and MultiNLI inference, substantially extending both visual coverage and language-task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 removes PPL from the reported selector comparisons, including comparisons where it was v1's strongest vision selector. It adds decision-tree comparisons in Table 5 and uniform ensembling in Table 19. These materially revise the alternatives evaluated, although the five downstream candidate algorithms remain, with logits correction renamed logits adjustment.

Fixed single-shift values are replaced by randomly sampled degrees. New protocols include BERT-based language experiments, training and evaluation with average-group error, and training on tasks of at most 1,000 samples before testing on 2,000–3,000 samples.

E4.justification: v2 adds suitability-threshold sensitivity, highest-logit versus random suitable-algorithm selection, and alternative-metric analyses in Appendix E. Appendices I–J add dataset-size extrapolation and detailed decision-tree interpretation and distillation analyses. Existing descriptor-removal, fine-tuning, and inferred-attribute studies remain, although some are relocated or revised.

E5.justification: v1 Table 1 explicitly states that synthetic results average over three seeds. v2 retains the corresponding means and ± values but omits that seed-count disclosure. This is a loss of statistical reporting detail, not evidence that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: Many real-data results are replaced: CelebA/ResNet MLC changes from 69.1% selection accuracy and 42.7% worst-group error in v1 Table 2 to 75.0% and 47.7% in v2 Table 2. Shared synthetic rows and retained fine-tuning entries remain unchanged.

Appendix D.2 also changes the reported real-data MLP from four layers to two.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method explanation, and conclusions are extensively rewritten. v2 consolidates algorithm selection in Section 2, gives dataset construction its own Section 3, and organizes experiments by domain and interpretation in Section 4. The appendices are substantially reorganized, including relocation of existing fine-tuning and inferred-attribute material.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text to two columns, redraws the overview and shift-quantification figures, removes the three-formulation diagram, and replaces the algorithm-difference histogram with a violin plot. Table 1 is transposed and other tables are restructured. New dataset-example displays, diagnostic tables, and decision-tree figures substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the new datasets, BERT, class balancing, and logit adjustment, including Idrissi, Menon, and Kini, while removing PPL-related references such as Bradley–Terry and Copeland voting. Its positioning relative to algorithm selection, meta-learning, AutoML, and Bell et al. remains broadly intact. Bibliographic publication updates are not treated as new works.

T1.justification: v2 adds Conjecture 1, explicitly conditioning selector learnability on sufficiently diverse, densely sampled training shifts and generalization within their support. v1 discusses the no-free-lunch motivation without this explicit conjecture. The principal dataset-construction mathematics remains, and no new proof or generalization bound is provided.

improvement.justification: v1's transfer evidence was concentrated on CelebA and a small COCO evaluation. v2 substantially strengthens the central learnability claim through broader visual transfer and CivilComments-to-MultiNLI evaluation, targeted sensitivity tests, and interpretable decision rules. Clearer limitations and implementation details further improve assessability. Removing the strong PPL comparisons and explicit three-seed disclosure are losses, but the broader validation and diagnostic evidence provide a substantial net improvement. Revised settings do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OOD-Chameleon by the same authors. All 20 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable and support comparison of text, equations, tables, and figures.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic, CelebA, and COCO experiments, including algorithm-selection results, ablations, and estimated-attribute experiments in Appendix E.

results.title: OOD-Chameleon: Is Algorithm Selection for OOD Generalization Learnable?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claim that gated, locally regularized adapters improve the learning/forgetting trade-off over finetuning, LoRA, and vanilla adapters. The α discussion changes from acknowledging no downstream benefit in v1 to interpreting small α as beneficial under v2's revised configuration.

German-as-new-language experiments disappear; German instead appears among retained languages in Appendix F.

Revised Gemma French scores use changed training budgets and therefore do not establish same-setting gains.

The frozen backbone, parallel adapters, low-variance initialization, mixed-data training, and local sparsity-loss approach remain. The main-results and ablation narratives are rewritten, initialization receives separate treatment, and existing capacity analysis moves into a structured appendix sequence alongside detailed results. These changes extend beyond terminology and routine copyediting.

The math failure case and Wikipedia-only control expose meaningful boundaries, while explicit loss details and per-task ablations improve inspectability. Removing the controlled Transf-EN/Transf-ML comparison is a tradeoff, and retained Table 2 is not clearly reconciled with revised defaults. results.title: Neutral Residues: Revisiting Adapters for Model Extension

A new Section 3.5 footnote explains that missing actual data ultimately causes implementation failure. Original model defaults and SR/NPS/CS definitions remain. Table 5 also gives split counts differing from retained descriptions, such as Software Defects training/validation counts; whether the original experiments were actually re-split or rerun is unresolved.

E4.justification: V1's component ablations and plan-count study are retained. V2 adds tests of sensitivity to agent-role wording and robustness to two noise-injection locations (Figure 6a-b). Appendix A.2 also newly reports qualitative code-generation failures of several smaller language models, extending the analysis of backbone limitations.

E5.justification: Both versions report five independent runs and standard deviations for the main performance tables, with unchanged values and reporting practice. No new seed, confidence-interval, or significance-testing procedure is documented. Table 13's Agent K ranges reflect rank-derived score approximations, not repeated-run variability.

E6.justification: V1 Tables 5-10 retain their numerical results as v2 Tables 6-11. Substantial new results appear in Figure 6 and Tables 12-13. Table 12 reports average search times of 249.91 seconds for AutoML-Agent versus 2037.18 for SELA, with NPS of 0.612 versus 0.599. Agent K comparisons show mixed outcomes; these are additional evaluations, not improvements over v1 under identical conditions.

M1.justification: The five-agent architecture, retrieval-augmented planning, plan decomposition, prompting-based search, and three verification stages are unchanged. Algorithm 1 and the matched appendix prompts retain the same procedures. The additional adversarial agent generates experimental noise rather than becoming a component of the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition and appendix examples remain textually stable. V2 consolidates the experimental analyses under Section 4.3, moves limitations into a discussion appendix, adds an appendix roadmap, and makes local wording, heading, affiliation, and cross-reference edits. This is a limited reorganization rather than an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout, substantially resizing and relocating existing displays. V2 adds a prompt-parsing illustration, a three-panel analysis figure, a dataset-statistics table, and two comparison tables. The framework-comparison table also gains rows.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Table 1 expand positioning against SELA, Agent K, and newer general-purpose agent research. Appendix A substantially develops the motivation for non-expert users and distinctions from generic LLM-agent frameworks, supported by additional literature. Publication updates to existing references, such as AgentHPO and AutoMMLab, are not treated as new works.

T1.justification: The mathematical descriptions of instruction data, planning, decomposition, and verification retain their substance, as do the NPS and CS formulas. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and v2 introduces no new mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: V1 supports efficiency mainly through absolute resource costs; v2 directly tests the central training-free-search rationale against SELA and adds controlled prompt and retrieval-noise experiments. These address important gaps in comparative and robustness evidence, while the code-access statement and additional documentation strengthen reproducibility. The gains remain substantial despite conflicting split counts, Figure 6's CS label versus Table 12's NPS label, and limited protocol detail for the rank-derived Agent K comparison.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoML-Agent, with matching algorithms, original experiments, prompts, and generated-code examples. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison. V1 Appendices A-E largely correspond to v2 Appendices B-F, alongside newly added material.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds prompt-sensitivity experiments, noise-injection tests, and evaluations involving SELA and Agent K.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations across fourteen datasets, including five-run performance summaries, component ablations, plan-count experiments, and measured resource costs.

results.title: AutoML-Agent: A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Full-Pipeline AutoML

C1.justification: The central method contribution is retained, but v2 broadens its principal empirical claims to both inductive trajectory prediction and transductive node classification. Its abstract and introduction explicitly claim superiority over existing hypergraph predictors, strengthening v1's claims of useful, interpretable latent structures and improved trajectory prediction.

C2.justification: v2 adds the qualification that annotated real-world hypergraphs need not be optimal for the downstream task and interprets TDHNN's dense structures as attention learning rather than useful sparse connectivity. It further interprets quantitative diversity and redundancy findings. Existing fixed-cardinality, maximum-slot and temporally static-structure limitations remain, while the oracle-performance-gap discussion is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds classification feature sources and split provenance, documents the shared-decoder baseline control and specifies the NBA structural-analysis configuration. It also promises a future full-code release, without providing a released SPHINX resource. The existing tuning grids, training details and dependency-code links are largely retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds transductive object classification on NTU and ModelNet40, substantially extending coverage beyond trajectory prediction. NBA is retained, while the reported synthetic evaluation concentrates on the former Two-Triangles setup, now called Particle Simulation; the separate One-Triangle evaluation is removed, although illustrative trajectories remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds GroupNet and TDHNN to the particle comparisons and TDHNN to both NBA comparison tables. The new classification comparison includes static and dynamic methods such as GCN, HGNN+, HNHN, HyperGCN, DHGNN, DeepHGSL and HSL. Conversely, v1's synthetic LSTM and ground-truth oracle comparisons are removed.

E3.justification: The added classification evaluation uses three feature configurations—GVCNN, MVCNN and their combination—and splits attributed to Zhou et al. v2 also specifies a common decoder for its added synthetic predictor comparisons and a six-hyperedge, four-node configuration for NBA structural analysis. The retained trajectory horizons and stated training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 retains the sequential-prediction, sampling and slot-count studies but substantially expands structural diagnostics: Figure 2b compares reconstruction overlap across predictors and ablations, Appendix D quantifies NBA node degrees and duplicate hyperedges, and Table 5 measures unique hyperedges under excess slots. The oracle-gap and LSTM temporal-degradation analyses from v1's Appendix D.1 are removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates and plots without explicit repeated-run uncertainty. v2's new Table 2 reports means and standard deviations over 20 runs for classification. This introduces uncertainty reporting for those experiments without establishing additional runs or changed statistical practices for the retained trajectory results.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive classification results, including NTU/GVCNN scores of 94.80±0.90 for SPHINX and 92.70±1.61 for TDHNN*, plus new predictor and structural-diagnostic results. It reports 90% versus 67% synthetic overlap for SPHINX versus TDHNN. Retained NBA entries are unchanged. One-Triangle, LSTM and oracle result entries from v1 disappear.

M1.justification: The sequential slot-attention predictor, binary history features, constrained k-subset sampling and hypergraph processing remain unchanged. Equations 1–2 and the decoder formulation match. The added classification experiments do not document a new algorithm or architectural component.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially reframed around three design requirements, related work is rewritten, and the experimental narrative is reorganized around inductive and transductive settings. The appendix is restructured, including a separate complexity section and predictor overview, although much of the method and limitations prose is retained.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from one to two columns, reformats and transposes the NBA tables, and combines revised performance plots, a new overlap panel and the retained decoder-learning curves into Figure 2. It adds classification, predictor-overview and unique-hyperedge tables while removing the detailed synthetic result tables. Several appendix graphics are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around static versus learned structures and inductive versus transductive applicability. New Appendix B and Table 4 compare differentiability, discreteness and regularization requirements across predictors, incorporating works such as TDHNN, DynGroupNet, DeepHGSL and MHSL. Earlier discussion of differentiable cell complexes and supervised set-to-hypergraph inference is removed.

T1.justification: The mathematical model, higher-order dynamics assumption, slot-update equations and permutation-matched overlap definition remain unchanged. The computational-complexity analysis moves from v1 Appendix C.2 to v2 Appendix C with the same bound. No new theorem, proof or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's broad applicability claim was supported principally by trajectory tasks and limited direct predictor comparisons. v2 substantially strengthens that foundation through transductive classification, controlled predictor comparisons, 20-run uncertainty reporting and quantitative structural diagnostics. Removing the oracle/LSTM comparisons and exact synthetic tables reduces diagnostic transparency, and the broader superiority wording exceeds the mixed long-horizon NBA rankings. Nevertheless, the new evidence meaningfully addresses the earlier validation gap and yields a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SPHINX by the same authors. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, allowing reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original trajectory experiments and reports additional NTU and ModelNet40 classification results, predictor comparisons and quantitative analyses of inferred hypergraphs.

before.justification: v1 reports original particle simulations and NBA trajectory-prediction experiments, including structural recovery, ablations and slot-count sensitivity results.

results.title: SPHINX: Structural Prediction using Hypergraph Inference Network

C1.justification: v1 presents joint one-shot adaptation and history-only prediction as a central contribution. v3 refocuses the advertised evaluation scope on one-shot adaptation and adds an explicit contribution claiming orders-of-magnitude faster inference. Generation and uncertainty capabilities already existed in v1, although v3 gives them greater prominence.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations connecting generative training to reduced error accumulation, codebook size to prediction tradeoffs, and reconstruction limits to turbulent forecasting. Its limitations now explicitly address data scarcity and high-dimensional attention costs. Some new interpretations overreach: Appendix D.2 claims consistent calibration superiority, although Table 10 gives worse Combined-equation RMSCE for Zebra than both ViT variants.

D1.justification: v3 adds implementation information for the hybrid, including [DYN] placement, frozen transformer weights with LoRA updates, and UNet bias conditioning. Appendix D.5 also specifies inference hardware, token throughput, and timing-step accounting. The original numerical-solver descriptions and transformer/VQ-VAE hyperparameter tables are substantially retained.

E1.justification: The seven PDE families remain. However, v3 removes the history-only, two-frame zero-shot benchmark from v1 Section 4.3 and adds explicit distribution shifts involving Heat forcing, Vorticity viscosity, and Wave 2D parameters. These materially change the evaluated input conditions and adaptation scenarios.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds ViT-in-context to the retained one-shot comparison with CAPE, CODA, and [CLS] ViT. Appendix D additionally evaluates a deterministic next-token alternative and noise/DropPath variants of ViT for uncertainty comparison. The MPP[2] and MPP[3] comparisons disappear with v1's zero-shot benchmark.

E3.justification: New protocols include training-data sweeps from 10 to 12,000 trajectories, codebook sizes from 32 to 512, CRPS/RMSCE evaluation, and Sinkhorn-based Wasserstein comparisons. The new timing study uses 100 adaptation steps, versus 250 in accuracy experiments. The retained core protocol is largely unchanged; the new Wave 2D distribution-shift description conflicts with Appendix B.7 about training parameter ranges.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantial tests of deterministic versus generative pretraining, distribution-shift robustness, training-data scaling, codebook sensitivity, reconstruction bottlenecks, calibration over rollout time, and inference cost. Existing context-count, temperature, and generation analyses are retained or revised. The earlier zero-versus-one-shot comparison and five-shot qualitative panels are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions estimate predictive means, standard deviations, and three-standard-deviation interval coverage using ten generated trajectories. v3 supplements this uncertainty reporting with CRPS and RMSCE calibration diagnostics, including their evolution over time. Neither version reports independent training-seed variability, significance tests, or confidence intervals on benchmark averages.

E6.justification: The shared rows in v1 Table 3 and v3 Table 1 are numerically unchanged, including Zebra's 0.207 on Wave 2D and 0.119 on Vorticity. v3 adds extensive new results, including hybrid inference times of 0.14 seconds versus 21 seconds for original Zebra on Vorticity. Context-count results change between v1 Figure 2 and v3 Table 18, while zero-shot benchmark results are removed.

M1.justification: The original VQ-VAE and next-token transformer remain, but v3 adds Zebra + UNet (Section 4.5; Appendix C.2). A new [DYN] token extracts a context embedding, the transformer receives LoRA fine-tuning, and a conditioned UNet predicts complete frames. This adds a substantially different inference procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution list, and problem-setting narrative are extensively revised. Experiments are reorganized around in-distribution adaptation, distribution shifts, generation, and acceleration. VQ-VAE mathematics, uncertainty discussion, and reproducibility material move into expanded appendices. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column formatting. The leading diagram is redrawn around inference, while the training overview moves to the appendix. New hybrid, robustness, and ablation displays are added; zero-shot and five-shot panels are removed. The context-count plot becomes a table, and the temperature analysis gains a CRPS panel.

R1.justification: The introduction and Appendix A substantially expand positioning against in-context operator learning, including Yang et al., VICON, and Chen et al., and against diffusion-based PDE surrogates. v3 explains differences in prompting, adaptation tasks, deterministic versus stochastic modeling, and scalability, rather than merely adding citations.

T1.justification: v3 Section 5 adds a brief mathematical complexity argument: extending the context sequence to 3D yields quadratic attention cost in NThwd. Existing PDE formulations and training objectives remain, with VQ-VAE equations relocated to Appendix C.4. Neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for Zebra's central contribution through a direct in-context comparator, explicit distribution-shift tests, analyses of modeling choices and reconstruction limits, and a measured speed/accuracy tradeoff for accelerated inference. These address important validation and practical-cost gaps in v1 despite unchanged core benchmark scores. The gains outweigh the loss of history-only evaluation, although inconsistent Wave 2D parameter documentation and the overstated calibration summary remain weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Zebra and retain matching methods, datasets, and experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v3 retains original prediction results and reports additional out-of-distribution experiments, accelerated inference results, calibration comparisons, and ablations in Sections 4 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original PDE prediction experiments, including one-shot and zero-shot comparisons in Tables 3–4, uncertainty analyses, and trajectory-generation results in Appendix D.

results.title: Zebra: In-Context Generative Pretraining for Solving Parametric PDEs

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes three training improvements, including angular embeddings, and headline scaling to N=256, q=3329. V2 centers two innovations—custom distributions and loss regularization—and changes the headline range to N=128, q=974269. It newly claims recovery of '2x harder' secrets and improved learning on non-arithmetic tasks, substantially broadening the stated contributions.

C2.justification: Regularization is reinterpreted from broadly improving accuracy and consistency in v1 Section 5.3 to offering little benefit on easier addition but helping harder recovery in v2 Sections 4.2–5. V2 adds interpretations concerning arbitrary padding values, repetition, and empirical sample-complexity scaling. Limitations shift toward large N, multiplication/scalar-product failures at larger q, and the need to extend noiseless recovery to actual noisy LWE.

D1.justification: V2 newly provides a code-repository URL, secret-recovery data budgets and recovery instructions, decoder/RoPE specifications, polynomial encoding and output criteria, and curriculum hyperparameter ranges in Appendix F. Reported main-training resources change from eight V100 GPUs and approximately 30 hours per GPU to one V100 and approximately three hours. V1's tail-generation instructions and detailed architecture-selection table are removed.

E1.justification: V2 retains addition and asymmetric functions but adds noiseless secret recovery, modular multiplication, scalar products, copy, associative recall, parity, selective copy, and polynomial sums. Modulus coverage expands substantially, including additional composite moduli in Appendix A. V1's Appendix D reaches N=384; v2 retains N=256 experiments in Appendix A but does not retain the N=384 cases.

E2.justification: V1 Table 4 directly evaluates implementations of Gromov, Doshi, and Jelassi. V2 retains a Jelassi-style standard encoder baseline but removes the direct Gromov and Doshi MLP comparisons. It adds evaluated curriculum-learning comparisons in Table 4 and cross-entropy-loss comparisons in Table 22, substantially changing the comparator set.

E3.justification: The main configuration changes from 12 to 4 encoder layers, batch size 256 to 250, and learning rate 0.0001 to 0.00003. Training changes from 614.4M examples to 100M presentations of 10M distinct examples. Addition evaluation drops exact accuracy and the 0.3% tolerance, retaining 0.5% and adding 1%. New secret-recovery and sequence-output experiments introduce additional evaluation procedures.

E4.justification: Sparsity and easy-before-hard analyses are retained with revised experiments. V2 removes tail-augmentation, input/output embedding, and detailed internal-layer PCA analyses. It adds curriculum sensitivity, arbitrary padding-value tests, controlled example repetition, sample-efficiency comparisons, longer-training/larger-model tests, and MSE-versus-cross-entropy analysis. Appendix E newly examines loss-dependent collapse in noiseless secret recovery.

E5.justification: V1 Table 9 reports best/average/worst accuracy over four loss-ablation trials. That summary disappears. V2 Table 4 reports averages with ± quantities described as variance across eight curriculum-comparison trials, while Table 8 reports recovery frequencies over 20 random model initializations. These are changed reporting designs across different experiments, rather than an established increase in repetitions of the same experiment.

E6.justification: The addition result grids are substantially replaced, and many new task results appear. Asymmetric-function accuracy changes from 90.3–91.0% at N=20 in v1 Table 10 to 95.1–96.2% at N=16 in v2 Table 9; different settings prevent interpreting this as a matched performance gain. V2 Table 8 newly reports 10–20% noiseless recovery with custom loss versus 0% with MSE, alongside new synthetic and polynomial outcomes.

M1.justification: V2 drops v1's g_interval tail-augmentation component and f_inv sampling option. For addition, the loss changes from alpha R + (1-alpha)MSE with alpha=0.01 to alpha R + MSE with alpha=0.0001, retaining the radial penalty R. New adaptations include token embeddings for multiplication and variable-length decoder-only training without custom loss for synthetic tasks. The precise sparsity-weight revision is ambiguous because v2's zero-count formula conflicts with Figure 1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around training distributions and cryptanalysis. The former standalone ablation section becomes exploration within Section 4; Section 5 becomes the LWE application; Section 6 gains task-specific subsections. The appendices are substantially reorganized and rewritten.

P2.justification: V2 redesigns the title block, typography, captions, and table arrangements. The introductory results table disappears, and numerous new comparison/task tables appear. The sampling plot changes from zero-count to nonzero-count axes, the learning curve uses training-completion percentage instead of epochs, and earlier tail/PCA displays are replaced by a noiseless-recovery output figure. Appendix tables also receive new side-by-side layouts.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around static sampling versus curriculum learning, repeated examples, optimization failures, and cryptanalysis. New discussions include Bengio et al., Charton and Kempe, and Shalev-Shwartz et al., alongside references supporting the added synthetic tasks and LWE setting. Angular embeddings are more clearly positioned as an inherited technique rather than one of the paper's central innovations.

T1.justification: The unit-circle MSE identity is retained. V1's formal g_interval construction in Appendix A is removed. V2 adds a conditional derivation of origin collapse under approximately constant predictions and uniform targets in Section 5, plus a finite-difference definition and claimed bound in Appendix D. These are localized changes to supporting mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation through tuned curriculum comparisons with repeated-run reporting, controlled repetition and sample-efficiency studies, and transfer tests on synthetic and polynomial tasks. These address important gaps in v1's evidence about why the approach helps and how broadly it applies. The gains outweigh reduced exact-addition reporting and removed diagnostics, although the '2x harder' cryptanalysis claim remains supported only by noiseless experiments and the revised sampling formula conflicts with Figure 1. The improvement is stronger empirical support, not an established same-setting performance gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable throughout, including figures, equations, tables, and appendices. V2 explicitly identifies itself as an update of v1's original title. The substantial restructuring does not prevent reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original modular-arithmetic experiments, noiseless secret-recovery results, synthetic-task evaluations, and polynomial-sum experiments, including Tables 8, 12, and 20–21.

before.justification: V1 reports original transformer experiments on modular addition and asymmetric modular functions, together with sampling, embedding, loss, and architecture ablations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Making Hard Problems Easier with Custom Data Distributions and Loss Regularization: A Case Study in Modular Arithmetic

C1.justification: The central contribution remains domain-independent test-time adaptation through idempotence. However, v2's abstract newly claims a theoretical connection to prediction confidence and consistent superiority over existing approaches, extending v1's emphasis on versatility across tasks and architectures.

C2.justification: The new appendices substantially develop the internal-representation projection interpretation and assert that small residuals indicate reliable predictions. Meanwhile, v2 removes v1's explicit CIFAR single-instance failure discussion, the explanation that the objective lacks independent input information, and the qualification that domain-specific methods may outperform IT3. A shorter general single-instance limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 supplies code and project links absent from v1 and newly discloses typical adaptation of 1–3 optimization steps and the CUDA peak-memory measurement function. These additions improve documentation but do not establish changed update budgets for retained experiments. Most existing architecture and training details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds large-scale ImageNet/ImageNet-C classification coverage in Section 4.7. Conversely, v1 Appendix A.1's separate evaluation on RoadTracer cities excluded from training disappears. The other datasets and principal task scenarios remain represented.

E2.justification: v1 principally compares against non-adapted models, with TTT included for CIFAR-C. v2 adds ActMAD comparisons for tabular data, CIFAR-C, roads, airfoils, and cars, and adds TTT to road segmentation. Its new ImageNet-C comparison evaluates TENT, ETA, MEMO, and ActMAD. Despite broader wording in Section 4, the age-prediction figure still shows only the non-adapted model and IT3.

E3.justification: The reported CIFAR-C TTT settings change from one instance augmented to 32 examples in v1 to batches of 8, 32, and 128 in v2. New ImageNet-C experiments use ResNet-18, 15 corruption types, five severity levels, and batches of 16–128. Appendix A adds relative inference-time comparisons and peak reserved GPU-memory measurement at batch 128.

E4.justification: v2 adds airfoil idempotence-error distributions before and after adaptation, an ImageNet-C accuracy-versus-idempotence analysis, and computational-cost comparisons. Its appendix segmentation montage compares TTT, ActMAD, and IT3 with per-example quality scores, replacing v1's additional iteration-progress examples. These substantially expand diagnostic and supplementary evidence without introducing component ablations.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 15 introduces Pearson correlation estimation across inference batches to quantify the relationship between idempotence error and accuracy. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the statistical addition does not establish improved run-to-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds ImageNet-C and comparator outcomes, a Pearson correlation of -0.94, and resource results: IT3 inference costs 4×, 5×, and 6× the base model for airfoils, cars, and roads, respectively, and uses 7.4 GB in the ImageNet-C memory comparison. Table 1 is unchanged, including online road quality 69.8, airfoil MAE 34.1, and car MAE 0.385. The held-out-city RoadTracer results are removed.

M1.justification: The auxiliary label input, supervised training loss, frozen-reference test-time loss, batch resetting, and online EMA variant remain unchanged. The expanded method discussion and appendices explain these procedures without establishing a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, the introduction and method exposition are extensively revised, and the experimental comparison narrative changes throughout.
