Separate limitations and conclusion sections become a combined section with a different future-work emphasis. New explanatory appendices and an impact statement substantially reshape the document's narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout and extensively redesigns comparative plots, legends, and colors. Separate mean-error plots are removed while corresponding boxplots remain; new diagnostic and ImageNet-C figures and four resource tables are added. The appendix's road displays are replaced by a cross-method segmentation montage.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning through ActMAD, depth-completion adaptation, a TTA survey, and ETA/MEMO references. Section 2.1 adds an explicit TTT-versus-TTA distinction and recognizes ActMAD's potential across modalities, replacing v1's position that suitable adaptation comparators were unavailable outside classification. The relationship to IGN receives extensive additional discussion.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds an explicit joint fixed-point-set formulation and categorical claims that the residual is zero in-distribution and positive for OOD inputs, extending v1's approximate consistency relation and possible OOD deviations. Most Appendix C equations restate existing mathematics. No general theorem or proof connecting self-consistency to prediction correctness is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's central empirical weakness: reliance mainly on non-adapted baselines and an explicitly mismatched CIFAR TTT comparison. Broader evaluated competitors, aligned reported CIFAR batch sizes, ImageNet-C validation, and resource measurements make the method's benefits and costs much easier to assess. These gains outweigh the removed held-out-city experiment and shortened limitations, although the stronger appendix claims about reliability exceed what self-consistency alone establishes.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IT3 research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds ImageNet-C evaluation, comparator results, idempotence diagnostics, and inference-time and memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original IT3 experiments on tabular regression, corrupted-image classification, age prediction, road segmentation, and aerodynamic prediction, including online adaptation and appendix results.

results.title: IT$^3$: Idempotent Test-Time Training

C1.justification: The central contribution remains uncertainty-adaptive conservative off-policy search that improves biological sequence design while balancing exploration and proxy reliability. The introduction and conclusion retain the same DNA, RNA, protein and peptide claims; added experiments primarily support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains arbitrary-position masking versus LS-GFN's suffix edits, connects smaller δ to uncertainty on harder GFP scenarios, and explicitly acknowledges that δ-CS does not resolve underlying active-learning and proxy-estimation weaknesses. These elaborate and qualify v1's retained conservative-search interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents δ clipping, TuRBO's continuous-to-one-hot conversion and the LS-GFN matching rule. Conversely, v1's stated 1,000 policy updates and exact 1,000-sequence AMP query budget are no longer specified. Core architectures, most hyperparameters and code-access information remain.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix B.5 adds GFP Medium and Hard benchmark scenarios characterized by low-scoring initial sequences distant from high-fitness sequences. This extends coverage within protein design; the existing biological task families, including AMP and Hard TF-Bind-8, were already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds TuRBO to all six main benchmark comparisons, LS-GFN back-and-forth search in Sections 6.4 and B.3–B.4, and SQL, VarGrad and Soft PCL comparisons in B.2. LatProtRL also enters the additional GFP comparison through explicitly literature-sourced results in Table 4.

E3.justification: Added protocols include 1,000-example GFP/AAV initialization tests, AAV reward-percentile truncations, LS-GFN backtracking matched through K=δL, and expanded δ sweeps. The additional GFP benchmark uses 15 rounds with 256 queries per round; the retained FLEXS experiments still use 10 rounds with 128 queries.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled search-strategy comparisons, alternative RL-objective analyses, reduced-data and degraded-proxy tests, and broader δ sensitivity and Pareto analyses. Conversely, v1 Appendix B.4's rank-reweighted proxy-training ablation is removed. Existing Hard TF-Bind-8 and RNA adaptive-δ studies are retained and reorganized.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five independent runs and retain the same mean-and-standard-deviation reporting for matched results. No changed run count, seed-reporting scheme, confidence-interval procedure or significance test is introduced.

E6.justification: Original Appendix C and AMP table values are retained, but v2 adds substantial results for new comparators, RL objectives, robustness tests and parameter sweeps. Table 4 newly reports GFP Medium/Hard scores of 1.06 ± 0.1 and 0.86 ± 0.0 at δ=0.01 under the added benchmark protocol. The rank-reweighting ablation results are removed.

M1.justification: v2 Appendix B.2 adds δ-CS variants using SQL, VarGrad and Soft PCL training objectives beyond the original trajectory-balance implementation. The central rank-based sampling, Bernoulli masking, sequential denoising and uncertainty-adaptive δ rule remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are edited, experiments are reorganized to lead with proxy failure, FLEXS tasks are grouped, and AMP and pseudocode move into the appendices. Related work gains thematic subsections, and the conclusion gains limitations and discussion. This substantially reorganizes the existing narrative.

P2.justification: The main text adopts two columns, with new radar, robustness and sensitivity displays. Pseudocode is split and relocated, the proxy-correlation bar chart becomes a numerical table, and main benchmark curves display means instead of medians. The maximum-summary and rank-ablation tables are removed; the AMP table is relocated.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands related work with a dedicated GFlowNets subsection covering foundations, credit assignment, exploration and RL connections, plus additional trust-region and generative Bayesian optimization research. It explicitly distinguishes δ-CS from exploration methods that assume accurate rewards and develops its relationship to LS-GFN.

T1.justification: The mathematical core, including the trajectory-balance objective and masking/denoising distributions, is retained. Expanded discussion of GFlowNet/RL equivalences cites existing work and introduces no new theorem, proof or substantive derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens direct testing of the central robustness claim through matched LS-GFN comparisons, degraded-proxy experiments, broader δ sensitivity tests and harder GFP evaluation. These address v1's limited validation of robustness and generality. Removing the rank-reweighting ablation, omitting budget details and introducing Figure 9's conflicting mean/median labels weaken documentation, but the more informative validation and explicit limitations provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same δ-Conservative Search work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, added and removed material to be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds RL-objective comparisons, protein-data robustness tests and GFP benchmark results. Appendix B.5 explicitly distinguishes borrowed comparator results.

before.justification: v1 reports original biological sequence-design experiments, proxy-failure analyses and ablations in Section 6 and Appendices B–C.

results.title: Improved Off-policy Reinforcement Learning in Biological Sequence Design

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion expand the demonstrated scope from natural-image restoration to medical reconstruction. The abstract replaces v1's significantly reduced runtime across all tasks with competitive or superior similarity metrics and runtime; Section 4.2 acknowledges faster baselines. This materially broadens applicability while qualifying the central efficiency claim. The triple-consistency contribution remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds an interpretation through grouped DPS updates and Adam, explains the cost of backpropagation versus fewer sampling steps, and discusses ODE quality/stability tradeoffs. v1's noise-estimation limitation is reconsidered using threshold-sensitivity evidence. Appendix B adds a 2D-only limitation and possible difficulties extending to 3D, while retaining the non-blind restriction.

D1.justification: New disclosures specify latent-model sources and hyperparameters, the Euler solver and five ODE steps, and MRI preprocessing, BART sensitivity estimation, pretrained-model sources, and sampling parameters. v2 explicitly identifies Adam as the experimental optimizer and adds links to extended ablations. Conversely, v1's explicit phase-retrieval oversampling-rate statement is omitted, without establishing a changed setting.

E1.justification: The eight FFHQ/ImageNet restoration tasks remain. v2 adds fastMRI multicoil reconstruction with uniform and Gaussian undersampling masks, truly noiseless Gaussian deblurring, and Poisson-noise super-resolution/nonlinear-deblurring scenarios. These extend the domain and measurement conditions; the latent experiments themselves reuse existing dataset/task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated DMPlug and PGDM comparisons, ReSample and Latent-DAPS comparisons in Table 5, and MRI comparators including DDS, Score-MRI, E2E-VarNet, and TV-ADMM. v1 Table 3's DDRM and PnP-ADMM comparisons disappear. RED-Diff was already evaluated, but its participation changes from FFHQ/ImageNet nonlinear tasks to ImageNet SR, motion deblurring, nonlinear deblurring, and HDR.

E3.justification: The original restoration test sets, metrics, and main hyperparameter table are retained. New protocols include 8,000 training images for supervised MRI baselines and 50 MRI test images, latent-model evaluation, five-step ODE reconstruction, component-removal controls, and runtime comparisons using N/K adjustments to approximately match PSNR. The N/K and stopping-threshold sweep designs also expand.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds full-trajectory backward-consistency ablations and separate measurement- and forward-consistency tests, beyond v1's intermediate-image demonstrations. Appendices I–J add matched-quality timing analyses, convergence curves, threshold sensitivity, and Poisson-noise robustness. The original four-task N/K table is replaced in the PDF by a broader Gaussian-deblurring sweep; the regularization and stopping-on/off studies remain.

E5.justification: The retained RED-Diff ImageNet nonlinear-deblurring and HDR comparisons acquire standard deviations in v2 Table 1, whereas v1 Table 3 gives only sourced point estimates. The general mean-and-standard-deviation convention and best-of-four phase-retrieval procedure remain unchanged. No increase in repeated-run counts or new significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Many original image-quality values remain, but Table 1 reverses FFHQ phase-retrieval PSNR ordering: SITCOM/DAPS changes from 30.97/30.67 to 30.67/30.97. Reported runtimes also change beyond unit conversion: DCDP FFHQ super-resolution changes from 0.52 minutes to 19.10 seconds. Substantial new latent, ODE, MRI, ablation, and robustness results accompany removal of v1 Table 3's comparisons.

M1.justification: The core pixel-space Algorithm 1 remains, but Appendix E adds Latent-SITCOM with a decoder-composed measurement objective and latent-space resampling. Appendix F implements SITCOM-ODE, replacing the Tweedie reconstruction in S2 with an ODE solver. v1 mentioned the ODE replacement only as an unused possibility and listed latent sampling as future work.

P1.justification: The contribution narrative becomes an explicit list, the experimental discussion is substantially rewritten into Settings and Main Results, and detailed task descriptions move to Appendix K. Retained appendix material is reorganized around individual consistencies, comparisons, sensitivity studies, and implementation details. These structural changes accompany substantial new explanations, although much of the core method exposition remains.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column manuscript to the two-column ICML layout. Table 1 gains comparator rows, the conceptual schematic is revised, and new analysis tables, convergence plots, and MRI panels appear. The phase-retrieval montage gains SITCOM-ODE examples. v1's introductory FFHQ figure is relocated to Appendix L rather than newly added.

R1.justification: Section 3.2.1 newly positions backward consistency through CSGM generative priors. Relationships to DPS, RED-Diff, and DMPlug receive substantial additional treatment, and PGDM/MRI literature expands the comparison context. RED-Diff is reframed from computationally expensive to fast but limited in reconstruction quality and requiring an external denoiser. DDRM and PnP-ADMM references are removed.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds Proposition D.1 and an approximation-based proof connecting K=1 SITCOM to DPS with resampling. This is a limited formal extension: the backward-consistency definition and Appendix A sampling derivation remain, and the broader acceleration argument is explicitly presented as heuristic rather than a performance guarantee.

improvement.justification: Controlled consistency ablations and matched-quality timing comparisons substantially strengthen v1's support for its mechanism and efficiency claims. Threshold and Poisson-noise studies address practical robustness, while latent and MRI experiments replace proposed extensions with implemented evidence. These gains outweigh removed comparator coverage and reporting weaknesses. However, v2 still needs correction: its blanket latent-superiority statement conflicts with Table 5, and default runtimes differ without explanation between Table 1 and Tables 11–12.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SITCOM research. The complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, revised, and added material.

after.justification: Original restoration experiments remain, supplemented by latent-space, ODE, MRI, consistency-ablation, and noise-robustness results.

before.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original image-restoration experiments on FFHQ and ImageNet, including quantitative comparisons, ablations, and reconstructed images.

results.title: SITCOM: Step-wise Triple-Consistent Diffusion Sampling for Inverse Problems

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the empirical claim from outperforming existing methods to achieving strong generalization while combining their strengths. The central claims about collapse avoidance, jointly clustered and decorrelated embeddings, and the hyperdimensional-computing connection remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds the hypersphere-versus-hypercube rationale for tanh, attributes faster convergence to quasi-orthogonal codes, and discusses checkpoint-storage limitations and possible bipolar-code efficiencies. It elaborates the explanation of excessive-beta collapse. The earlier finite-capacity qualification is retained.

D1.justification: The promise to release code becomes a stated public repository link, whose availability cannot be independently verified from the PDFs. New ResNet-18 optimizer, learning-rate, batch-size, hardware, and training-budget details accompany checkpoint-size, training-time, and ImageNet computation-cost disclosures. These substantially expand practical reproducibility information.

E1.justification: The same four image datasets are retained. ImageNet-100 evaluation expands from linear probing to include clustering. The additional ResNet-18 experiments reuse CIFAR-10 and do not introduce another dataset or domain.

E2.justification: The ImageNet-100 comparison expands from DINO alone in v1 Table 2 to DINO, Barlow Twins, SwAV, and GEDI no gen in v3 Table 3. v3 Figure 6 also introduces cross-method collapse comparisons. The original Table 1 comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: v3 adds a 1000-epoch ResNet-18 protocol using LARS, revises reported beta settings, and changes the ImageNet dictionary-size grid and evaluation metrics, adding NMI and dropping top-5 accuracy. Section 4 and Table 3 change ImageNet training from 100 to 300 epochs, although Appendix M still states 100; the actual budget is therefore inconsistently documented.

E4.justification: New analyses compare L2 normalization with tanh, compare collapse behavior across methods, examine training convergence, measure time and storage costs, and test a finer beta range (Table 4, Figure 6, Appendix L). Earlier dictionary-size and collapse analyses remain, including those moved from the main text to Appendix K.

E5.justification: Five-random-initialization averaging and existing uncertainty displays are retained for the small-benchmark and collapse studies. The activation comparison follows the same practice. No changed repeated-run counts, new uncertainty-estimation procedures, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: v1's L2 results survive in v3 Table 4, while tanh results appear in the main Table 1; for example, SVHN accuracy at c=16384 is 0.78 for L2 versus 0.75 for tanh. New ResNet-18, sensitivity, convergence, and resource results are added. ImageNet results are replaced under revised settings, including 70.9% NMI and 78.0% top-1 accuracy at c=131072, not a demonstrated same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 introduces tanh in place of L2 normalization, changing the projector's embedding constraint. The frozen random dictionary and loss framework remain intact. Reverse-KL stabilization was already documented in v1 Appendix L and is retained in v3 Appendix N.

P1.justification: The title changes from Failure-Proof to Collapse-Proof, with localized rewriting of the abstract, practical discussion, and conclusion. The collapse subsection moves to an appendix, new experimental subsections are introduced, and an impact statement replaces the separate reproducibility statement. Most theoretical prose and the principal section sequence remain.

P2.justification: v3 adds activation, ResNet-18, resource, and beta-sensitivity tables plus comparator-collapse and convergence plots. The ImageNet table is reorganized into clustering/linear-probing and small/large-projector groups. Figures 1 and 5 are enlarged, and v1's main collapse Figures 6–7 move to the appendix as Figures 12–13.

R1.justification: v3 adds the Kleyko et al. hyperdimensional-computing survey and additional Sansone–Manhaeve references, and identifies the dictionary encoding as multiply-add-permute. The broader positioning around unifying feature-decorrelation and clustering approaches remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 5 corrects the displayed expectation from a self-inner-product expression to cosine similarity between two code vectors, fixing its scaling and indexing. The principal lemma, embedding theorem, corollaries, and appendix proofs otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The expanded ImageNet comparisons directly test the central claim of jointly useful clustering and classification representations, addressing v1's reliance on linear probing against DINO alone. ResNet-18 experiments and activation, sensitivity, convergence, and resource analyses substantially strengthen empirical scrutiny and practical usefulness. The narrower superiority claim is also better calibrated. Important limitations remain: conflicting 100/300-epoch descriptions, and the assertion that tanh preserves the guarantees without a corresponding revision of the normalization-dependent proof.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FALCON research, despite the revised title. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and reports additional activation comparisons, ResNet-18 experiments, expanded ImageNet-100 comparisons, and sensitivity and resource analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original clustering and linear-probing experiments, dictionary-size studies, and collapse analyses on SVHN, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-100.

results.title: Collapse-Proof Non-Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning

C1.justification: The central claims about sign-consensual unlearning, knowledge preservation, and computational efficiency persist. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the explicitly claimed validation scope to twelve datasets and four architecture families, including VGG and Swin.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking sparsity to retention, averaging to outlier suppression, and layer depth to knowledge specificity, plus storage and memory arguments. Appendix D.2 qualifies robustness by warning about poorly constructed model pools. Appendices E–F add heuristic mechanism reasoning and prospective applicability beyond image classification.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands documentation with attention-layer freezing, incremental consensus-mask storage, VGG/CUB training settings, and detailed alternative model-pool configurations (Section 3.3; Appendices A and D). These are disclosures and specifications, not evidence of changes to retained experiments. Existing core hyperparameters and the code-access URL remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds CUB-200-2011 and Tiny ImageNet evaluations and CIFAR-10 class-wise forgetting (Tables B8, B9, B13). The original eight CLIP target datasets, ImageNet retain control, and CIFAR-10 remain. Discussion of LLM applicability adds no evaluated language task.

E2.justification: The main unlearning comparator sets remain unchanged. However, the task-vector-addition comparison drops TIES-Merging and MagMax from v1 Table 3 to v2 Table 5. Their continued participation in other experiments does not preserve this particular comparison.

E3.justification: v2 adds VGG-16 and Swin-T configurations, a 50% random-forgetting split, and systematic experiments varying pool size and hyperparameter composition (Tables B10–B12, B7, D1–D4). Primary retained settings remain stable. Newly disclosed attention-layer freezing does not establish that the original experiments changed.

E4.justification: New analyses examine pool size and composition, averaging versus minimum/maximum merging, and sparsity across methods, depths, and components (Tables 4, 6, B7, C1–C3, D1–D4). Earlier sign-conflict and task-addition analyses largely remain. The retain-set sensitivity panel and island Grad-CAM example are removed.

E5.justification: Table C3 newly defines and reports variability across layers for component sparsity. Existing three-trial classifier statistics and three-run timing reporting remain unchanged. Table B7 extends the existing mean/standard-deviation convention to a new ablation; it does not establish increased run counts for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and v1 Tables A1–A6, matched to v2 Tables B1–B6, retain their numerical values. Substantial new results cover additional benchmarks and sensitivity analyses. For example, newly evaluated CUB gives average gaps of 7.30 for NegMerge versus 7.41 for Task Arithmetic; class-wise CIFAR-10 gives 3.73 versus 4.18. Some diagnostic result entries are removed.

M1.justification: Both versions average task-vector coordinates with unanimously consistent signs and subtract the scaled merged vector from the original model. Equation (1) is algebraically equivalent. Newly documented storage procedures and experimental min/max alternatives do not establish a change to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, motivation, and method exposition are extensively rewritten and reorganized. Computational cost becomes a separate subsection, implementation details move to Appendix A, and the appendices expand into sections A–F. The title and terminology also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout. Figure 1 is redesigned and loses its retain-set panel; Figure 3 loses one example. Numerous new tables are introduced, existing tables are resized or shortened, and retained appendix displays are relocated.

R1.justification: Related work adds focused positioning against Skill Localization, Localize-and-Stitch, and TALL Mask. New representation and linear-mode-connectivity references support added explanations, while some broad pretraining and continual-learning context disappears. The central task-arithmetic/model-merging positioning remains; publication-year updates are not new works.

T1.justification: The core mathematics is unchanged. New Appendix E offers qualitative arguments involving sparsity, linear mode connectivity, and a conjectured stable merged point, but supplies no formal assumptions, derivation, theorem, or proof. Both conclusions acknowledge the absence of theoretical justification.

improvement.justification: v2 directly tests the pool-size and composition robustness that v1 largely asserted, and expands standard-classifier validation beyond one dataset, backbone, and forgetting setup. These additions substantially strengthen empirical support for the method's central rationale and applicability. Some diagnostic evidence is trimmed, several new benchmark margins lack uncertainty estimates, and Appendix E remains heuristic, but the broader and more targeted validation provides a clear net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NegMerge and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Renamed and relocated material can be matched reliably despite extensive revision and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds dataset, architecture, forgetting-scenario, sparsity, and model-pool evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original CLIP and CIFAR-10 unlearning experiments, sign-conflict analyses, and Grad-CAM examples, alongside explicitly attributed baseline results.

results.title: NegMerge: Sign-Consensual Weight Merging for Machine Unlearning

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, Remark 3.2, and discussion replace the central claim of a dimension-independent non-private term with a sqrt(d)-dependent, sublinear term. This materially narrows the claimed guarantee. The Ω(sqrt(d)) improvement over Zhang et al. and the multi-pass contributions remain.

C2.justification: New Remark 3.3 discusses trading sample complexity against oracle complexity. Remark 6.2 additionally contrasts the retained first-order oracle saving with the smaller non-private oracle gap. Existing limitations concerning approximate versus Rényi privacy and unresolved lower bounds remain.

D1.justification: The explicit single-pass tuning prescriptions change: Σ gains an α/(D sqrt(d)) term, and D gains an additional dimension-dependent cap in Theorems 3.1 and 6.1. These revise documented algorithm settings; no code release, hardware information, or experimental implementation details are added.

E1.justification: Neither version actually trains or evaluates on datasets or concrete test scenarios. Both study the same abstract nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization problems.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains Zhang et al. (2024) as the theoretical comparator. Neither version reports an experimentally evaluated baseline set, and the added citations do not introduce evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Neither version contains experimental evaluation protocols, splits, metrics, or training budgets. Revisions to theoretical algorithm parameter prescriptions are covered under M1 and D1.

E4.justification: Neither version reports empirical ablations, robustness tests, or case studies. The first-order analysis and optimal-smoothing extension already exist in v1; their relocation does not introduce supplementary experiments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The concentration results concern theoretical guarantees rather than uncertainty estimated from experiments.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the single-pass sample-complexity expression 1/(αβ³) + d/(εαβ²) + d^(3/4)/(ε^(1/2)αβ^(5/2)) with sqrt(d)/(αβ³) + d/(εαβ²), suppressing the same factors. These are substantially revised theoretical results, not measured performance changes. The multi-pass entries remain unchanged.

M1.justification: V2 revises the single-pass algorithms' period and clipping-parameter prescriptions and corrects Algorithm 1's node-selection condition from k' <= k to k' <= t. The underlying O2NC framework and gradient-oracle constructions remain; the first-order algorithm already appeared in v1 Appendix B.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the exposition: v1 Appendix B becomes Section 6 and Section 7.4, and the techniques explanation moves into a new introductory subsection. It also expands the introduction and tree-mechanism explanation and foregrounds the existing first-order contribution.

P2.justification: Both versions retain Table 1 and Algorithms 1–5. V2 lightly restyles the table, places Algorithms 1 and 2 together, moves Algorithm 5 into the main text, and reflows mathematical displays. There is no substantial addition or replacement of visual content.

R1.justification: V2 adds supporting references to Abadi et al., Kulkarni et al., LeCun et al., Keskar et al., and Villalobos et al., principally for privacy composition and motivation. The central relationship to Zhang et al. remains, with the novelty claim narrowed to sublinear dimension dependence. Grimmer and Jia's publication update is the same cited work.

T1.justification: V2 repairs the single-pass derivation by retaining L/sqrt(B1), hence L/sqrt(Σ), in Equation (9), where v1 mishandles and drops this contribution. Revised parameter choices yield corrected Theorems 3.1 and 6.1, the latter corresponding to v1 Theorem B.4. V2 also uses AM-GM to absorb the mixed term and corrects smaller indexing and variance-factor errors.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves an important deficiency in a central guarantee: it restores the omitted variance contribution, revises the parameter choices and bounds, and withdraws the unsupported dimension-independent claim. Although the corrected guarantee is less ambitious, these changes substantially improve the paper's internal consistency and reliability. The pseudocode correction and clearer organization provide additional benefits.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and provide readable main text, Table 1, algorithm listings, proofs, and appendices. Material moved between the appendices and main text can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 remains a theoretical paper. Neither its main text nor its appendices report original empirical measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports theoretical algorithms and guarantees, including in its appendices, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes. Its empirical-risk results are mathematical guarantees.

results.title: Improved Sample Complexity for Private Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization

C1.justification: The central generalization, flatness, and efficient-ensembling claims remain. However, v1's claim to demonstrate the effect theoretically and empirically becomes an empirical demonstration supported by analytical insights in v2's contributions and conclusion, narrowing the claimed strength of the theoretical contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges that flatter minima do not universally imply better domain generalization, explains aggressive quantization through over-regularization, and distinguishes structured quantization noise from random uniform perturbations. The original limitations concerning ensemble training cost and bit-width selection are retained in Appendix C.

D1.justification: v2's abstract announces released code and supplies a project link, replacing v1's future-release promise, although Appendix M retains future-tense wording. v2 also documents additional model configurations and ablation settings and changes the reported CUDA version from 11.1 to 12.1. Most original implementation details are relocated unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluations on the WILDS Amazon and Camelyon datasets (Section 4.1.4, Table 3), extending coverage beyond the five retained DomainBed datasets and explicitly including text inputs. WILDS was only cited in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds an evaluated CLIPood comparator alongside ERM in the CLIP-based comparison (Table 6). CLIPood was cited but not evaluated in v1. Comparator membership in the retained DomainBed, quantization-method, and appendix comparisons is unchanged.

E3.justification: Added evaluations introduce Amazon 10th-percentile accuracy, Camelyon average accuracy, a BERT model, and CLIP ViT-B/16 settings. New controlled experiments vary scaling granularity, quantization timing, and uniform-noise amplitude. Existing DomainBed splits, training budgets, and model-selection procedures are retained in Appendix B.

E4.justification: Appendices H–J add PACS ablations testing channelwise versus layerwise scaling, quantization at 1000–4000 steps, and uniform weight-noise amplitudes. Section 3.2 and Appendix L add weight-distribution, symmetry, and quantization-error analyses. Earlier flatness, bit-precision, and GradCAM analyses remain.

E5.justification: Section 3.6 newly states that ensemble members are trained independently from initialization using random seeds. Both versions retain the stated three-trial standard-error reporting and omission of ensemble confidence intervals. No increase in repetitions or new significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark values are retained, including Table 1 averages of 66.2 for QT-DoG and 68.4 for EoQ. New Table 3 reports QT-DoG versus ERM OOD scores of 55.9 versus 53.8 on Amazon and 78.4 versus 70.3 on Camelyon. Table 6 adds CLIP averages of 70.6 for QT-DoG and 70.3 for CLIPood. New ablation and noise-distribution findings substantially expand the reported results.

M1.justification: The proposed weight-quantization procedure, integration with ERM, and EoQ prediction aggregation remain unchanged. The ensemble initialization clarification and additional evaluations do not establish a revised algorithm or training objective.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the document: dataset descriptions, implementation details, and limitations move from the main text to Appendices A–C; experimental subsections are reordered; and the appendix structure expands around new analyses. Contributions and analytical explanations are revised, and acknowledgements and an impact statement are added.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference paper, with extensive resizing and relocation of existing displays. v2 adds Tables 3, 6, and 13–15 and distribution Figures 2 and 8. The vision-transformer table drops its redundant backbone column. Existing GradCAM images are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds quantization-noise references such as Gray and Neuhoff and Boncelet, qualifies the flatness discussion using Andriushchenko and Mueller, and adds recent quantization and CLIP-related works. These refine the supporting literature and positioning without replacing the paper's central novelty claim.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 and Appendix L introduce assumptions and an approximate derivation for uniformly distributed quantization error, using small quantization bins, smooth symmetric weight distributions, and piecewise-linear density approximations. The existing quantization equations, Taylor expansion, flatness expression, and ensemble equation are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support for the paper's generality and mechanism claims. WILDS, text, and CLIP evaluations extend evidence beyond v1's DomainBed image settings, while Appendices H–J directly test previously unexamined scaling, timing, and generic-noise explanations. More cautious theoretical framing also improves claim calibration. The added protocols remain tersely documented, the uniform-noise argument is approximate, and code-release wording is inconsistent, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe QT-DoG and EoQ. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds WILDS and CLIP evaluations, configuration ablations, and measurements of quantization-noise distributions.

before.justification: v1 reports original DomainBed experiments, quantization ablations, flatness measurements, training trajectories, and GradCAM analyses, including additional appendix results.

results.title: QT-DoG: Quantization-aware Training for Domain Generalization

C1.justification: The abstracts, contribution lists, and conclusions retain the same central claims: implicit multi-hop retrieval uses deeper MLPs, shallow editing leaves relevant knowledge unchanged, and IFMET improves multi-hop recall through shallow and deep editing. The revised introduction makes the existing hypotheses more explicit.

C2.justification: Appendices F-G add substantive interpretations of component necessity, transfer to LLaMA-2, and model-generated prompts. They also acknowledge specificity loss and editing-time overhead, qualifying v1's largely benefit-focused discussion. For example, Table 7 reports specificity of 69.87 for IFMET versus 78.60 for PMET and discusses the resulting tradeoff.

D1.justification: v3 supplies the model-generated prompt template, a limit of one to five prompts per case, and the absence of additional filtering for that variant. It also reports per-edit times. Existing WikiData queries, GPT-J layer ranges, optimization settings, and editing equations are retained.

E1.justification: MQuAKE remains the benchmark family. v3 constructs paraphrase and neighborhood sets from a MQuAKE-3K subset, extending evaluation to reworded queries and preservation of neighboring facts (Appendix F). COUNTERFACT supplies the construction approach, rather than becoming an additional evaluated benchmark.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain their baseline methods. FT already appears in v1's appendix CoT tables, which become v3 Table 3; MeLLo remains in the batch comparison in v3 Figure 7. The new analyses reuse existing comparison methods, chiefly PMET.

E3.justification: v3 introduces LLaMA-2-7B experiments and component-ablation protocols using edit batches of 1 and 100, with efficacy, paraphrase, specificity, and editing-time measurements. Existing GPT-J few-shot and CoT evaluations remain; moving the CoT results into the main text does not establish a changed protocol.

E4.justification: v3 adds ablations of the first editing stage, multi-hop prompts, token position, and layer depth, plus LLaMA-2 causal interventions, prompt-source comparisons, and timing analyses (Tables 5 and 7-9; Figure 6). The earlier Pre/Post analysis remains, but its batch-100 row is omitted from v3 Table 2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The added relative percentage changes and average editing times do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial ablation, LLaMA-2, prompt-source, and timing results. The main CoT scores are retained from v1's appendix. In matched Table 4, IFMET+CoT's unedited-answer average changes from 21.62 to 21.32 and its Mid score from 30.51 to 28.20. Figure 7 also changes some batch results and plots zeros for batched ROME entries that v1 marked unavailable.

M1.justification: The two-stage editor, PMET-based Search/Calculate procedures, losses, and weight updates remain unchanged. v3 adds an alternative procedure that obtains supporting knowledge from the model itself to construct multi-hop editing prompts, alongside the existing WikiData procedure (Appendix D.1 and Table 13).

P1.justification: The introduction is reorganized around explicit hypotheses, Section 3 becomes a sequence of three research questions, and the method and experimental narratives are substantially rewritten. Existing appendix material is reorganized into separate dataset, intervention, method, settings, results, and prompt sections, alongside the new analyses.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main text, merges v1 Tables 5-6 into Table 3, splits Table 4 into two panels, and redraws the batch comparison as Figure 7. It adds ablation, timing, and prompt tables and a LLaMA-2 heatmap, while enlarging or redisplaying several retained figures.

R1.justification: Appendix A is largely unchanged. New Appendix G.1 positions locate-then-edit against weight-preserving/RAG approaches through internal-knowledge, retrieval-cost, and security arguments, adding Jin et al. (2024) and Upadhayay et al. (2024). The Levy et al. (2017) citation is removed.

T1.justification: The LogitLens information definition, causal-intervention equations and approximation, key-value assumptions, and IFMET optimization/update formulas are retained. The added evaluation metrics do not introduce new theoretical results or substantive mathematical revisions.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's lack of component ablations, validation beyond GPT-J, and assessment of editing side effects. The new experiments strengthen attribution of the gains and expose specificity and runtime costs. These benefits outweigh limited reporting defects, including Table 8's incorrect percentage-baseline caption and runtime ratios in Appendix G that disagree with Table 9.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IFMET study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across the substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds component ablations, LLaMA-2 evaluations, model-generated editing prompts, and editing-time measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-J mechanistic investigations, causal interventions, and IFMET knowledge-editing experiments on MQuAKE, including additional appendix results.

results.title: Locate-then-edit for Multi-hop Factual Recall under Knowledge Editing

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from VIRT with cognitive-science-inspired RIP and robotic gaze to VIP pre-training using sparse flows and progressive masking. The vision-over-text claim remains but is framed around current robotic-data diversity. v1's abstract claim of improving success from nearly zero to over 65% is dropped.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations concerning reliance on privileged flow information, pre-training/inference mismatch and world-model prediction failure. It attributes harmful small-data pre-training to domain overfitting and identifies Gaussian noise as the strongest tested disturbance. Baseline explanations also change: Diffusion Policy's data demands and VIRT's encoder representation replace much of v1's feature-compression and ambiguity discussion.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies 120K pre-training and 8K fine-tuning iterations, a 20-step horizon, 0.5 image-masking ratio, YOLOv10-small, and CoTracker sampling/filtering and masking procedures. Previously unstated budgets are disclosures, not established budget changes. Conversely, v1's stage-supervision, detector-freezing and appendix completion-step details are no longer provided.

E1.justification: Droid and the six real-robot/simulation tasks remain. v2 adds unseen brightness, Gaussian-noise and image-blur conditions on the simulated tasks (Section 4.3, Table 5), extending input-environment coverage without adding a dataset or core manipulation task.

E2.justification: ConvMLP, Diffusion Policy and ACT remain the external policy families. v2 Table 1 adds VIP-pretrained counterparts and no longer separately reports single-step ConvMLP. Table 2 also introduces a world-model-generated future-image instruction comparator. The evaluated alternatives change, but the main policy families remain stable.

E3.justification: v1 supplies CLIP-encoded text to comparison policies for instruction-following tasks; v2 supplies cropped-image instructions to every policy and evaluates each with and without VIP pre-training. Completion-score evaluation disappears. New protocols vary training-data fractions and introduce visual corruptions. Demonstration counts and 100 evaluation trials per policy/task remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's RG/enlargement/RIP/uncertainty ablation is replaced by instruction-source and backbone/uncertainty/image-mask studies on the three simulated tasks. v2 additionally studies data scaling, visual-corruption robustness, attention maps and world-model failures (Tables 2–5; Figures 1, 4 and 9). The original Open the Lid component ablation is absent.

E5.justification: Both versions report 100 evaluation trials per policy/task without training-seed information, confidence intervals or significance tests. Predicted Laplacian uncertainty concerns the model's loss and outputs, not statistical uncertainty reporting for experimental performance.

E6.justification: VIRT's reported Transport/Stack success rates change from 0.69/0.65 in v1 Table 2 to 0.74/0.68 in v2 Table 1; its three real-task rates remain 0.42/0.71/0.37. Many baseline scores are replaced, completion-score entries disappear, and new instruction, scaling and robustness outcomes are reported. Changed methods and settings prevent interpreting these as controlled cross-version gains.

M1.justification: v1's RIP predicts trajectories from endpoint observations using L1 loss. v2's VIP adds CoTracker-derived sparse motion flows, an MLP flow encoder and progressive flow masking, and applies uncertainty-weighted supervision during pre-training. VIRT also gains random image masking. These change the procedure despite retaining the 12-encoder/3-decoder architecture and cropped-object instructions.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten around VIP. Method subsections are reorganized, experimental setup becomes introductory paragraphs, and the evaluation narrative shifts toward pre-training effectiveness and instruction comparisons. Related work is condensed and the completion-score appendix is removed.

P2.justification: v2 adopts two columns, replaces the opening schematic with attention maps, redraws the pipeline and adds flow, world-model and disturbance figures. Existing platform/task figures are resized and rearranged. Real and simulated results are merged into a redesigned table, with additional analysis tables. An erroneous ICML formatting-instructions running header also appears.

R1.justification: v2 removes motor-imagery, gaze-anchoring and foveal-vision references supporting RIP/RG, while adding CoTracker, diffusion-image-generation and uncertainty references. The three related-work themes and principal positioning against text-conditioned robotic manipulation remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: v1's explicit MDP/demonstration-data formalization in Section 3.1 and completion-score definition i/k in Section 4.2 are removed. The Laplacian-loss formula is essentially retained, although its training role changes. Neither version contains theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's main comparisons confound policy differences with different instruction modalities. v2 gives every policy cropped-image instructions and adds within-policy pre-training controls (Table 1), while Table 2 compares instruction choices within VIRT. This substantially strengthens evidence for the central claims; scaling and robustness studies also expose failure conditions. Partial-completion reporting is lost, and the DINOv2 ablation changes backbone architecture as well as initialization, but these limitations do not outweigh the improved experimental controls.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe successive versions of the same robotic-manipulation work. Their text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison. v1 includes Appendix A.1; v2 ends with references and contains no appendix.

after.justification: v2 Tables 1–5 report original manipulation results, pre-training comparisons, instruction studies, ablations, data-scaling experiments and robustness tests.

before.justification: v1 Tables 1–3 report original real-robot and simulated manipulation results, including policy comparisons and component ablations.

results.title: VIP: Vision Instructed Pre-training for Robotic Manipulation

C1.justification: Both versions claim that logits-only L2H efficiently constructs hierarchies without fine-tuning, outperforms specialized hierarchical models, and supports interpretation of supervised classifiers. V2 foregrounds the critique more strongly but preserves these contributions. Its under-a-minute runtime wording was already stated in v1 Appendix A and supported by Table 2.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations concerning generality across backbones, robustness to misspecified K, normalized training loss as guidance for choosing K, and benefits of predicting at coarser taxonomy levels. The conclusion also introduces a concrete limitation: poorly calibrated logits may invalidate their use as a cluster-similarity proxy. These materially expand the applicability and limitations discussion beyond v1.

D1.justification: V2 documents the added taxonomy-level training and hierarchy-cutting procedure, the K sensitivity grid, and iTOL as the visualization tool. The existing implementation and baseline details remain largely unchanged. V1's separate statement advertising supplementary code disappears, although the complete Appendix A implementation is retained; this does not establish that external code availability changed.

E1.justification: V2 adds iNaturalist21, with 2.7 million natural-species images and evaluation across family, order, class, phylum, and kingdom labels. This substantially extends coverage to a taxonomy-based task testing predictions at multiple granularities. The four datasets used in v1 remain; ImageNet itself is not newly introduced.

E2.justification: The original Table 1 comparators remain. Appendix C adds the Lowe et al. (2024) UMAP-plus-Ward comparator, CLIP-based agglomerative and TreeVAE comparison variants, and separately trained flat TURTLE models for the taxonomy-level comparison (Tables 5, 6, and 8). These substantially broaden the alternatives evaluated against L2H.

E3.justification: The original benchmark splits and six evaluation metrics are retained. Added experimental designs include CLIP-input controls, fitting and evaluating the Lowe comparator on the test set, varying K from 85 to 115, and comparing a family-level hierarchy with separately trained models at coarser taxonomic levels. These are substantive new protocols, without evidence that the original experiments changed their settings.

E4.justification: V1's hierarchy visualizations and case studies are retained. V2 adds tests of dependence on foundation-model backbones using TCL, aggregation-function choice, sensitivity to over- and underestimated K, an alternative all-pairs merging strategy, and the benefit of hierarchical predictions over separately trained flat models (Tables 4 and 7-9; Figure 5). These address several previously untested assumptions and design choices.

E5.justification: V1 reports five-run comparison means and three-run runtime means without variability estimates. V2 adds runtime standard deviations over the same stated three runs, five-run standard-deviation bands in Figure 5, and statistical-indistinguishability markings in Table 8. However, Table 1 loses its five-run disclosure, and Table 8 specifies neither the statistical test nor its threshold. The change concerns reporting practices, not an established increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises values, including Food-101 leaf purity from 0.881 to 0.913 for L2H-TEMI and from 0.843 to 0.877 for L2H-TURTLE; Table 2 also revises runtimes. Tables 3-9 and Figure 5 add extensive results. The new iNaturalist findings are mixed: kingdom accuracy favors L2H-TURTLE, 0.734 versus 0.663, while class-level leaf purity favors standalone TURTLE, 0.827 versus 0.797.

M1.justification: The standard L2H procedure and Appendix A implementation remain unchanged. However, Appendix C introduces an alternative merging procedure that searches all group pairs instead of first selecting the lowest-scoring group (Table 9). This is a limited algorithmic variant evaluated as an ablation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental narrative, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting, with the critique of specialized models foregrounded and the contribution bullets reordered. Method explanations are repaired and clarified, and the end matter gains acknowledgements and an impact statement while losing the standalone reproducibility statement. These are broad language and narrative revisions beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout, with reformatted tables and repositioned figures. V2 adds Tables 3-9 and the multipanel sensitivity plot, enlarges retained appendix hierarchies, and stacks the final ImageNet visualizations vertically. Existing tree results are retained under new numbering, and their ImageNet captions are corrected.

R1.justification: V2 adds relevant citations for unseen-dataset clustering, hierarchical and hyperbolic representations, TCL, iNaturalist21, and iTOL, including Lowe, Khrulkov, Linderman, and Sinha. The central positioning against specialized deep hierarchical clustering remains. Publication and bibliographic updates to existing references do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: Appendix B.3 corrects both pair-set definitions from the impossible condition x_j != x_j to x_i != x_j. This repairs a mathematical error in the written definitions underlying DP and LHD. The remaining mathematical formulation is retained, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens weaknesses in v1's empirical support through CLIP-based comparison controls, a non-foundation-model backbone, and tests of aggregation, merging, and cluster-count choices. The iNaturalist experiment also directly examines the benefit of hierarchical predictions over separate flat models. Added variability reporting and the calibration limitation improve assessment of the evidence. Unspecified statistical tests in Table 8 and the lost Table 1 run-count disclosure are drawbacks, but the stronger controls and analyses provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same L2H research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A-C support reliable comparison, including matching retained content across layout changes and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds quantitative ImageNet results, iNaturalist21 experiments, additional comparisons, and ablations in Appendix C.

before.justification: V1 reports original clustering evaluations on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Food-101, runtime measurements, and an ImageNet hierarchy case study.

results.title: From Logits to Hierarchies: Hierarchical Clustering made Simple

C1.justification: V2's abstract adds the claim that KinDEL is the first public DEL dataset containing molecular docking poses and frames its contribution as encompassing both 2D and 3D structures. This expands the central resource claim beyond v1. The conclusion also qualifies the earlier drug-like characterization to many molecules having properties within approved-drug ranges.

C2.justification: V2 interprets cluster splits as offering limited additional difficulty, tentatively associates MAPK14 disynthon degradation with overfitting, and explains objections to scaffold splitting. It adds qualifications about preselection-normalization errors and kinase-only coverage while retaining the principal denoising interpretation and existing applicability limitations.

D1.justification: V2 adds Chemprop hyperparameters, clustering configuration and GPU/runtime information, BCA preparation and assay protocols, and detailed docking software, conformer, receptor and SDF specifications. It newly discloses sequencing depths and the cloning kit and corrects DDR1 gene labels. The existing repository link remains available in the text.

E1.justification: V2 extends experimental coverage beyond two kinases by adding Bovine Carbonic Anhydrase screening with replicate analysis (Section 4; Figure 7c). Appendix F also reports docking 234k ligand states against six kinase receptor models. The tabulated machine-learning affinity benchmarks still concern MAPK14 and DDR1.

E2.justification: Tables 1-2 newly evaluate Chemprop DMPNN against the existing methods, including within the retained random and disynthon comparisons. Counts, Poisson, RF, XGBoost, kNN, DNN, GIN and both DEL-Compose variants remain.

E3.justification: V2 adds a third evaluation split based on UMAP-reduced fingerprints, HDBSCAN clustering and whole-cluster assignment (Section 3.1; Appendix E). Appendix F introduces a specified multi-receptor docking protocol. The original top-1M training selection, random/disynthon protocols, affinity test-set sizes and Spearman metric remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds cluster-split generalization comparisons and an empirical scaffold-frequency analysis assessing the suitability of scaffold splitting (Appendix E; Figure 9). It also adds held-out affinity distributions, BCA replicate diagnostics and qualitative docking cases (Figures 7-10), substantially extending v1's supplementary analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five training runs per splitting strategy, report performance with ± values, and use triplicate DEL measurements. V2 extends these practices to additional results without introducing a new uncertainty-estimation procedure, significance test or changed run count for retained experiments.

E6.justification: All 28 pre-existing model/split rows in Tables 1-2 retain their numerical values. V2 adds Chemprop and cluster-split results, including MAPK14 cluster on-DNA correlation 0.713 ± 0.013 for Chemprop and off-DNA correlation 0.766 ± 0.012 for DEL-Compose(S). BCA replicate plots, scaffold statistics, affinity distributions and docking examples add further findings.

M1.justification: The retained predictive architectures, objectives and DEL-Compose variants remain unchanged in Section 3.2 and Appendix D. Chemprop is an added comparator; the new splitting and docking procedures extend evaluation and data generation without modifying these predictors.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the abstract and expands selected dataset, evaluation and discussion passages while retaining the main section order and much existing prose. It updates authorship, adds an Impact Statement and Appendices E-F, and removes the standalone Reproducibility Statement while retaining the repository reference elsewhere.

P2.justification: The main text changes to a two-column conference layout. V2 redraws synthesis/selection graphics, adds a data-schema panel, separates the UMAP and splitting diagrams, and expands the benchmark tables. New appendix displays include BCA replicates, affinity histograms, scaffold structures and docking poses.

R1.justification: Section 5.1 adds AIRCHECK (Wellnitz et al., 2024), contrasting its masked structures with KinDEL's representation. Additional citations support Chemprop, clustering and docking, and the abstract adds docking-related novelty positioning. The established related-work discussion remains largely intact.

T1.justification: No new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are introduced. The fluorescence-polarization and binding-curve equations in Appendix A remain mathematically equivalent; the new clustering and docking descriptions specify procedures rather than theoretical results.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens KinDEL's usefulness and reproducibility through a non-kinase screen with replicate diagnostics, documented 3D pose generation, and explicit implementation details. Chemprop comparisons, the additional split and scaffold diagnostics make the evaluation more informative and its design easier to assess. These gains extend beyond presentation, although the unchanged small affinity test sets and absence of BCA/3D predictive benchmarks still limit generalization claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KinDEL study and retain identifiable experiments on the same molecular library. Their text, tables, figures, equations and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial formatting changes.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds Chemprop and cluster-split evaluations, BCA screening replicate analyses, scaffold statistics and molecular docking outputs.

before.justification: V1 reports original MAPK14 and DDR1 screening data, on- and off-DNA biophysical measurements, model evaluations in Tables 1-2, and experimental replicate analyses in Appendix B.

results.title: KinDEL: DNA-Encoded Library Dataset for Kinase Inhibitors

C1.justification: The three central contributions—performance prediction through PMF, uncertainty-based active evaluation and sparse-data enhancements—are retained. v2's introduction additionally claims demonstrated generalization through expanding the matrix to new models and datasets, modestly broadening the stated contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations based on benchmark redundancy, shared architectures/training data, and differences between transfer to new models and new datasets. It interprets coreset and PMF predictions as complementary. The conclusion drops v1's cautions about uninformative high-uncertainty evaluations and identifying needed benchmarks; the existing zero-observation limitation is retained and promoted to the conclusion.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information with DMF/GCMC training configurations, exact prompts and decoding settings, coreset embedding/selection details, A100 timing measurements, additional model checkpoints, and new dataset counts and access links. These largely document added experiments rather than establish changes to existing implementations. The project's code-access information is retained.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original benchmark coverage and adds MathVision, EMMA, Video-MME and LongVideoBench, expanding mathematical/multimodal reasoning and video evaluation, including long-video understanding. Section 5.2 also introduces corrupted-image testing. These extend the represented tasks and input conditions beyond the original matrix.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's mean-based prediction baselines, v2 Table 10 evaluates Deep Matrix Factorization and Graph Convolutional Matrix Completion. Tables 4 and 14 additionally compare Random Selection, Herding and K-Center Greedy coreset predictors and their combinations with PMF. TinyBenchmarks' earlier citation alone did not constitute these comparisons.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 changes the reported active-evaluation design from initially masking 80% of scores to explicit 20% training, 60% acquisition-pool and 20% test partitions. Added protocols include observing 20% or 50% of new matrix blocks, ranking metrics, confidence-based prediction filtering, coreset sampling fractions and controlled prompt/decoding variations. The original NUTS sampling schedule is retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test Gaussian image noise, prompt changes, sampling temperatures and beam search; compare coreset fusion strategies and sampling fractions; and examine retaining only confident predictions. The earlier low-rank, profile, vision-encoder and zero-observation generalization analyses remain present, sometimes relocated to appendices.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 4 displays shaded ranges around its repeated-run curves, whereas v2 Figure 4 omits them. Their precise statistical meaning was not specified in v1. Both versions retain ten-seed averaging for active evaluation and enhancement experiments, and other error-bar displays remain.

E6.justification: v2 adds transfer, robustness, timing, ranking, neural-baseline and coreset results. For example, new Table 10 reports overall RMSE of 0.193 for PMF versus 0.225 for DMF at 20% masking. The original detailed PMF/PTF tables retain their numerical values. Figure 4 supplies replacement results under the revised protocol, while its MAE panel and Table 1's MAE entries are removed.

M1.justification: The Section 3 PMF/PTF framework remains unchanged. Sections 5.2–5.3 add bounded adaptations: representing evaluation settings through additional model rows or profiles, and combining PMF with coreset predictions through averaging or uncertainty-guided fusion. These change parts of the prediction procedure without replacing its core.

P1.justification: The introduction and related-work prose are revised, and the discussion is reorganized around predictability, varying evaluation settings and coreset integration. The original low-rank discussion moves to Appendix B; the appendices are reorganized into A–C with five experimental subsections. Publication information and an impact statement are also added.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main document to a two-column conference layout, redraws Figure 1, and restructures Figure 4 from three panels into two with different axes. Table 1 drops its MAE columns, numerous experimental tables are added, and existing analyses and figures are redistributed between the main text and appendices. The original heatmaps are retained.

R1.justification: Focused additions distinguish the work from Zhang et al. (2024c)'s concurrent LLM performance-prediction study and explicitly position it as complementary to coreset methods. References also expand to neural matrix completion, newer models/benchmarks and benchmark redundancy. The central positioning around PMF for efficient LVLM evaluation remains.

T1.justification: Appendix C.2 adds explicit top-K hit-rate definitions: Precision@K tests whether the predicted best model belongs to the true top K, while Recall@K tests whether the true best belongs to the predicted top K. The PMF/PTF likelihoods, priors, assumptions and profile equations remain mathematically unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps by explicitly separating acquisition from held-out testing and adding substantive matrix-completion comparisons. Transfer experiments and controlled setting perturbations substantially strengthen evidence about applicability beyond the original matrix. Reporting shortcomings remain: Figure 4 loses shaded ranges, and Table 13 leaves its two result blocks unlabeled. These limited drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger experimental validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PMF-based LVLM performance-prediction study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained content across substantial reformatting and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations involving newer models and benchmarks, alternative predictors, evaluation-setting perturbations, coreset combinations, ranking metrics and computational costs.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 108 LVLMs across 176 datasets, performance-prediction experiments, active evaluation, ablations and appendix generalization results.

results.title: Can We Predict Performance of Large Models across Vision-Language Tasks?

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds persistence similarity, pruning and consistent topology across models. v2 makes identification of four processing phases and quantitative discrimination between models and datasets central contributions, explicitly emphasizes the kNN-based zigzag framework, and recasts pruning as a showcase application.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 expands the mobile-versus-stationary interpretation into four phases linked to contextualization, stable relations, specialization and output preparation. It adds qualifications concerning last-token proxies and terminal-layer persistence, and discusses unexplained code and shuffling behavior. The earlier limitation concerning evaluation at only two pruning thresholds is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds the code-dataset source and execution details for the calendar example, including its prompt, token positions, k=2 and simplex dimension 3. Existing pseudocode, repository, computational libraries and hardware/runtime example are retained or relocated. The weighting exponent used for the pruning score remains unspecified.

E1.justification: Beyond retained SST and Pile coverage, v2 evaluates MATH and GitHub code, including five language subsets. It adds calendar-arithmetic prompts, shuffled SST inputs, and pruning evaluations on CMMLU, Commonsense-QA and WSC, substantially broadening domains and test scenarios.

E2.justification: The pruning comparators remain angular-distance pruning from Gromov et al. [6] and Block-Influence/ShortGPT from Men et al. [7], grouped as 'Other works.' The additional benchmarks use this same comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 specifies size-matched datasets of 8,000 prompts analyzed in 500-prompt subsets and changes the representative kNN setting from 5 to 4. It drops the aggressive condition selecting layers within 20% of peak similarity and the Llama2-13B pruning evaluation. New sliding-window experiments remove blocks of 5, 3 or 2 layers with corresponding strides of 2, 1 or 1; five-shot benchmark evaluation remains.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of weighting sensitivity, subset-size dependence, token-order disruption, code-language differences and calendar-token positions. Sliding-window layer ablations test the proposed connection between processing phases and performance. The existing kNN–Vietoris–Rips robustness analysis is retained in Appendix D, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1's descriptor curves lack sampling-variability bands. v2 reports means and standard deviations across 16 subsets of 500 prompts, or eight subsets of 1,000 for language-specific code analyses, and studies variance versus subset size. These quantify input-subset variability; pruning accuracies still lack reported uncertainty.

E6.justification: The surviving Table 1 scores exactly match v1's conservative-pruning results, while all aggressive-pruning entries and the Llama2-13B row disappear. New Table 3 adds benchmark scores, including Mistral CMMLU accuracy of 38.84 versus 29.68 for 'Other works.' New descriptor, calendar, shuffling and sliding-window findings substantially expand the results; revised topology plots should not be interpreted as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The kNN complexes, intersection filtration and FastZigZag pipeline remain. However, v2 Section 3.3 adds births' relative frequency and generalizes unweighted average persistence similarity to power-weighted inter-layer persistence. These expand the method's central analytical outputs beyond merely renaming the existing similarity measure.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion are substantially rewritten around processing phases. Method and experiment sections are reorganized, both algorithms move to appendices, and a separate interpretation subsection is introduced. Terminology changes throughout from persistence similarity and p-cycles to inter-layer persistence and p-dimensional holes.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the main similarity heatmaps and kNN-sweep display with weighted-descriptor plots and sliding-window accuracy plots. It redraws persistence images, introduces uncertainty shading, converts the pruning schematic into Table 2, simplifies Table 1, and adds calendar barcodes, model-difference panels, supplementary analyses and Table 3.

R1.justification: A new 'Distinguishing Transformer Stages' discussion substantially expands positioning relative to research on processing phases. Sections 3.2–3.3 also distinguish the method from prior kNN filtrations, spatiotemporal persistence, persistent clustering and generalized rank invariants, with additional citations supporting these comparisons.

T1.justification: The zigzag-module formulation and interval decomposition in Appendix A are retained. v2 adds definitions for birth frequency and power weighting, specifies the zero-Betti case, corrects the persistence index endpoint to 2(Nlayers−1), and states a computational-complexity bound in Appendix B. These are limited mathematical extensions and corrections, without a new proof.

improvement.justification: The controlled layer removals, shuffled-input test and calendar example provide substantially stronger evidence about what the descriptors capture than v1's broad similarity patterns alone. Subset uncertainty and size-sensitivity analyses address an important reliability gap. Lost aggressive-pruning and 13B comparisons, unspecified pruning weights, and inconsistent variance-scaling descriptions in Appendix E.4/Figure 12 are drawbacks, but the net improvement in empirical grounding is substantial. The four-phase explanation remains interpretive.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same zigzag-persistence study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original representation and pruning results and adds calendar-token experiments, shuffled-input tests, subset analyses, sliding-window ablations and additional benchmark results.

before.justification: v1 reports original measurements of LLM representations on SST and Pile, topology sensitivity analyses, and comparative pruning accuracies in Table 1.

results.title: Persistent Topological Features in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions add an isotropic-noise convergence regime for GaLore beyond v1's deterministic and large-batch regimes, with additional conditions formalized in Appendix C. This materially expands the answer to a central research question. The principal GoLore convergence claim and sparse-extension contribution are retained.

C2.justification: v2 refines the failure explanation around anisotropic noise, adds task-dependent switching guidance, and attributes importance sampling's weaker performance to residual projection bias. It also explains equal WinoGrande test accuracy through overfitting and extends the stated theoretical limitation to variants such as Fira. v1 provided the simpler noise-dominance explanation and the MSGD-versus-Adam limitation.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies quadratic-experiment batch sizes, FLORA's scaling factors, the OPT-13B training duration, and simulation/gradient-diagnostic details. Existing hardware disclosures, most retained hyperparameters, and the code link remain. OPT-13B's rank is ambiguous: Section 6 associates Table 2 with rank 4, while Appendix E describes reuse of a rank-1024 setup.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds a distinct synthetic scenario: Gaussian-noise matrix simulations assessing the leading property across three noise scales. C4, GLUE, WinoGrande, and BoolQ were already evaluated in v1. LLaMA-350M and OPT-13B extend model configurations on retained datasets rather than adding dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds FLORA to the GLUE comparison and evaluates importance sampling and Adam@40% against GoLore in the new LLaMA-350M comparison (Figure 12). These introduce substantive alternatives to the projection strategy. The full-parameter curve in v1's LLaMA-60M comparison is absent from v2 Figure 4, although the accompanying prose still lists full-parameter training.

E3.justification: LLaMA-60M pretraining changes from 10,000 to 30,000 iterations and from GoLore@20% to GoLore@50%. v2 adds LLaMA-350M and OPT-13B configurations, switching/frequency sweeps, and a gradient-error evaluation using 32 MRPC sequences; the 8-bit pretraining experiment is removed. The new WinoGrande accuracy column says 80 epochs while Appendix E specifies 30, leaving that evaluation budget unclear.

E4.justification: New Appendix F tests switching-point sensitivity, subspace-update frequency, singular-value-based importance sampling, and gradient approximation error on quadratic and MRPC tasks. Appendix C additionally tests the leading-property assumption under Gaussian noise. These substantially expand investigation of robustness and the proposed mechanism beyond v1's fixed-configuration demonstrations.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix C introduces Monte Carlo estimation of expected projection properties using 200,000 sampled matrices. This is a new statistical estimation procedure. LLM results remain without reported repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds FLORA's GLUE average of 84.72, OPT-13B BoolQ accuracies of 79.79 for GaLore and 81.96 for GoLore@30%, and WinoGrande accuracies of 68.51 for both GaLore and GoLore versus 69.85 for full-parameter training. It also adds simulation and ablation findings, replaces the C4 curves under changed settings, and removes the 8-bit results. Previously reported GLUE rows and LLaMA2-7B BoolQ scores are unchanged.

M1.justification: The core random projections, momentum transfer, hybrid training, and sparse variants are retained. Algorithm 1 changes Adam's bias-correction denominator from 1-beta_i^t to 1-(1-beta_i)^t. This is a local revision of the stated update; appendix Algorithms 2 and 6 retain the old expression, so a corresponding implementation change is not established.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: theoretical challenges move from Appendix A to Section 1.3, experiments precede algorithm connections, and the ReLoRA-like implementation moves from Appendix D to A. Main theorem statements are shortened by referring hyperparameter choices to the appendices. The introduction and related-work discussion are revised, and acknowledgements and an impact statement are added.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout and extensively rearranges displays.
