It adds a conceptual illustration, simulation and ablation figures, and an OPT-13B table; expands the GLUE and BoolQ tables; and removes the 8-bit figure. Figure 1 changes its vertical axis from loss to objective gap, while several retained displays are relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through LDAdam, Fira, APOLLO, noise-geometry research, zeroth-order optimization, and gradient sketching. It explicitly contrasts GoLore's assumptions with LDAdam's error-feedback analysis and narrows the first discrete-time convergence positioning from memory-efficient LLM training generally to GaLore-like algorithms under standard assumptions.

T1.justification: New Appendix C introduces isotropic-noise and leading-property assumptions, projection and momentum lemmas, and Theorem 18/Corollary 19 establishing conditional small-batch GaLore convergence. Gaussian validity of the leading property is supported empirically rather than proved. Existing large-batch GaLore and GaSare bounds also revise constants, including doubling the lower bound on the subspace-update period.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the practical hybrid method: Appendix F tests previously unexamined switching and projection choices, measures gradient error directly, and complements new comparator evidence. The conditional isotropic-noise analysis also sharpens the convergence discussion. These gains outweigh the lost 8-bit and full-parameter C4 comparisons, although conflicting rank/epoch descriptions and the additional leading-property assumption limit the precision and scope of the new conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GaLore/GoLore research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds Gaussian-noise simulations, OPT-13B results, and sensitivity and gradient-error analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original quadratic optimization experiments, C4 pretraining, and GLUE, WinoGrande, and BoolQ fine-tuning results, including appendix results.

results.title: Subspace Optimization for Large Language Models with Convergence Guarantees

C1.justification: The central claims of exact FRT type I error control and individualized conformal borrowing remain. V3 adds a prominent contribution claiming non-asymptotic guarantees for adaptive MSE-based threshold selection, while shifting emphasis away from presenting fixed and adaptive thresholds as parallel recommendations. Adaptive MSE selection itself was already proposed in v1.

C2.justification: V1 already explains power losses and borrowing trade-offs. V3 adds a rationale for optimizing MSE rather than family-wise error or false discovery rates, connects difficult-bias behavior to Hodges estimation and transferability detection, and explicitly discusses the absence of uniform improvement over RCT-only analysis. These refine existing interpretations rather than reverse them.

D1.justification: V1's clinical execution details—5,000 FRT iterations taking about 10 minutes on an eight-core MacBook—are omitted. The revised bootstrap algorithm specifies an input L without reporting its numerical value, whereas v1 specified 100 splitting repetitions. The intFRT repository disclosure and clinical preprocessing software information remain available; matching details move to Appendix D.

E1.justification: V3 changes the main simulated covariate population from two-dimensional normal covariates to uniform covariates on [-2, 2], and adds a five-dimensional correlated Gaussian scenario in Appendix C.6. The hybrid-trial task and CALGB 9633–NCDB clinical population remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The NB, FB, and ALSB point-estimator comparators are retained. ALSB newly participates in type I error and power comparisons using asymptotic inference, and v3 Figure 7 compares NB, ALSB, and CSB under asymptotic inference. V1 evaluated ALSB's estimation and selection performance but omitted its testing results. FB is also omitted from the corresponding fixed-threshold comparison plots in v3.

E3.justification: V3 adds an effect-size sweep for power curves at hidden-bias magnitudes 0 and 8 and introduces explicit asymptotic-versus-FRT evaluation protocols. The false-selection-rate metric reported in v1 is dropped. The principal sample sizes, 10-fold CV+, clinical preprocessing, and outcome definition remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds power-versus-effect-size curves, analyses comparing asymptotic inference with FRT, and robustness results for five dependent covariates. These substantially expand checks of power, calibration, and robustness. Conversely, v1's quantitative false-selection-rate analysis is removed, although selection scatterplots remain. Larger-EC-sample and fixed-threshold analyses were already present in v1.

E5.justification: V3 adds error bars to simulated type I error rates, including Figure 2 and appendix comparisons; v1 presents these rates without error bars. Their construction and coverage level are not explained. Both versions report 500 simulation replications and 5,000 FRT draws and provide asymptotic standard errors and confidence intervals for the clinical analysis.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes CSB's clinical estimate from 0.236 to 0.138, its confidence interval from (0.114, 0.359) to (0.024, 0.252), and its FRT p-value from 0.028 to 0.046. Selected controls change from 178 to 264 in the table, although v3's prose still says 178. Simulation results also change: the reported no-bias CSB power gain over NB rises from 38% to 45%, and new appendix results are added. Changed tuning and covariate generation prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The adaptive threshold algorithm changes substantially. V1 Section 3.2 estimates MSE through repeated two-fold splitting; v3 Section 3.3 and Algorithm 1 instead use the full-sample squared difference from the no-borrowing estimator, subtract its bootstrap-estimated variance, and add the borrowing estimator's bootstrap variance. The underlying FRT and four conformal variants remain; full conformal and jackknife+ move to Appendix A.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution narrative, method exposition, and discussion are extensively rewritten and compressed. Section 3 is reorganized around an estimator class and adaptive selection; full conformal and jackknife+ move to a new appendix section. Clinical matching details also move, and separate Software and Data and Impact Statement sections are introduced.

P2.justification: The manuscript changes from a spacious single-column format to a two-column conference main text. Figures are substantially recomposed: Figure 1 loses the CSB histogram row, performance and selection plots are merged, threshold boxplots are removed while histograms remain, and new comparison figures appear. Simulation axes and error-bar displays change, and the relocated clinical selection plot gains a shaded quantile-regression region.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands the literature coverage and positioning around test-then-pool methods, Bayesian borrowing, control variates, and bias modeling. It adds connections to causal model selection, Hodges estimation, transferability costs, and regulatory guidance. Examples include Li et al. (2020), Schmidli et al. (2014), Rothenhäusler (2020), and Cai et al. (2024). The Gao ALSB citation's publication update is not a new comparator.

T1.justification: V3 adds Theorems 3.4 and 3.5, establishing uniform MSE-estimation error and oracle excess squared-error bounds under sub-Gaussian assumptions, with proofs in Appendices B.7–B.8. V1 has no corresponding adaptive-selection guarantees. V3 also tightens the model-correctness condition used to infer the full-borrowing variance advantage. Earlier FRT and conformal results are largely retained.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the previously unanalysed adaptive-selection component through an explicit revised criterion and non-asymptotic guarantees in Theorems 3.4–3.5. Added inference-calibration comparisons and correlated-covariate tests also better establish where the approach works and fails. These gains outweigh the loss of false-selection-rate diagnostics and some reproducibility details. However, undefined simulation error bars and the unresolved 264-versus-178 clinical control-count discrepancy remain material weaknesses. The improvement rests on stronger justification and validation, not higher reported performance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FRT and Conformal Selective Borrowing study, with matching authors, clinical application, and substantial retained material. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: V3 reports revised simulations, additional empirical analyses in Appendix C, and the CALGB 9633–NCDB clinical analysis.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations and an analysis combining CALGB 9633 trial data with NCDB external controls, including additional simulation results in Appendix B.

results.title:
Enhancing Statistical Validity and Power in Hybrid Controlled Trials: A
  Randomization Inference Approach with Conformal Selective Borrowing

C1.justification: The abstract and central claim that FLU improves robust editing/unlearning remain unchanged. The contribution summary shifts emphasis toward editing and explicitly claims that latent representations reflect the desired replacement answer, extending v1's claim that less original information remains recoverable.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies what its robustness tests establish: whole-sport relearning is described as invalid because facts are dependent, and held-out CounterFact relearning is too weak to distinguish methods reliably. It acknowledges difficulties averaging probes across unequal layer counts, discusses competitive Gemma-2 baselines and limited soft-prompt effectiveness, and interprets sequential editing as potentially beneficial. v1 presents its related relearning experiments primarily as positive robustness evidence.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix A.6 adds sweep ranges, a selection objective, hyperparameter-sharing rules, model/task-specific learning rates and loss coefficients, and an 8-bit optimizer disclosure. Appendix A.2 provides an explicit CounterFact localization threshold. However, v1's ordinary 80/20 split specification and detailed weight-masking optimizer, learning-rate, batching and regularization settings are omitted.

E1.justification: Sports Facts and CounterFact remain the datasets, but v2 adds sequential editing and adaptive soft-prompt recovery scenarios. It extends whole-sport replacement from basketball to baseball and football, while dropping v1's separate athlete-subset unlearning experiment (Table 5). Whole-sport editing itself already appeared in v1 Appendix A.1 and is not wholly new.

E2.justification: The six-localization comparison expands to nine with Causal Tracing MLPs, Attribution Patching MLPs and Random MLPs. These controls are actually evaluated in v2's appendix comparisons, substantially strengthening the comparison of mechanistic selection against simply restricting updates to MLPs. Manual interpretability is renamed FLU; the existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: v2 evaluates three models across both datasets, adds 64-fact settings, changes athlete-edit targets from golf to randomly selected incorrect sports, and introduces hyperparameter tuning. Relearning changes from rank-64 LoRA on two athletes or all CounterFact forget facts to rank-512 LoRA with separate training and evaluation halves. Probe training and scoring change, edited-answer metrics are added, and sequential editing uses 100 total training steps versus 50 for batch editing.

E4.justification: v2 adds OT attribution profiles, learning-rate and loss-coefficient sensitivity analyses, adaptive soft-prompt attacks, and model-specific probes measuring both original and edited answers (Appendices A.3, A.6–A.8). The earlier sports attention-head ablation displays disappear. Much of v1's weight-masking analysis is retained in Appendix A.4 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix A.8 newly states that soft-prompt evaluations are averaged over four prompts, adding limited information about evaluation repetition and aggregation. This does not establish independent seeded training runs. Neither version provides confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests for its main comparisons.

E6.justification: v2 adds or replaces extensive results for edited-answer accuracy, sequential editing, expanded models, probing and soft-prompt attacks. Under its revised relearning protocol, Figure 6 reports final forget accuracies of 0.199 for FLU, 0.469 for Causal Tracing and 0.631 for Causal Tracing MLPs; these are not same-setting comparisons with v1. Conversely, v1 Table 1 and mechanism-weight Tables 6–7 retain their numerical entries as v2 Tables 1–3.

M1.justification: The proposed editor still localizes fact-lookup MLPs and restricts fine-tuning to them using injection, retention and Pile losses. Unlearning and weight masking remain in the appendices. The expanded probe/path-patching explanation elaborates v1 Appendix A.2; sequential editing repeatedly applies the existing editor rather than introducing a new component.

P1.justification: The methods and evaluation narrative are extensively rewritten around explicitly named editing tasks and revised metric terminology. Localization explanations expand, manual interpretability becomes FLU, and unlearning and the detailed weight-masking discussion move into a reorganized appendix. These changes substantially restructure the exposition despite the retained title and abstract.

P2.justification: Main results shift from accuracy tables and relearning trajectories to radar charts, grouped metric bars and before/after relearning bars. v2 adds multi-model probing and attribution panels, soft-prompt figures and tuning tables. Existing weight-masking displays move to Appendix A.4; Figure 1 and several tables and plots are retained despite renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of residual-knowledge tracing, representation engineering, circuit breakers and tamper-resistant safeguards, plus references for path patching and soft prompting. The book-unlearning and inserted-unlearning-layer discussion disappears. The central positioning against Hase et al.'s critique of localization remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The component-graph and importance-threshold formulation and the editing, unlearning and masking losses remain substantively equivalent. There are no added or removed theorems, proofs or substantive derivations. Expanded path-patching explanations and standard accuracy/error definitions concern exposition and evaluation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical case through MLP-only controls, evaluation across models, explicit measurement of successful replacement answers, and held-out relearning. These address important ambiguities in v1's evidence for robust editing. Tuning documentation and qualifications about weak robustness tests further improve assessability. Some earlier reproducibility details are lost, and sequential comparisons use unequal training budgets, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger validation of the central contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. The revisions can be matched reliably, including relocated unlearning and weight-masking results.

after.justification: v2 reports original editing comparisons, held-out relearning, probing, hyperparameter sweeps and soft-prompt attacks throughout the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning, unlearning/editing, relearning, probing and weight-masking experiments on Sports Facts and CounterFact in Section 3 and Appendix A.

results.title:
Mechanistic Unlearning: Robust Knowledge Unlearning and Editing via
  Mechanistic Localization

C1.justification: v2 explicitly frames POROver as targeting already highly safe but overrefusing models and claims that no existing post-training method specifically targets this setting. The three central contributions concerning general-purpose overgeneration, toxic-prompt overgeneration and preference optimization remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of unconditional compliance at zero toxic preference data, low usefulness at the opposite threshold extreme and diminishing returns from additional safety data. Limitations shift from a single student family/size to unresolved scaling near teacher size and language/domain transfer. It also newly interprets POROver as preserving adversarial robustness, although Table 6 shows increased GCG and PAIR attack success.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly specifies ten epochs, 40 warm-up steps, checkpoint-selection rules, evaluation frequency and GPU hours; additional model-specific decoding and generation settings are documented. These disclosures do not establish changes to earlier runs. Conversely, v2 omits v1's selected threshold of 0.01, its 2,013-plus-166 preference-sample breakdown and several exact checkpoint links. The code/data access link remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Section 3.3.4 adds JailBreakBench with 100 prompts evaluated under GCG, PAIR and hand-crafted JBC attacks, substantially extending coverage to adversarial input conditions. The original training datasets and capability, safety and overrefusal benchmarks remain represented.

E2.justification: The GPT-3/GPT-3.5 baselines and random, DeBERTa, ArmoRM and Llama Guard 2 selection comparisons remain. New experiments reuse these comparator sets. Llama-3-70B is an alternative teacher configuration, while GCG, PAIR and JBC are attack conditions; no new competing alignment method is evaluated.

E3.justification: The experimental design expands from Phi-3-7B to five students, adding Llama-3.1-8B, Falcon-3-7B and Llama-3.2-3B/11B, plus a Llama-3-70B teacher configuration. New protocols include transferred Vicuna attack artifacts, attack-success-rate evaluation and an ASD grid adding 5,000 and 10,000 examples. The retained Phi-3 decoding settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds adversarial robustness tests, student/teacher generalization checks, finer safety-data saturation analysis in Section 4.3 and qualitative threshold-sensitivity findings in Section 4.2. Figures 7–8 add teacher-response case comparisons. The original human-versus-automatic annotation analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report means with standard errors and error bars. Neither specifies repeated-training run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures. The expanded results do not establish a changed statistical estimation practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for new students, the open-weight teacher and jailbreak attacks. Its headline OR-Bench F1 comparison changes from Phi-3's 70.81 to 88.33 to Llama-3.1-8B's 74.39 to 91.78, using different student and selection settings. Retained Phi-3 safety results match Table 7 and Figures 10–11, but its AlpacaEval results and additional-benchmark results from v1 Figure 4 are omitted.

M1.justification: The overgeneration, rejection sampling, preference-pair construction, containment-threshold rule and DPO procedure remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 formalize previously described steps; additional teacher and student configurations reuse the existing procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, results and limitations undergo substantial rewriting. Llama-3.1-8B becomes the main experimental narrative, retained Phi-3 results move to Appendix D, limitations move to Appendix A, and the supplementary narrative is reorganized by evaluation and model.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column layout to a two-column conference format. It adds algorithm blocks, response-comparison figures, a saturation plot and numerous model-specific and adversarial displays. Retained Phi-3 figures are relocated, its results table loses the AlpacaEval column, and the main capability table is restructured.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 positions POROver explicitly as complementary to traditional safety alignment. v2 adds references supporting the new models, jailbreak evaluations and reward-model choices, including RewardBench and OpenAssistant, while removing several reinforcement-learning references such as Dai, Kundu and Pang. The overall research positioning remains recognizable.

T1.justification: The Llama Guard 2 score-normalization equation and preference-selection mathematics are unchanged. The new pseudocode restates existing procedures; neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's explicit single-family/single-size evidence gap through multiple student families and sizes, an open-weight teacher and adversarial evaluation. Added sensitivity analyses and training details strengthen validation and reproducibility. Qualifications include omitted Phi-3 results and preference-data details, plus overstated robustness preservation: Table 6's GCG and PAIR attack success rises from 0.08 to 0.13 and 0.16 to 0.22 after POROver. These weaknesses temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same POROver research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained experiments can be matched despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: The main results and Appendix D report original experiments across multiple students, teachers and adversarial attacks, alongside retained Phi-3 results.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.2 and Appendix C report original Phi-3 finetuning, preference-optimization and human-annotation results.

results.title: POROver: Improving Safety and Reducing Overrefusal in Large Language Models with Overgeneration and Preference Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the claims of KG-grounded zero-hallucination reasoning, complementary specialized/general LLMs, state-of-the-art KGQA performance and transfer to unseen KGs. Additional evidence does not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: New Appendices F.5 and G explicitly acknowledge that KG-valid paths can be irrelevant and that incomplete or incorrect KGs undermine answer correctness. They explain concrete failures and computational limits for longer paths. This substantially qualifies v1's predominantly successful-case discussion and brief medical-domain limitation.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds CPU/memory specifications and construction-stack details, including Virtuoso SPARQL, Pickle, spaCy, ColBERTv2, the tokenizer and MARISA Trie. Figure 8 supplies the new coherence-evaluation prompt. Existing training hyperparameters and resource measurements are retained, although the coherence judge model and sample size remain unspecified.

E1.justification: v2 adds zero-shot evaluation on 100 FreebaseQA questions, extending question coverage on the existing Freebase KG. WebQSP, CWQ, CSQA and MedQA remain; the addition does not introduce a new KG domain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds UniKGQA, reporting WebQSP Hit/F1 of 77.2/72.2 and CWQ Hit/F1 of 51.2/49.1. Existing comparator sets are otherwise retained. Newly discussed methods in Appendix A are not additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 1–5 LLM scoring protocol for logical coherence and construction-efficiency evaluations across path lengths, pipeline stages and 1/4/10/20 processing threads. It also introduces answer-count and reasoning-hop breakdowns. The original QA splits, training recipe and main L=2, K=10 settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component, model, constraint and parameter studies, Appendices B and F.2–F.5 add construction-overhead and parallel-scaling analyses, multi-answer and multi-hop comparisons with RoG, logical-coherence evaluation and failure cases involving irrelevant paths and incomplete KGs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added mean timings and coherence score do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Main GCR benchmark scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds FreebaseQA scores, construction timings, stratified F1 results, failure examples and a mean coherence score of 3.9/5. Table 4 also changes the Llama-3.1-70B general-LLM Hit/F1 from 90.24/71.19 to 89.85/71.47 under the same reported setting.

M1.justification: The BFS-to-KG-Trie construction, constrained decoder, fine-tuning objective and beam-search/general-LLM aggregation remain unchanged. Appendix B elaborates optional construction, caching and deployment strategies without establishing a revised evaluated GCR algorithm.

P1.justification: Most original main-text prose and section order are retained. v2 adds localized clarifications, organizes the expanded appendix into lettered sections, and updates authorship, affiliations and acknowledgments while adding an Impact Statement. The scientific additions do not amount to a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column format to an ICML two-column layout, extensively resizing and relocating displays. v2 adds a cache schematic, evaluation-prompt figure and construction, subgroup and failure-case tables, and extends Table 6 with FreebaseQA. Existing parameter-analysis plots are retained.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands the prior-work discussion with GFM-RAG, Plan-on-Graph, Debate on Graph, SymAgent and temporal-KG research. The retrieval-versus-agent framing remains, but positioning now covers additional graph models, planning approaches and methods addressing KG incompleteness.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2.1 adds construction-complexity reasoning: O(E^L) time and O(E^L × T) space, with E denoting average edges per entity and T tokens per path. The original probabilistic formulations and training objective are retained; no substantial new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves assessment of the central efficiency and faithfulness claims. Where v1 lacked construction-cost accounting and explicit treatment of KG-grounded failures, v2 provides stage timings, failure evidence and clear limitations concerning incorrect, incomplete or irrelevant KG information. These address important applicability and interpretation gaps. Broad headline claims and the underspecified coherence evaluation remain weaknesses, but the added evidence and qualifications provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GCR research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds construction-efficiency measurements, FreebaseQA results, stratified evaluations and logical-coherence assessment.

before.justification: v1 reports original GCR benchmark results, efficiency measurements, ablations, parameter analyses and zero-shot transfer experiments.

results.title: Graph-constrained Reasoning: Faithful Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs with Large Language Models

C1.justification: The principal contributions remain global TC rainfall forecasting, ARP-based change awareness, multimodal conditioning with NWP information, and claimed superiority over competing forecasts. v2 explicitly describes forecasting around an existing TC or given track location, consistent with v1's TC-centered task definition.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for Persistence's strength under a moving TC-centered window, interprets spectral agreement as capturing TC-scale structure, and attributes weaker phase/intensity performance to irregular cloud structures and rainfall-intensity variability. It also discusses stochastic samples as forecast uncertainty, hypothesizes why FuXi struggles, and qualifies usefulness when NWP forecast inputs are unavailable.

D1.justification: Appendices A–C supply detailed variable and pressure-level lists, split-selection information, denoising steps N=200, network depth K=4, noise settings, hardware/software versions, timing, and metric calculations. v2 states that code has been released at a repository, replacing v1's future-release promise; the earlier data-release commitment is absent. These are documentation and access-information changes, without evidence that existing training settings changed.

E1.justification: Both versions use MSWEP, ERA5, and IBTrACS data for the same global TC-centered, 10-degree rainfall forecasting task, covering 1980–2020 and predicting 12 hours at three-hour intervals. The new 2020 subset, phase/intensity breakdowns, and case visualizations remain within this coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains Persistence, U-Net, PreDiff, and NowcastNet. v2 adds ERA5-IFS alongside ECMWF-IFS in Table 2 and introduces FuXi in Appendix D.6/Table 6. These materially broaden comparisons to the input forecast system itself and a learned global weather model.

E3.justification: The reported main evaluation changes from repeated selections of half the test set to stochastic predictions across the full test set. Added evaluation protocols include RAPSD diagnostics, separate lead-time scores, timing comparisons, and a FuXi comparison using 349 samples from 2020 at 6–12-hour leads. The stated dataset split counts and six-hour NWP alignment remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original component ablation remains, while v2 adds substantial analyses of spatial fidelity through RAPSD, lead-time-dependent skill and rainfall distributions, and errors across cyclone lifecycle phases and intensities. Figures 9 and 13 additionally examine eight stochastic predictions and an Olivia case against NWP forecasts.

E5.justification: v1 averages ten random half-test-set evaluations without reporting dispersion. v2 describes eight independent diffusion-noise predictions per test case and reports individual scores, means, and standard deviations in Table 5. This changes the estimation procedure and introduces explicit uncertainty reporting; the eight predictions are inference samples, not separate training runs.

E6.justification: Table 1's TCP-Diffusion ETS-6/24/60 and TPMAE values change from 0.43766/0.14971/0.00742/0.42582 to 0.43788/0.14703/0.00644/0.42344, while comparator values and rankings remain unchanged. Tables 2–3 also revise TCP-Diffusion scores. Numerous new runtime, FuXi, spectral, lead-time, stochastic-sample, and cyclone-stratified results substantially expand the evidence. Changed sampling limits direct performance comparisons between versions.

M1.justification: The ARP targets, rainfall reconstruction, conditional EA-3DUNet, historical encoders, ResNet-18 forecast encoder, and denoising objective remain unchanged. New pseudocode and expanded input and hyperparameter descriptions document the existing method; they do not establish an implemented algorithm or architecture change.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes existing material: model design precedes dataset discussion, detailed data descriptions and 3DUNet equations move into appendices, and evaluation methods and results receive separate sections. The abstract and introduction are revised, training/inference pseudocode is added, and structured appendices integrate technical explanations and extended analyses.

P2.justification: Figure 1 expands into a fixed-versus-moving forecast-window explanation, and Figure 2 is redrawn with explicit denoising, network, and reconstruction panels. New input visualizations, spectral and lead-time plots, sample grids, case comparisons, and Tables 4–8 substantially expand the visual presentation. Table 2 gains an ERA5-IFS row, and the document adopts a different conference layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds context from diffusion-based climate emulation, TC forecasting, FuXi, and residual prediction in global weather models, including Price, Nguyen, Oskarsson, and Hu. It removes the Hersbach ERA5 reference. These additions refine the surrounding literature while retaining the original central novelty positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 newly specifies beta_s = 1 - cos(pi*s/(N-1)) and sigma_s = sqrt(beta_s), where v1 left these generic. This is a limited mathematical specification; as written, the schedule exceeds the stated beta_s range of (0,1). The principal equations remain unchanged, including Equations 12–14 moved to Appendix B.3. Appendix C explains existing metrics without adding theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses the supplied v1's limited implementation documentation, absent dispersion reporting, and narrow diagnostic analysis. Appendices A–D and the added comparisons make the method easier to assess and reveal performance weaknesses across cyclone phases and intensities. These gains outweigh remaining reporting problems, including the newly specified noise schedule's conflict with the stated variance range, which limits direct reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TCP-Diffusion work, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures. v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–D. Supplementary material mentioned but not included in v1 cannot establish what was previously documented outside the supplied PDF.

after.justification: v2 retains original forecasting experiments and adds repeated stochastic predictions, runtime comparisons, spectral diagnostics, FuXi comparisons, and cyclone phase and intensity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original TC rainfall forecasting experiments, comparisons with DL and NWP methods, component ablations, and qualitative predictions in Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–4.

results.title: TCP-Diffusion: A Multi-modal Diffusion Model for Global Tropical Cyclone Precipitation Forecasting with Change Awareness

C1.justification: The central claims remain consistent estimation of arbitrary PD functions, linear sample-size scaling for moderately deep trees, recovery of SHAP and functional decompositions, and possible inconsistency of path-dependent TreeSHAP. The expanded experiments support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's existing memory and extrapolation caveats, v2 explains finite-sample TreeSHAP-path error through reduced effective sample size and interprets high-correlation failures to recover ground truth. It adds guidance on checking background-sample adequacy, truncating higher-order interactions, and supplementing exploratory ground-truth explanations with semiparametric or doubly robust estimators.

D1.justification: v2 documents Rcpp bindings, pltreeshap and the VanillaPD implementation, plus Adult preprocessing, selected hyperparameters, benchmark configurations and multiclass explanation targets. Code-access instructions change from the explicit simulation-repository URL to the existing glex package and a named attached codeforsimulations repository; this does not establish newly available code.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic Gaussian regression settings only. v2 adds 35 OpenML-CTR23 regression datasets and 61 OpenML-CC18 classification datasets, including a dedicated Adult analysis. Additional simulations cover different correlations and eight-covariate inputs.

E2.justification: The reported runtime comparison expands from FastPD and TreeSHAP-int in v1 Figure 3 to five methods in v2 Figure 4, adding VanillaPD, Zern et al. (2023) and TreeSHAP-path. Zern was previously discussed theoretically but not included in the runtime results.

E3.justification: New benchmark protocols introduce 100-setting cross-validation searches, component-importance and relative-discrepancy metrics, and multiclass score aggregation; Adult uses a separate 25-trial tuning protocol. The illustrative SHAP plots also change from selecting FastPD's median-MSE run for both methods to selecting each method's own median run. Existing main simulation tuning was already documented in v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds correlation sensitivity analyses in Figures 7–10, including uncorrelated and strongly correlated inputs, eight-covariate experiments, and comparisons between fitted-model and ground-truth components. The Adult age–relationship interaction case study adds an application-level examination of conflicting explanations. These analyses are absent from v1.

E5.justification: v1's runtime figure reports medians over 100 runs and mentions 95% confidence bands; v2 reports means over 100 runs and drops that confidence-band statement. New Figure 10 specifies 150 runs. This does not establish an increase in repetitions for the retained main experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive attribution results: discrepancies exceeding 30% occur in 33, 18 and 9 of 96 datasets for Friedman-path, FastPD-50 and FastPD-100, respectively, matching the non-intercept appendix entries. It also adds correlation findings and replaces runtime results, reporting 1.26 seconds for both FastPD and Zern at 8000 points. Changed implementation descriptions, timed outputs and summary statistics preclude treating the runtime revision as a clean same-setting speedup.

M1.justification: FastPD retains the same tree augmentation, empirical leaf probabilities, evaluation traversal and caching procedure. Revised pseudocode makes inputs, outputs and previously described caching more explicit; it does not establish a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the introduction and algorithm exposition, reorganizes motivation and complexity explanations, and converts the simulation paragraphs into numbered subsections. Separate real-data sections and appendix material reshape the narrative, beyond merely adding result entries.

P2.justification: v2 adds an augmentation diagram, an Adult interaction figure, four supplementary sensitivity figures and extensive color-coded benchmark tables. The runtime figure changes from a two-method linear-scale plot to a five-method log-log plot with slopes and numerical summaries. Algorithms and several existing plots are also reformatted.

R1.justification: Targeted additions include FastSHAP, further functional-ANOVA connections, and references supporting doubly robust estimation and ALE. SHAP-definition attribution changes from Lundberg and Lee (2017) to Strumbelj and Kononenko (2010). These broaden context without fundamentally changing FastPD's positioning relative to existing tree-based methods.

T1.justification: The two propositions and Appendix B proofs are retained. v2 introduces the component-importance definition in Equation (10). Its rewritten SHAP definition in Equation (5) omits the 1/d normalization required for inverse-binomial weights, unlike v1's factorial formula and the retained two-feature proof. This introduces a localized mathematical error.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's validation through real-data attribution comparisons, runtime evaluation against the efficient Zern method, and sensitivity analyses exposing model-versus-ground-truth limitations. These substantially strengthen the evidence for practical applicability and clarify its boundaries. The gains are tempered by the missing SHAP normalization in Equation (5), inconsistent simulation references in Appendix A, and reduced runtime uncertainty reporting, but the retained FastPD derivation and proofs together with the broader validation support a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FastPD research, with matching algorithms, propositions and proofs. Their main text, figures, tables and appendices provide sufficient material for a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original simulations, additional correlation experiments, regression and classification benchmarks, and an Adult dataset case study, including extensive appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations of SHAP estimation error, runtime and functional-component recovery in Figures 1–4 and Appendix A.

results.title: Fast Estimation of Partial Dependence Functions using Trees

C1.justification: The abstract and discussion extend the claimed performance benefit from 17 to 19 SR methods, with the real-data claim changing from 16/17 to 18/19. The central contributions—nonparametric prescreening for scalable SR and high-dimensional benchmark construction—remain the same.

C2.justification: V2 explains the relevance of class imbalance to clustering choice and interprets the new robustness tests. The discussion newly acknowledges physical inconsistencies in the Feynman benchmark and describes complementary refinements from Matsubara et al. The existing cautions about low-SNR screening failures and noise-sensitive SR remain.

D1.justification: The stated repository changes from Scalable_SR to PAN_SR. Appendix B clarifies sampling and the sample variance used to set response noise, while Appendix D supplies RF tuning information and a scikit-learn version for the clustering ablation. Existing BART hyperparameters, hardware and reproduction commands are largely retained.

E1.justification: The 35 PMLB and 100 extended Feynman problems remain. Appendix D.4 adds Friedman-based variable-selection tests with predictor noise, a redundant feature x6 = x1 + x2, and correlated predictors. This is a bounded extension of the represented input conditions.

E2.justification: Figures 1–2 add DySymNet and TPSR to the 17 existing SR methods. Appendix D.2 adds PySR's random-forest selector to the three BART selector alternatives and introduces BART-G.SE+Operon in the downstream comparison with VIP Rank+Operon and standalone Operon. These substantially broaden the directly evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: The original splits, metrics, evaluation budgets and sample-size/SNR grid remain. New protocols include five-fold cross-validation over k = 1–20 for RF selection and controlled Friedman scenarios with n = 1000, p = 100 and SNR = 10, specified predictor-noise variance, and correlation structure.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's noise/sample-size sensitivity and ranking analyses, v2 adds downstream replacement of VIP Rank by BART-G.SE, a ten-algorithm clustering ablation, and noisy/redundant/correlated-predictor tests in Appendices D.2–D.4. These directly examine component choices and input assumptions that v1 did not test.

E5.justification: Appendix D.4 newly specifies 100 trials per Friedman scenario. Both versions retain ten seeded trials for the original benchmarks and 95% confidence intervals. V2 also explicitly identifies the confidence intervals in the retained Operon appendix plots; it does not report increasing repetitions of the original experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds results for the new comparators, clustering ablations, predictor scenarios and the Operon solution-rate grid. New Table 3 reports R2 values of 0.892, 0.860 and 0.846 for VIP+SR, GSE+SR and standalone SR at n = 500 and SNR = 20. Table 4 reports 100% TPR across four scenarios, with FPR ranging from 10.58% to 26.42%.

M1.justification: Both versions average VIP rankings from 20 independent BART fits, apply Euclidean average-linkage hierarchical clustering, and retain the low-mean cluster before SR. These details already appear in v1 Supplementary Section 3.2; v2's expanded explanation and ablations do not establish a changed proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction, method explanation, results narrative and discussion undergo substantial rewriting. Section 4 gains a detailed BART/VIP explanation and worked example. The separate supplement is reorganized into integrated Appendices A–D, with ranking visualization separated from selector comparisons and new analysis subsections.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and extensively redraws and rearranges plots, including colors, legends and panel arrangements. It adds Tables 3–4 and clustering and solution-rate figures, expands comparator displays, and splits v1's supplementary Figure 5 into Figures 11–12.

R1.justification: V2 expands positioning against PySR's RF prescreening and Matsubara et al.'s benchmark. It adds references including Chipman et al., DySymNet, Friedman and materials applications, while removing the Rockova–van der Pas and Luo–Li citations. The central positioning as an extension of SRBench to high-dimensional SR remains.

T1.justification: After matching v1's q0 to v2's p0, Section 4 corrects the irrelevant-feature rank support from {p0, ..., p} to {p0 + 1, ..., p}, changing its expected mean from (p0 + p)/2 to (p0 + 1 + p)/2. This is a limited mathematical correction; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central design choices: RF and downstream BART-G.SE comparisons test the selector's value, and the clustering ablation supports choosing hierarchical clustering. Predictor-robustness tests address assumptions untested in v1, while the expanded explanation and benchmark limitations improve assessability. The Friedman evidence remains limited to screening on one function, and Table 1 retains unchanged comparison totals despite added methods, but these reporting limitations are outweighed by the stronger empirical justification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PAN+SR work and retain matching methods and core benchmarks. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix D retain original benchmarking results and add comparator evaluations, clustering ablations and predictor-robustness simulations.

before.justification: Section 6 and Supplementary Section 4 report original benchmarking and variable-selection experiments on PMLB and extended Feynman datasets.

results.title: Ab Initio Nonparametric Variable Selection for Scalable Symbolic Regression with Large $p$

C1.justification: The single-model arbitrary-conditioning claim remains, but the stated contributions change substantially. v2 removes irregular-data handling from the abstract and contribution list, claims stabilization through zero regularization, and adds comparative claims about completion accuracy, uncertainty calibration and generation quality comparable to unconditional diffusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking zero-target regularization to stability and conditional training to completion quality. It interprets MFD comparisons as preserving unconditional generation quality and discusses masking sensitivity. Appendix D also qualifies efficiency claims: cheap epochs do not eliminate the larger training budget or higher total training time than FNO and DON.

D1.justification: v2 provides an ACM-FD code-release link and documents the summed pointwise/whole-function masking losses, Simformer's DDPM and linear-attention adaptations, its tuning ranges, diffusion-reaction data preparation, and A100 hardware and training/runtime details. v1's irregular-data sampling and interpolation instructions are removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds PDEBench diffusion-reaction data with four prediction mappings and half-domain function completion on Darcy Flow and Convection Diffusion. Conversely, v1's irregularly sampled prediction and generation scenarios disappear. Regular-grid coverage of the original three systems remains.

E2.justification: v2 adds an adapted Simformer for prediction and calibration, unconditional MFD for generation and ablations, and MFD-Inpaint plus interpolation for completion. The original operator baselines and beta-VAE remain in the retained comparisons; PODDON is relocated to Appendix Table 5 rather than removed.

E3.justification: New protocols include observing one domain half and completing the other, evaluating empirical coverage at three confidence levels across eight tasks, and timing computation with and without Kronecker structure. Runtime comparisons aggregate neural-operator training across tasks. The original 1,000/100/200 training/validation/test split and 64-by-64 regular grids are retained.

E4.justification: v1 has no component ablation suite. v2 Appendix D tests removing random masking, varying masking probability around 0.5, and removing Kronecker computation, with results in Tables 6–8. Figures 2 and 6 also add prediction-error/uncertainty and completion case studies.

E5.justification: Both versions report prediction means and standard deviations over five training runs. v2 additionally constructs 90%, 95% and 99% predictive intervals from 100 samples, evaluates their empirical coverage, and displays predictive standard deviations in Section 5.4. This substantially expands uncertainty assessment without establishing an increase in training-run counts.

E6.justification: Original regular-grid prediction values are unchanged in v2 Tables 1 and 5, and regular generation scores are retained in Table 2. v2 adds diffusion-reaction, new-baseline, completion, calibration and ablation/runtime results while removing irregular-sampling results. For example, the new diffusion-reaction f1,u1-to-f2 task reports errors of 0.0144 for ACM-FD and 0.0107 for FNO.

M1.justification: The GP diffusion, masked zero-target loss and FNO denoiser are retained. Algorithm 2 corrects the sampling-noise multiplier from beta_hat_t to sqrt(beta_hat_t). The described GP-interpolation route for irregular inputs is omitted; the combined pointwise and whole-function masking strategy is newly documented within the existing flexible-mask framework.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution discussion, related-work section and experimental narrative are substantially reworked. Qualitative generation discussion moves from the main text into Appendix C, while experiments gain separate completion, calibration and ablation sections. Much of the core mathematical exposition remains unchanged.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout. v2 adds a method schematic, uncertainty and completion visualizations, and several analysis tables. The original generation comparison is expanded with MFD and moved to Figure 3; v1 Figure 2 survives as Figure 4. PODDON results are split into an appendix table.

R1.justification: Section 4 replaces much of the general generative-model survey with focused discussion of functional diffusion and conditional inference. Added predecessors include Kerrigan et al. (2023), Lim et al. (2023), Franzese et al. (2024) and Gloeckler et al. (2024). v2 acknowledges conceptual similarity to prior GP-based diffusion and distinguishes Simformer through zero regularization.

T1.justification: Algorithm 2 replaces beta_hat_t times epsilon with sqrt(beta_hat_t) times epsilon, correcting the sampling variance to match Equation 8. The principal diffusion derivations and Kronecker complexity analysis otherwise remain, without a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's missing validation of completion, predictive uncertainty and individual design choices through Tables 3–4 and 6–8. Relevant diffusion comparators, clearer prior-work positioning and additional reproducibility information strengthen the evidence. Irregular-sampling validation is lost, and Section 5.1 overstates superiority over GNOT relative to Table 1, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in support for the central claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ACM-FD, with matching authors, core equations and retained experimental results. The complete main texts, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds diffusion-reaction predictions, function completion, uncertainty calibration and component ablations, reported throughout Tables 1–8.

before.justification: v1 reports original prediction and generation experiments on Darcy Flow, Convection Diffusion and Torus Fluid, including numerical results in Tables 1–3.

results.title: Arbitrarily-Conditioned Multi-Functional Diffusion for Multi-Physics Emulation

C1.justification: The abstract and three contribution bullets retain the same central claims: reward-free world models for online imitation learning, planning without explicit reward modeling, strong complex-control performance and reward recovery. The shortened conclusion preserves this scope; the new analyses primarily support existing contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of regularization sensitivity and recovered-reward variance, acknowledges the method's primarily deterministic design, and discusses limited noise robustness and computational overhead. The introduction also shifts attribution for distribution-shift and bias mitigation from the novel formulation to online interaction. These substantially expand the interpretation and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: Appendix F newly specifies a single RTX 2080 Ti for the timing comparisons and reports training time in seconds. The detailed architecture and default hyperparameters in Appendix A remain unchanged, and no new code or data access information is provided.

E1.justification: The benchmark tasks and visual-input coverage are retained. Appendix E.5 adds stochastic-transition Walker Run scenarios with trembling probabilities 0.01 and 0.02. The other new analyses reuse environments already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: HyPE joins the main locomotion and MyoSuite comparisons in Figures 2–3 and Table 1. HyPER is added specifically to the computational-cost comparison in Figure 16. Table 7 also introduces IQL+SAC as a reward-recovery comparator, whereas v1's recovery analysis showed IQ-MPC alone.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include an alpha sweep over 0.25, 0.5 and 1, controlled transition noise, Pearson correlation as a reward-recovery metric, and training-time comparisons with MPC versus policy-prior interaction. Existing architecture and default settings remain. Shorter Figure 2 time ranges establish changed reporting windows, but do not establish reruns or reduced actual training budgets.

E4.justification: V2 adds regularization sensitivity on Humanoid Walk, robustness to noisy Walker Run transitions, quantitative reward-recovery analysis across four tasks, and computational analysis including the cost of planning. These address questions absent from v1. The original demonstration-count, objective-formulation and gradient-penalty ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Three-seed averaging, success-rate tables with plus/minus values, and shaded variability already appear in v1 and remain in v2. No increased run count or new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedure is stated. The added Pearson coefficients serve as evaluation metrics.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds HyPE success rates of 0.55±0.09, 0.13±0.10 and 0.00±0.00 for Key Turn, Object Hold and Pen Twirl; retained methods' entries are unchanged. New Table 7 reports, for example, Hopper Hop correlations of 0.88 for IQ-MPC versus 0.49 for IQL+SAC. New findings also cover alpha sensitivity, noise degradation, computational cost and comparable performance with HyPE on Cheetah Run and Quadruped Run.

M1.justification: The encoder, latent dynamics, critic, policy prior, learning losses, gradient penalty and MPPI planner remain unchanged. Algorithm 2 drops an unused reward field from the buffer-insertion tuple, without changing the learning equations. Policy-prior-only interaction appears as a timing-study variant.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify reward-free modeling and regularization, shorten the conclusion, and update affiliations and publication headers. Visual experiments and reward recovery move from the main text to Appendices E.4 and E.6. Much of the original prose and broad section sequence remains intact.

P2.justification: Figures 2–3 and Table 1 expand for HyPE, with revised legends and colors; Figures 12, 14 and 16 and Table 7 add new displays. Existing visual-control and reward-recovery plots are relocated. Figure 2 shortens Walker Run, Quadruped Run and Hopper Hop from 4M to 1M displayed steps, and Cheetah Run from 2M to 1M.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to model-based imitation approaches including MAIL, EfficientImitate, V-MAIL, CMIL, Ditto and DMIL, alongside hybrid inverse RL and LS-IQ. The methodology now explicitly positions critic-derived rewards against prior approaches using separate reward models, sharpening a previously limited comparison with this literature.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 adds a return-gap bound attributed to Kolev et al. Appendix G.3 introduces Gaussian and approximately matched-variance assumptions, then uses Pinsker's inequality and a KL derivation to connect consistency loss with transition-distribution error. V1's objective-equivalence and policy-update proofs are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens comparative evaluation and support for reward recovery through HyPE comparisons, four-task correlation measurements, and sensitivity, noise and computational-cost analyses. These address important gaps in v1 and make performance limitations more assessable, including ties with HyPE and higher costs than model-free baselines. Four shorter learning-curve windows reduce long-horizon evidence, and the new theory remains assumption-dependent, but the additional comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a clear net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IQ-MPC research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated and newly added content to be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, regularization sensitivity, noisy-dynamics evaluation, reward correlations and training-time measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original DMControl, MyoSuite and ManiSkill2 experiments, including learning curves, success rates, visual control, reward recovery and ablations.

results.title: Reward-free World Models for Online Imitation Learning

C1.justification: The core claims about Laplace-resolvent learning, small-lag robustness, broad process coverage, and linear dependence on state dimension remain. The introduction broadens the empirical superiority claim from molecular-dynamics performance under computational constraints to estimation performance against TO and other IG methods.

C2.justification: V2 explains the resolvent's relevance to non-normal transient dynamics and discusses forecasting full distributions with an additional projection error. Its conclusion expands the limitations from uniform sampling to full-state observation, identifying partially observed systems as an unresolved extension.

D1.justification: V2 adds an implementation-and-experiments repository link, identifies Nüske et al. as the source of the two alanine trajectories, and specifies experimental kernel/feature configurations. These improve documentation; the newly identified trajectory source does not establish a change of dataset.

E1.justification: V2 adds an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck experiment with a non-normal 2×2 drift matrix, extending empirical coverage beyond the retained triple-well Langevin and alanine settings. This tests non-normal generators, an important part of the claimed scope previously supported only theoretically.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained transfer-operator comparator, v2 Figure 5 evaluates Hou et al.'s Galerkin projection and Kostic et al.'s Dirichlet-energy regression. These generator methods were only analytically compared in v1. Although Section 7 also mentions Cabannes and Bach, Figure 5 does not separately identify that comparator.

E3.justification: The triple-well evaluation changes from signed to absolute relative error and adds systematic time-lag sweeps using both implementations. The new OU protocol uses 1,000 Fourier features and 10,000/100,000 samples at time steps 0.01/0.001. Alanine's reported time step changes from 25 to 50 ps, retaining 250 ns training and test durations.

E4.justification: V2 Figures 2 and 4 directly test sensitivity to decreasing time lag for dual and primal LaRRR versus TO RRR. Appendix D Figure 5 adds an analysis of spurious eigenvalues from generator estimation. Neither analysis is present in v1's experimental figures.

E5.justification: The triple-well experiment reports 10 independent trajectories and fitted models instead of 100. V2 adds quartile bands across time lags alongside violin distributions, whereas v1 shows violin distributions with mean bars. The new OU experiment explicitly reports ten trials.

E6.justification: V2 replaces the original triple-well distributions with results showing comparatively stable LaRRR error as TO error increases at small lags. It adds non-normal OU recovery results and evidence of Galerkin's spurious near-zero eigenvalues. Changed metrics and protocols prevent interpreting the revised distributions as same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The Laplace-resolvent objective, trapezoidal weighting, Toeplitz construction, and primal and dual LaRRR algorithms are retained. The extension to multiple non-uniformly sampled trajectories already appears in v1 Appendix B. Newly evaluating the primal implementation does not introduce a new method.

P1.justification: V2 expands the introduction and resolvent explanation, locally reorganizes the risk formulation and approach, and adds Appendix D. The main section sequence and most algorithm and proof exposition remain, so the narrative revision is limited despite extensive visual reformatting.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column conference formatting. V2 redesigns the triple-well display as lag-dependent curves with inset distributions, adds OU and appendix figures, updates the alanine display, and introduces a full-page notation table.

R1.justification: The introduction expands application positioning through graph-clustering and neuroscience references, including Klus and Djurdjevac Conrad, Marrouch et al., and Ostrow et al. Several general Koopman citations are pruned. The central methodological positioning and Table 1 comparisons remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: V1 Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 become Proposition 6.1 and Theorem 6.2, with minimum combinations replaced by maxima in their bounds, including Equation 22. These are weaker mathematical statements, not equivalent notation. The convergence-rate exponents, principal assumptions, and most appendix derivations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially closes an empirical gap: v1 does not directly test its central small-lag robustness claim or demonstrate non-normal recovery. The targeted lag sweeps, OU experiment, and generator-baseline analysis connect evidence to those claims. Reproducibility pointers and fuller limitations also help. The reduction from 100 to 10 triple-well repetitions and inconsistent baseline attribution temper, but do not outweigh, these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LaRRR research. Their main text, algorithms, equations, experimental figures, and complete appendices support comparison across the substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: Section 7 and Appendix D report original Langevin, non-normal Ornstein–Uhlenbeck, and alanine experiments, including time-lag sensitivity and generator-baseline comparisons.

before.justification: Section 7 reports original eigenvalue-estimation experiments on triple-well Langevin dynamics and eigenfunction recovery for alanine dipeptide.

results.title: Laplace Transform Based Low-Complexity Learning of Continuous Markov Semigroups

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a unified, efficient evolutionary framework for three compression approaches, a convergence guarantee for linear fitness, and competitive compression quality across the same model families. The rewritten abstract and conclusion alter emphasis without substantively changing these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the monotonicity argument by describing useful prediction at low compression and deterioration at medium sparsity. It also interprets seed consistency as evidence against problematic local optima and explains EvoPress–BESA complementarity. Appendix G adds qualifications about runtime/data tradeoffs, differing sparsity granularity, and incomplete tuning-cost accounting.

D1.justification: v2 adds RTX 4090 hardware information for Table 17, runtime-accounting exclusions for BESA, and vLLM precision/grouping requirements. Figure 3 newly clarifies minibatch fitness versus full-test-set perplexity measurement. The original hyperparameter table and code URL remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same calibration and evaluation corpora and the same language-model compression tasks, including the five zero-shot benchmarks. The added runtime studies, Wanda implementation, and vLLM precision restrictions change configurations and procedures within retained task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix G adds evaluated comparisons against SLEB and BlockPruner for depth pruning and against layerwise and rowwise BESA for sparsity allocation. These substantially expand comparison with competing search procedures beyond v1's baseline set; the original comparisons remain elsewhere.

E3.justification: The original Table 8 settings remain, but substantial additional protocols appear: 1000-generation seed experiments, stopping after 20 generations without training-perplexity improvement, Wanda-based sparsity comparisons, and vLLM-compatible 4/8-bit search with coupled projection precisions. Table 17 adds runtime and forward-pass measurements on an RTX 4090. These are additional settings, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds seed sensitivity and configuration-consistency analyses in Appendix C.2, and tests layerwise perplexity prediction when removing 2, 4, or 6 blocks in Appendix D.4. Table 18 also examines combining EvoPress with BESA. These materially extend robustness and mechanism validation beyond the retained mutation, selection, and fitness ablations.

E5.justification: v1 contains no empirical repeated-seed uncertainty study. v2 reports 16 independent runs, standard-deviation bands in Figure 7, and mean C4 perplexity 33.82 with standard deviation 0.61 for Llama-3-8B at 70% sparsity. This substantial addition is confined to the new robustness study; uncertainty is not added throughout the benchmark tables.

E6.justification: Most matched original scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results in Figures 4, 6, 7, and 10 and Tables 17–18. For example, Table 17 reports C4 perplexity/runtime of 19.87/53 minutes for EvoPress versus 20.91/159 minutes for SLEB at 37.5% depth pruning. Conversely, Tables 2–3 lose individual task scores for compressed models and the Llama-3.1 compressed-model rows, without restoring those scores in the appendices.

M1.justification: The level database, KL-divergence fitness, level-switch mutation, and multistage selection remain unchanged. Appendix G adds an early-stopping variant and a two-stage EvoPress+BESA procedure that refines EvoPress-derived block sparsities through rowwise allocation.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are revised, several passages and the conclusion are shortened, and the baseline list becomes prose. Appendix C gains subsections, Appendix G and an impact statement are added, and the contents page disappears. Most existing exposition and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column conference layout. Tables 2–3 are substantially condensed; Figure 2 loses its profile panel and changes its vertical scale. New quantization, seed-robustness, and correlation figures and runtime tables are added, while numerous retained displays are resized, reordered, or redrawn.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to SLEB, BlockPruner, BESA, Wanda, and straight-through estimation, and positions BESA as complementary to EvoPress. The Kwon et al. reference is removed. The main related-work organization and unified-compression novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 becomes Theorem 3.1, retaining the linear-fitness assumptions and expected O(k(n-k)/lambda) convergence bound. Appendix A preserves the supporting definitions, lemmas, and drift proofs. Changes are numbering, typography, and explanatory wording.

improvement.justification: The 16-seed study addresses an important reliability gap for stochastic search, while comparisons against competing search methods substantially strengthen evidence for practical efficiency. The added low-compression analysis also clarifies the motivating argument's limits. These gains outweigh the loss of detailed scores in Tables 2–3, although runtime comparisons retain stated comparability limits and Figure 4 does not quantify its claimed vLLM speedups.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EvoPress despite the revised title and formatting. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds seed-robustness results, constrained quantization results, and runtime comparisons in Appendix G.

before.justification: v1 reports original compression experiments, perplexity and zero-shot accuracy results, convergence measurements, and ablations across depth pruning, sparsity, and quantization.

results.title: EvoPress: Accurate Dynamic Model Compression via Evolutionary Search

C1.justification: Both versions claim a data-to-data bridge framework for I2V, effective diffusion-to-bridge transfer through SAF, and improved generation through neural priors. Updated headline scores and broader supporting experiments do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix C newly discusses the tradeoff between motion and consistency and the content bias of FVD. It also interprets the added curves as evidence of faster convergence and effective reduced-step sampling. The original explanation based on informative priors and frame-to-frames generation remains.

D1.justification: V2 adds training/sampling pseudocode, discrete-timestep SNR interpolation details and CogVideoX implementation sources, and updates the project-page address. Most existing hyperparameters remain documented. However, v1's explicit general specification of first-order, 250-step sampling is no longer retained as such.

E1.justification: V2 adds VBench-I2V evaluation inputs, including 50 sampled prompts used in the human study. WebVid-2M, UCF-101, MSR-VTT and the original class-conditional and text-conditional I2V tasks remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 expands the zero-shot comparator set beyond DynamiCrafter and SEINE to include SVD, ConsistI2V, SparseCtrl and I2VGen-XL. The neural-prior ablation also adds a VDT-I2V baseline conditioned on the neural prior, providing an important additional control.

E3.justification: V2 adds 100k-step fine-tuning alongside 20k steps and evaluates a CogVideoX-2B backbone. The UCF-101 SAF ablation changes from uniformly 20k iterations to 5k/10k configurations. New protocols include VBench-I2V, CD-FVD, human rankings from 18 participants on 50 prompts, and sampling-step/runtime comparisons.

E4.justification: New analyses examine motion versus consistency using noisy image conditioning and increased frame stride, FVD content bias, training convergence and sampling efficiency. V2 also adds WebVid-2M SAF ablations for both backbones and the neural-prior-conditioned diffusion control; v1 mainly ablated SAF and prior choice.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed variability, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's user-ranking averages introduce a metric and study sample size, but no uncertainty analysis.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises multiple results: SEINE's MSR-VTT FVD changes from 176 to 245, and FrameBridge's SAF result changes from 83 to 99 for the reported 20k-step configuration. V2 separately adds a 100k-step result of 95, CogVideoX results and extensive new analyses. The neural-prior diffusion control scores 132 FVD; FrameBridge-NP's original 122 remains. These are revised and additional results, not uniform performance improvements.

M1.justification: Appendix A.3 extends SAF with output reparameterization for v-prediction models such as CogVideoX-2B, beyond v1's input and timestep alignment. The core bridge process, replicated prior and neural-prior construction remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial motivation/SAF passages are rewritten. Background and motivation are consolidated, the main experimental setup discussion is compressed, and the appendices are reorganized around new pseudocode and analysis sections, moving the original related-work appendix from B to E.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main layout, redesigns comparison tables with training-budget columns and ranking markers, and adds analytical plots, tables and algorithm boxes. Qualitative displays are reorganized: the rabbit example moves from Figure 5 to Figure 9, while v1 Figures 6–9 are retained as v2 Figures 12–15.

R1.justification: V2 expands discussion of coupled flow matching, noise calibration, newer bridge models and additional video-generation methods. It adds benchmark-related citations while retaining the central positioning against noise-to-data diffusion. Numerous venue/year updates refer to works already cited in v1.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds the mathematical construction of the aligned v-prediction output target. The bridge derivations and Propositions 1–3 with their proofs are otherwise retained. Removing the separately displayed neural-prior bridge loss from the main text is an equivalent restatement through prior substitution.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's limited empirical validation through broader baselines, explicit training-budget comparisons and the missing neural-prior-conditioned diffusion control. VBench-I2V, CD-FVD and human judgments better examine whether apparent gains reflect consistency at the expense of motion. Cross-backbone and efficiency analyses further support applicability. Uncertainty remains unreported and some sampling-plot labeling is inconsistent, but the added controls and complementary evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FrameBridge. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds benchmark comparisons, efficiency analyses, further ablations and an 18-participant user study.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-to-video benchmark results, SAF and neural-prior ablations, and generated-video examples, including appendix results.

results.title: FrameBridge: Improving Image-to-Video Generation with Bridge Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion recast the contribution from a joint perplexity/FLOPs-constrained threat model to an N-gram perplexity constraint with separate compute reporting. v2 additionally argues for N-gram perplexity over self-perplexity. The central claims about interpretable benchmarking and the strength of discrete-optimization attacks remain.

C2.justification: v2 drops v1's interpretation that filtering can improve PRS success and revises the model-robustness conclusions. Transfer is reinterpreted relative to declining source-model ASR, rather than simply as an absolute decline under tighter constraints. New discussions address multilingual and tokenizer limitations, Gemma's refusals after the target token, and whether self-perplexity confounds attack cost with robustness.

D1.justification: v2 adds explicit HarmBench judge templates, judge precision, PRS reimplementation/caching information, and self-perplexity thresholds and context-handling details in Appendices B, F, G, and I. The main code-repository link remains, while the standalone reproducibility statement and separate baseline-repository links disappear. These extend and revise existing documentation.

E1.justification: v2 adds filter-rejection evaluation on translations of the 300 HarmBench queries into 12 languages, substantially extending the previously English-focused evaluation population (Section 5.3 and Table 2). The existing Dolma, Alpaca, and HarmBench coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated windowed and full-query self-perplexity comparators; the full-query result explicitly transfers the windowed attack (Table 3). BEAST and PAIR also enter comparisons on six retained target models where v1 reported no results. The preliminary COLD evaluation reported in v1 is removed.

E3.justification: Appendix F changes the reported PRS budget from 10,000 to 100,000 steps and its stopping condition from target probability above 0.1 plus a refusal check to probability above 0.99, followed by checkpoint judging. New self-perplexity experiments use separate stopping settings. The target-model configuration also changes: Zephyr-7b-R2D2 is removed, and transfer evaluation adds three large open-source models.

E4.justification: v2 adds multilingual utility tests and adaptive self-perplexity comparisons, and expands transfer analysis with additional targets and source-model ASR references. Figure 5 revises the threshold-sensitivity study and removes the separate GCG ASR-versus-FLOPs panel. The human evaluation and N-gram order/window ablations are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 5 explicitly reports average ASR and standard deviation over three seeds, with uncertainty bands. v1's corresponding figure provides neither a seed count nor uncertainty reporting; the PDFs establish newly reported uncertainty, not a known increase from a specified earlier run count.

E6.justification: PRS results are extensively replaced: baseline/adaptive ASR on Llama3.1-8b changes from 0.16/0.28 in v1 Table 4 to 0.97/0.96 in v2 Table 1, alongside the revised search procedure and budget. Perplexity distributions and transfer results also change, and new multilingual and self-perplexity entries are reported. Table 3 reports ASR 0.62 for all three filtered PRS conditions.

M1.justification: The central bigram filter and most attack adaptations remain unchanged.
