However, Algorithm 2 changes adaptive PRS candidate generation to sampling the 100,000 most likely bigrams, and Appendix I introduces a PRS adaptation using self-perplexity as its rejection criterion. These are limited procedural extensions.

P1.justification: Beyond retitling and widespread prose editing, v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative and experimental sections. Human evaluation moves from Appendix B to Section 5.6, filter-construction material moves into Appendix C, and related work and interpretation receive newly separated subsections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout, with extensive figure and table relocation and redesigned algorithms. v2 adds multilingual and self-perplexity tables and Figure 14, removes v1's attack-metric overview table, redraws transfer displays, and adds uncertainty bands to the PRS threshold plot.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citations concerning circuit breakers and latent-space defenses, multilingual tokenization, N-gram modeling, and layered safety measures. It also develops the comparison with earlier self-perplexity filters. The principal positioning around HarmBench and adaptive jailbreak evaluation remains intact.

T1.justification: The formal threat-model definition changes: v1 Section 3.3 requires FLOPs below a fixed budget of 10^19, whereas v2 Section 3.4 treats FLOPs as a reported resource measure rather than a membership condition. The judge-success requirement remains in Equation 1, and the N-gram and adaptive-GCG mathematics are otherwise equivalent.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens scrutiny of the central threat model: it documents a more thorough PRS search, fills previously missing attack comparisons, and directly tests adaptive self-perplexity alternatives. Multilingual tests and three-seed uncertainty reporting expose important applicability and variability limits. Conflicting calibration descriptions in Table 3 versus Appendix I and some mismatched captions weaken reporting, but the more complete and diagnostic evaluation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same N-gram perplexity threat-model research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and reports additional multilingual filter evaluations, self-perplexity comparisons, and expanded transfer experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original HarmBench jailbreak experiments, filter ablations, transfer results, and a human evaluation of 2,000 responses.

results.title: An Interpretable N-gram Perplexity Threat Model for Large Language Model Jailbreaks

C1.justification: V1 presents reflection as a criterion for AI intelligence and emphasizes shortcomings relative to human intelligence. V2 explicitly targets intrinsic epistemic agency, treats reflection as a process, and acknowledges rudimentary agency. It also adds central claims about contamination minimization and a three-tier performance hierarchy, substantially redefining the paper's contribution.

C2.justification: V2 replaces v1's cost-based criticism of CoT with task- and model-dependent interpretations supported by prompting comparisons. It expands discussion of local adaptation, global understanding and cognitive coordination. New applicability boundaries distinguish base LLMs from augmented or multi-LLM agents and address ecological validity, modalities and naturalistic interaction. It also interprets Centaur's results as evidence of contamination resistance.

D1.justification: V1's appendix supplies only Oddball prompts and annotation examples. V2 Appendix A documents system prompts and worked interactions across all seven tasks and gives the three strategy prompts; Appendix D explains the embedding scorer. Conversely, v1's explicit temperature-zero settings, API costs/counts and WPT last-20-of-100 estimation detail are omitted. These are substantial documentation changes, not proof that every underlying implementation changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same seven text-based cognitive tasks. V2's harder evaluations vary memory depth, reward probabilities and reversal intervals within those tasks; they do not introduce a new dataset domain, language or distinct task.

E2.justification: The main comparison changes from 13 to 16 models, adding models including DeepSeek-Reasoner/V3, QwQ, Grok-2 and Claude-Haiku while removing GPT-4, Gemini-1.5-pro and the Llama-3.1 variants from that comparison. Table 9 adds Centaur versus Llama-3.1-70B and chance baselines. The original 13 models remain represented in Appendix D's Oddball validation.

E3.justification: V1 generally restricts responses to choices; v2 evaluates direct generation, free output and zero-shot CoT, with only two strategies for reasoning models. Easy-setting WCST changes from 108 to 72 trials, PRLT probability from 0.9 to 0.8 and its smoothing window from 3 to 5, and MBT reversal interval from 3 to 2. V2 also adds hard configurations and automated Oddball scoring.

E4.justification: V2 adds systematic prompting comparisons, difficulty sensitivity tests, a Centaur comparison intended to investigate contamination, and human-versus-automated Oddball scoring validation. Existing behavioral analyses are substantially extended, including five WPT response patterns and quantitative DC-IGT switching and earnings analyses (Appendices C–D).

E5.justification: Both versions describe two sessions for most tasks and three for Oddball; an increase in these counts is not reported. V2 adds one million random simulations per applicable task to estimate 95th-percentile chance thresholds, plus Pearson correlations, p-values and confidence intervals for Oddball scoring validation (Figures 18–19). These substantially expand statistical reporting beyond v1's averages.

E6.justification: V1 Table 2 ranks o1-preview first at 80.97; v2 Table 2 ranks Claude-3.5-Sonnet with CoT first at 68.78, ahead of o1-preview's direct-generation 66.57. These are revised-setting results, not a same-setting performance decline. V2 adds extensive strategy, difficulty and Centaur results. Some entries conflict internally: Grok-2's easy CoT PRLT score is 68.34 in Table 8 but 48.86 in Table 9.

M1.justification: The seven-task benchmark design is retained. V2 adds an automated Oddball scoring component: split responses into sentences, embed them and select the maximum cosine similarity to a reference surprise sentence (Appendix D). This changes one scoring procedure without redesigning the benchmark.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V2 adds a dedicated explanation of agency dimensions, reorders task descriptions, separates discussion from experiments and reorganizes the appendix into prompts, results, secondary analyses and scoring validation. This is substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1 and rearranges Figure 2. The original consolidated results table becomes an overall model-strategy table plus task-specific and easy/hard comparison tables. Behavioral plots are redesigned and moved to the appendix, alongside new interaction diagrams, switching analyses and correlation panels. The original Oddball MMN-style results plot is removed.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from emergent intelligence and first-principles accounts toward LLM agents, epistemic agency and cognitive-psychology evaluation. V2 adds substantial positioning around AgentBench, ReAct, MetaGPT, cognitive evaluation, philosophical agency and benchmark contamination, while retaining relevant cognitive-task foundations.

T1.justification: The weather transition matrices and MAE-based score normalization are retained. V2's expanded epistemic-agency framework is conceptual, while its new scoring and statistical procedures are empirical; no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's acknowledged choice-only prompting limitation through direct strategy comparisons, replacing speculative CoT interpretation with experimental evidence. Full task prompts, harder-setting tests, chance thresholds and empirical validation of automated scoring improve the benchmark's interpretability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting defects, including conflicting PRLT entries in Tables 8–9, although the Centaur comparison supports a narrower conclusion than v2's strong contamination-resistance claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Reflection-Bench and its seven cognitive tasks. Their full text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial changes in framing and evaluation.

after.justification: V2 reports original model-by-prompting evaluations, harder-setting experiments, Centaur comparisons, random simulations and automated-scoring validation in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 13 LLMs across seven tasks, including numerical scores in Table 2 and behavioral analyses in Figures 3–7.

results.title: Reflection-Bench: Evaluating Epistemic Agency in Large Language Models

C1.justification: v2 adds superiority over alternative architectures as its first main contribution and broadens the abstract's empirical scope to fish milling. v1's three listed contributions concern the expected-transformer construction and approximation theory; those central theoretical objectives remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the reported transfer from 20 training particles to 30 simulation particles as evidence of learning the interaction kernel. It also replaces v1's explicit short-horizon qualification with discussion of approximation over a prescribed finite interval, while retaining the exponential error-growth warning.

D1.justification: Appendix E newly supplies hyperparameter ranges, optimizer and scheduler choices, batch sizes, and epoch budgets. Section 3 expands neural-network data-generation details and adds a code-access link. These substantially improve documentation, although v1's BDF solver specification and 16,834-sample count are omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds real fish-milling data spanning 5,000 time steps, with incomplete observations and changing particle identities/counts. This substantially extends coverage beyond v1's synthetic Cucker-Smale and neural-network training examples, both of which remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated cylindrical networks, GraphConv and TransformerConv with 3- and 20-neighbor graphs, plus FNN and kernel-regression baselines on Cucker-Smale only. v1 contains no corresponding architectural benchmark; its comparisons with true dynamics and gradient-based training remain.

E3.justification: The added benchmark study introduces validation-selected comparisons and 3-/20-neighbor graph controls. Figure 4 adds Gibbs sampling over five fixed positions and an 11-by-11 velocity grid. v2 also reports 30 simulated Cucker-Smale particles instead of ten, although Figure 3 still captions ten; this inconsistency prevents establishing whether that experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 and Figure 4 add a focused diagnostic comparing sampled expected-transformer errors with the theoretical bound across position/velocity settings. The trajectory and neural-network parameter-error analyses already present in Figures 1–3 are retained.

E5.justification: v2 specifies five trials per hyperparameter configuration and introduces plus/minus uncertainty entries in Table 1, without defining the uncertainty statistic. The existing 100-trial median and interquartile-range reporting in Figures 1–2 remains unchanged.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds substantial comparative results: the transformer has the lowest reported MSE on both Cucker-Smale (1.9e-6) and fish milling (2.2e-2). Figure 4 newly reports maximum sampled error 0.025 against a stated bound of at least 0.05. Figures 1–3 retain their earlier results.

M1.justification: The transformer architecture, expected-transformer construction, and mean-squared-error vector-field learning procedure are retained. The architecture definitions move from Section 3.1 to Appendix D; additional training specifications do not establish a changed proposed method.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and experimental narrative are extensively revised. Experiments move ahead of theory, notation becomes an introduction subsection, architecture definitions move to Appendix D, and related work becomes a dedicated later section. This is substantial restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 switches the main text to a two-column conference layout, adds Table 1 and the five-panel heatmap Figure 4, and substantially resizes and relocates Figures 1–3. The retained plots preserve their underlying results.

R1.justification: The broad neural-network/PDE approximation background is replaced by a focused Section 5 comparison of measure roles, architectures, and guarantees. v2 adds positioning against Kratsios and Furuya (2025), alongside new citations for probabilistic transformers, fish data, GNN baselines, and attention regularity, while removing much of the earlier general background.

T1.justification: v2 replaces Wp-based regularity with W1 regularity, removes the explicit smoothness assumption, and revises approximation bounds and their proofs. Theorem 4.12 and Appendix B add an existence-and-uniqueness argument using a cutoff, replacing v1's Assumption 2. The dynamics theorem is reformulated in W1, although inconsistent p/Wp expressions remain elsewhere.

improvement.justification: Table 1 supplies architectural comparisons and real-data validation absent from v1, while Appendix E substantially improves reproducibility information. These materially strengthen the paper's empirical support and auditability. The added existence-and-uniqueness argument also addresses a previously assumed condition, although theoretical consistency remains imperfect. The ambiguous '80-20-20' split, conflicting particle counts, and residual W1/Wp expressions limit confidence but do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same expected-transformer approach to mean-field dynamics, despite the changed title. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison.

after.justification: Section 3 retains the original simulations and adds comparative results on Cucker-Smale and real fish-milling data. Section 4.3 also reports a new approximation-error analysis.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figures 1–3 report original Cucker-Smale simulations and experiments approximating two-layer neural-network training dynamics.

results.title: Universal Approximation of Mean-Field Models via Transformers

C1.justification: v3 adds resistance to existing prompt-based defenses as a central claim in the abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion. This extends the claimed findings beyond attacks on undefended agents. The main-text 'first framework' novelty language is softened, while the underlying method and controllability claims remain.

C2.justification: v1 describes position transfer as broadly robust; v3 explicitly acknowledges the unchanged 26.0% Finance result and suggests position sensitivity and task-specific tuning. It also interprets the new baseline and defense findings. The substantive offline-feedback and step-level-evaluation limitations are retained, moving from Appendix D to E.

D1.justification: v3 explicitly documents GCG's target-action-triplet objective and describes the new baseline and defense adaptations. It omits v1's disclosure of 50 successful attacks per domain for position/field tests, while retaining core hyperparameters. The release statement mentions code rather than code and data; these documentation changes do not establish changed sample sizes or actual resource availability.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Mind2Web task coverage across Finance, Medical, Housing, and Cooking. The added defense experiments change agent configurations within this coverage, without introducing another dataset, domain, or task requirement.

E2.justification: Table 1 replaces AutoDAN, COLD-Attack, and Cat-Jailbreak with Agent-Attack and InjecAgent, while retaining GCG. Separately, all four baseline rows disappear from the GPT-4V and Gemini controllability comparisons: v1 Tables 2 and 5 become proposed-method-only v3 Tables 3 and 6.

E3.justification: v3 Section 6 adds Gemini 1.5 evaluations with random-sequence enclosure, instruction defense, and sandwich defense, compared with no defense. The retained experiments keep the 240/200 training/test split, step-based exact-action ASR, model identifiers, and stated training hyperparameters.

E4.justification: New Section 6 and Table 5 extend robustness analysis to whether three prompt-based defenses mitigate the attack, a question not experimentally examined in v1. The existing SFT/DPO ablation, controllability tests, position/HTML-field variations, cross-model transfer tests, and qualitative cases remain.

E5.justification: Corresponding tables retain means and standard deviations across domains, rather than uncertainty across repeated runs. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or experimental seeds, or introduces confidence intervals or significance tests; the additional results do not establish a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v3 Table 1 adds Agent-Attack/InjecAgent mean ASRs of 45.4/64.3 on GPT-4V and 25.0/28.0 on Gemini. New Table 5 reports defense-condition means of 89.8, 88.8, and 89.8, versus 99.8 without defense. Removed comparator rows also remove results. The proposed method's corresponding original scores, including standard ASRs of 97.5 and 99.8, remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The renamed framework retains hidden HTML injection, target placeholders, feedback collection, positive-example SFT, and positive/negative-pair DPO. Algorithms 1–2 and the training objectives describe the same procedure; the revised explanations and diagrams do not establish a method change.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming AdvWeb to AdvAgent, v3 extensively rewrites the abstract, threat-model explanation, framework overview, results discussion, and conclusion. It reorders analyses, moves LLM related work into an appendix, and adds mitigation, acknowledgements, and impact-statement sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from predominantly single-column presentation to a two-column conference layout. Figures 1–2 are redesigned, tables adopt abbreviated domain headings and backend sections, and controllability tables are shortened. A new defense table is added, while existing figures and analyses are resized or relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds discussion of Agent-Attack and InjecAgent and references for three prompt defenses, while removing Mo et al. (2024). It moderates prominent novelty language and contextualizes existing black-box approaches more explicitly. Most related work remains; the LLM-attack discussion moves to Appendix D rather than being deleted.

T1.justification: The agent/action formulation, visual-invariance constraint, target-substitution formulation, and SFT/DPO objectives remain mathematically equivalent. Neither version contains additional theoretical propositions or proofs, including in the appendices.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central comparative evidence: v1's four baselines all scored zero, whereas v3 Table 1 includes relevant agent-injection methods with substantial nonzero success, making the retained performance advantage more informative. Defense testing adds meaningful security context, and the position-transfer discussion better reflects its evidence. Removing controllability baseline rows and a sampling disclosure reduces some completeness, but these losses are outweighed by the stronger comparisons and more calibrated interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, renamed from AdvWeb to AdvAgent. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains the original experiments and reports additional baseline comparisons and evaluations against three prompt-based defenses.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack experiments, controllability and transfer tests, training ablations, and qualitative examples, including additional results in Appendix B.

results.title: AdvAgent: Controllable Blackbox Red-teaming on Web Agents

C1.justification: v1 presents two conditions as predicting CoT failures and describes the three mismatch tasks as showing no negative effects. v4 explicitly acknowledges mixed positive, neutral and negative effects and frames the approach as an imperfect heuristic. It also claims statistically demonstrated enrichment of failure cases and introduces a released six-task benchmark.

C2.justification: The logical-inconsistency explanation shifts from low baseline performance toward differences in formal-logic knowledge. New controls support interpretations concerning image ordering and distracting features, while successful steering qualifies CoT failures as dependent on its default reasoning strategy. Appendix F.1 adds explicit discussion of the apartment implementation favoring models and possible memory restrictions.

D1.justification: v4 supplies decoding temperatures and output-token budgets throughout Appendices A–F, including the o1 temperature exception and an 8000-token apartment budget. It also provides a repository link for the six task datasets. These substantially extend v1's construction instructions and prompts; newly disclosed settings do not establish changes to earlier runs.

E1.justification: The six task families remain, but v4 adds simpler grammar distributions, faces with differing descriptions, binary face matching and vehicle classification with a binary oracle feature. Appendix G additionally analyzes 378 published model-task comparisons as a new data source, without rerunning those benchmarks.

E2.justification: The model comparator sets in Tables 1–6 are unchanged, and tree-of-thought was already evaluated in v1. v4 adds comparisons involving bigram-guided CoT and progressively stronger license-plate steering alongside ordinary prompting conditions (A.7, C.6).

E3.justification: New protocols include temperature sweeps over 4400 grammar problems, a balanced 100-problem binary face test and a vehicle-oracle experiment capped at seven iterations. The bootstrap analysis uses vehicle classification accuracy instead of rounds to permit aggregation. These supplement the retained main experimental protocols.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing tree-of-thought and learning-curve analyses, v4 tests grammar complexity, sampling temperature, face-task difficulty, image-ordering explanations, oracle features and steering strength. It also adds three failure examples and tests whether the task-selection heuristic disproportionately identifies CoT failures.

E5.justification: Section 4.5 and Appendix G add two bootstrap tests, each using 100000 resamples of size 50, assessing failure magnitude and frequency. Appendix C.6 also reports independent trial counts and an uncertainty interval for steering experiments. Existing main-table p-values and learning-curve error bars are retained.

E6.justification: Tables 1–6 and the original tree-of-thought results retain their values. Substantial new results include direct/CoT accuracies of 61%/32% with differing face descriptions and 72%/62% for binary face matching; combined vehicle steering achieves perfect classification by iteration two in both conditions. These are newly evaluated conditions, not improvements to the original results.

M1.justification: Appendices A.7 and C.6 introduce task-specific inference instructions directing reasoning toward bigrams or retrieval of matching license plates. These modify prompting procedures in supplementary conditions; the underlying models and original direct/CoT procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, task discussions and concluding discussion are extensively rewritten. Task-specific Hypothesis paragraphs become Human failure descriptions, the numbered limitations/future-directions structure is consolidated, and a heuristic-effectiveness section is introduced. v4 also repairs malformed prose in v1.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from one to two columns, with substantially resized tables and revised captions. The existing learning curve moves from appendix Figure 5 to main-text Figure 2. v4 adds two task-variation figures and three failure-example tables, while relocating many appendix tables to the document's end.

R1.justification: v4 adds relevant work on fragile mathematical reasoning, CoT-related bias/toxicity and long-context retrieval, including Mirzadeh, Shaikh and Liu. It also positions the heuristic empirically against Sprague's metastudy. The principal psychology-based research positioning remains intact; publication updates to existing references are not new works.

T1.justification: The finite-state grammar definitions, logical-consistency formulation, Gaussian distractor construction and additive apartment-utility assumption are retained. v4 adds empirical procedures and interpretations, without new theoretical propositions, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the evidence through targeted robustness and steering tests and corrects the categorical no-harm claim that conflicted with v1's own tables. Dataset access and decoding details improve reproducibility. Appendix A.7 still mixes a stated subset experiment with full-dataset reference accuracies, limiting that comparison, but the broader gains in evidential support and calibration of claims are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same six-task study. Their main text, tables, figures, equations and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds controlled task variations, steering experiments, failure examples and an original bootstrap analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original model experiments on six tasks in Tables 1–6, plus tree-of-thought results and a vehicle-learning analysis in the appendices.

results.title: Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central accuracy, 6× batch-size, and 3.04× throughput claims. The introduction adds an explicit claim of higher accuracy than approaches applying low-rank approximations to weights, sharpening the comparative claim without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix A.8 connects the first outlier chunk to attention sinks and adds a specific qualification: inadequate outlier handling can make mean-based landmarks worse than Quest's min-max selection. v2 also interprets the new FP8 tests as precision robustness and expands explanations of its advantages over InfiniGen.

D1.justification: Appendix A.4 newly discloses BF16 weights and KV caches for the main experiments and specifies torch.float8_e5m2 for the additional FP8 tests. The implementation framework, kernel descriptions, default hyperparameters, and repository address are otherwise retained in Appendix B.1.

E1.justification: The benchmark and task families remain unchanged, including InfiniteBench already present in v1's appendix. v2 extends RULER's tested input conditions to 512K and 1M contexts (Appendix A.5), beyond v1's 128K main evaluation and MInference experiments through 256K.

E2.justification: InfiniGen, previously discussed but not evaluated, and its value-only variant join the RULER and LongBench comparisons across all four original models (Table 1, Appendix A.3). Quest also becomes an explicit throughput comparator in Table 14; v1's throughput comparison used full attention.

E3.justification: v2 adds FP8 evaluation, Llama-3-70B-1M, expanded batch-size and context-length sweeps, operation-level timing experiments, and a batch-three, 1M-context offloading comparison. These substantially expand the evaluation design. The original default rank, chunk size, outlier count, and benchmark filtering remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test generated-key compression, FP8 sensitivity, outlier counts from zero to 48, scaling, and prefill/decoding latency contributions (Appendix A). These directly examine previously untested components and operating conditions. The original budget, rank, and chunk-size analyses remain, although the detailed chunk-size versus hit-rate panel is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or an uncertainty-estimation procedure. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: The original tabulated RULER, LongBench, MInference, throughput, and InfiniteBench scores are retained after matching relocated content. v2 adds extensive results for the new comparisons and analyses; Table 14 reports 45.32 tokens/s for ShadowKV versus 9.34 for Quest with CPU offloading at 3×1M. Figure 1 also reports substantially lower SVD overhead without explaining the revision, so it does not establish a same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: v1 describes compressing newly generated keys but explicitly excludes it from the implementation. v2 implements and evaluates this extension as ShadowKV+, reusing the prefill projections (Section 4.1, Appendix A.1). The base ShadowKV algorithms remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose remain recognizable. v2 clarifies sparse budgets and temporal locality, revises selected paragraphs and author information, and separates additional results into Appendix A while moving the former experiment-details appendix to Appendix B.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the single-column main text with a substantially redesigned two-column layout. It merges the main accuracy tables, moves Yi results to the appendix, splits the original overview figure, adds a scheduling diagram and numerous tables, and removes the detailed prefill/decoding illustrations and chunk-hit-rate panel.

R1.justification: v2 expands the distinction from the already-cited InfiniGen, especially its offline selection projections versus ShadowKV's prompt-dependent compression. It adds references including MatryoshkaKV, Eigen Attention, and Effectively Compress KV Heads for LLM, while removing several general application citations. The broader research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds a GPU-memory-savings expression and a worked 7.08× example. The subspace-similarity definition, its bounds, and the equivalent-bandwidth derivation remain unchanged. The new expression omits the M factor from its sparse/outlier term, unlike Section 4.2's byte accounting.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support by addressing v1's missing InfiniGen evaluation, directly testing the importance of outliers, and providing operation-level latency evidence. Generated-token compression, FP8, and larger-model tests further establish applicability. The unexplained SVD-plot revision, inconsistent new memory formula, and denser tables are drawbacks, but they do not outweigh the stronger validation of the central system claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ShadowKV. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial formatting changes.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, precision tests, scalability experiments, and component analyses in Section 5 and Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark accuracy, A100 throughput measurements, and ablation results in Section 5 and Appendix A.

results.title:
ShadowKV: KV Cache in Shadows for High-Throughput Long-Context LLM
  Inference

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: text filters detect existing prompt attacks, image-conditioned attacks expose an overlooked vulnerability, and adaptive attacks bypass safeguards. The expanded appendix evidence does not redefine these principal contributions.

C2.justification: v3 replaces the architectural explanation for weak SDv3.0 transfer with a conjecture about filtered training data, explicitly conditioning attack applicability on the model's existing NSFW capability. It removes the earlier architecture/resolution rationale for omitting InstructPix2Pix transfer and adds interpretations concerning image-quality tradeoffs, generator-based purification robustness and potential defensive use.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies five SLD parameters, identifies the ViT-L/14 safety checker and names the TOPIQ evaluation checkpoints. It removes v1's 256x256 resolution statement and Table 6's explicit InstructPix2Pix identification. The code-access link is unchanged; these disclosures do not establish changes to the original implementation.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained nudity and violence tasks, v3 evaluates political extremism in Appendix G and introduces suppression of explicit-prompt attacks using benign image conditioning in Appendix I. These substantially broaden task coverage, while the original image-text dataset remains unchanged.

E2.justification: The principal Attack VAE, MMA and text-filter comparisons remain. v3 adds Face-Adapter to the image-quality comparison, DiffPure as a purification defense, and a ViT-B/32 safety checker in Tables 15, 17 and 13, respectively. These are focused extensions of the comparison methods.

E3.justification: v3 introduces additional model and checker configurations, transfer-under-defense evaluations, image-quality metrics including LPIPS, SSIM, TOPIQ and FID, and an original-image versus benign-conditioned-image control. The original 1800/200 training/evaluation split is retained. Newly disclosed SLD parameters do not establish that the earlier experiments used different settings or were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantial investigations of transfer under defenses, transfer to different safety checkers, perceptual-quality tradeoffs, DiffPure robustness and potential defensive use. The existing generator ablation and concept-strength sweep are retained as Tables 10–11, corresponding to v1 Tables 8–9.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 2–6 and the relocated ablation tables retain their numerical results. Table 7 changes all eight ASRs, including AdvI2I transfer to SDv2.1 from 86.0% to 84.0% and SDv3.0 from 36.0% to 34.0%. New results include 74.0% FLUX transfer, 72.5% ASR under DiffPure, image-quality measurements, and a 96.5% versus 24.5% ASR comparison within the new defensive experiment.

M1.justification: The concept-vector construction, VAE generator, latent-matching objective, clipping and adaptive training remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 explicitly includes the safety-checker vision encoder, whose feature-comparison role was already described in v1. The additional concepts and defensive application reuse the existing procedure.

P1.justification: There are localized wording clarifications, introductory revisions, an expanded conclusion and a new generic Impact Statement. Appendix A.1–A.2 becomes B–C within an expanded appendix structure. The main section order and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The single-column ICLR-style presentation becomes an ICML-style two-column main text. Existing figures are enlarged and repositioned, Algorithm 1 is reflowed, and Tables 5–6 appear side by side. Nine additional appendix tables materially expand the visual presentation; the two existing figures retain their substantive content.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for TOPIQ, rectified-flow transformers, Face-Adapter and DiffPure to support the appendix evaluations and revised transfer interpretation. The main related-work discussion and positioning of AdvI2I against prompt-based attacks remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Algorithm 1 revises the formal safety-checker loss to apply the vision encoder V to the decoded image before comparison with concept embeddings. This corrects an omitted operation in the written expression, although Equation (3) remains unchanged. No new theoretical results or proofs appear.

improvement.justification: v1 supported image fidelity mainly through constraints and examples; v3 adds quantitative quality measurements and tests against alternative safety checkers and purification defenses, addressing important gaps in the evidence for fidelity and robustness. Explicit SLD settings and qualified transfer explanations also help. Sparse protocols, absent uncertainty estimates and untested causal explanations remain limitations, but the central claims receive substantially broader empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdvI2I research, with matching authors, methods and core experiments. Text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial layout changes.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds model-transfer, image-quality, safety-checker, purification, extremism and defensive-application evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack-success measurements, defense comparisons, transfer experiments, ablations and qualitative examples in the main text and Appendix A.

results.title: AdvI2I: Adversarial Image Attack on Image-to-Image Diffusion models

C1.justification: The central claim of shared cross-modal task representations remains. V2 adds the explicit claim that task-level sharing coexists with modality-specific context embeddings and describes compressed-vector superiority over full prompting as peculiar to the cross-modal case. LLM-to-VLM transfer and instruction-derived vectors receive greater prominence but were already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: V2 develops a substantive distinction between modality-specific context embeddings and integration within task vectors. It replaces the out-of-domain explanation for prompting failures with an ignored-prefix/forced-application interpretation and explains stronger syntax prompting through potentially compatible instructions. Conversely, it removes the explicit harder-task overriding failure qualification. Image-to-text weaknesses remain discussed in the appendix.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands documentation through the overriding evaluator prompt and success rule, task pools, VQA construction details, visualization pseudocode, and t-SNE normalization/sampling instructions. It also drops explicitly listed optimal layer indices and changes the stated Animal-Latin label source from iNaturalist 2017 to 2021; the PDFs do not establish whether the evaluated samples changed.

E1.justification: V2 extends the six constructed tasks with Food-Class, Shirt-Color, and Man-Holding tasks from VQAv2, using LLaVA-ReCap descriptions as textual counterparts. It expands task-conflict coverage to semantic, formatting, creative-generation, and factual-recall scenarios, including OK-VQA/A-OKVQA, and evaluates typo-corrupted instructions. Earlier image-to-text examples remain in Appendix A.7.

E2.justification: The main comparator set is retained under Prompt/Patch terminology. V2 adds an explicit system-prompt comparator for task overriding in Table 5 and adds Image Examples Patch to the model-specific template comparison in Table 10; that row was absent from v1 Table 6.

E3.justification: New protocols include question-stratified VQA evaluation, 1000 samples for each of three overriding settings, and 148 factual-recall images. Overriding uses GPT4o to judge attempted task adherence, counting responses addressing both tasks as successes. V2 also introduces character-swap corruption and timing with 30 examples. The original six-task splits, five-example setup, models, and first-token accuracy metric remain.

E4.justification: V2 adds instruction-typo robustness and computational-overhead analyses, substantially expands task-conflict testing, and compares context embeddings against task vectors. It replaces v1's multi-layer t-SNE sweep with this single-layer comparison and removes the car-manufacturer overriding failure example. Existing template, modality-combination, and representation-evolution analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V2 explicitly reports three-seed averaging and identifies the ensemble plot's shaded regions as variance across those seeds. It also states that timing measurements average 100 runs. V1 already displayed variability and reported aggregation over 100 example sets for representation analyses; the new disclosures do not establish increased run counts for retained experiments.

E6.justification: The matched main transfer, LLM-to-VLM, and modality-combination tables retain identical numerical entries. Substantial new results include VQA average accuracy of 0.69 for text patching versus 0.63 for text prompting and 0.52 for image prompting, overriding scores, timing/VRAM measurements, and noisy-instruction averages of 0.39, 0.37, and 0.35. The template ablation gains an image-patching row averaging 0.22.

M1.justification: Both versions extract task activations at a delimiter token, patch them into a selected layer for another query, and average instruction- and example-derived vectors for ensembling. V2 reformulates the explanation and notation; the added evaluations do not establish a changed extraction, patching, or ensembling procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and much explanatory prose are rewritten. Related work moves near the beginning, representation evolution follows the experiments, and image-to-text transfer moves into the appendix. Terminology changes from ICL/Base/xPatch to Examples/Prompt/Patch, with reorganized experimental subsections, explicit findings, and a new impact statement.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the conceptual and patching diagrams, introduces finding boxes and new experimental tables, and adds evaluator-prompt and pseudocode figures. It reorganizes retained displays, adds a cross-modality column to the main results table, replaces the multi-layer t-SNE figure, and removes the standalone instruction examples and one overriding example.

R1.justification: V2 adds connections to simplicity bias, cross-modal few-shot learning, in-context vectors, and modality separation, alongside references supporting the new evaluations. Its Lin et al. citation now identifies cross-modal few-shot learning rather than the earlier VILA paper. These changes broaden the context while preserving the central positioning around cross-modal task vectors.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs. V2's patching equation restates the existing extraction-and-application mapping. Its softmax and logit-lens pseudocode explains an existing visualization rather than introducing a new mathematical result or demonstrated change in its definition.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence beyond v1's constructed task suite and qualitative overriding examples through VQA transfer, controlled overriding comparisons, and robustness and efficiency analyses. Seed reporting, evaluator instructions, and visualization pseudocode improve auditability. Removing the overriding failure example and multi-layer t-SNE sweep reduces some transparency, and the new overriding scores measure attempted adherence rather than answer correctness. Nevertheless, the broader validation and clearer documentation substantially improve the paper's evidential support and assessability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research despite the changed title and substantial reorganization. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable matching.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds VQA transfer results, quantitative task-overriding evaluations, computational measurements, and instruction-noise experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original cross-modal transfer experiments on three VLMs, LLM-to-VLM transfer, instruction ensembling, and analyses of internal representations, including appendix ablations.

results.title: Vision-Language Models Create Cross-Modal Task Representations

C1.justification: The central claims of scalable, non-myopic RL-based BO and improved optimization performance remain. v2 broadens the contribution framing toward a modular framework accommodating alternative encoders, RL algorithms, and initialization methods, while explicitly characterizing its learning as model-based.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of SAASBO's advantages on additive, unimodal functions, interprets the new dimensional and encoder results, and discusses when computational overhead is justified by expensive function evaluations. These substantially expand applicability and tradeoff discussion; the earlier planning-delusion explanation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds per-iteration computational requirements, rollout timeout and Monte Carlo settings, and approximately 1600-second runtime information for 30-D Ackley. Existing hardware, hyperparameters, preprocessing, fallback details, and baseline access links are largely retained. Implementation details for the newly evaluated SAASBO baseline are not supplied.

E1.justification: Section 4.1 adds 30-dimensional versions of Ackley, Levy, Rosenbrock, and Sum Squares beyond v1's 2-D, 5-D, and 8-D synthetic coverage. This substantially extends the dimensional conditions tested. The three HPO-B search spaces remain unchanged.

E2.justification: SAASBO is newly evaluated in the retained synthetic and HPO comparisons, as confirmed by Figure 2 and v2's Figure 4. Conversely, Figure A2 removes the TuRBO comparator present in v1's sparse-initialization experiment. The existing UCB, EI, PI, and EARL-BO curves remain there.

E3.justification: Retained benchmark ranges, initialization sizes, regret metric, and Table 1 hyperparameters remain unchanged. New analyses introduce an attention-only control, additional one- and seven-step horizons, and a timing protocol specifying 1000 Monte Carlo iterations and a 3600-second timeout for rollout.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds an Attention-DeepSets versus attention-only comparison at two horizons and extends horizon analysis to 1, 3, 5, and 7 steps. New Appendix C examines computational overhead and dimensional scaling. The earlier learning-rate, sparse-data, and training-convergence analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly identifies Figure 2's lines as ten-run means and its shading as one standard deviation. v1 already reports ten repetitions and discusses standard deviations, but does not specify this band convention there. This is a reporting clarification, not evidence of increased replication.

E6.justification: New results show EARL-BO leading all four 30-D comparisons, while added SAASBO results outperform it on lower-dimensional Sum Squares. Figures A5–A6 add encoder and horizon findings. Table 2 reports 840 ± 147 seconds for three-step EARL-BO versus rollout exceeding 3600 seconds. Figure A2 removes TuRBO's result.

M1.justification: The Attention-DeepSets encoder, PPO objectives, GP virtual environment, TuRBO initialization, layer freezing, and fallback procedure are retained. Algorithm 1 preserves the procedure. Describing the framework as modular and Dyna-style, with optional alternative components, does not establish a changed implemented method.

P1.justification: The principal section sequence and much existing exposition remain. Focused rewrites shorten the abstract, clarify modular and model-based terminology, and expand the algorithm explanation. A new L2O subsection, computational-cost appendix, and impact statement extend the existing structure without wholesale reorganization.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with substantial figure and algorithm resizing. Figure 2 gains consolidated legends, new Figure 3 and Figures A5–A6 are added, and Table 2 presents runtimes. Figure A2 changes from logarithmic to linear scaling; the HPO figure moves from Figure 3 to Figure 4.

R1.justification: v2 adds a Learning to Optimize subsection discussing RIBBO, POM, and broader L2O research, expands coverage to SAASBO, and positions EARL-BO within model-based RL and Dyna-style learning. Additional acquisition-optimization and dataset-encoding references further expand its relationship to prior work.

T1.justification: The GP equations, MDP formulation, reward definition, encoder equations, PPO losses, and parameter-freezing expressions retain their mathematical substance. Renumbering and notation cleanup introduce no new derivation, assumption, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for v1's scalability and architectural claims through 30-D benchmarks, SAASBO comparisons, encoder and horizon ablations, and explicit runtime analysis. These additions make both effectiveness and computational tradeoffs more assessable. Missing SAASBO implementation details and removal of TuRBO from Figure A2 limit the revision, but the overall gain in empirical support and practical transparency is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EARL-BO and retain matching methods and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including v2's new Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds 30-dimensional benchmarks, encoder and horizon ablations, and computational-cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original optimization experiments on four synthetic functions and three HPO-B search spaces, together with learning-rate, sparse-data, and training-convergence analyses.

results.title: EARL-BO: Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Step Lookahead, High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization

C1.justification: V2 removes the introduction's claim to consider BPs with MLLMs 'for the first time in the literature.' The main contributions and central claim that poor performance reflects broader reasoning limitations rather than synthetic imagery alone remain intact.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning color/layout sensitivity, structural versus surface-level recognition, the insufficiency of model scaling alone, and human evidence for dataset solvability. New Appendix A substantially discusses applicability beyond BPs, fine-grained perception and relationships to other AVR settings. These extend v1's explanations of model failures.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents stratified sampling from test splits, fixed negative-label selection with manual checking, image-resizing details and human-study instructions. These disclosures do not establish changes to the original samples. V2 explicitly announces code availability alongside data, while v1's prospective MIT-license statement disappears.

E1.justification: The four underlying BP datasets are retained, but v2 adds a human-solving population and multiple-choice concept selection across all four datasets. These substantially extend population and task coverage. The grayscale and square-image RWR variants reuse existing problems rather than introducing new concepts.

E2.justification: V2 substantially expands the evaluated systems. Figure 10 adds GPT-4o mini, Gemini 1.5 Flash and larger InternVL2/LLaVA variants; Tables 2–3 include InternVL2.5 variants and Qwen2VL 72B-Instruct. Appendix B also supplies a human benchmark absent from v1.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a 30-participant open-ended study with manual adjudication, multiple-choice testing with varying candidate counts, and model-size comparisons using Direct and Descriptive strategies. New RWR preprocessing includes grayscale conversion and square cropping, with 512×512 panels and 1024×763 matrices. The original benchmark sample counts are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds color/cropping ablations, sensitivity to the number of candidate concepts, and model-scaling analyses in Appendices C–D. Appendix B examines human solvability, problem difficulty and human/model coverage. V1's evaluator-validation, strategy-overlap and synthetic-versus-real-world case analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V2 adds human-score variability reporting through a histogram and boxplot, mean/median/range summaries, and independent human-rater agreement reporting of 94.5% (Appendix B). Neither version reports repeated-model-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: All 320 entries in v1 Table 1 are retained in v2 Table 4. Substantial new results include human performance averaging 39.2/60, image-variant scores, concept-selection accuracies and scaling results. For example, Table 2 reports Phi-3.5-Vision solving 16 grayscale problems versus 1 under the original input condition. Figure 23 changes the aggregate RWR caption from 23 to 22, matching the unchanged plot, although Section 5 and Appendix G still state 23.

M1.justification: V2 adds a constrained concept-selection procedure in which the model chooses among 2, 4, 8 or 16 supplied concepts. This is a limited input/output adaptation; the seven original generation strategies, four-model voting evaluator and Bongard-RWR generation algorithm remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 substantially condenses the abstract and reorganizes the narrative and appendices. Detailed binary-classification discussion moves from Section 5 to Appendix C, prompts move from Appendix A to Appendix I, and evaluation, dataset and coverage material are integrated into a new appendix structure.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, replaces examples in Figure 1, and redisplays original results through a compact generation table and new binary/strategy-effect plots. The complete original table moves to Appendix C. Human-study, concept-selection and scaling displays are added, while existing appendix graphics are largely retained and relocated.

R1.justification: Section 2 replaces the assertion that MLLMs had not tackled BPs with explicit positioning against concurrent work by Wüst et al., emphasizing synthetic-versus-real-world comparisons. It also adds Perception Test and KiVA. Appendix A substantially expands connections to ConceptARC, VCog-Bench, MindSet: Vision and cognitive-assessment research.

T1.justification: The BP formalization and dataset-generation mathematics are substantively unchanged, and neither version develops formal theorems or proofs. Newly specified candidate counts and negative-label indexing concern evaluation procedures rather than theoretical developments.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked human validation of its new benchmark. V2's 30-person study establishes that every RWR problem was solved by at least one participant, addressing a central uncertainty about dataset solvability. Color/cropping controls and broader model comparisons also test alternative explanations for poor performance. The convenience sample, different human/model grading procedures and unresolved aggregate-count inconsistencies limit some comparisons, but the additions substantially strengthen the paper's empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Bongard Problems study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original human-study, image-variant, concept-selection and model-scaling results in Section 5 and Appendices B–D.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments with eight MLLMs across four BP datasets in Table 1, together with evaluator-validation and problem-coverage analyses in the appendices.

results.title: Reasoning Limitations of Multimodal Large Language Models. A Case Study of Bongard Problems

C1.justification: The central contributions remain curated training data, a scaled MAE-G/8, and intermediate-block selection through biological probes. v2 extends the abstract's best-performance claim to compound–gene activity prediction and emphasizes efficient use of experimental data, while preserving the original methodological contribution and scaling claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning unsuccessful DINO training, the resulting allocation of compute to MAEs, and the unresolved potential of other SSL and fine-tuning recipes. It attributes lower external-data recall to assay differences and variability, and interprets continued MAE reconstruction-loss improvement as suggesting further scaling potential. These materially expand the interpretation and qualification of the findings.

D1.justification: v2 announces inference, visualization and benchmarking code plus CA-MAE-S/16 weights, and supplies RxRx3-core access information. Appendices A.9 and A.11 add DINO hyperparameters and CellProfiler extraction, aggregation and missing-data details. Existing MAE hyperparameters are retained. Some disclosure remains inconsistent: Section 6 calls the baseline CellProfiler 4, whereas A.11 specifies version 2.2.0.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on external JUMP-CP images covering 7,976 gene knockouts and introduces compound–gene activity prediction on RxRx3-core, containing 735 genetic knockouts and 1,674 compounds across eight concentrations. These extend both acquisition conditions and task requirements beyond v1's genetic-perturbation evaluations. Existing RxRx1, RxRx3 and Anax coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds CellProfiler comparisons on JUMP-CP and RxRx3-core, a random baseline for compound–gene prediction, and microscopy-trained DINO models, including an MAE initialized variant in Appendix A.9. It removes the ImageNet WSL ViT-L/16 comparator from the original whole-genome comparison. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparison approaches while changing membership in the retained benchmark.

E3.justification: Whole-genome recall changes from four database-specific columns to an aggregate over five databases, including Signor. New evaluations introduce PCA-based alignment, four-crop well averaging, concentration-dependent compound–gene ranking, and exclusion of 4,749 wells lacking CellProfiler features for all RxRx3-core models. Original MAE training budgets and probing settings remain unchanged. Appendix A.6 still lists only the original four relationship databases.

E4.justification: v2 adds an explicit generalization test across laboratories and assay protocols, examines trimming and compound concentration in the new prediction task, and diagnoses unsuccessful DINO training through loss curves and scratch-versus-fine-tuning results (Figure 7 and Table 6). The original Anax cell-condition checks and FLOP correlations are retained, with the latter moved from Appendix A.9 to A.10.

E5.justification: Beyond v1's existing permutation and replicate-consistency tests, v2 introduces mean and standard deviation over three null-sampling seeds for whole-genome recall, uncertainty reporting for JUMP-CP, and standard deviations and error bars over 100 benchmark seeds for RxRx3-core. It also reports improvement z-scores. These quantify benchmark sampling variability; they do not establish repeated model training.

E6.justification: v2 replaces database-specific whole-genome table entries with aggregate recall and adds substantial new results. JUMP-CP StringDB recall is 0.235 for trimmed MAE-G/8 versus 0.191 for CellProfiler; RxRx3-core mean average precision is 0.309 ± 0.015 for trimmed MAE-G/8 versus 0.290 ± 0.017 for the previous MAE-L/8. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over corresponding v1 experiments. The stated 42% gain concerns z-scores, 3.77 to 5.38. Original probing and KS/CVM results are largely retained.

M1.justification: The proposed Phenoprints-16M curation procedure, MAE architectures and losses, and linear-probe selection of intermediate blocks remain unchanged. The newly reported DINO training attempts are comparison experiments, rather than changes to the proposed MAE method.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around data efficiency, replacing the original contribution bullets with a developed narrative. Related-work topics are reordered, the discussion is expanded, and dedicated external-evaluation, compound–gene benchmarking, limitations/reproducibility and impact sections restructure the paper.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, moves the model inventory into the appendix, restructures the whole-genome table, and adds benchmark tables, a concentration plot and a DINO loss plot. The original replicate-similarity distribution figure is removed, while retained figures are resized or relocated. Figure 1's caption loses its detailed model-to-bar mapping and ends after introducing that mapping.

R1.justification: The principal positioning relative to Kraus, Celik and intermediate-layer research remains intact. v2 adds contextual references on language-model data curation, mechanistic interpretability, alternative SSL/fine-tuning approaches, CellProfiler and RxRx3-core, while removing some broad biological foundation-model background. This updates and extends the context without fundamentally redefining the claimed relationship to prior work.

T1.justification: The block-selection definition and perturbation-consistency, permutation-p-value, KS and CVM equations remain unchanged. v2 adds no original theorem, proof or substantive derivation; its discussion of MAE–contrastive relationships cites existing work.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of validation on data from other laboratories and direct compound–gene prediction. JUMP-CP and RxRx3-core results, additional comparison methods, sampling uncertainty and documented DINO failures make the conclusions better supported; code and small-model access information also improves reproducibility. Aggregate recall loses database-level detail, and the 42% wording requires qualification as a z-score comparison, but these reporting weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite substantial reformatting and added evaluations in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds JUMP-CP evaluation, RxRx3-core compound–gene prediction, and microscopy DINO training experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original MAE training experiments, RxRx1 and Anax linear probes, whole-genome RxRx3 benchmarks, and supplementary cell-condition and scaling analyses.

results.title: ViTally Consistent: Scaling Biological Representation Learning for Cell Microscopy

C1.justification: The central gradient-bottleneck and LASER contribution claims remain. The abstract and introduction extend the reported scale from 2.2B to 7.7B parameters and add a fine-tuning benefit claim. The conclusion also moderates 'fix' to 'alleviate' when describing the gradient problem.

C2.justification: Appendix A.5 adds a substantive explanation linking fewer training spikes to reduced gradient saturation and conjectured residual-like behavior during strong self-attention. Section 4.3 newly interprets temperature and QK-normalization effects and attributes poorer per-dimension-temperature results to hyperparameters tuned without that component. These explanations extend the original gradient-magnitude interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 adds architecture and training-budget details for the larger and differential models, a per-dimension-scaling implementation reference, and reconstruction-test details: 4,800 cached tensors of shape (1024, 8, 256), four TPUv5 chips, and sixteen A100s. The core JAX implementation and original hyperparameter search tables are retained.

E1.justification: The represented datasets and tasks remain C4, the existing downstream language tasks, Wikipedia/MLPerf BERT, ImageNet, and LibriSpeech. SuperGLUE fine-tuning uses tasks already evaluated in v1. ARC Easy disappears from the 2.2B table but remains in v2 Tables 6–7; the new experiments principally change models and procedures within retained coverage.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares LASER with standard attention. v2 adds evaluated temperature-tuned and per-dimension-temperature comparators in Table 2, QK-normalization and temperature variants in the vision/speech comparisons (Tables 4–5), and DiffTransformer against LASER+DiffTransformer in Table 7.

E3.justification: v2 introduces 7.7B models trained on 44B tokens, 2.2B DiffTransformer models trained on 24B tokens, ten-epoch SuperGLUE fine-tuning, and BF16 training and reconstruction tests. These are additional protocols, not replacements for the retained C4 setup. The OPTList evaluation protocol is removed, and vision/speech reporting expands beyond validation results to training and test results.

E4.justification: v2 adds temperature and normalization ablations, a parameter-versus-loss power-law fit, DiffTransformer compatibility tests, and Appendix A.5 analyses of early training spikes, BF16 training, and numerical reconstruction on TPUs and GPUs. The original depth/MLP and LAMB analyses remain, while the OPTList comparison is removed.

E5.justification: Appendix A.4 and Table 10 newly report downstream means and standard deviations across five checkpoints. This is a focused uncertainty-reporting addition, not evidence of five independent training runs or increased seed counts. The primary vision/speech experiments retain their five-initialization reporting.

E6.justification: v2 revises the downstream and vision/speech results and removes OPTList scores. For example, ViT validation errors change from 0.2527/0.2412 in v1's text to 0.2532/0.2417 in v2 Table 4 for Standard/LASER. New LASER/comparator averages include 53.97/52.53 for 7.7B models and 51.52/50.59 for DiffTransformer variants; these use new experimental settings. Table 1 and BERT results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The central LASER formula, stabilization trick, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Section 4.4 adds LASER+DiffTransformer, applying the exponential/logarithmic transformation separately to two attention branches before their weighted subtraction. This is a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the introduction, method exposition, and original experimental prose remain. Targeted rewrites update the abstract, related work, and experiment summaries. New experimental and appendix subsections, acknowledgements, and an impact statement are added, while the standalone limitations section is removed.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Table 2 is reoriented and expanded, Figure 2's panels are stacked, and vision/speech curves are replaced by multi-metric tables. New scaling and stability figures appear. v1 Figure 4 is retained as v2 Figure 5 in Appendix A.3, rather than deleted.

R1.justification: Related work shifts substantially from efficient attention, sparse attention, and state-space models toward softmax sharpness, QK-normalization, and Lipschitz properties. v2 adds discussion of Veličković et al., Dehghani et al., and Kim et al., plus Differential Transformer elsewhere, while removing much of the Mamba, routing, Longformer, and context-parallelism discussion.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 corrects causal masking from multiplying logits by a binary mask to adding a mask with zero for permitted positions and negative infinity otherwise. This changes the mathematical specification without establishing a code change. Lemmas 3.1–3.2 and the Appendix A.2 proof remain substantively unchanged; the new residual-connection explanation is conjectural.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's empirical support through temperature and normalization controls (Tables 2, 4–5) and direct precision and stability checks (Appendix A.5). These address important gaps in attributing benefits to LASER and assessing practical reliability. Removed OPTList evidence, checkpoint-only uncertainty, a conjectural stability explanation, and inconsistencies between some Table 2 summaries and entries limit the gains, but the stronger controlled evaluation provides a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LASER attention. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial layout changes and relocation of training curves.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds larger-model evaluations, SuperGLUE fine-tuning, attention variants, and numerical-precision and training-stability experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original training and evaluation results for C4 language models, BERT, ImageNet ViT, and LibriSpeech Conformer, including architecture and optimizer ablations.

results.title: LASER: Attention with Exponential Transformation

C1.justification: The finding that intermediate encoder representations can compromise safety is retained. However, the abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the contribution from diagnosing this vulnerability to proposing L-PPO and claiming effective mitigation, theoretical improvement guarantees and preserved utility. These are substantive new claims beyond renaming the vulnerability ICET.

C2.justification: Beyond the retained OOD explanation, v2 explains disagreements between binary safety judgments and reward scores, discusses incoherent early-layer outputs and evaluator errors, and explicitly limits L-PPO to per-layer alignment. It also distinguishes partial improvements from failures and frames ICET as an architectural safety blind spot rather than a new jailbreak attack (Section 4.2, Appendices E-G).

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial implementation information absent from v1: LoRA rank 8, scaling 16 and dropout 0.05; Adam optimization; PPO epoch ranges; value-loss and adaptive-KL settings; PyTorch; and 2-4 NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPUs (Appendix F). It also supplies additional data-construction details and promises code, preprocessing scripts and aligned weights, without establishing their actual availability.

E1.justification: The original 100-pair dataset is retained as Custom Prompts (CP). v2 adds broader harmful-query categories and natural, generated and noisy image inputs through RedTeam/Jailbreak-V28K, plus AdvBench-COCO evaluation and HH-RLHF reward-model training. VQA-v2 and safe XSTest prompts introduce distinct utility and over-refusal tasks (Section 4.1, Appendices B-C and J-K).

E2.justification: v1 compares default inference with intermediate-layer inference without evaluating an alternative alignment method. v2 adds one explicit alignment comparator, supervised fine-tuning, against L-PPO and the original model using RedTeam-2K training and CP testing (Appendix L, Tables 21-22).

E3.justification: v2 adds alignment train/test protocols and LLaVA-NeXT experiments, supplements mean ASR and toxicity with reward scores, VQA accuracy and refusal metrics, and drops maximum-ASR/toxicity summaries. New procedures include blinded, shuffled human judging by three annotators assessing 200 outputs each, and string-matched refusal evaluation on 150 safe XSTest prompts (Appendices H and K).

E4.justification: v2 adds utility-preservation and over-refusal analyses, a reported value-loss-coefficient sensitivity search, and strong, partial and failed mitigation case studies (Table 3, Appendices F-G and J-K). Conversely, the separate Llama Guard 2 and 3 robustness checks in v1 Figures 4-5 are no longer reported.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports aggregation across three human annotators and inter-annotator agreement using Fleiss' kappa, 0.8916 (Appendix H). Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive mitigation, utility, refusal and human-rated results. For example, CP average ASR is 64.62% before alignment, 37.96% after L-PPO and 55.14% after SFT (Tables 2 and 21); human-rated CP ASR changes from 50.21% to 16.74% (Table 15). The reported original early-layer LLaVA-1.5 AASR also differs between versions: 49.995% in v1 Table 2 versus 75.38% in v2 Table 2. This unexplained baseline revision cannot establish a same-setting performance gain or loss.

M1.justification: The intermediate-layer projection procedure is retained and renamed ICET. The substantive addition is Layer-wise Clip-PPO: reward-guided optimization of the language backbone using a selected intermediate layer's embeddings, with clipped updates and KL regularization while freezing the image encoder and projector (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten around ICET and mitigation. Background becomes a broader related-work and research-gap section; methodology and experiments gain substantial internal structure; and a discussion section is introduced. The appendices are reorganized into dedicated datasets, metrics, limitations, implementation, analysis and theory sections.

P2.justification: The overview is redrawn to incorporate L-PPO (v1 Figure 1 becomes v2 Figure 2), and v2 adds a first-page demonstration and three-panel before/after results. v1 Table 1 becomes the expanded, color-coded v2 Table 4. New human-evaluation, utility and SFT tables substantially change the presentation, while retained examples and Llama 3.2 plots are relocated or regrouped.

R1.justification: The research positioning expands from cross-modal attacks and LLM layer analysis to dynamic early exiting, preference optimization and multimodal RLHF, with new discussions of works by Bakhtiarnia, Xu, Uzkent, Schulman, Rafailov and Sun. The new gap analysis and discussion also connect the vulnerability to multilayer feature fusion, including DenseConnector (Sections 1-2 and 5).

T1.justification: v1 provides forward-pass and metric equations without policy-improvement theory. v2 adds MDP definitions, a policy-improvement lemma, a cited performance bound and an argument extending it to L-PPO (Section 3.3), together with GAE derivations and a formal expected-regret interpretation of ICET (Appendices I and M).

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's narrow 100-pair exploratory evidence through broader evaluation, an implemented mitigation, an SFT comparison and blinded human validation. Utility controls address an important alternative explanation: VQA accuracy changes only from 48.73 to 48.23, while average safe-prompt refusal falls from 0.047 to 0.040 (Tables 3 and 20). Unexplained baseline revisions and the unsupported leap from a conditional policy bound to guaranteed safety improvement remain weaknesses, but the expanded empirical validation and implementation disclosure provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same intermediate-image-encoder safety vulnerability. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title, terminology and substantially expanded scope.

after.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original vulnerability and alignment experiments, including LLaVA-NeXT results, human evaluations, visual-question-answering utility and over-refusal measurements.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix E report original layer-wise attack-success rates, toxicity scores and generated responses for LLaVA-1.5 and Llama 3.2.

results.title: Layer-wise Alignment: Examining Safety Alignment Across Image Encoder Layers in Vision Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same central claims: compute-optimal scaling laws occur in world modeling and BC, tokenizer compression affects their coefficients, and architecture changes the optimal model/data allocation. The added experiments support these existing headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 2.2 adds substantive arguments for treating loss as a performance proxy, attributes earlier weak-correlation findings to finite-data and overfitting settings, and discusses how improved prediction could reflect richer behavioral and environmental understanding. Appendix A.1 newly explains that 256-token reconstructions miss details such as enemy health bars. The general limitations in Section 6 remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 supplements the existing hyperparameter tables with previously undisclosed learning-rate sweep procedures and tokenizer-resolution selection rationale. Appendices C–D document RT-1 preprocessing, the VQVAE implementation source, 40,000 tokenizer updates with batches of 128, transformer settings, and video-evaluation procedures. These are substantial documentation additions, without establishing that the original experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: v2 adds real-world robotic manipulation through the RT-1 dataset, extending the embodied experiments beyond Bleeding Edge. It also analyzes previously published BC results for NetHack, Bank Heist, Breakout and Space Invaders, explicitly as a meta-analysis rather than new environment runs. The Bleeding Edge, Shakespeare and BookCorpus coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The existing architecture comparisons and fitting-method comparisons are retained. No competing method is newly evaluated against the authors' models in a matched comparison. The Tuyls et al. meta-analysis supplies evidence about loss and return, rather than adding a baseline to the authors' experiments.

E3.justification: New protocols include the RT-1 sweep over five tokenization resolutions and 0.08M–0.99M-parameter models, with two-step sequences and four action dimensions discretized into 500 buckets. Appendix D adds evaluation using 1,024 ten-second generated videos and FVD/LPIPS across checkpoints. The retained Bleeding Edge splits and tabulated training settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 adds a direct robotics sensitivity study of whether tokens per image affect scaling coefficients, supplementing the retained language analogies. Section 2.2 and Appendix D add analyses testing whether pre-training loss tracks online return and world-model video quality.
