These substantially expand the evidence addressing mechanism and proxy validity.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports three repeated runs per VQVAE for the new RT-1 analysis and displays individual coefficient estimates in Figure 12. v1 has no corresponding replication analysis. This is a localized addition; confidence intervals and significance tests are not added, and increased repetition of the retained experiments is not established.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original scaling and extrapolation findings are retained. New results include RT-1 example model-size exponents of 0.56 at 16 tokens and 0.65 at 256 tokens (Figure C.2), loss-return correlations from -0.98 to -0.94 (Figure 2), and correlations of 0.83 with FVD and 0.77 with LPIPS (Figure 3). Figure 1 newly labels the BC-Token data exponent as 0.78, conflicting with the retained 0.68 in Table 1.

M1.justification: The existing WM-Token, BC-Token and BC-CNN procedures and scaling-fit methods are retained. The added RT-1 experiments introduce VQVAE image tokenizers, whereas the original embodied experiments use VQGANs. This is a limited tokenizer-component adaptation, without redesigning the transformer learning procedure.

P1.justification: Related Work becomes Background, with separate related-work and performance-proxy subsections. The extended related-work appendix is incorporated into the main text, and the remaining appendices are reorganized and relabeled. There are local rewrites and expanded explanations, but most existing methodological, results and concluding prose is preserved.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 2, 3, 12, C.1 and C.2 and Table C.1, moves the gameplay montage from appendix Figure 9 to main-text Figure 5, and adds coefficient annotations to retained plots. A new Microsoft report format changes typography, spacing, headers, footers and figure placement throughout. Some new annotations contain errors, including the exponent 85 in Figure 11.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hussenot et al. (2021) and Li et al. (2024) when discussing weak relationships between validation loss and policy performance. It also explicitly claims first-time study of world-model scaling and develops its relationship to Tuyls et al. through the meta-analysis. Most cited works and the broader positioning are retained.

T1.justification: Equation 6 corrects the model- and data-size scaling exponents from -a and -b to a and b. A new footnote derives a + b = 1 from C = 6ND, although its final proportionality is incorrectly written as N proportional to D^(1-a). The remaining mathematical framework is retained.

improvement.justification: v1 supported the tokenizer effect through two different Bleeding Edge setups and language analogies, while largely motivating pre-training loss as a convenient intermediate signal. v2 substantially strengthens both foundations through a repeated, five-resolution robotics study and empirical loss-versus-quality analyses, including direct measurements on its world models. These additions improve the support and generality of the central conclusions. New exponent-label errors, notably Figures 1 and 11, reduce reporting precision but do not outweigh these substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and retain matching core methods and experiments. The complete documents, including their figures, tables, equations and appendices, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds RT-1 world-modeling experiments and measurements relating world-model loss to generated-video quality.

before.justification: v1 reports original Bleeding Edge scaling experiments, an 894M-parameter extrapolation experiment, and language-modeling analyses in Section 5 and Appendix C.

results.title: Scaling Laws for Pre-training Agents and World Models

C1.justification: The central claims remain offline task-agnostic world modeling, zero-shot visual-goal planning without reward models or inverse models, and generalization to unseen configurations. The introduction retains the 56% LPIPS and 45% planning-improvement claims. Expanded evaluations support these existing contributions rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses difficulty obtaining sufficient state-action coverage in complex environments and proposes exploration and model updates. New ablation interpretations explain future-frame leakage without causal masking and benefits from richer training data. Section 3.2 replaces v1's gradient-terrain explanation for GD's weakness with a proposal to investigate regularization.

D1.justification: Appendices A.8–A.9 add substantial specifications: transformer depth, attention heads, parameter count, feature dimensions, image resizing, frame skips, trajectory lengths and timing hardware/settings. Section 4.2 clarifies offline, reward-free baseline training and MPC evaluation. Code/models change from promised release to reported open-source availability. Some details remain inconsistent: Table 11 lists five-step Rope/Granular trajectories while Appendix A.1 still states 20 steps.

E1.justification: v2 adds Reacher, requiring a two-joint arm's entire pose to match a target image (Appendix A.1; Tables 1–2). This is a focused extension into articulated-arm pose control. The five existing environments and three generalization families remain; Maze is a shortened name for PointMaze.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain IRIS, DreamerV3, TD-MPC2, AVDC/AVDC-AC, R3M, ResNet and DINO CLS. Reacher extends existing comparator sets. The new masking and decoder-loss variants are controlled DINO-WM ablations, rather than newly introduced baseline methods.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands the experimental design with PushT dataset-size sweeps, history-length/masking controls, decoder-loss controls and a timing protocol using CEM with 100 samples and 10 optimization steps. Reacher uses 3,000 training trajectories and 50 evaluation instances. Appendix A.1 also revises Wall's reported training count from 2,000 to 1,920 trajectories, without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix A.4 tests how performance depends on training-data quantity, whether causal masking prevents failures as history increases, and whether reconstruction-loss backpropagation helps the predictor. These provide substantial new analyses of data dependence and design choices beyond v1's retained encoder, planner and generalization comparisons.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The existing evaluation practice of 50 navigation/pushing instances and 10 deformable-object instances remains; additional result rows do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds Reacher results, including success rates of 0.92 for DINO-WM and 0.64 for DreamerV3, plus substantial ablation and timing results (Tables 5–7 and 10). DreamerV3's PushT score in Table 1 changes from 0.04 to 0.30; DINO-WM remains 0.90, while new ablation tables separately report 0.92. Existing generalization and planner scores are retained, and relocated LPIPS/SSIM results differ only by rounding.

M1.justification: Both versions use frozen DINOv2 patch features, an action-conditioned causal transformer, latent prediction loss, an independently trained optional decoder and CEM/MPC planning. v2 clarifies removal of the transformer's tokenization layer and provides architecture details; it does not establish a changed proposed procedure. Decoder-loss and masking variants are ablation controls.

P1.justification: The abstract and several explanatory passages are tightened, Section 4.1's environment descriptions are condensed, and metric discussion is redistributed between main text and appendix. The standalone reproducibility statement disappears, the ethics statement becomes an impact statement, and acknowledgments are added. The overall argument and main section sequence remain.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main text and references, redesigns the environment montage, and expands/reorders benchmark tables. The full LPIPS/SSIM table and planning-comparison visualizations move to the appendix. New ablation/timing tables and an all-six-environment trajectory figure accompany substantial resizing, relabeling and relocation of existing displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Chain-of-Thought Predictive Control, Diffusion World Model, Manipulate by Seeing, Embed to Control and DeepMind Control Suite. These supplement existing context and benchmark attribution; the positioning against task-dependent and pixel-generative world models remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation, latent-model definitions, losses and planning equations are mathematically unchanged. The new 'Scaling Laws' subsection presents empirical trends, not a new formal law, derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility by directly testing previously untested masking and decoder-loss choices, measuring data dependence and computational cost, and documenting architecture and preprocessing. These address important evidential and implementation gaps in v1. The gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including unexplained 0.90 versus 0.92 PushT reference scores and conflicting trajectory lengths; uncertainty reporting remains absent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DINO-WM research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting and relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Reacher evaluations, controlled ablations, timing measurements and planning visualizations.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated planning, generalization, reconstruction-quality and planner-comparison results across five environment suites, including appendix results.

results.title:
DINO-WM: World Models on Pre-trained Visual Features enable Zero-shot
  Planning

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the HSPI identification objective and the two proposed methods. The headline claims of 83.9%–100% white-box accuracy and up to three times random-guess performance in black-box settings remain; the new experiments primarily broaden their supporting evidence.

C2.justification: Sections 6.1–6.2 add interpretations concerning applicability to optimized serving, label merging as a scalability solution, and acceptable query costs. Section 4.4 also explains random-word prompting as encouraging closer top-k logits and avoiding negative infinity. Existing equivalence-class, batch-size, and black-box limitations largely survive in Appendices E–F.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 substantially expands the previously underspecified LLM sampling pipeline: prompt template, NLTK word source, three versus eight leading words, 256 queries per class, top-256 logits, and four responses per SVM sample. New tables specify device counts and parallelism configurations. The abstract advertises a code repository, although the conclusion still promises future code and logit-data release. These disclosures do not establish changes to the original experiments.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from direct model-inference experiments on NVIDIA hardware to optimized SGLang cloud serving and distributed, cross-vendor environments, including AMD MI300X and Amazon Inferentia. These additions substantially broaden the serving conditions and target hardware population; the original vision and random-word language tasks remain.

E2.justification: The HSPI-BI, HSPI-LD, and random-guess comparisons are retained without adding an evaluated external fingerprinting method. SGLang is a serving environment, vLLM is cited context, and the additional hardware configurations are identification targets rather than competing methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include 16-way GPU/precision/kernel/sharding classification in Table 6, distributed Llama-3.1-70B configurations in Table 10, and two-class merged-label evaluation in Table 12. Separately, v1 Table 1's RTX8000/H100 condition becomes RTX8000/A100 in v2 Table 8, although Section 5.2 still names H100. This is a reported setting inconsistency, not evidence establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D.3 newly tests whether merging software labels preserves GPU identification using the same samples as Table 6. The original batch-size and iteration sensitivity plots remain as Figure 7, while v1's illustrative DistillGPT2 border-request case in Figure 7 is removed. Proposed noise and bit-flip mitigations remain untested discussion.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seed-based uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional result tables retain this reporting practice.

E6.justification: The numerical values in v1 Tables 2–6 and Appendix A.2 are retained after renumbering. New v2 Tables 6, 10, and 11 report average accuracies of 0.991, 0.973, and 0.964, respectively; Table 12 reports 0.985 accuracy and F1. These are results under new conditions or prediction targets, not improvements over the retained 0.839 result under identical settings. The original DistillGPT2 response example is removed.

M1.justification: The core PGD border-input and SVM logit-distribution methods remain. Section 6.2 and Appendix D.3 add an adaptation that merges software configurations into GPU-only labels and trains a new classifier, changing the prediction target. Section 4.4 largely reorganizes model-specific adaptations already described in v1.

P1.justification: Background and methodology prose are extensively condensed and reorganized. A model-specific adaptation subsection is created, detailed settings move into Appendix B, limitations and robustness move into Appendices E–F, and much of the governance discussion moves into an Impact Statement. The discussion is substantially restructured around serving, scalability, and cost.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference paper, with widespread resizing and relocation of figures and tables. New displays include the summary matrix, Tables 6 and 10–12, and the prompt-template Figure 8. The original DistillGPT2 figure is removed, and the fine-tuning hyperparameter table becomes prose.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds explicit positioning against the side-channel work of Hua et al. and Gongye et al.; serving-framework and pricing citations are also added. The training-variability discussion and its Pham, Zhuang, and Alahmari references are removed, along with several convolution-background references. The central relationship to prior numerical fingerprinting work remains.

T1.justification: The access assumptions, equivalence-class concept, and mathematical content of Equations (1)–(6) remain. The newly explicit N(N−1)/2 classifier count explains the existing pairwise construction rather than introducing a substantive formal derivation, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important validation gap between v1's practical serving motivation and its simpler NVIDIA experiments. SGLang, distributed-model, and cross-vendor evaluations substantially strengthen deployment relevance, while label-merging evidence and detailed sampling instructions improve practical usability and reproducibility. The H100/A100 inconsistency and conflicting release statements are limited drawbacks. The additions remain principally white-box evidence and do not resolve the retained black-box limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HSPI work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained experiments can be matched across the substantial reformatting and relocation.

after.justification: The original empirical results remain, supplemented by SGLang serving, distributed and cross-vendor hardware experiments, and label-merging results in Section 6 and Appendix D.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A report original experiments involving vision models, LLMs, quantization formats, and GPU identification.

results.title: Hardware and Software Platform Inference

C1.justification: The central theoretical contribution shifts from linear-mapping identification up to an invertible matrix to permutation/scaling identification with nonlinear invertible mappings under revised premises. The abstract and introduction newly emphasize avoiding assumptions about instantaneous effects or sufficient variability. The conclusion expands the claimed climate discoveries from NAO/AAO to include MJO.

C2.justification: V2 adds arguments about applicability to finite grids and distinguishes latent recovery from graph recovery requiring Rhino's assumptions. It introduces explanations of baseline mode collapse, interprets precipitation/temperature teleconnections, and discusses isotropic kernels as a simplification justified by localized physical mechanisms. These substantially expand the interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents graph-density and DAG-generation rules, simulator architecture, burn-in, multivariate implementation and baseline adaptations, and irregular-factor generation. It changes the anonymous code-access disclosure to a named SPACY repository and revises hyperparameter documentation. However, v1's PyTorch 2.1, NVIDIA A10 and fixed 700-epoch disclosures disappear. Newly disclosed simulator details do not establish that existing experiments changed.

E1.justification: V2 adds two-variate synthetic experiments and expands the existing climate ensemble from temperature alone to temperature, precipitation and their cross-variate relationships. It also evaluates data generated with irregular, spatially warped factors. The four original univariate synthetic configurations remain.

E2.justification: CDSD, discussed but not evaluated in v1, joins the synthetic accuracy, scalability and spatial-factor comparisons in v2 (Figures 4, 5 and 8). The new multivariate comparison additionally evaluates TensorPCA-PCMCI alongside Mapped-PCMCI (Table 3). LEAP, TDRL and Linear-Response remain in the main comparisons.

E3.justification: The scalability experiment changes from linear to nonlinear spatial mapping. The main synthetic comparisons now report Rhino-based SPACY where v1 used SPACY-L for linear-SCM cases. Climate evaluation changes from a linear SCM with 25 latents and three-month lag to a nonlinear SCM with 50 latents and six-month lag; batch size changes from 100 to 500 and sparsity weight from 10 to 40 (v1 Table 1; v2 Table 2). These are reported setting changes, not evidence of same-setting performance gains.

E4.justification: V2 adds an over-specification sweep using D* + {0, 2, 5, 7, 10}, tests isotropic estimation of irregular spatial factors, and expands qualitative analysis to baseline spatial-recovery failures (Appendix D). V1's D* + 10 and Matérn-kernel ablations are retained and relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-run or five-seed averages and display error bars or ± values. V2 extends this existing practice to additional experiments; no changed uncertainty definition, increased repeated-run count, confidence-interval procedure or significance test is reported.

E6.justification: Figures 4–5 contain revised benchmark values and new CDSD results. New multivariate Table 3 reports, for linear SCM and linear mapping, F1 scores of 0.656 for SPACY, 0.334 for Mapped-PCMCI and 0.127 for TensorPCA-PCMCI. New Figure 14 reports irregular-factor F1 of 0.624 ± 0.12 and MCC of 0.889 ± 0.06. Climate outputs are replaced by multivariate graphs including MJO-related findings.

M1.justification: V2 implements multivariate SPACY using variate-specific spatial factors, encoders and decoder embeddings, followed by causal discovery over concatenated latent representations (Section 3.3; Appendix B.4). V1 leaves this extension as future work. The original nonlinear observation mapping, ELBO and linear/nonlinear SCM variants already existed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work and theoretical narrative are extensively revised. The linear variant and main-text ablations move into the appendices, which are reorganized into Theory, Implementation Details, Experimental Details and Additional Results. This is substantial rewriting and restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws benchmark plots, expands spatial-factor comparisons, and replaces the two climate subgraphs with a nine-panel multivariate display. It adds assumptions and multivariate-results tables and new robustness figures. Existing kernel and over-specification displays are retained under new locations and numbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds substantive positioning against dynamic causal modelling and newer identifiability and spatial-representation work, including Li, Lachapelle and Zhao. New Table 1 compares methodological assumptions, emphasizing SPACY's claimed weaker restrictions on latent dynamics. Additional real-analysis, tensor-PCA and climate references support the expanded research scope.

T1.justification: V2 revises linear SFP identifiability and replaces v1's invertible-matrix marginal-distribution theorem with a nonlinear theorem stated under equality of conditional observation distributions. It claims permutation/scaling recovery under explicit diffeomorphism, analyticity, shared-function-family and noise conditions, with new supporting lemmas and proofs (Appendix A.2). Appendix A.3 also formalizes Rhino's assumptions. The ELBO derivation is substantively retained.

improvement.justification: V2 closes important validation gaps: CDSD, identified as the closest approach in v1 but unevaluated there, is now tested, and irregular-factor experiments probe spatial-model mismatch. Multivariate discovery moves from future work to an implemented method with synthetic validation and a climate application. These gains substantially strengthen the evidence and demonstrated applicability. Some software/hardware and training-budget disclosures are lost; climate evidence remains qualitative, and the revised theory uses different premises rather than providing a straightforward strengthening of v1's marginal-distribution guarantee.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPACY research, despite the revised title and substantial expansion. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthetic and climate experiments, including multivariate results, expanded baseline comparisons and additional robustness tests.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic causal-discovery and representation-recovery results, runtime measurements, climate analyses and ablations.

results.title: Discovering Latent Causal Graphs from Spatiotemporal Data

C1.justification: V1's contribution list groups training data with architecture and model size as not qualitatively meaningful factors. V2 removes training data from that dismissal and presents objective as a crucial factor. The framework, superior consistency of SSL models, and dataset-dependent relationship with performance remain central claims.

C2.justification: V2 limits weak training-data effects to large, diverse datasets and mainly dataset size. Appendix I distinguishes convergence to specialized solutions from general representations. Appendix F explains local/global differences through fine-grained classes and acknowledges that sigma=0.4 partly captures global structure. Appendix H adds explanations for natural/non-natural subgroup differences.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents L2 feature normalization, expands model and dataset provenance, adds a source column to Table 2, and provides weight sources for Appendix I. It clarifies ImageNet validation-set evaluation and states that data accompany the existing code release. These disclosures do not establish that normalization or the original evaluation split actually changed.

E1.justification: The same 23 downstream evaluation datasets remain. Appendix I adds models pretrained for scene recognition on Places365, extending training-domain coverage beyond the original general-purpose model collection. Natural versus non-natural stratification reuses existing evaluation datasets.

E2.justification: The reported comparison-model roster changes: Table 2 replaces vit-large-patch14-clip-224.laion2b with barlowtwins-rn50. Appendix I adds matched ImageNet/Places365 comparisons using AlexNet, DenseNet161, ResNet18, and ResNet50. The PDFs do not establish whether the Table 2 revision reflects rerunning experiments or correcting the inventory.

E3.justification: V1 uses RBF CKA with sigma=0.4 and a 10,000-sample cap for its local analyses. V2 uses sigma=0.2 with up to 30,000 samples, retaining 10,000 for linear CKA (Appendix C). New protocols separately analyze natural/non-natural datasets and compare four architectures under ImageNet versus Places365 pretraining while controlling objective and architecture/size categories.

E4.justification: V2 substantially extends the existing sensitivity analyses with bootstrap checks of stimulus-sampling stability, natural/non-natural subgroup robustness, and a controlled training-domain comparison (Appendices C, H, I). Appendix F expands local/global metric validation, and the anchor analysis now examines the more localized sigma=0.2 setting.

E5.justification: Appendix C newly reports 500 bootstrap iterations for six anchor models, displaying sampling distributions for linear CKA on 10,000 images and RBF CKA on 30,000 images (Fig. 12). This adds uncertainty estimation for the central similarity measurements. The existing three-seed averaging of linear-probe accuracy remains unchanged.

E6.justification: New results include higher consistency among Places365-trained pairs, natural/non-natural subgroup differences, and local/global ranking reversals (Figs. 16, 19, 20). Fig. 3 replaces the 0.98 linear/RBF correlation at sigma=0.4 with 0.85 at sigma=0.2, under different settings. The linear/RSA consistency correlation also changes from 0.68 to 0.69 (v1 Fig. 12; v2 Fig. 15).

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the framework: extract representations, compute pairwise similarities, correlate similarity vectors across datasets, and examine correlation distributions. The revised kernel bandwidth and sampling budgets concern evaluation settings; newly documented normalization does not establish a methodological change.

P1.justification: V2 shortens the title, tightens prose, merges contribution bullets, updates affiliations, removes Author Contributions, and adds an Impact Statement. Appendix headings and explanations are expanded, but the main section sequence and most of the narrative remain recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column conference layout and extensively resizes and rearranges displays. Fig. 7 changes panel arrangement; Fig. 8 is condensed while v1's full plot survives as v2 Fig. 21. Tables are relocated or restructured, and new heatmaps, bootstrap plots, and controlled-comparison figures substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds Dwivedi and Roig and Borup et al. on similarity-based model selection, and engages Conwell et al. when motivating the training-domain analysis. Additional model/dataset references accompany expanded provenance, while discussion of formal metric requirements is shortened. The central positioning relative to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis remains.

T1.justification: The definitions of representations, similarity vectors, and cross-dataset correlation distributions remain mathematically equivalent. Neither version contains a theorem or proof that is added, removed, or substantively revised.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's central conclusions. Bootstrap checks and the more localized RBF analysis improve validation of sampling reliability and metric robustness (Appendices C, F). The ImageNet/Places365 comparison directly tests training-domain effects and corrects v1's overly broad dismissal of training data (Appendix I; Section 4.5). These gains outweigh the reduced readability of some smaller main-text figures, although model-attribute confounding still limits causal conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same similarity-consistency framework and corresponding empirical study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains the original empirical study and adds bootstrap, dataset-subgroup, and training-domain results in Appendices C, H, and I.

before.justification: V1 reports original representational-similarity analyses across 64 pretrained models and 23 datasets, linear-probe performance results, and supplementary sensitivity analyses.

results.title: Objective drives the consistency of representational similarity across datasets

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions broaden the central theoretical claim from linear/logistic two-expert models to general MoE with conditionally exponential-family distributions, characterized by projected mirror descent. The original direct-MD and SNR results become special cases. The empirical claim that EM can outperform GD remains.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability qualifications: Appendix A.2 explains that the projection set need not be convex and the required Pythagorean inequality is not automatic; Section 4.2 identifies stochastic/mini-batch guarantees as open; Appendix D.4 discusses combinatorial costs of deep/sparse EM. The earlier simplified best-case SNR interpretation is removed, while most original MIM discussion is retained.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies retained experiments as full-batch and documents the CIFAR-10 architecture, including 100-unit ReLU hidden layers and unit-row-norm initialization. Appendix D adds explicit standard-EM pseudocode alongside the retained Gradient EM/GD algorithms. These are useful documentation additions, but numerical learning rates, batch size, and inner-loop budgets remain unspecified.

E1.justification: Appendix C.1 adds grayscale CIFAR-10 object classification to the retained synthetic regression and original/inverted Fashion-MNIST evaluations. This is a limited domain extension within image classification; the proposed deep/sparse architectures are not separately evaluated.

E2.justification: The corresponding experiments retain EM, Gradient EM, and Gradient Descent, while Table 1 retains the single-logistic-expert controls. CIFAR-10 uses the same optimizer comparison set. Newly discussed methods such as EIM are not evaluated.

E3.justification: The new CIFAR-10 evaluation introduces mini-batch training for 50 epochs with five experts and nonlinear MLP gates/experts, substantially extending the earlier experimental configurations. Retained experiments are newly described as full-batch, which establishes disclosure rather than a setting change. Synthetic Figures 1–2 now extend to 100 iterations instead of 50, but the prose still specifies 50, leaving the actual revised budget unclear.

E4.justification: The Fashion-MNIST inversion controls and existing convergence/parameter-recovery analyses are retained. CIFAR-10 supplies another benchmark comparison, not a controlled ablation, sensitivity study, or robustness test.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages without error bars or significance tests. v2 adds error bars to Figures 1–3 and paired t-tests, reporting T-statistics at least 22 for synthetic results and at least 17 for Fashion-MNIST; CIFAR-10 also includes bars and a paired test. The retained 50/25-instance counts do not establish additional runs. The meaning of the error bars remains unspecified.

E6.justification: Table 2 accuracy/cross-entropy pairs change from 79.2%/0.801 to 78.5%/0.827 for EM, 65.7%/1.30 to 66.0%/1.29 for Gradient EM, and 61.9%/1.33 to 62.4%/1.30 for GD. Synthetic curves are revised and extended. Appendix C.1 adds CIFAR-10 accuracies of 41.6%, 37.4%, and 34.5%, respectively. These substantially expand reported results while retaining the optimizer ranking; Table 1 is unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 and Appendix D.4 introduce an EM-like formulation for deep and sparse MoE, using latent expert-selection sequences across layers and a greedy-path approximation to avoid combinatorial evaluation. This substantially extends the proposed procedure, although it is not experimentally validated. Classical EM and Gradient EM remain unchanged; the projected-MD correspondence is an analytical characterization.

P1.justification: The narrative is reorganized around general MoE followed by symmetric special cases. Much of v1's main convergence analysis moves into Appendix B, while the abstract, contributions, and discussion are rewritten. v2 also adds a contents section, notation guide, separate algorithms appendix, and revised symmetric-model terminology.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are redrawn with error bars and revised displays; synthetic plots extend their horizontal range, and Figure 1b changes from logarithmic to linear vertical scaling. v2 adds CIFAR-10 Figure 4 and an EM algorithm box, reformats existing pseudocode with line numbers, and relocates figures and tables.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion adds foundational Jacobs et al. work and EIM, clarifies earlier EM-for-MoE results and Makkuva et al.'s frozen-expert procedure, and adds sparse-MoE and mini-batch literature. Positioning relative to Kunstner et al. becomes more explicit. KKS22-to-KKS21 and several other reference changes identify the same works rather than new citations.

T1.justification: New Theorems 4.1–4.2 and Appendix A establish a conditional-exponential-family formulation, expected-KL projection characterization, and convergence bounds with regularity, average-convexity, and projection-inequality assumptions. The original symmetric-two-expert theory largely survives in Section 5 and Appendix B. The simplified parallel-vector SNR derivation in v1 Section 5.2 is removed.

improvement.justification: The new general-MoE analysis and explicit projection assumptions address v1's central restriction to symmetric two-expert guarantees, making the broader applicability substantially more assessable. CIFAR-10 adds evidence beyond the engineered two-expert examples, and uncertainty reporting strengthens empirical scrutiny. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses, including undefined error bars and the synthetic 50-versus-100-iteration inconsistency; the deep/sparse extension remains unvalidated.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EM-for-Mixtures-of-Experts study and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The original two-expert results can be matched across renaming, renumbering, and relocation in v2.

after.justification: Section 6 retains original empirical evaluations, and Appendix C.1 adds experiments on grayscale CIFAR-10.

before.justification: Section 6 reports original synthetic regression and Fashion-MNIST experiments, including convergence curves, parameter-recovery results, and classification scores.

results.title: Learning Mixtures of Experts with EM: A Mirror Descent Perspective

C1.justification: V2's abstract and conclusion explicitly extend the empirical claims to LLM fine-tuning, and its contribution statement emphasizes benefits across AdaGrad-based optimizers as well as Adam. The two central techniques, memory-scaling claims, convergence guarantees, and headline token-efficiency and memory benefits remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds hypotheses connecting momentum benefits to subspace noise, explains the grouping heuristic through architectural noise correlations, and attributes GaLore switching spikes to incompatible optimizer statistics. It discusses SFT's SVD runtime cost and activation/gradient memory bottlenecks, and qualifies the revised SM rate as requiring problem-parameter knowledge. Higher-order tensor projections become an explicit applicability limitation; the unresolved combined SNSM guarantee was already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: V2 adds a PyTorch implementation link and hardware, model identifiers, learning-rate grids, and timing configurations for new experiments. The existing optimizer pseudocode, memory-measurement listing, and core pretraining details largely persist or relocate to Appendix A. Some new documentation remains inconsistent: the CIFAR prose says no update gap, while Table 11 specifies g = 1000.

E1.justification: C4 pretraining and GLUE fine-tuning are retained. V2 adds LLaMA 7B supervised fine-tuning on UltraFeedback, CIFAR10/CIFAR100 image classification, and DiT-L/2 image-generation experiments. This substantially expands data and task coverage beyond v1's language experiments. The diffusion experiment's dataset is not identified.

E2.justification: V2 Table 8 adds reported pretraining comparisons with FLORA, LoRA, and ReLoRA. AdaGrad and AdaGradm join the main multi-scale comparison, although both existed in v1's ablations. Table 13 also adds Gaussian, OPCA, and Oja projection comparators. Adam-mini receives discussion but no corresponding reported experimental comparison.

E3.justification: V2 adds a fixed-1.3B-token batch-size sweep from 4 to 1024 alongside v1's retained fixed-step experiment, plus cross-scale fixed-subspace and longer-gap protocols. New SFT and vision experiments introduce distinct budgets and metrics. Table 3 changes the reported 350M AdaGradSNm/AdaGradmSN learning rate from 1 to 2. The main pretraining budgets otherwise persist.

E4.justification: V2 extends subset-size ablations to 130M, tests projection refresh schedules across model sizes, and investigates online/streaming subspace selection. Appendix C.3 and Figure 18 test whether the architectural grouping heuristic concentrates gradient noise. Fixed-token batch-size analyses address a control missing from v1. Existing clipping, rank-gap, and momentum/step-size ablations are retained, often relocated.

E5.justification: V2 Appendix B.11 introduces three-seed performance experiments with means and standard deviations in Tables 17–18, and discloses seed matching across comparisons. V1 estimates gradient-noise variance but does not report comparable training-run uncertainty. The new reporting does not establish that all retained results were rerun or averaged.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive results, including 1B AdaGradSNSM perplexity 13.96, UltraFeedback final perplexity 2.580 for rank-32 SNSM, vision scores, timings, and seed summaries. The 350M AdaGradSNm/AdaGradmSN entry changes from 16.99 at learning rate 1 to 17.14 at learning rate 2, so this is not a same-setting performance change. V2 Table 8 conflicts with Table 3 for 1B AdamSNSM (13.96 versus 14.05) and 350M GaLore (20.51 versus 18.95).

M1.justification: The core SN/SM updates and main SVD implementation remain unchanged; AdaGradSNSM already appeared in v1. However, v2 Appendix B.8 introduces online-PCA and Oja subspace-update variants that retain optimizer statistics during updates. These are limited procedural extensions to the existing momentum framework.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: optimizer background moves into Preliminaries, related work moves near the end, experimental setup moves to Appendix A, and several main-text ablations move into Appendix B. Contributions, interpretations, and future-work passages are rewritten, and the title changes.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, with substantial table restructuring and relocation. Figure 1 becomes a single panel on the first page; v2 adds an SN schematic, new analysis plots, and numerous experimental tables. The old noise histogram is retained as Figure 11, while Figure 3 gains a secondary axis showing noisy-coordinate fractions.

R1.justification: V2 substantively positions the methods against Adam-mini and AdaMeM, discusses second-order approaches including Shampoo, Sophia, and SOAP, and incorporates momentum and online-PCA literature. It also removes v1's citation and disclosure identifying the preliminary Subset-Norm workshop version. These changes extend and revise the relationship to closely related research.

T1.justification: V1 Theorem 2's SM guarantee uses eta = 1/(alpha sqrt(T)); v2 Theorem 4.1 uses a capped, noise-dependent step size and obtains an O(1/T) deterministic term with an O(sigma/sqrt(T)) stochastic term. Appendix D revises the derivation and removes its separate bounded-variance expectation bound. The Subset-Norm theorem and Appendix E proof remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central efficiency and robustness claims. Table 9 adds measured runtimes and realistic peak memory; Table 17 controls total data when varying batch size, and Tables 17–18 report three-run variability. These address important gaps in v1's token-based speed evidence and fixed-step batch analyses. Added SFT and vision experiments broaden validation. Conflicting values in Tables 3 and 8 and inconsistent CIFAR settings weaken specific new results, but do not outweigh these substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Subset-Norm and Subspace-Momentum research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison despite the changed title and extensive reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds UltraFeedback fine-tuning, vision evaluations, runtime measurements, and repeated-seed analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original LLaMA pretraining experiments, GLUE fine-tuning results, optimizer ablations, memory measurements, and gradient-noise analyses.

results.title: Lean and Mean Adaptive Optimization via Subset-Norm and Subspace-Momentum with Convergence Guarantees

C1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the contribution from ARC abstract reasoning to few-shot learning across ARC and BBH, including a new claim of a 7.3-percentage-point BBH improvement. The emphasis shifts toward limitations of ICL and model adaptability. v1's overall state-of-the-art ensemble claim is dropped, while the narrower open-source neural ARC comparison remains.

C2.justification: v2 explains why shared adapters may help BBH but hurt ARC, hypothesizes benefits for structural patterns and limitations for sequential computation, and discusses the semi-private decline as possible distribution shift. It extends leakage concerns to BBH and removes v1's hardware-based submission barrier and promised future uncertainty analysis. These substantially revise applicability and limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix F adds BBH hyperparameter search spaces, training-step budgets, evaluation implementation information, libraries, and A100 runtime; a separate BBH code link is supplied. Table 6 newly identifies preferred ARC learning rates by model size. Conversely, v1's disclosure of approximately 600,000 generated fine-tuning tasks is omitted, without evidence that the underlying dataset changed.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates ARC visual-grid reasoning only. v2 adds all 27 BIG-Bench Hard tasks across 23 task types and an ARC semi-private hidden-task evaluation, substantially expanding both task requirements and evaluation populations. The original 80 ARC development tasks are identical across versions.

E2.justification: ARC Table 1 adds reported comparisons with OpenAI o1 preview, DeepSeek r1, and OpenAI o3 while retaining the earlier comparison rows. BBH adds a zero-shot reference and new permutation/loss controls. E2E and Direct I/O are matching comparators, and the QLoRA comparison survives in Appendix C.2.

E3.justification: The new BBH evaluation introduces Llama 3.1-8B, ten demonstration examples per task with the remaining examples held out, 40 demonstration shuffles, rank-64 LoRA, and greedy decoding with custom answer extraction. Semi-private ARC testing adds an external evaluation procedure. The original ARC development set and pass@2 scoring remain.

E4.justification: Sections 5.3–5.4 and Appendix F add BBH ablations of example permutations, training losses, and adapter sharing, plus task-specific gains and failures. The semi-private ARC result adds a generalization check. Existing ARC analyses remain, including the QLoRA result moved from the main figure to Appendix C.2.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports no comprehensive standard-error analysis. v2 reports BBH averages over five demonstration-selection seeds, identifies seeds 42–46, and provides per-method standard errors in Table 7. This introduces substantive uncertainty reporting, although corresponding ARC uncertainty estimates remain absent and no increase in ARC run counts is established.

E6.justification: New results include BBH accuracies of 50.5% for ICL, 57.8% for TTT, and 59.8% for shared TTT, plus 47.5% on semi-private ARC. Most matched ARC results remain unchanged. Table 1 changes the ensemble entry from 61.9% to 62.8%, but v2's abstract, caption, and prose still say 61.9%, leaving that revision unresolved. Section 4.6 corrects the original prose baseline from 39.3% to 18.3%, matching both versions' tables.

M1.justification: The core leave-one-out, LoRA, and ARC hierarchical-voting procedure remains. v2 adds an inputs-and-outputs loss variant in Section 3.2 and adapts the procedure to BBH without synthetic preliminary fine-tuning or geometric augmentation/voting. These are limited extensions; renaming E2E as Direct I/O does not itself change the method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and preliminaries are extensively rewritten. The method-centered narrative becomes general TTT design followed by separate ARC and BBH sections and related work. Fine-tuning and detailed inference material move into reorganized appendices. The title, author list, and E2E terminology also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns, Figure 1 is redesigned, and a new design-summary diagram and BBH figures/tables are added. Existing diagrams and tables are relocated and resized; the model-size panel is separately redisplayed. QLoRA disappears from the ARC ablation chart while its numerical result remains in appendix prose.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning through local and transductive learning, retrieval-based TTT, MetaICL, BBH, and an explicit distinction from recurrent-state interpretations of TTT. New references include Bottou and Vapnik, Joachims, Hardt and Sun, and Hübॉटter and colleagues. Earlier Krause dynamic-evaluation and Cole citations disappear; publication-metadata updates are not counted as new works.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 adds a mathematical definition of the inputs-and-outputs objective by adding conditional input losses to the output objective. Existing leave-one-out, augmentation, and inference mathematics is largely restated or relocated. Neither version contains a theorem or proof development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence beyond v1's public-ARC-only evaluation: BBH tests applicability without ARC-specific augmentations, five-seed estimates quantify reliability, and semi-private ARC testing addresses a stated evaluation limitation. Task-specific analyses also reveal important boundaries and reversals in adapter-sharing benefits. These gains outweigh reporting defects, including the 62.8%/61.9% ensemble inconsistency and newly presenting ARC task counts as percentages. ARC uncertainty reporting remains incomplete.

A1.justification: Both complete PDFs describe the same test-time training study, despite the broadened title and substantial reorganization. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison. Numerical inconsistencies can be identified directly rather than treated as missing evidence.

after.justification: v2 retains the original ARC experiments and adds original BIG-Bench Hard experiments, task-level analyses, and an ARC semi-private evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original ARC experiments, including training and inference ablations, model-size comparisons, and full public-validation results.

results.title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning

C1.justification: Both versions claim a continuously updated daily forecasting benchmark and persistent temporal degradation despite retrieval, motivating ongoing model updates. Revised headline percentages, expanded supporting experiments, and stronger descriptive wording do not materially redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of refusals as potentially alignment-related and indicative of insufficient actionable knowledge, while distinguishing them from degradation that remains after refusals are excluded. Appendix C develops explanations involving market-question quality, sparse early coverage, and changing source/category composition, and qualifies Daily Oracle as complementary to human-curated benchmarks rather than inherently superior in question quality.

D1.justification: v2 documents supplementary collection with Newspaper3k, the timing and roles of the generation-model switch, human annotation instructions, market-data selection and balancing, and budget-limited proprietary open-book evaluation endpoints. The exact forecasting-model versions, retrieval parameters, and full prompts were already supplied in v1 and are retained.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix C adds actual closed-book evaluations on raw and filtered human-authored questions from five forecasting platforms. This introduces a substantially different question population beyond Daily Oracle's news-generated questions. Daily Oracle also extends through December rather than September 2024; its languages, news outlets, and TF/MC task types remain stable.

E2.justification: v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 5 list the same eight evaluated LLM versions, and BM25 remains the retriever. GPT-3.5 remains excluded from constrained open-book evaluation. The market experiments reuse existing models; GPT-4o-family models serve question generation, while ForecastBench appears in the literature comparison rather than as an evaluated forecasting system.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a human evaluation design with four annotators rating 30 TF and 30 MC questions, balanced market evaluations containing 12,438 raw and 3,232 filtered questions, and additional accuracy calculations excluding refusals. The retained Daily Oracle evaluation grows from 29,988 to 31,510 questions and extends its observation window. These are substantial added evaluation protocols, while the original BM25 top-five retrieval and five-month smoothing remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's closed-book refusal rates and temporal regressions, v2 tests whether degradation persists after excluding refusals across all three settings. It also adds human validation of filtering, category distributions over time, forecasting-market quality and distribution analyses, and a Mixtral case study showing responses under different information settings (Appendices A–C).

E5.justification: v2 introduces inter-rater reliability estimation using Fleiss' kappa across four independent annotators, reported separately for seven criteria and as an average in Table 4. Neither version reports repeated model-run counts, seed variability, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests; the new statistical reporting is confined to annotation agreement.

E6.justification: Reported endpoint accuracy declines change from 20.14%/23.26% to 21.55%/11.33% for TF/MC, using September versus December 2024 endpoints, so these are extended-series results rather than same-setting gains. Table 3 also revises retained entries, such as GPT-4's 2023 MC accuracy from 56.40% to 56.36%. Substantial new results include 89.52% human–LLM criterion agreement, 85.00% acceptance agreement, refusal-excluded degradation, and volatile forecasting-market trends.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 explicitly reports switching the generation pipeline from GPT-3.5/GPT-4 to GPT-4o-mini/GPT-4o for later questions. This is a limited model-component substitution: the four construction stages, article-selection scheme, seven filtering principles, and generation/evaluation prompts remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The five-section main narrative and most existing prose remain recognizable. v2 makes targeted revisions to contributions, related work, dataset analysis, discussion, and conclusion; adds a human-evaluation subsection and Impact Statement; and expands the appendices. The prompt appendix moves from C to D with its substantive text unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 reformats the main paper into two columns, rearranges the temporal-regression panels, and moves the construction diagram from main-text Figure 1 to appendix Figure 7. It adds the human-agreement table and new distribution, refusal-control, case-study, and market-comparison figures. These substantially alter both the visual organization and the evidence displayed.

R1.justification: v2 adds ForecastBench and materially expands positioning against forecasting-market benchmarks in Section 2 and Appendix C. The earlier argument that sustained degradation demonstrates a more challenging benchmark becomes a broader argument about longitudinal coverage, consistency, and confounding, supported by analyses of Halawi et al.'s data. Publication updates to existing references are not counted as new works.

T1.justification: The accessible-article date-range definition and exponentially weighted temporal regression formulation are retained. Neither version presents theorem or proof contributions, and v2's added agreement metrics and empirical analyses introduce no new mathematical derivation or formal property.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked independent question-quality validation and evidence separating temporal degradation from increasing refusals. v2's human audit and refusal-excluded analyses address these important gaps, while the market comparisons strengthen the rationale for the benchmark's longitudinal design. The audit remains small with only fair average agreement, and the generator switch is not controlled experimentally, but the new validation and robustness evidence substantially improve the paper's overall evidential quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Daily Oracle study. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains and extends the model evaluations and adds original human annotation results, refusal-controlled analyses, and forecasting-market experiments in Section 3.3 and Appendices A–C.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of eight LLMs, including temporal accuracy, constrained retrieval, gold-article performance, and refusal analyses in Section 4 and Appendix B.

results.title: Are LLMs Prescient? A Continuous Evaluation using Daily News as the Oracle

C1.justification: The continuous Bayesian MAP discovery contribution remains, but v2 adds an explicit theoretical contribution explaining multivariate distinguishability. Its introduction and conclusion strengthen competitive-feasibility claims to outperforming Bayesian and non-Bayesian alternatives across multiple settings. Explicit claims of demonstrated real-world dataset performance disappear with the Sachs evaluation.

C2.justification: v2 adds qualifications connecting estimated error to model misspecification through total variation, interprets the new ablation through Bayesian Occam's razor, and attributes DiBS's poor performance to Bayesian neural-network inference. Appendix I discusses sparse-graph and small-sample exceptions. The Sachs ground-truth uncertainty discussion and associated interpretation are removed.

D1.justification: v2 revises optimization, stopping and restart specifications, documents spectral-penalty tuning and new baseline implementations, and adds a code/data repository link and A100 hardware information. Reproducibility ambiguities remain: Appendices C.3 and C.6 describe penalty increments differently, and Algorithm 1 places score storage outside the restart loop despite the accompanying restart description.

E1.justification: v2 removes Sachs and adds sparse/dense 20- and 50-variable ER/SF scenarios and Gaussian-process additive-noise datasets. Three-variable synthetic data and Syntren remain. The ten-variable ER/SF benchmark evaluation is replaced, although ten-variable ER graphs remain in v2 for hyperparameter tuning.

E2.justification: The corresponding three-variable and Syntren comparisons replace GraN-DAG and GraN-DAG++ with SDCD and DiBS. v2 additionally evaluates a uniform-random DAG baseline in Figure 1 and the restricted CGP comparator in Figure 4. NOTEARS, CAM, SCORE, NOGAM and the three-variable DGP-CDE comparison remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds normalization during synthetic data generation, beyond v1's final standardization. Reported CGP-CDE settings change from 128 to 256 examples per minibatch, 100 to 50 latent Monte Carlo samples, and 30,000 to 25,000 warm-up/cool-down iterations. NOTEARS switches from a fixed 0.3 threshold to binary-search thresholding. Appendix I.2 adds evaluation at 100, 500 and 1,000 samples.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix I adds a latent-variable ablation comparing CGP-CDE with CGP on additive and non-additive data, and a sample-size sensitivity study. These directly examine flexibility and data requirements. The DGP-CDE restart analysis is retained, while v1's Sachs PKA-to-ERK model-fit case study is removed.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 5 introduces standard-error bars across five graphs. The existing restart analysis retains standard deviations over 50 restart-order permutations. Reported CGP-CDE optimization restart counts also change: three to two for the three-variable experiment and two-to-five to two for Syntren. These are changed restart budgets, not evidence of increased independent replication.

E6.justification: v2 adds larger-graph, ablation and sample-size results and updates the three-variable/Syntren comparisons. It removes the ten-variable benchmark results and Sachs Table 1, where CGP-CDE scored SHD 17, SID 59 and F1 0.48. New Figure 4 shows comparable CGP/CGP-CDE performance on additive-noise data and an advantage for CGP-CDE on non-additive data. Changed settings prevent a clean same-setting performance comparison between versions.

M1.justification: v1 uses matrix-exponential acyclicity with augmented-Lagrangian optimization. v2 replaces this with a largest-eigenvalue constraint, power-iteration gradient approximation and an increasing linear penalty, substantially changing the optimization procedure. The GP-CDE representation and hyperparameter-based adjacency remain. Appendix I.1 also introduces the latent-free CGP ablation.

P1.justification: The introduction and Bayesian background are substantially rewritten around explicit research questions and expanded explanations. Causal-model and continuous-optimization background moves into Appendix A, a theory section enters the main text, and the experiments, conclusion and appendix organization are reworked. These are extensive narrative changes beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: v1's combined four-row benchmark figure is reorganized into separate main-text displays. v2 adds multi-panel ablation and graph-regime figures plus a sample-size plot, while removing the Sachs illustration, Sachs results table and identifiability schematic. The encoder table and restart plot are retained and relocated; the optimization pseudocode is reformatted.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands the literature supporting its optimization and theoretical positioning, including NOBEARS/SDCD, Bayesian consistency and standardized structural causal models. It explicitly positions the nonparametric MEC result relative to earlier parametric results and the prior bivariate framework. This extends v1's research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v1 Appendix A primarily discusses identifiability informally. v2 Section 3 and Appendix B add formal error and equivalence definitions, a lemma, theorems, a corollary and proofs concerning recovery across MECs and distinguishability within an MEC, with explicit consistency and prior-separability conditions. Appendix A.2 also introduces the spectral constraint and its gradient mathematics.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central flexibility claim through explicit theoretical conditions and proofs, a targeted CGP ablation, sample-size sensitivity tests and broader graph regimes. Generation-time normalization improves experimental controls, and code/data access instructions aid reproducibility. Removing Sachs weakens real-data validation, and optimization documentation contains inconsistencies, but these drawbacks are outweighed by the stronger justification and targeted empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CGP-CDE research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic and Syntren evaluations, including larger graphs, an additive-noise ablation and sample-size sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on three-variable and ten-variable synthetic data, Syntren and Sachs, plus a DGP-CDE restart analysis.

results.title: Continuous Bayesian Model Selection for Multivariate Causal Discovery

C1.justification: The central claims about reference-free, trigger-agnostic defense, limited clean data, preserved utility and computational efficiency remain. The introduction drops v1's explicit claim to the most comprehensive evaluation, retaining the contribution of evaluation across six attacks, five models and three tasks.

C2.justification: New appendix discussion interprets the ablations as explaining why adversarial perturbations and consistency across layers are needed, and expands CleanGen deployment tradeoffs. Section 3.3 clarifies that stable behavior refers to the regularized model. The existing hyperparameter-tuning and adaptive-attack limitations remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies five-epoch LoRA finetuning for CROW, clarifies elementwise embedding perturbations, and documents semantic-experiment hyperparameters. Conversely, v1's 200-sample Figure 1 diagnostic count and 32 GB RAM detail are omitted. The code repository disclosure is retained.

E1.justification: Appendix C.4 adds SST-2 alongside Alpaca and two semantic/entity-trigger scenarios targeting negative sentiment about Joe Biden. This is a focused extension of data and trigger coverage; the original sentiment-steering, refusal, code-injection and jailbreak evaluations remain.

E2.justification: v1 explicitly excludes CleanGen from evaluation, whereas v2 Table 9 compares it with CROW across five attacks and two Llama-2-7B tasks. This adds a directly relevant LLM defense beyond the retained finetuning, pruning and quantization baselines. Tables 10–11 also introduce comparisons with two component-removal variants.

E3.justification: The added semantic experiments specify 1% poisoning, three epochs, batch size 128 and learning rate 2e-5; Appendices C.2–C.3 introduce controlled component-removal comparisons. The original main evaluation settings and metrics are retained. Newly specifying five-epoch LoRA training for CROW does not establish a change to the earlier experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained perturbation-magnitude, weighting-factor and similarity-measure studies, v2 tests removing adversarial perturbations (Table 10) and restricting consistency to embeddings (Table 11). It also adds semantic-trigger robustness experiments and training-stability curves. These directly examine previously untested design choices and robustness questions.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or seeds, reports uncertainty intervals or error bars, or provides significance tests. The added tables and training curves do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–8 retain their numerical values, but Tables 9–12 and Figure 3 add substantial results. Pure Consistency leaves 48.97% BadNets refusal ASR versus CROW's 19.63%; the new semantic-instruction experiment reports 89.10% without defense versus 3.52% with CROW. Table 9 also reveals tradeoffs: CleanGen has higher MT-Bench scores throughout, while CROW has lower ASR on four of five refusal attacks.

M1.justification: CROW retains FGSM perturbations of input embeddings and finetuning with language-modeling loss plus weighted, perturbed layer-consistency loss. The algorithms are consolidated. Pure Consistency and embedding-only consistency are added as experimental ablations, without changing the proposed CROW procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodology and results discussion are extensively condensed and rewritten. Background and experimental details move into Appendices A–B, method subsections are merged, the separate Key Observations section is removed, and ethical considerations move into an Impact Statement.

P2.justification: The conference layout substantially reflows and restyles the document and tables, consolidates two algorithm displays into one, and adds Figure 3 and Tables 9–12. Figures 1–2 retain identical images. The original attack-example Table 9 is retained as Table 13 with revised formatting.

R1.justification: Section 6 substantially expands positioning against closely related mechanisms, including trigger-activated change and channel Lipschitzness, layer-wise feature analysis, EP-BNP, adversarial-training defenses and W2SDefense. CleanGen changes from an excluded comparator to an evaluated complementary approach. These revisions materially sharpen CROW's relationship to prior defenses.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 adds a bounded-hidden-state-norm assumption and an order-(tau/c)^2 argument connecting cosine consistency to Euclidean distances. It also changes the final perturbation comparison from a strict non-amplification inequality in v1 Equation 14 to approximate equality in v2 Equation 10. The underlying Jacobian/Lipschitz argument remains.

improvement.justification: The CleanGen comparison and component ablations address important gaps in v1: no evaluated LLM-specific defense and no direct tests isolating CROW's defining components. Together with semantic-trigger experiments and closer prior-work positioning, they substantially strengthen the empirical justification. Some new experimental settings remain unspecified and uncertainty reporting is still absent. Rewritten prose also incorrectly describes the 91.50% to 85.28% ASR change as an increase, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the stronger validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CROW study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive restructuring.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original baseline comparisons, component ablations, semantic-backdoor results and training-loss plots.

before.justification: v1 reports original backdoor-mitigation results, helpfulness evaluations, ablations and jailbreak experiments in Tables 1–8.

results.title: CROW: Eliminating Backdoors from Large Language Models via Internal Consistency Regularization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: combining visual demonstrations and VLMs with IRL and iterative self-reflection. The headline claims of 42.3% better benchmark performance and 41.3% better generalization remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 expands interpretations of the existing normalization, textual-input, and random-demonstration ablations. Its limitations section develops demonstration-quality dependence and possible runtime remedies, while Appendix C.2 discusses nonlinear feature expressiveness and inspectability. These extend v1's existing discussion without changing its central interpretation.

D1.justification: v1 refers to supplementary prompts and hyperparameters but does not include them in the supplied PDF. v3 Appendices A-B provide actual prompts, TorchScript interface requirements, grid-search disclosure, learning rate, IRL iterations, policy-training steps, code-sampling counts, and network architecture. These substantially expand reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same nine IsaacGym tasks and the same Ant scenarios: original, reversed observations, lighter gravity, and backward running. The new Humanoid case study examines an existing task rather than extending coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1-3 retain the same comparators and ablation variants. The normalization, text-demonstration, and random-visual-demonstration rows already appear in v1; v3 expands their descriptions and renames the normalization rows without adding comparison methods.

E3.justification: Both retain GPT-4o, five RL-generated demonstrations per task, final-100-step evaluation, and the same Ant modifications. Newly specified hyperparameters, expert keyframe selection, and text-demonstration sampling document existing experiments rather than establish protocol revisions. Appendix C traces the retained procedure.

E4.justification: Appendix C.2 adds a Humanoid case study tracing two rounds of feature generation, feedback, rescaling, and introduction of a lateral-velocity feature. This provides a limited new examination of self-reflection. The systematic ablations and generalization tests were already present in v1.

E5.justification: v3 Table 5 newly reports means and standard deviations across three seeds for the Ant generalization comparisons. Both versions already disclose three seeds and retain best-seed results in the main tables. The addition does not establish more runs or introduce significance testing.

E6.justification: Tables 1-3 retain their numerical results. New Table 5 supplies seed-aggregated results, including original-Ant performance of 6.80±1.17 for ELEMENTAL and 4.44±2.45 for EUREKA. Appendix C.2 adds Humanoid feature values, learned weights, and episode-length outcomes across iterations.

M1.justification: The three-phase procedure remains VLM feature generation, Approximate MaxEnt-IRL with PPO and gradient/weight normalization, and feature-count-based self-reflection. Algorithm 1 is unchanged. The appended prompts and worked example disclose implementation details without establishing an algorithmic revision.

P1.justification: Most of the main narrative and section sequence remain intact. v3 tightens prose, expands explanations of existing ablations, separates limitations from the conclusion, and adds an Impact Statement and appendices. Author and conference-header text also change.

P2.justification: The paper is substantially reformatted from a single-column layout to a two-column main text, with resized and relocated figures, tables, and algorithm display. v3 also adds hyperparameter and uncertainty tables and boxed prompts and case-study outputs. The original figure content is retained.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive positioning relative to EUREKA, Peng et al. (2024b), and other language-model-assisted robotics methods are retained. Reference-style changes, shortened venue descriptions, and related-work copyediting do not introduce new research positioning.

T1.justification: The linear reward formulation, MaxEnt likelihood, feature-expectation gradient approximation, and normalization equations retain their mathematical substance. Equations are renumbered and the linear reward formula moves inline; no new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears.

improvement.justification: Appendices A-C address a substantial reproducibility gap: v1 promises supplementary material but omits the actual prompts and key training settings, whereas v3 supplies them and a worked execution trace. Table 5 also makes generalization variability across seeds inspectable. These additions substantially improve the paper's transparency and assessability, although the main claims still rely on unchanged best-seed summaries and uncertainty reporting remains limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ELEMENTAL, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures supporting direct comparison. The supplied v1 ends after its references; v3 includes Appendices A-C. This difference is confirmed by inspection, not an extraction gap.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and additionally reports seed-aggregated generalization results and a Humanoid case study in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original IsaacGym benchmark experiments, component ablations, Ant generalization experiments, reward correlations, and code-execution measurements.

results.title: ELEMENTAL: Interactive Learning from Demonstrations and Vision-Language Models for Reward Design in Robotics

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add significant compression-rate improvement over canonical tokenization as a main empirical claim. v1 instead emphasized approximation accuracy and speed, including a specific Llama result. The central claims about character-level conversion and resolving the prompt boundary problem remain.

C2.justification: v2 explains surprisal gains through noncanonical probability mass and high-probability noncanonical tokenizations. It also explicitly identifies stochastic tokenizers, including UnigramLM and BPE-Dropout, as potentially requiring expensive large beams. These additions refine the retained explanation and limitation concerning concentration on relatively few tokenizations.

D1.justification: The code pointer changes from token-to-char-lm to genlm-bytes, and v2 documents the GenLM interface with a vLLM backend. Reported hardware changes from an A100 with 80GB to an L40S with 40GB. Appendices F and G provide implementation pseudocode for the new baseline and pruning variant; detailed trie implementation already existed in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate next-symbol language modeling on WikiText-103 test text and retain the illustrative GPT2 prompts. Surprisal adds a measurement of the existing task, without introducing another dataset, domain, or downstream task.

E2.justification: v1's aggregate experiments compare beam configurations against a K=128 reference. v2 adds a canonical-tokenization surprisal baseline and an implemented character-level token-healing comparator across four models (Appendix A.2 and Appendix F, Table 1). Token healing was previously illustrated but not quantitatively benchmarked.

E3.justification: v2 retains Llama 3.1 8B but replaces GPT2-large in the aggregate evaluation with Llama-3.2-1B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, and phi-4. It reports a 4000-byte prefix where v1 reported characters, adds K=2 and surprisal measurements, changes hardware, and introduces joint beam-size and pruning-threshold sweeps.

E4.justification: Beyond the existing beam-size error/speed analysis, Appendix G and Figure 2 systematically examine probability-threshold pruning across beam sizes and four models. They measure effects on error, speed, and surprisal, explicitly identifying empty-beam failures and infinite surprisal under excessive pruning.

E5.justification: Both versions report bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals for experimental averages. The additional results extend this reporting practice; no new repeated-run counts, seed information, or statistical testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v2 replaces and expands the benchmark results and adds surprisal, token-healing, and threshold-pruning outcomes. For Llama 3.1 8B at K=4, v1 reports 0.00021 JSD/character and 46.31 characters/second; v2 reports 0.00005 JSD/byte and 32.06 bytes/second under revised settings. Newly reported v2 surprisal is 0.53173 bits/byte, versus 0.66 for canonical tokenization and 2.116 for token healing.

M1.justification: The core covering enumeration, bucket pruning, trie bundling, and conditional generation procedures remain. Appendix G adds optional probability-threshold pruning that skips low-probability bundle extensions. Appendix D also corrects the unbundle end-of-token lookup to use the currently visited prefix.

P1.justification: v2 substantially condenses and edits the introduction, background, and algorithm exposition, removes redundant helper listings, and relocates the main correctness proofs to appendices. It separates the conclusion and limitations, adds an impact statement, and reorganizes the appendix structure around results, proofs, implementation, and additional experiments.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference paper with reformatted examples and pseudocode. The two-model error/speed display becomes a four-model figure with an additional surprisal row; numerical tables move to Appendix A. A token-healing table and a separate pruning-sensitivity figure are added.

R1.justification: v2 adds Loula et al. on constrained generation and Provilkov et al. on BPE-Dropout, while removing several background references, including Blum, Cotterell, and Goubault. Its positioning relative to token healing and prior tokenization-marginalization work remains largely unchanged. Gastaldi's publication update represents the same cited work.

T1.justification: The principal propositions and proofs are retained, with the correctness proofs moved to Appendices B and E and covering-size analysis moved to C. v2 formalizes prompt-boundary consistency through relative probabilities, introduces the token-healing covering and its size bound, and changes an equality to a lower bound in Proposition 4's proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical validation beyond v1's internal approximation/runtime comparison. Quantitative canonical-tokenization and token-healing comparisons establish practical benefits, while Appendix G examines pruning tradeoffs and failures. More specific tokenizer limitations improve qualification of the claims. Evaluation remains restricted to a short WikiText prefix, but the new comparisons resolve an important gap in the earlier paper's evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across the extensive reformatting and relocation.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices A, F, and G report original experiments across four models, including approximation error, runtime, surprisal, baseline comparisons, and pruning sensitivity.
