E5.justification: The general five-run convention, with four runs for Peptides, remains unchanged. Appendix G.3.2 additionally specifies ten-fold cross-validation and averaging for Reddit, introducing a resampling-based performance estimate. It does not establish increased seed counts for retained experiments or a new uncertainty-estimation method.

E6.justification: Substantial classification, timing, and ablation results are added. Examples include MalNet-Tiny's 92.84 ± 0.52 for HyMN with T=1 without CSE and Reddit accuracy of 93.2 ± 2.2 for T=2. These are newly evaluated settings; existing scores such as MOLHIV's 81.01 ± 1.17 are retained.

M1.justification: Centrality ranking, top-T node marking, CSE construction, feature augmentation, and subgraph processing remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 is identical and moves to Appendix C. Additional backbone evaluations and disclosure of tie handling do not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are rewritten to emphasize scalability, and task and metric explanations are expanded. Algorithm 1 and the ZINC discussion move to appendices, whose outline is updated. The main section sequence and most methodological and theoretical prose remain.

P2.justification: The main text changes to a two-column conference layout with reformatted tables and captions. The combined ZINC/MOLHIV table is split and relocated, and the NCI1 panel moves to the appendix. A sampling diagram, ER perturbation panel, and multiple experimental tables are added.

R1.justification: v2 adds Bresson and Laurent for GatedGCN, Freitas et al. for MalNet, and Dupty and Lee for the connection to node individualization. The Murphy et al. citation and CSL discussion disappear. The broader research positioning remains stable; publication-metadata updates concern existing works.

T1.justification: Observation 1, the two expressiveness theorems, their existing top-k extensions, the CSE-probability and DSS-GNN propositions, and the perturbation derivations are retained. Renumbering and relocation to Appendices D and E introduce no substantive proof or assumption changes.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central scalability claim, which v1 chiefly demonstrated on molecular benchmarks including Peptides. MalNet graphs with up to 5,000 nodes, Reddit, timing comparisons, additional relevant baselines, and backbone and selection controls address an important validation gap. MalNet preprocessing costs remain unreported, its parameter count is incomplete, and Reddit dataset descriptions are inconsistent, but these reporting weaknesses do not outweigh the stronger empirical validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HyMN research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds MalNet-Tiny and Reddit experiments, additional backbone evaluations, and minimum-centrality analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original perturbation, substructure-counting, molecular-prediction, ablation, and timing results in Sections 3 and 5 and the appendices.

results.title: Balancing Efficiency and Expressiveness: Subgraph GNNs with Walk-Based Centrality

C1.justification: The abstract and principal noise-dependent and countable-class contributions are retained. However, introduction contribution (4)'s finite-union sufficiency claim now invokes the stronger total-example noise-independent notion; v1's corresponding premise used positive-example counting. This narrows that stated sufficient condition beyond merely renaming it.

C2.justification: Section 3.2 adds a quantitative sample-complexity interpretation of the Noisy Closure dimension and changes the comparison with learning theory to emphasize deterministic online learning. Section 4 removes v1's Questions 4.3–4.4 and their discussion of possible noisy/noiseless separations requiring uncountable classes. The information-theoretic scope and unresolved characterization/computability questions remain.

D1.justification: Neither version supplies implementation environments, hardware, experimental hyperparameters, runtime measurements, or code/data access information. The revised mathematical generator constructions are covered under M1 and T1.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or empirical training/evaluation tasks. The added discussion of training LLMs on generated outputs is motivation, not evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates empirical comparison methods or baselines. Comparisons with earlier work concern theoretical guarantees.

E3.justification: Neither version contains experimental protocols, splits, evaluation metrics, or training budgets. Revisions to theoretical sample thresholds belong under T1.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, sensitivity experiments, robustness tests, or empirical case studies. Noise tolerance is studied through mathematical arguments.

E5.justification: Repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, and statistical uncertainty estimates are absent from both versions.

E6.justification: Neither version reports empirical scores, rankings, or qualitative experimental findings. Changes to mathematical results and guarantees are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: Appendices E–F restrict generator index searches to {1,...,t}, whereas v1 maximizes over all natural numbers. Algorithm 1 changes its loop endpoint from r_t to r_t-1 and its fallback output from candidate r_t+1 to r_t. Appendix C also supplies a related closure-based generator. These are procedural additions and corrections within the retained approach.

P1.justification: v2 systematically replaces the easily confused noisy/uniform terminology with noise-dependent and noise-independent terminology. It moves noiseless definitions and background results into Appendices A–B and several proofs into E–G, replacing them with main-text summaries. It also shortens the discussion and adds acknowledgements and an impact statement, substantially reorganizing the narrative.

P2.justification: The single-column manuscript becomes a two-column conference paper for the main text and references, with single-column appendices. Typography, headers, author information, and equation wrapping change throughout. Algorithm 1 is reformatted into a narrow column without its previous line numbering. Neither version contains empirical figures or tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds Burns et al. (2023) and Briesch et al. (2023) to motivate noisy training on LLM outputs. It also revises the relationship to online-learning results, replacing v1's broad equivalence comparison with a distinction for deterministic algorithms. The central positioning relative to Kleinberg and Mullainathan and Li et al. remains.

T1.justification: v1 Definition 2.5 counts distinct positive examples; v2 retains it as Definition C.1 but introduces total-example counting in Definition 2.4 and replaces Theorem 3.1's proof. Appendix C restricts the earlier proof argument to an explicit subclass condition in Lemma C.2 and adds the characterization sup_n(NC_n(H)-n) < infinity with a proof sketch. Appendices E–F revise sufficient sample bounds to accommodate bounded index searches, and Algorithm 1's proof receives indexing corrections. Appendix G also drops v1's explicit late-noise cutoff from its final guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important theoretical defect: v1's Theorem 3.1 relied on an unjustified minimal-subclass step for positive-example counting. v2 separates total-count and positive-count guarantees, replaces the main proof, and supplies a separate characterization in Appendix C. Bounded index searches in Appendices E–F also repair generator definitions. Incorrect Appendix C cross-references and Appendix G's dropped late-noise cutoff remain weaknesses, but the central mathematical corrections provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Generation from Noisy Examples. All 19 pages of v1 and 15 pages of v2, including their appendices, support comparison; definitions and proofs can be matched across renaming and relocation.

after.justification: v2 remains entirely theoretical, including Appendices A–G. Its added LLM motivation cites other work rather than reporting original empirical results.

before.justification: v1 reports mathematical definitions, algorithms, theorems, proofs, and counterexamples, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

results.title: Generation from Noisy Examples

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add an explicit contribution concerning acceleration of Langevin sampling for unnormalized distributions. v1 contained only a general applicability remark about other discretized diffusions. The central claims of exact DDM sampling, maximal acceptance, training-free drafting, and fewer target evaluations remain.

C2.justification: The discussion adds a substantive qualification: diffusion models already exploit parallelism, so LLM-style speculative-decoding latency benefits need not transfer. Section 5 and Appendix K distinguish exact reproduction of ULA from its biased approximation to the desired density. Appendix J adds an interpretation of the combination results as evidence of complementarity.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly defines NFE as a batched target-model call regardless of batch size, labels sequential and parallel algorithm operations, and documents cached-drift initialization and reuse. It also supplies ULA pseudocode and parameters for the added experiments. Existing architecture and training details in Appendix I are largely retained.

E1.justification: Appendix K adds sampling from an unnormalized phi-4 energy model on an 8-by-8 grid, extending evaluation into physical-system MCMC. The Gaussian-mixture, image-generation, latent CIFAR-10, and PushT coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's draft and target comparisons, v2 Table 3 evaluates uniform, EDM, and learned LD3 timestep schedules and multistep moment-matching distillation. It separately includes published DPM-Solver++ results with naive, AYS, and LD3 schedules. Table 9 adds ordinary Langevin sampling as the comparator for the new application.

E3.justification: Appendix J introduces a 30-step CIFAR-10 combination experiment, selecting the best FID over window sizes 5, 10, and 20, plus approximately 15-NFE baseline comparisons. Appendix K adds a 100,000-step ULA protocol with stepsize 0.001 and speculative window 20. These are additional protocols rather than established reruns of the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Table 8 adds a focused composability study varying parallel-call count p=0, 1, and 5 alongside temperature and stochasticity. Figure 6 adds a comparison of the acceptance-bound factor under linear and cosine schedules. Earlier temperature, dimension, and window-size analyses remain.

E5.justification: Appendix K newly specifies 500 runs and reports energy means and standard deviations using the last 500 simulated samples. The existing PushT episode count and uncertainty entries are unchanged; the PDFs do not establish additional repetitions of the original experiments.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in v1 Tables 1–6 are retained in v2 Tables 1, 2, and 4–7. New Tables 3 and 8 add acceleration comparisons, including hybrid CIFAR-10 FID 2.07 at 15.42 NFE with p=1, epsilon=0.25, and tau=10. Table 9 reports Langevin versus speculative NFE of 100000 versus 48564 and mean energies of 62.27 versus 65.90.

M1.justification: Appendix B adds an efficient frozen-draft variant that reuses previously computed verification drifts, changing proposal construction after rejection. Section 5 and Algorithm 11 additionally specialize speculative sampling to ULA with proxy-energy or frozen-gradient drafts. The original reflection coupling and Picard-based drafting were already present in v1.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized prose edits, standardizes draft/output notation, reorders contribution bullets, and subdivides Appendix H. It inserts a Langevin section, Appendix K, and an impact statement while retaining most of the original narrative and appendix organization.

P2.justification: v2 adds three substantive result displays—Tables 3, 8, and 9—and the schedule plot in Figure 6. Figures 2 and 3 change from side-by-side to vertically stacked panels, captions are expanded, and several displays move. The original tables and plotted results are retained rather than replaced.

R1.justification: Section 5 and Appendix K substantially expand positioning into MCMC prefetching, delayed acceptance, multifidelity methods, and parallel Langevin algorithms, with corresponding new references. Appendix J also establishes comparisons with AYS, LD3, and moment-matching distillation. These extend the research context beyond the retained LLM and diffusion-acceleration discussion.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds a formal counterexample showing why independently resampling from the target upon rejection is incorrect. Appendix H expands the acceptance-ratio derivation and restricts Lemma H.6 from alpha>=1 to even alpha>=2 while revising its proof constants. Section 4.1 replaces constant acceptance probability with a lower-bound assumption; the central coupling results remain.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly compared against its own draft and target samplers. v2 substantially strengthens comparative evidence through additional acceleration baselines and a direct composability study in Tables 3 and 8, while developing and testing the broader Langevin application. Its latency qualification also improves interpretation. These gains outweigh remaining limitations: the best hybrid result uses non-exact tau=10 sampling, wall-clock acceleration remains unmeasured, and Algorithm 11's rejection update prints E where Equation 38 specifies its gradient.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same speculative-sampling research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds acceleration-method comparisons, parallel-sampling experiments, and a phi-4 Langevin simulation in Appendices J and K.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian-mixture, CIFAR-10, LSUN, latent-diffusion, and PushT experiments in Section 6 and Appendix J.

results.title: Accelerated Diffusion Models via Speculative Sampling

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add PAC learnability as a main contribution: proper learning for bounded single-head rank, improper learning for bounded multi-head rank, and conditional hardness of proper learning already for two-head rank one. Multi-head rank itself was already introduced in v1.

C2.justification: Section 6 explains why efficient learning through a larger single-head hypothesis class yields only improper learning of the multi-head class. New Section 7 qualifies comparisons with multilayer soft-attention results by explaining their different input encoding, with an entire function supplied in one token.

D1.justification: Neither version supplies implementation, hardware, training, or code/data-access information. The new constructive algorithm is described mathematically rather than accompanied by implementation details.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or tasks for empirical training or evaluation. The new PAC-consistency problems are studied mathematically.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing methods. The added comparison with hardness results for 2-term DNFs concerns theoretical positioning, not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Neither version contains experimental evaluation protocols. Section 6's sample-access assumptions and accuracy parameters define a theoretical learning model.

E4.justification: Neither version reports empirical ablations, robustness tests, or supplementary experimental analyses. The new examples and gadgets support proofs.

E5.justification: Neither reports repeated experimental runs or statistical uncertainty estimates. v2's PAC confidence parameter is a formal guarantee, not uncertainty reporting from experiments.

E6.justification: Neither version reports measured performance, empirical rankings, or observed qualitative outcomes. The added learnability and hardness results are mathematical contributions assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The decoder architecture and existing constructions remain unchanged, but Section 6.1 introduces a recursive consistency algorithm for fixed-rank functions over arbitrary fixed finite alphabets. It identifies lower-rank-consistent subsamples, recursively processes the remaining samples, and assembles a decision tree. v1 contains no corresponding learning procedure.

P1.justification: The earlier sections remain largely intact. v2 makes local language and notation edits, clarifies the Section 5.2 proof, moves Proposition 6's discussion after that proof, adopts author–year citations, and extends the abstract and roadmap for Sections 6–7.

P2.justification: v2 adds an unnumbered paired tabular display of positive and negative gadget samples in Section 6.2, page 23. Equation displays and bibliography formatting also change, while the overall single-column presentation is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Valiant, Kearns and Vazirani, Pitt and Valiant, Schaefer, and Chen et al. It positions its learning-hardness theorem as incomparable with 2-term-DNF hardness and distinguishes Chen et al.'s composition setting. The existing Transformer-expressivity positioning remains largely intact.

T1.justification: New Section 6 formalizes PAC learning and consistency, proves polynomial-time consistency for fixed single-head rank over finite alphabets (Theorem 4), and proves NP-completeness for Boolean two-head rank at most one (Theorem 5). Lemmas 3–6 provide the algorithmic argument and reduction machinery. The original rank/decoder equivalences and CoT bounds are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 motivates rank through PAC learning but does not examine learnability of its multi-head generalization. Section 6 of v2 addresses that substantive question with a constructive algorithm and detailed hardness reductions, distinguishing efficient improper learning from conditional proper-learning hardness. This substantially deepens the computational implications of the characterization while preserving the original CoT results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same rank/Chain-of-Thought research, with readable definitions, equations, constructions, and proofs. All 20 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v2 support comparison. Neither contains a separate appendix.

after.justification: v2 adds theoretical learning algorithms and complexity proofs. Its labeled samples and sample matrices are mathematical constructions, not empirical study outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports mathematical characterizations and proofs of decoder-depth bounds, without original experiments, simulations, user studies, or empirical data analyses.

results.title: Ehrenfeucht-Haussler Rank and Chain of Thought

C1.justification: The central claims of efficient constrained RL, fidelities above 0.999 across three systems, and noise robustness remain. V2 explicitly quantifies the Λ-system advantage as almost two orders of magnitude lower infidelity and extends the conclusion's applicability claim to noisy physical control more generally.

C2.justification: V2 substantially develops practical applicability through measurement-budget estimates in Appendix F and hardware-bandwidth interpretations in Fig. 15. Appendix G.3 attributes much of the runtime advantage to compilation and automatic differentiation, qualifying the role of constraints. The conclusion adds error-correction relevance and cross-device policy generalization, while retaining the principal modelling and non-adiabatic limitations.

D1.justification: V1 promises future code and data release; v2 states that code is open source and supplies a repository address. V2 also adds a detailed PPO/DDPG/TD3 hyperparameter table, CleanRL implementation information, and hardware, batching, and timing details. These materially expand reproducibility documentation; repository contents were not independently checked.

E1.justification: The three quantum platforms and their control tasks remain. Noise-test coverage expands modestly: v2 Fig. 9 includes a Λ-system amplitude-noise level of 3 MHz alongside the 0.1 and 1 MHz levels shown in v1 Fig. 7. The new hardware-feasibility discussion does not introduce a physical-device study.

E2.justification: V2 adds Krotov to the Λ-system comparison and evaluates vanilla PPO plus constrained and vanilla DDPG/TD3 variants in the Λ and two-photon Rydberg environments. These substantially expand the evaluated comparator set beyond v1. The retained 0.83 entry is relabeled PINN, rather than representing an additional baseline.

E3.justification: V2 introduces controlled RL comparisons with common batches and update budgets, CPU convergence-time benchmarking, and a 1 GSa/s waveform-analysis protocol. The reported Λ-system BFGS iteration limit also changes from 10,000 in v1 Table II to 1,000 in v2 Table 1 despite an unchanged score; this does not establish that the experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds constrained-versus-vanilla algorithm ablations in Figs. 2 and 12, an RL-versus-optimal-control state-evolution comparison in Fig. 10, and smoothing-dependent waveform analysis in Fig. 15. It revises the Λ noise study and omits v1 Fig. 10's quantitative single-photon Rydberg noise analysis. Existing pulse-area and smoothing ablations are retained.

E5.justification: The main comparison table retains its 32-seed reporting. New Fig. 2 explicitly reports two seeds and one-standard-deviation shading. For Λ noise robustness, v1 Fig. 7 reports min/max envelopes, whereas v2 Fig. 9 reports standard-deviation envelopes. These are reporting changes, not evidence of increased replication for existing results.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial numerical comparison and timing results, including Krotov fidelity 0.99 ± 0.001 and CPU convergence times of 239.1 seconds for PPO versus 3997 seconds for Krotov. The reported 0.25-microsecond Rydberg pulse fidelity changes from 0.9993 to 0.99958 alongside a revised waveform. Noise curves and the transmon solver-step curve also change; the principal Λ and transmon headline fidelities remain.

M1.justification: The constrained PPO framework, filtering, endpoint constraints, and multi-step feedback procedure remain. However, the stated low-pass smoothness penalty changes from an integrated signed residual in v1 Eq. E4 to an integrated absolute residual in v2 Eq. 23, altering the documented reward component. The PDFs do not establish whether this also changed the implementation.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and method explanation undergo substantial rewriting. Quantum-control background moves from the main text to Appendix B, implementation material is reorganized into Appendix G, and experimental-feasibility and impact sections are added. Terminology and section conventions are revised throughout.

P2.justification: V2 adopts an ICML layout, expands and restructures the main comparison table, adds hyperparameter and timing tables, and introduces several analytical figures. V1's two-panel multi-step figure is redrawn as a combined main-text plot; noise and Rydberg plots are revised. The conceptual comparison table and single-photon noise plot are removed.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against Krotov, hybrid optimal control, logical-level quantum RL, error correction, compilation, and recent transmon-control work. It revises the discussion of model-based RL and replaces v1's categorical RL-versus-direct-differentiation table with more contextual comparisons. These changes extend beyond bibliographic formatting.

T1.justification: The absolute-value addition changes the mathematical smoothness definition, and v2 Fig. 15 introduces a sampled-waveform diagnostic. Most quantum and PPO equations are retained or relocated, without new proofs. The printed single-photon Hamiltonian summation limit also changes from 2 to 1 in Eq. 14 without explanation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central constrained-RL claim through vanilla-versus-constrained comparisons and broader baselines, addressing important gaps in v1. Hyperparameter disclosure, runtime benchmarks, and the code-access statement also materially improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removed single-photon robustness evidence and localized equation/reporting inconsistencies. Physical-device feasibility remains an extrapolation rather than experimentally validated evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same constrained reinforcement-learning work for quantum control. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains original simulation results and adds algorithm comparisons, runtime measurements, and analyses of learned control signals. These are simulation results, not new physical-device experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations of population transfer, Rydberg gates, and transmon reset, including fidelity, robustness, ablation, and computational timing results.

results.title: Reinforcement Learning for Quantum Control under Physical Constraints

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same two decentralized CP protocols, coverage claims, and trade-off between Q-DCP's tuning requirements and H-DCP's communication overhead. The added experiments support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains that suitable epsilon_0 selection depends on network size and interprets the resulting coverage failures in Appendix B.3. It also motivates the torus experiment through intermediate connectivity, discusses medical applicability, and adds asynchronous networks as future work. These refine the existing interpretation and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-release repository address in the abstract. Appendix B.6 documents the PathMNIST split sizes, small-resnet14 shared model, device allocation, and communication settings. Existing algorithm descriptions and CIFAR100 implementation disclosures largely remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates CIFAR100 classification only. v2 adds nine-class PathMNIST medical-image classification in Appendix B.6 and Figures 16–17, substantially broadening the evaluated domain while retaining CIFAR100.

E2.justification: v1's empirical comparisons use centralized CP; FCP, FedCP-QQ, and WFCP appear as background methods. v2 Table 1 adds evaluated FCP and FedCP-QQ comparisons on a CIFAR100 star topology, with WFCP represented by the combined H-DCP(WFCP) column.

E3.justification: The original Section 6 settings remain. New protocols include 100-device experiments with 3000 iterations and varying network size and epsilon_0 on Erdős–Rényi graphs. PathMNIST uses eight devices, Q-DCP with 8000 iterations, and H-DCP with 80 iterations and 100 quantization levels to match communication costs.

E4.justification: Appendix B.3 adds substantial scalability and sensitivity analyses: 100-device tests and experiments examining how network size interacts with epsilon_0 and coverage. Figures 10–11 expose undercoverage with epsilon_0 = 0.1 as the network grows. Existing convergence and smoothing, regularization, and quantization ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages over 10 randomly generated calibration sets without plotted variability. v2 adds uncertainty bands to Figures 2–5 and standard deviations in Table 1. Figure 2 identifies its bands as intervals covering 95% of realized values. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting; no increase in repetitions is stated.

E6.justification: New Table 1 reports coverage/set-size pairs of 0.913/11.35 for Q-DCP, 0.920/12.16 for H-DCP(WFCP), 0.918/11.98 for FCP, and 0.996/45.32 for FedCP-QQ. Figures 8–11 and 16–17 add larger-network, network-size sensitivity, and PathMNIST findings. These expand the reported evidence rather than establish performance improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: Q-DCP retains its smoothed, regularized quantile loss, ADMM updates, averaging, and threshold correction. H-DCP retains its quantization, histogram consensus, and coverage correction. Algorithms 1–2 are relocated from Appendix C without procedural changes.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include localized explanations, notation corrections, affiliation and publication text updates, expanded Appendix B organization, and relocation of the algorithm descriptions from Appendix C into Sections 4–5.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 1 and six experimental figures, redraws main plots with uncertainty bands, and relocates the algorithm tables into the two-column main text. The original ablation Figures 8–11 remain as Figures 12–15. These substantially expand and reorganize the visual evidence.

R1.justification: v2 adds references on Bayesian conformal prediction, federated learning, and asynchronous optimization, including Clarte and Zdeborova, McMahan et al., Kairouz et al., Wei and Ozdaglar, and Tian et al. The central research positioning remains; several other reference changes merely update publication metadata.

T1.justification: The assumptions, propositions, coverage theorems, bounds, and Appendix A proofs retain their mathematical substance. Changes such as Z_i to S_i in Equation 8 and p to x in Equation 34 correct notation without changing the reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical validation beyond v1's 20-device CIFAR100 study against centralized CP. Table 1 addresses the missing evaluated federated baselines, while Appendices B.3 and B.6 test scalability and a medical domain. Added uncertainty reporting and the network-dependent coverage failure analysis make reliability and practical limitations easier to assess, supporting a substantial overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Q-DCP and H-DCP research. Their main text, equations, figures, proofs, and experimental appendices are readable and support comparison. The algorithms in v1 Appendix C are relocated into v2's main text.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds federated-baseline comparisons, larger-network and sensitivity experiments, and PathMNIST results in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR100 experiments on coverage, prediction-set size, communication costs, convergence, and hyperparameter sensitivity in Section 6 and Appendix B.

results.title: Distributed Conformal Prediction via Message Passing

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: external search mitigates snowball errors, and reward-function reliability and reasoning resources matter more than the particular search framework. New supporting analyses do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix D.2 interprets declining accuracy on easier problems as harm from overthinking and argues that length effects persist within difficulty groups. Appendix D.3 attributes faster PrOntoQA gains with increasing k to a more reliable value function. These extend interpretation without revising the central account.

D1.justification: v3 documents Game24 tree settings and cost-calibration quantities, names the larger evaluated models, and specifies the search-width sweep. Existing prompts, ten-answer MI sampling, HSIC bandwidth 50, reward-model information, and code-access statement are retained.

E1.justification: Appendices D.2 and D.4 add MATH-500 mathematics across five difficulty levels and Game24 arithmetic-puzzle planning. These substantially broaden coverage beyond the retained GSM8k word problems and PrOntoQA logical reasoning.

E2.justification: The corresponding GSM8k and PrOntoQA comparisons retain MCTS against BoN with Self-Consistency, ORM Vote, and ORM Max. Game24 evaluates existing MCTS and ORM-based BoN methods; no new comparison method is introduced.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include Qwen2.5-14B/32B tests, difficulty-stratified MI and accuracy analyses, and an MCTS max-action sweep from k=1 to 8 with other hyperparameters held fixed. Game24 adds maximum tree width 20 and depth 4. The original GSM8k/PrOntoQA settings and MI workflow remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendices D.1–D.3 add targeted checks of whether snowball patterns persist at larger model sizes, whether length effects persist within difficulty groups, and how accuracy responds to search width. These substantially expand robustness and sensitivity analysis beyond v1's original experiments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports run-level uncertainty, confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-based variability. The new experiments continue to present point estimates and curves without adding statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original Figures 2–3 are retained, while Figures 4–6 add model-scale, difficulty, and search-width findings. New Table 3 reports Game24 MCTS accuracy of 64.80%, versus 66.85% for ORM-Vote and 67.13% for ORM-Max at N=18. These are newly reported results, not improvements over a corresponding v1 experiment.

M1.justification: The BoN, MCTS, and answer-selection procedures are retained. v3 introduces no new algorithm or architecture; its relaxed probability assumptions extend the theory, while additional model sizes extend evaluation.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain largely unchanged. v3 adds brief explanations and cross-references, reorganizes the appendices around new theoretical and empirical sections, updates affiliations and publication information, and adds acknowledgments and an impact statement.

P2.justification: v3 adds substantial visual material: larger-model curves, difficulty-stratified MI and accuracy panels, a search-width plot, and the Game24 results table. Table 2 gains a Game24 column. Figures 1–3 retain their displays, while Table 1 is relocated.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds Wu et al. (2024), Inference Scaling Laws, as empirical support for inference scaling. The remaining cited works and the paper's positioning relative to information theory and external search are retained.

T1.justification: New Appendix B replaces the specific exponential form, for its extended analysis, with a nonnegative function decreasing monotonically to zero. Proposition B.1 and bounds B.2–B.7 generalize the reasoning and search analyses. Existing main-text results and Appendix A proofs are retained; the lookahead derivation moves from Appendix C to E.

improvement.justification: v1 did not test length effects within difficulty groups or across larger models, and its probability analysis used a specific exponential form. Appendices B and D address these gaps and add search-width sensitivity and planning-task evidence, substantially strengthening the scope and support of the central account. The overthinking interpretation remains observational, and uncertainty estimates are still absent, but the targeted additions provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, and their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison. The original experimental settings and lookahead analysis are retained as v3 Appendices C and E.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds larger-model evaluations, MATH-500 difficulty analyses, search-width experiments, and Game24 comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments measuring mutual information and reward on GSM8k, and comparing BoN with MCTS on GSM8k and PrOntoQA.

results.title: Rethinking External Slow-Thinking: From Snowball Errors to Probability of Correct Reasoning

C1.justification: The central contribution remains diffusion finetuning that preserves the original model while enabling additional inference computation. The abstract and introduction qualify superiority from 'is more effective' to 'can be more effective' and extend the claimed complementarity from traditional finetuning to search. These refine the scope without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: Section 6 and Appendix D.6 newly acknowledge limitations in accessing confidence scores and directly controlling sampling through logits. V2 explains that relaxed GSM8K evaluation changes comparative advantages, that oracle verification can favor repeated sampling, and that R1-style reasoning introduces substantial costs and task tradeoffs. These materially qualify applicability and strengthen the interpretation of complementarity.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the promised code release with a repository link and a statement that code is provided, while removing Appendix B.1's separate data-release promise. It adds beam-search scoring and sampling details, clarifies the main evaluation's untempered generation, and describes new prompt-generation and parsing procedures. The existing hyperparameter table and dataset preparation recipe remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same curated SmolTalk training coverage and nine evaluation benchmarks, including the appendix tasks. V2's additional models, prompting variants, answer extraction, and pass@K evaluations change procedures within these retained tasks rather than adding datasets or domains.

E2.justification: V1 primarily compares against untuned models, LoRA, and full finetuning. V2 adds evaluated token-search and chain-of-thought comparators and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, together with combinations involving L2D (Tables 2 and 16–18). This substantially broadens comparison with alternative inference-scaling approaches.

E3.justification: The original training settings and main evaluation remain. New protocols include 15-hypothesis beam search, pass@5/10 evaluation for mathematics and knowledge, and a separate GSM8K setup using eight examples, greedy baseline decoding, and relaxed extraction. Appendix D.7 also introduces modified reasoning-model prompts and parsing, plus longer chain-of-thought demonstrations. These are additional settings, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The existing learning-rate, noise-scale, initialization, velocity, and solver analyses are retained. V2 adds substantial analyses of oracle best-of-N scaling, sensitivity to GSM8K evaluation choices, and complementarity with search, chain-of-thought prompting, and an R1-distilled model. These test additional questions about when L2D helps and how its benefits combine with other approaches.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-training uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional pass@K evaluations concern sampling budgets and success metrics, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Matched original results are retained, including Table 1 and the existing appendix ablations. Substantial new results appear in Tables 13 and 15–17 and the search rows of Tables 2 and 18: token search scores 33.83 overall and its L2D combination 38.57. The new relaxed GSM8K evaluation gives Llama 1B full finetuning 46.36 versus L2D 43.41; the original setup's 33.48 versus 38.86 remains unchanged. These are additional conditions, not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The core architecture, diffusion objective, conditioning, and training procedure remain unchanged. Section 4.3 adds an evaluated inference extension combining L2D with beam search, allocating half the original budget to each component. This extends decoding without redesigning L2D.

P1.justification: V2 makes targeted wording corrections, clarifies method explanations, and revises the related-work and discussion prose. It inserts search and expanded appendix subsections, acknowledgements, and an impact statement. The main six-section organization and Appendices A–D remain recognizable; the revision is chiefly added scientific content rather than extensive narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: V2 adds four substantive comparison tables for best-of-N, relaxed GSM8K, R1-style reasoning, and chain-of-thought, and expands the extension tables with search rows. Existing plots retain their content but are resized or relocated, and Figure 5's reversed math/coding caption is corrected. The new Table 13 introduces a labeling error by placing MMLU columns under 'Coding'.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens positioning relative to search, repeated sampling, and contemporary reasoning approaches, adding discussion and citations for DeepSeek-R1, s1, inference-compute scaling, and diffusion alignment. Sections 6 and D.4–D.7 explicitly position L2D as complementary to these approaches. The earlier diffusion-model relationships remain, while the Lightman and Ye references are removed.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(8), the single-step diffusion interpretation, and the midpoint integration derivation are retained. V2 adds no substantive formal assumptions, theoretical results, or proofs; its beam-search scoring description supplies implementation information.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central test-time-scaling argument by adding direct comparisons with alternative scaling approaches, which v1 largely lacked. More importantly, Table 15 exposes evaluation-dependent rankings, while Section 6 and Appendix D.6 explain consequential sampling and confidence limitations. This improves the credibility and calibration of the conclusions. Differing comparison settings and the continued absence of uncertainty estimates still limit some conclusions, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same L2D research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite additions and renumbering in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds original search, best-of-N, evaluation-sensitivity, reasoning-model, and chain-of-thought comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original Llama and Qwen experiments on mathematics, coding, and knowledge tasks, with ablations and additional evaluations in Appendices C–D.

results.title: Large Language Models to Diffusion Finetuning

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the claims of temporal-wise distillation, convergence across implicit timestep models, flexible deployment without timestep-specific retraining, and strong benchmark performance. The expanded evidence and more explicit logit-based title do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands practical interpretation: it distinguishes inference-budget flexibility from benefits of additional training resources and explains how timestep robustness supports early exits. Appendix C discusses transformer teacher-selection difficulties, temporal averaging weakening the DVS teacher, and potential feature-alignment problems with adaptive input encoders. These applicability considerations were absent from v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit code-availability link in the abstract and measured per-batch training time and memory in Table 9. Existing software, hardware, optimizer, preprocessing and hyperparameter disclosures move to Appendix B without substantive changes. The PDFs alone do not establish the linked repository's contents or accessibility.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate classification on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet and CIFAR10-DVS. The additional architecture and early-exit experiments use existing datasets and tasks; they change model configurations and inference procedures rather than data or task coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 1 replaces the direct-training comparator with standard logits-based distillation. v2 Table 7 adds logits-KD controls to the full-range comparison previously containing only proposed-method models in v1 Table 8. The comparator sets in the principal dataset benchmark tables remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Original splits, preprocessing, training budgets and hyperparameters are retained in Appendix B. Appendix C substantially broadens evaluation procedures through Spikingformer, MS-ResNet and VGGSNN configurations, time/memory and firing-rate measurements, and SEENN-I confidence thresholds from 0.7 to 0.999 with accuracy and average inference timesteps reported.

E4.justification: v2 adds a self-distillation-without-teacher ablation in Table 5, objective ablations on VGGSNN/CIFAR10-DVS, and explicit logits-KD controls for timestep robustness. Appendix C also adds training-overhead diagnostics, firing-rate analysis and an early-exit case study. These substantially extend the retained hyperparameter, loss and clustering analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three-run averaging for the CIFAR and CIFAR10-DVS benchmark tables. v2 introduces no new seed disclosures, uncertainty intervals, significance tests or repeated-run procedures. Its firing-rate means are measured outcomes, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Existing headline scores, including 71.04% on ImageNet, remain unchanged. New results include 78.94% and 79.63% for the teacher-free ablation, logits-KD full-range controls, and Appendix C measurements across costs, firing rates, architectures and early exits. Table 14 reports 79.05% at 1.690 average timesteps for the proposed T=6 model at confidence threshold 0.9.

M1.justification: Equations (1)–(9) and Algorithm 1 retain the same temporal cross-entropy, teacher distillation and ensemble self-distillation objectives. Additional backbones, teacher-free ablations and application of SEENN-I evaluate the existing framework without revising its proposed training algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the document by moving proofs and the experimental-details subsection into Appendices A–B, adding Appendix C, and expanding the practical discussion. It also revises the title, adds acknowledgments and an impact statement, and adopts author–year citations. Much of the retained scientific prose remains verbatim.

P2.justification: v2 adds six appendix tables, expands the objective-ablation and full-range comparison tables, redraws Figure 1's baseline panel, and annotates the existing t-SNE plots with red boxes. The hyperparameter table moves to the appendix, and the document adopts ICML formatting with running headers and single-column appendices.

R1.justification: Section 2 newly discusses Ding et al.'s adjacent-timestep ensemble distillation and distinguishes the present ensemble-to-submodel supervision. References to SEENN, additional architectures, recent transformers and adaptive encoding support the expanded discussion. The broader positioning around efficient logits-based SNN distillation remains intact.

T1.justification: Lemma 1, Propositions 2–3 and their derivations are retained. Appendix A relocates the proofs and repeats the existing statements as Equations (13)–(15); it does not introduce new assumptions, bounds or mathematical corrections.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's central efficiency and deployment claims. The added matched logits-KD timestep controls, measured training overhead and SEENN-I accuracy–cost tradeoffs address important validation gaps in v1. Teacher-free ablations and additional architectures further test the framework's usefulness. These gains improve empirical credibility despite unchanged uncertainty reporting and limited implementation detail for some new experiments.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same temporal-wise distillation framework. Text, equations, figures and tables are readable. v1 contains proofs and experimental details in the main text; v2 relocates these to Appendices A–B and adds supplementary experiments in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds experiments measuring training costs, firing rates, additional architectures and confidence-based early exits.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification results on four datasets, objective ablations, loss and clustering visualizations, and evaluations across training and inference timesteps.

These claims are not substantively reframed despite the revised results.

C2.justification: Section 6 strengthens the qualification concerning SAE labels. v1 notes shallow concepts and possible changes in benchmark rankings; v3 explicitly attributes part of SAE underperformance to limitations of automatic interpretation, even after supervised feature selection, and suggests better labeling could improve SAE performance.

D1.justification: v3 documents removal of gradients parallel to learned weights for Probe and ReFT-r1, specifies equally weighted MSE and cosine losses for the affine mapper, and supplies BoW tokenization and hyperparameter grids. These are additional implementation disclosures; the original unit-norm constraint, prompt templates, and code/data access information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use CONCEPT10, CONCEPT500, CONCEPT16K, the same text/code/math instruction sources, and Alpaca-Eval steering instructions. Balanced and imbalanced detection, cross-model transfer, and English/Chinese examples are retained; the added comparator introduces no new dataset or task coverage.

Conversely, generated-vector and affine-transfer comparisons shrink from broad baseline lists in v1 Tables 4–7 to ReFT-r1, DiffMean, and SAE in v3 Tables 4–5, removing prompting and finetuning comparators from those comparisons.

E3.justification: v3 divides the ten steering instructions per concept equally between steering-factor selection and held-out evaluation; v1 selects the factor maximizing the evaluation score without this separation. Prompting and finetuning also change from averaging factor-indexed generations to randomly scoring a generation on the testing instructions, equalizing sampling with steering methods. These substantially revise the central evaluation design.

E4.justification: BoW is added to the existing balanced-versus-imbalanced detection analysis. The data-scaling, generated-vector, affine-transfer, and SAE clamping studies remain, with revised steering outcomes rather than new analytical questions. The code-error clustering example also replaces one highlighted feature.

E5.justification: Both retain paired t-test reporting in Section 5.1, existing error-bar and distribution displays, and three data-scaling seeds, 42, 43, and 44. No new uncertainty estimator or increased replication count is reported. Condensed appendix tables omit duplicated significance markings that remain available in the main comparison.

E6.justification: Under the revised steering protocol, Table 2 replaces ReFT-r1's mean score of 0.735 with 0.543 and SAE's 0.315 with 0.165; ReFT-r1 moves from third to fifth. Table 3 changes ReFT-r1's mean win rate from 88.0% to 81.8%. v3 also adds BoW AUROC results, averaging 0.914, and 9B SAE-A entries, while updating generated-vector, transfer, scaling, and clamping results. These are not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The synthetic-data pipeline and core ReFT-r1 procedure remain: concept detection through a learned direction, top-k-dependent intervention training, and language-modeling loss with sparsity regularization. The equation corrections and newly documented optimization details do not establish an underlying algorithm change. Generated-vector and affine-transfer methods already appear in v1.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized wording and notation edits, moves the SAE concept-source footnote into Appendix B, consolidates the SAE ablation subsections, and adds an Impact Statements section. The main narrative, section order, and most appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The mean ROC plot moves from the main text to the appendix, comparison displays expand for BoW and 9B SAE-A, Figure 10 gains connecting lines, and Figure 11 is redesigned with a labeled cluster enlargement. Four large supplementary comparison tables become two compact paired tables, and hyperparameter tables gain BoW columns and rows. This substantially reorganizes the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds Bhalla et al. (2025) to the discussion of interpretability-based control and previous steering evaluations. The broader positioning and historical appendix remain substantially unchanged; other reference edits mainly concern bibliographic formatting.

T1.justification: Equation 9 corrects the ReFT-r1 intervention to add the mean top-k activation multiplied by the learned vector to each token representation. The appendix clamping equations now subtract the original latent activation, including for minimum clamping. These correct mathematical definitions; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: The held-out steering-factor evaluation and matched generation sampling address an important source of optimistic and uneven comparisons in v1's central benchmark. Corrected intervention equations and additional controls further strengthen validity and reproducibility. Reporting remains imperfect: Section 5.2 still quotes win rates of 88.0% and 61.6%, although Table 3 now reports 81.8% and 58.7%, and retains optimistic ReFT-r1 comparison prose. These inconsistencies temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial evaluation improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AxBench study and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Appendix renumbering and reorganized displays can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical studies and reports revised steering results, a new bag-of-words comparison, and additional SAE-A evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original concept-detection and steering experiments, plus appendix studies of data efficiency, generated steering vectors, cross-model transfer, and SAE interventions.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add an explicit claim of effective nudity removal on I2P. It explains cat–dog interference through early-timestep feature overlap and interprets object-attack failures partly as classifier artifacts, supported by qualitative examples and CLIPScore analysis.

Existing SAE optimizer, hardware, and training-time details remain. However, v1's explicit DDIM sampler, guidance scale of 9, and activation-dataset size disclosures disappear.

Table 1 replaces separate domain averages with an overall average. Added protocols include SD-v1.4 nudity evaluation with a 0.6 NudeNet threshold, Q16 evaluation, 49-of-50-style unlearning, and training-size sweeps.

E4.justification: V3 adds object and nudity attack analyses, training-data/time scaling, cat–dog feature-overlap failure studies, hyperparameter sweeps, classwise retention analysis, qualitative baseline comparisons, and automated feature annotations. The original block ablation, held-out-style generalization, and activation-steering studies remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report main UnlearnCanvas results averaged over five random seeds and retain the existing uncertainty presentation in sequential-unlearning plots. No changed repeated-run protocol, confidence-interval procedure, or significance-testing practice is documented.

E6.justification: Under revised selection and tuning, Table 1 replaces object UA/IRA/CRA of 84.23/90.05/76.78% with 78.82/95.47/95.58%; these are not same-setting gains. New results include 18 nudity detections (Table 2), 1.40% post-attack nudity ASR (Table 7), and 44.6% overall inappropriate content (Table 8). Reported inference overhead also changes from approximately 10% to 1.92%.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.2 replace percentile-threshold feature selection with explicit top-τ selection and add filtering of dead and excessively frequent features. These refine feature selection while retaining the SAE architecture, training objective, negative activation scaling, and inference intervention.

P1.justification: V3 edits the abstract and existing prose, converts several numbered subsections to paragraph headings, and reorders technical details. Pseudocode moves from Appendix I to S, while the style-classification and score-distribution appendices move from K–L to I–J. Much of the original narrative and section structure is retained.

P2.justification: V3 adds safety-result tables, feature visualizations, efficiency plots, failure analyses, sensitivity heatmaps, comparative image grids, and annotated examples. Table 1 is restructured around one overall average, the method diagram and score histogram exchange order, and the original feature-count bar chart is removed.

R1.justification: V3 acknowledges concurrent Concept Steerers work, explicitly distinguishes its intervention from changing prompt embeddings or model weights, and adds citations supporting safety baselines and automated feature annotation. The central positioning around sparse-autoencoder interpretability and mechanistic unlearning remains intact; publication-year updates are largely bibliographic.

T1.justification: Equation (5) revises the formal selected-feature set from threshold exceedance to top-τ ranking, also reflected in Appendix H. V3 corrects the input/latent dimension relationship and uses n rather than d in latent-feature summations. No new theorems or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: V1's broad practical claims rely mainly on UnlearnCanvas and brief cost limitations. V3 substantially strengthens their assessment through safety benchmarks, adversarial and sensitivity studies, and interpretable failure analyses. Its explicit deployment, similarity, and abstract-concept limitations improve claim calibration. Some sampling details are lost and revised results trade lower object-unlearning accuracy for better retention, but the broader evidence and clearer boundaries provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same SAeUron work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds nudity and inappropriate-content evaluations, adversarial tests, sensitivity studies, and feature-interpretation analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original SAeUron unlearning results in Table 1, feature-classification experiments, adversarial evaluation, and appendix experiments on generalization and activation steering.

Appendix B.5 also newly interprets SRCC 0.6860 as indicating independence between dimensions, an interpretation that the reported correlation does not establish.

The ten repetitions concern rating-consistency analysis, not additional model-training runs.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include the AGAVQA-3k name, localized wording edits, affiliation/publication information, an Impact Statement, and reorganized appendices separating human evaluation from dataset construction and experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds the scoring-interface figure and compact backbone, rating-variability, and category-accuracy tables. Table 3 gains rows and training-status headings; Tables 1–2 and Figure 2 receive label corrections. Existing MOS plots and instruction/latency tables are retained and relocated, with the overall visual format preserved.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for GroundingGPT, OneLLM, Krippendorff reliability, and three Sun et al. papers on visual attention/perception. The principal related-work discussion and positioning relative to existing audio-visual quality assessment remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 1 is retained. Appendix C.2 supplies standard formulas for the cross-entropy and PLCC objectives already specified in v1; it does not introduce new theoretical reasoning, assumptions, proofs, or substantively different mathematics.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps by reporting rating reliability and comparing selection against fine-tuned baselines, while substantially improving annotation and preprocessing documentation. Corrected metric headers also resolve inconsistencies between v1's benchmark and ablation tables. These gains strengthen the paper's evidential support and reproducibility despite conflicting scoring ranges, the pretraining-count mismatch, and the unsupported interpretation of correlation as independence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AGAV-Rater study. Their complete main texts, appendices, figures, tables, and equations support comparison, including matching renamed datasets and relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds backbone comparisons, annotator-reliability analyses, and category-specific selection results.

C1.justification: The introduction adds formal almost-colorings in two and three dimensions to the principal contributions, including the improved five-color bound. C2.justification: v2 explains how freedom to enlarge the removed region enables automated formalization, discusses neural representations' advantages and tuning limitations, and identifies finer discretization as a possible improvement for the three-dimensional construction. D1.justification: v2 adds a repository link for reproduction code and formalized constructions. Appendix B supplies previously absent instructions for detecting periodicity through translated radial evaluations, constructing cell conflict masks, and repairing conflicts. E2.justification: Section 5 newly reports experiments with Fourier bases and Voronoi diagrams, stating that neural networks performed best. These are additional evaluated alternatives, although the comparison is qualitative and supplies no scores or matched experimental settings.

These are reported setting changes, without establishing that all retained experiments were rerun.

Section 5 adds qualitative sensitivity observations concerning architecture, penalty scale, and box size. The triangle conflict-threshold analysis in Appendix E was already present.

E5.justification: v1's Table 1 explicitly reports the best of 60 runs; v2 removes that run-count and selection disclosure. The general experimental description changes from hundreds to thousands of runs to thousands of runs, without establishing a specific increase. Neither version supplies confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces numerical entries and adds formalized results: the five-color entry changes from 4.01% in a finite box to 3.60% numerically under periodic evaluation and 3.74% formalized, specified as 3.7356% in the text. These are not same-setting performance comparisons. Section 4.3 newly reports 2.3% numerical conflicts and a formal almost-14-coloring excluding 3.4622% of space. The formal triangle-bound regions also change between v1 Figure 3 and v2 Figure 4. Some prior-bound entries change beyond rounding, including 0.0143% to 0.02% for six colors.

M1.justification: v2 introduces Algorithm 1: extract periodicity, retrain with an exact periodic coordinate mapping, discretize the output, and repair conflicts through recoloring. It also applies this procedure in three dimensions. This substantially extends the procedure beyond v1's neural optimization and subsequent human formalization; the original losses remain.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution list are reorganized, the discussion is expanded, an Impact Statement is added, and terminology and prose receive local corrections. The section sequence, four-variant organization, and substantial portions of the narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 2 and an Algorithm 1 display, expands Table 1, and replaces Appendix B's numerical coloring displays with six formalized periodic constructions. It redraws the formal triangle-bound diagram, recolors other triangle plots, enlarges the three-dimensional visualization, and moves v1 Figure 7 into Appendix C as Figure 13. Together these substantially revise the presentation of constructions and verification.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to AlphaEvolve, Alfarano et al., Trinh et al., Gwyn and Stavrianos, and Croft, extending the discovery-method context and attribution of prior coloring bounds. The main positioning relative to combinatorial optimization and implicit neural representations remains. Several other reference changes merely update publication metadata.

T1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Appendix B add a mathematical construction using periodic parallelogram cells and explain reducing continuous unit-distance avoidance to stricter discrete cell constraints. Proposition 3.1, its proof, and the existing loss formulations remain unchanged. No separate new theorem or complete construction proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v1 left the five-color and three-dimensional almost-colorings unformalized. v2 substantially addresses that gap through Algorithm 1, Appendix B's procedural explanation, separately reported numerical and formalized results, and code-access information. This strengthens the connection between neural exploration and checkable mathematical constructions. Full construction accounts remain deferred and Table 1 loses explicit run-count detail, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in methodological completeness and evidential clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same neural approach to Hadwiger-Nelson coloring problems. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–F are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original numerical experiments and adds periodic almost-coloring evaluations and results from its automated formalization procedure.

before.justification: v1 reports original neural-network experiments, numerical conflict rates, and discovered colorings for planar, off-diagonal, three-dimensional, triangle-avoidance, and alternative-norm problems.

Algorithm 1 also omits the previously explicit initialization of the critic-loop convergence variable, without explaining an implementation change.

E1.justification: Appendix D.9 adds Vehicle Safety and Welded Beam evaluations, optimizing vehicle mass and beam manufacturing cost while assessing secondary safety and deflection objectives. It also evaluates GC content of candidates from the retained UTR task. The original six-task coverage remains.

E2.justification: The broader comparison adds Tri-Mentoring, ICT, PGS, Match-Opt and RGD, with results across the six original tasks and five quality/diversity metrics in v2 Tables A6–A8. These methods were absent from the corresponding v1 Tables A5–A6; existing comparators are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix E.5 introduces controlled Sobol-versus-top-k initialization comparisons using 64 initial designs, with gradient ascent except Adam for RoMA. Appendix D.9 introduces 800-design synthetic datasets and evaluates secondary-objective dispersion among 128 candidates; Welded Beam is evaluated without its original constraints. These are added protocols, not demonstrated changes to the retained experiments. The dispersion metric is inconsistently called standard deviation in the prose and variance in Table A10.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.5 and Table A14 test whether initialization explains DynAMO's diversity advantage. New Appendix D.9 and Table A10 investigate whether candidate diversity accompanies broader secondary-objective values. Existing component, hyperparameter, batch-size and oracle-budget ablations remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and 95% confidence intervals over ten random seeds. Added tables follow that practice, and original uncertainty information remains in the relocated tables. Secondary-objective dispersion is an additional evaluation outcome, not a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for five comparators, secondary-objective exploration and paired initialization. Existing per-task scores are retained, while ranks change with the expanded comparator set: DynAMO-BO-qUCB's Best@128 average rank changes from 4.8 in v1 Table A5 to 6.3 in v2 Table A6, with its optimality gap unchanged at 20.5. This is not a same-setting performance decline.

M1.justification: The KL-regularized objective, source-critic constraint, dual optimization, model architectures and candidate-generation procedure are retained. The mixed-divergence extension was already present in v1 Appendix D.3. Algorithm 1's documentation edits do not establish a changed underlying method.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact. Local expansions explain optimization families and source critics, elaborate limitations, clarify Algorithm 1's inputs/comments and update publication information. The revision is principally additive rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The full main-results table becomes appendix Table A1, while main Table 1 is redesigned as a compact rank/optimality-gap summary. Expanded comparison tables are reorganized, including splitting the former diversity table, and Tables A10 and A14 display new analyses. Figure 1's legend changes from DAAG-Modified to DynAMO-Modified; existing analysis figures are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantial coverage of first-order, evolutionary and Bayesian optimization, including a distinction between DynAMO and diversity-gated or BO-specific approaches. Appendix D.5 expands the discussion to five additional evaluated methods, and new references support the secondary-objective applications. This extends research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Lemma 3.1 and its proof are substantially rewritten using a point-mass/residual decomposition and a measure-based argument. New Remark A.1 derives equivalence to KL state matching against a rescaled reference distribution. The other principal derivations and Appendix D.4 bounds are retained. The revised lemma's statement omits the optimality condition needed for its conclusion.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by testing initialization as a possible explanation for diversity gains and directly examining the proposed benefit for secondary-objective exploration, neither addressed experimentally in v1. Five additional comparators and clearer applicability limits further improve the assessment of DynAMO. These gains concern evidential credibility, not higher retained benchmark scores. The missing optimality condition in revised Lemma 3.1 and inconsistent dispersion labeling are defects, but do not outweigh the substantial empirical improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DynAMO research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support comparison. Material relocated between the 43-page v1 and 52-page v2 can be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds evaluated comparators, secondary-objective evaluations and an initialization ablation.

before.justification: v1 reports original optimization experiments across six tasks and six backbone optimizers, with quality, diversity, computational-cost and ablation results.

results.title:
Diversity By Design: Leveraging Distribution Matching for Offline
  Model-Based Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain multivariate OT-based prediction regions, finite-sample marginal coverage, and asymptotic conditional coverage. The conclusion now explicitly qualifies the efficiency advantages by acknowledging potentially more conservative regression sets and greater computational cost, modestly narrowing the overall contribution narrative.

C2.justification: v2 explains why distribution-free fitted ranks alone do not justify the original coverage argument and motivates separate calibration. It adds substantive limitations concerning small-sample overcoverage, set-size and runtime costs, and opportunities for alternative reference distributions or entropic maps. Appendix D.4 also interprets classification benefits through label-confusion patterns.

D1.justification: Appendix D.1 newly identifies the network simplex solver in Python Optimal Transport; this is a disclosure, not evidence of a solver change. v2 adds neighborhood-size guidance and specifies the five-class MNIST labels. The CIFAR-10 neural-network architecture details disappear with that experiment.

E1.justification: v2 removes the five-class CIFAR-10 evaluation, eliminating the natural-image benchmark, and adds five-class MNIST and a synthetic classification scenario with less-confusable classes. The six regression datasets and full MNIST/Fashion-MNIST tasks remain. Thus represented image domains and classification scenarios change substantially.

E2.justification: Predictive baseline membership remains ELL/REC for synthetic regression, adaptive ELL for real regression, and IP/MS/APS for classification. Figure 12 newly compares OT-CP and OT-CP+ runtimes, adding a limited comparison between existing variants. Newly cited competing approaches are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: MNIST/Fashion-MNIST experiments change from 20,000 observations with a 10%/80%/10% train/calibration/test split to 25,000 with 10%/45%/45%. Calibration now includes D1/D2 splitting. Appendix D.2 additionally reports a square-root neighborhood rule for larger datasets, while new experiments vary calibration size and measure runtime, marginal coverage, and volume.

E4.justification: Appendix D.4 adds runtime scaling with calibration size and a controlled comparison of more versus less-confusable synthetic classes. These investigate computational scalability and when classification advantages arise, extending v1's existing five-versus-ten-class analysis. Figure 13 also exposes coverage, volume, and runtime tradeoffs in real regression.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten repeated random draws for the image-classification experiments and display error bars. v2 does not introduce a changed repetition policy, seed specification, confidence-interval definition, or significance-testing procedure. Changed error-bar magnitudes are result changes.

E6.justification: Numerous plotted results change. For example, Figure 4's low-data wq worst-set coverage for the adaptive method falls from approximately 0.92 to 0.79. New runtime, regression-efficiency, easier-classification, and five-class MNIST results appear, while CIFAR-10 results disappear. Given the method and protocol revisions, these are replaced or newly reported outcomes, not controlled same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: Section 2.3 replaces v1's fixed rank threshold with split calibration: D1 learns the transport map and D2 calibrates its threshold. OT-CP+ likewise replaces its fixed neighborhood-based threshold with a threshold calibrated across held-out conditional ranks. These change both procedures, rather than merely documenting them.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain. v2 expands procedural explanations, reorganizes the appendices into methodology, proofs, related work, and experiments, and adds an Impact Statement and affiliation edits. Much of the substantial rewriting accompanies scientific changes rather than an independent overhaul of the narrative.

P2.justification: Classification displays are reorganized into aggregated main-text metrics and paired label-wise coverage plots, with detailed results in the appendix. New runtime, regression-tradeoff, easier-classification, and MNIST-subset figures appear; CIFAR-10's figure disappears. Existing figures also receive layout, caption, and legend revisions, including identifying OT-CP+ correctly in Figure 4.

R1.justification: New Appendix C substantially expands positioning across copula, multiple-testing, latent-space, density/sampling, and shape-optimization approaches. v2 discusses concurrent work by Klein, Dheur, Braun, and Luo and Zhou, including the relationship between OT-CP and entropic transport-based conformal prediction.

T1.justification: Theorem 2.4 changes its upper bound from alpha + 2/(n+1) to alpha + n_ties/(n2+1), with rewritten exchangeability arguments and a generalized tie lemma. Theorem 3.2 now specifies convergence in probability as both calibration subsets grow. Appendix B adds threshold-consistency Lemma B.2 and substantially replaces the conditional-coverage proof.

improvement.justification: The separate map-fitting and threshold-calibration stages address the exchangeability gap underlying v1's central coverage argument, substantially improving the paper's theoretical foundation. Added computational evidence, implementation details, and explicit limitations improve assessability. Removing CIFAR-10 narrows empirical breadth, and Section 3.2 still overstates Figure 4's worst-set coverage, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the repair of the main validity argument and fuller accounting of practical tradeoffs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OT-CP research. Their main text, equations, figures, table, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial methodological revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original regression and classification experiments, supplemented by runtime measurements and additional classification scenarios in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments, regression evaluations on six real datasets, and classification results on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, including appendix experiments.

results.title: Optimal Transport-based Conformal Prediction

C1.justification: The central claims remain a general MI lower-bound approach for continuous MOBO, optimized mixing of over- and under-truncation, and particular benefits with three or more objectives. The added application experiments broaden supporting evidence without substantively strengthening or narrowing these principal claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of weaker method differences on high-dimensional, highly multimodal problems, argues that additional MC samples cannot remove frontier-discretization bias, and discusses potentially insufficient variational flexibility. It also explains the choice of DIRECT and explicitly qualifies comparison fairness across GPy and BoTorch. These substantially expand the interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix J newly specifies EHVI reference vectors using coordinatewise minima minus 10^-4 and maxima plus 1; v1's silence does not establish a changed setting.
