Appendices F/M provide BoTorch implementation names and configurations, while Section 6.3 supplies application dataset dimensions and split information. Core PFEV implementation details largely remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's GP-generated and analytic benchmark functions, v2 adds LightGBM class-weight optimization on Abalone, Waveform, Pageblocks, and Gesturephase, plus DTLZ1–7. Parallel, decoupled, and noisy scenarios were already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds Random to GP and main benchmark comparisons and qLogNEHVI to the GP comparison in Figure 29. Appendix F replaces the custom grid-based HVKG approximation with BoTorch's one-shot implementation. JES disappears from the matched d=10 FES panels. ParEGO, MOBO-RS, and MESMO remain in appendix comparisons despite their omission from main plots.

E3.justification: The decoupled PFEV population changes from the inherited size 50 to 10, alongside revised HVKG settings with 10 Pareto points and 10 fantasy samples. New LightGBM experiments use an 80:20 split and hypervolume of per-class test accuracies with reference zero. v2 also adds gradient-versus-DIRECT controls for qLogNEHVI and FES dimensions 5–9 alongside the existing d=10 setting.

E4.justification: v2 adds mixture-weight trajectories, analyses stratified by input dimension and length scale, FES dimension sweeps, truncation-volume error versus frontier sample size, and optimizer comparisons (Appendices C, K, L, and M). These substantially broaden mechanism and sensitivity evidence beyond the retained estimator and noise analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report 10 runs, standard deviations for the main benchmark curves, and standard errors for noisy-observation results. The new mixture-weight trajectory uses the existing 10-run mean-and-standard-deviation practice; no new significance testing, confidence intervals, or seed-reporting practice is introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds application, DTLZ, qLogNEHVI, dimension-sweep, and diagnostic results. Figure 27 reports PFEV advantages on DTLZ2/5/6/7 but better EHVI and MESMO performance on DTLZ4. Decoupled curves are replaced under revised settings, showing near parity with BoTorch KG at length scale 0.25; this is not a same-setting improvement. Table 1 timings remain unchanged.

M1.justification: New Section 7 proposes gradient-compatible adaptations, including replacing the hard Pareto-region indicator with a Gaussian-smoothed probability. These are prospective alternatives: the mixture, MAP acquisition, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged, and reported PFEV experiments still use DIRECT.

P1.justification: v2 copyedits terminology and grammar, changes lower-bound notation from L to LB, retitles Appendix C, and inserts application and gradient-discussion sections. Most existing prose and the overall narrative sequence are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds application, DTLZ, optimizer, mixture-weight, truncation, and stratified-boxplot displays. The original d=10 FES figure becomes three dimension-sweep grids. Main Figures 3 and 5 simplify displayed comparator sets while fuller comparisons appear in appendices; other figures and captions are relocated or revised.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ament et al. (2023), Daulton et al. (2020, 2021), Ke et al. (2017), and Ozaki et al. (2024), supporting the hypervolume baselines and LightGBM application. Positioning relative to PFES, JES, and PF2ES remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix C adds an existence argument for the MAP objective's maximizing mixture weight on (0,1], using its limit of negative infinity as the weight approaches zero. Appendix D.1 corrects the beta posterior from Beta(a+m,a+l) to Beta(a+m,b+l). The principal MI lower-bound derivation remains intact.

improvement.justification: v1's validation was confined to GP-generated and analytic functions. The LightGBM application, stronger comparator coverage, and direct mixture/truncation diagnostics substantially strengthen empirical relevance and the method's justification. The added existence argument and explicit limitations also improve rigor. BoTorch comparisons remain implementation-confounded, and Figure 29 omits the four benchmark comparisons mentioned in Appendix M, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PFEV research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including Appendices A–K in v1 and A–M in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds LightGBM optimization, DTLZ benchmarks, optimizer comparisons, and truncation diagnostics.

before.justification: Section 6 and the appendices report original optimization experiments, estimator comparisons, and evaluations of parallel, decoupled, and noisy settings.

results.title: Pareto-frontier Entropy Search with Variational Lower Bound Maximization

C1.justification: The abstract, three introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: high-temperature reverse-KLD training avoids mode collapse, iterative reweighting anneals to the target temperature, and molecular experiments achieve strong accuracy with up to threefold fewer energy evaluations. Added appendix evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies efficiency and scalability. Appendix J explains that additional flow evaluations make TA-BG slower than FAB in the current setup, with anticipated benefits for expensive potentials. Appendix F.4 discusses high-dimensional importance-sampling failure. The discussion adds permutation-invariance limitations, while Appendix K explains the illustrative scope of GMM results and exclusion of symmetric-particle benchmarks.

D1.justification: The Software and Data statement changes from a promised release to concrete GitHub and Zenodo access locations. v2 also documents million-sample validation datasets, cosine scheduling for forward/reverse KLD, regularized-energy use in ESS, GMM implementation settings, and CPU/GPU hardware with timing details. These materially expand reproducibility information; newly disclosed details do not alone establish changed experiments.

E1.justification: The three peptide systems are retained, while v2 extends evaluation beyond molecular distributions with a 40-component two-dimensional Gaussian mixture (Appendix K) and a Gaussian IS/AIS scaling experiment reaching 500 dimensions (Appendix F.4). These add distinct synthetic sampling scenarios, without demonstrating coverage of larger molecular systems.

E2.justification: The molecular comparator set remains forward KLD, reverse KLD, and FAB. The new GMM comparison adds PIS, DDS, iDEM, and Real-NVP FAB alongside neural-spline FAB (Table 15), substantially broadening comparison methods. Appendix K explicitly attributes the diffusion and Real-NVP FAB scores to prior work; they are reported comparisons, not new runs by these authors.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled annealing sweeps, Gaussian dimension-scaling protocols, and GMM-specific model configurations and evaluation using 1,000 samples per metric. It also revises molecular FAB's reported coordinate range from [-5,5] to [0,10] and initial HMC step size from 0.1 to 0.05 (v1 G.2; v2 G.1). These explicit setting revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained FAB ablations and qualitative workflow variations, v2 adds systematic TA-BG tests of direct reweighting, starting temperature, linear versus geometric schedules, final and intermediate fine-tuning, annealing count, and buffer size (F.3). Appendices F.4 and J additionally analyze dimensional scaling and computational cost.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains means and standard errors over four independent experiments. New Table 15 instead reports standard deviations, using four runs for the authors' GMM experiments and three for imported results. Appendix F.3 specifies single runs for most new ablations and four runs per starting temperature. No increase in the main experiments' run count is stated.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results change: Table 1's hexapeptide NLL becomes -501.511 instead of -501.523 for TA-BG, and -501.268 instead of -501.275 for FAB. Substantial new results include hexapeptide ESS of 15.38% versus 7.56% with versus without intermediate fine-tuning, GMM comparisons, and runtime measurements. Main molecular conclusions remain; revised settings prevent interpreting updated scores as demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The two-stage TA-BG algorithm and molecular flow architecture remain. Appendix C changes the specified regularized energy for E > E_max from E_max to log(E_max - E_high + 1) + E_high, a limited correction to the training loss definition. Whether implementation changed is unstated. The AIS extension in Appendix F.4 is proposed for future use.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain. v2 makes localized explanations of training, annealing, and metrics clearer, standardizes terminology, and reorganizes appendix hyperparameters by method. Acknowledgments and an impact statement are added. The retained narrative is refined rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 5–11 and Tables 6–9, 14, and 15 for ablations, scaling, runtime, and GMM results. Earlier appendix Figures 5–11 correspond to Figures 12–18, with several heatmaps updated. The ICML format also changes typography, title and affiliation layout, headers, captions, reference columns, and table placement throughout.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and context for diffusion samplers, transition-path sampling, adaptive AIS, and recent flow/protein-ensemble models. The central positioning against MD-dependent temperature-transfer approaches and FAB remains largely unchanged. Publication updates for existing works, such as TRADE, are not new research additions.

T1.justification: New Appendix F.4 introduces an independent-neighborhood clash model and derives expected normalized ESS = (1 - eta)^N, explaining exponential degradation with dimension. Appendix C also corrects the piecewise energy-regularization definition. These are limited mathematical additions and corrections; the main flow and reweighting derivations remain.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves important evidence and reporting gaps: Appendix F.3 tests design choices that v1 largely justified verbally, and Appendix J exposes the wall-time tradeoff behind energy-evaluation savings. Scaling limitations, implementation details, and concrete code/data locations improve interpretation and reproducibility. Most new ablations remain single-run and the Gaussian tests are limited demonstrations, but the stronger empirical justification and more transparent costs substantially improve overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Temperature-Annealed Boltzmann Generators by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite formatting changes and substantial additions.

after.justification: v2 retains original molecular experiments and adds TA-BG ablations, Gaussian dimension-scaling experiments, runtime measurements, and original Gaussian-mixture sampling results.

before.justification: v1 reports original sampling experiments on three peptide systems, molecular simulations, and FAB hyperparameter experiments, including Table 1 and Appendix H.

results.title: Temperature-Annealed Boltzmann Generators

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements retain the same central claims: a parameter-free loss modification produces sharper deterministic forecasts, improves effective resolution from 1,250 km to 160 km, and benefits ensemble spread, cyclone intensity and wind extremes. The added evidence supports these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds focused qualifications about the meaning of effective resolution, the untested use of AMSE throughout training, and possible regularization benefits of MSE. It also explains why multiscale separation is necessary to prevent coarse-scale variance from concealing missing fine-scale variability. Existing precipitation, lagged-ensemble and out-of-distribution limitations remain.

D1.justification: v1 promises training-code release upon publication. v2 instead reports access locations and licenses for the AMSE implementation, training code and fine-tuned checkpoints. It also documents the new loss-control configurations and filtering parameters. This substantially expands actionable reproducibility information, although external resource availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same HRES/ERA5 training coverage, 2022 weather evaluation, tropical-cyclone observations and North American station comparisons. The added controls reuse existing forecasting tasks, and the new filtered visualization examines the existing winter storm Eunice case.

E2.justification: Appendix B.5, Figure 14 and Table 2 add MSE AR12 and MAE AR12 as evaluated comparators. MSE AR12 is distinct from the retained, unmodified Control: it receives the fine-tuning curriculum, providing an important additional-training control. MAE AR12 adds a competing loss-function comparison.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes the reported warm-up from 128 to 64 batches per stage. Appendix B.4 revises SER to form spatially aggregated variance/error ratios; B.4.1 adds bias-adjusted ensemble-error evaluation. The new visualization uses a fourth-order high-pass filter with cutoff wavenumber 50, while the new loss controls reuse the existing curriculum. These are localized protocol additions and revisions; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained AR1/AR12 and spectral analyses, v2 adds matched-curriculum loss ablations testing whether extra training explains improved sharpness (B.5), a high-pass analysis of Eunice forecast structures (B.1), and an analysis of finite-ensemble error bias (B.4.1). The new training control addresses a central attribution question absent from v1.

E5.justification: v2 adds finite-ensemble bias estimation and a variance-subtraction correction for ensemble mean squared error, and explicitly uses unbiased ensemble variance in SER. The existing one-third-date bootstrap sampling and 90% significance threshold remain. No additional training seeds or repeated-run counts are reported.

E6.justification: New results establish that MSE/MAE fine-tuning retains fine-scale smoothing, although MAE improves intermediate-scale sharpness. Table 2 adds substantive comparisons: five-day z500 CRPS is 82.100 for MSE AR12, 80.621 for MAE AR12 and 80.469 for AMSE AR12; five-day q700 instead favors MAE, 0.499 versus AMSE's 0.510. Figure 13 adds results under the bias-adjusted metric, and some significance markers change in retained scorecards. The headline resolution and cyclone findings remain.

M1.justification: The proposed AMSE loss in Equation (6), variable/level weighting, GraphCast architecture and forecasting procedure are retained. The added MSE and MAE variants are comparison controls, rather than changes to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative are retained. Local changes expand the introduction and discussion, number the This Work subsection, rename Discussion as Discussion & Limitations, add appendix subsections, and update author, affiliation and acknowledgement text.

P2.justification: The main text and references are comprehensively reformatted from a single-column preprint into a two-column conference layout, with figures resized and relocated. v2 adds Figures 7, 13 and 14 and Table 2, adds a length-scale axis to the effective-resolution plot, and revises labels and captions in retained plots. These are substantial visual changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds relevant antecedents and approaches, including Weyn, Keisler, Allen, Han and Lippe, and relates AMSE to Chakraborty's binned spectral power loss. Kent and Leutbecher–Palmer support the new resolution discussion and bias analysis. The central positioning relative to ensemble methods and NeuralGCM remains; publication updates to retained references are not new works.

T1.justification: Appendix B.4.1 adds a derivation of the finite-ensemble squared-error bias, including the variance divided by ensemble-size term, and defines its correction in Equation (18). The SER definition also changes its normalization and spatial aggregation. The central AMSE derivation and Appendix A's KL-divergence analysis are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 compares AMSE fine-tuning principally with an untouched checkpoint, leaving extra training as a confound, and only promises future code. v2's matched-curriculum MSE/MAE controls directly address that attribution gap, while its code/checkpoint access information substantially improves reproducibility documentation. The finite-ensemble analysis and clearer resolution qualifications further strengthen evaluation. A local mean/median inconsistency in the new MAE explanation does not outweigh these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AMSE loss and GraphCast fine-tuning study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds MSE/MAE fine-tuning comparisons, filtered forecast visualizations and a finite-ensemble bias analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original GraphCast fine-tuning results, including spectral resolution, lagged-ensemble verification, tropical-cyclone prediction and comparisons with station observations.

results.title: Fixing the Double Penalty in Data-Driven Weather Forecasting Through a Modified Spherical Harmonic Loss Function

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about continuous noise distillation, cross-domain ICRL, self-correction and limited generalization. The added experiments support existing core claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: Appendix C newly interprets the controls as evidence that policy-improvement structure enables self-correction and reward feedback is essential for effective inference-time improvement. Existing interpretations and limitations concerning unseen-task generalization remain.

D1.justification: Section 2.3.1 clarifies that group identifiers concern shared dimensions and channel semantics. Appendix C documents architecture/loss matching and reward removal for its controls. Existing hyperparameters, hardware, dataset metadata and the promised code-release information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same four domains, 87 training tasks, held-out tasks and physical-parameter variations. The additional comparisons and controls reuse MuJoCo and Meta-World; they introduce no new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Section 3.2 and Appendix I add REGENT to the previously JAT-only cross-agent comparison, using published comparator scores. Appendix C additionally evaluates an architecture-matched Expert Distillation model and reward-masked AD, substantially expanding the comparison methods.

E3.justification: Appendix C adds expert-only training and reward-masking controls evaluated through cold-start inference. Figure 8 reports mean normalized scores, whereas the retained main adaptation plots use IQM. Existing benchmark splits, rollout settings and Vintix's 100-episode comparison protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Sections C.1–C.2 test whether policy-improvement trajectories outperform expert-only demonstrations under the same architecture and whether rewards contribute to adaptation. Figure 8 supplies direct controls for central mechanism claims that v1 lacked. Existing generalization analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 removes the explicit 100-trial JAT disclosure and Figure 5's Vintix error bars, while newly tabulating JAT scores with ± values in Tables 11–12. Other 95% confidence-interval displays remain. No increase in independent runs or seeds is documented.

E6.justification: Appendix C newly reports ED scores around 0.80 versus AD scores of 0.97 on MuJoCo and 0.95 on Meta-World, plus poorer reward-masked performance. Appendix I adds task-level REGENT and JAT results, and Figure 5 revises aggregate bars. Existing task-level Vintix tables retain their values; the new mean-based controls do not establish changes to earlier IQM results.

M1.justification: Continuous Noise Distillation, the Vintix architecture, prediction loss and inference procedure are retained. The added group-identifier explanation clarifies the existing architecture; Appendix C introduces experimental controls, not a revised proposed method.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section order are retained. Local revisions clarify group identifiers, update the comparison discussion, expand related work and introduce Appendices C and I. Author spelling, affiliations, publication information and several typographical details also change.

P2.justification: Figure 5 is redrawn for three comparators, Figure 8 and Tables 11–12 are added, and Figure 4 is relocated. The hyperparameter table is reformatted and captioned. Existing appendix plots and numerical tables are retained with renumbering and limited repositioning.

R1.justification: Section 4 adds a Sequence Modeling in RL discussion and five references covering Decision Transformer, Janner et al.'s sequence model, Online Decision Transformer, Decision Mamba and Reinformer. This extends positioning within an existing research lineage. REGENT was already cited in v1.

T1.justification: The trajectory and task notation, Algorithm 1 and Appendix A.3's noise-schedule formula are unchanged. No new formal assumptions, mathematical derivations, theorems or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 supported AD's advantage mainly through comparison with JAT, leaving architecture differences intertwined with the training approach. v2's architecture-matched ED control and reward-masking experiment directly strengthen evidence for the paper's central explanations; REGENT and task-level comparisons broaden scrutiny. These address important evidential gaps, although the new controls' training budgets and run details remain sparse and Figure 5 loses uncertainty bars.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Vintix and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Existing material can be matched reliably across appendix renumbering and layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds expert-distillation and reward-masking control experiments in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original Vintix experiments across four domains, including inference-time adaptation, parameter variations and held-out tasks, with detailed appendix results.

results.title: Vintix: Action Model via In-Context Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about dimensional soft advantages, autoregressive action dependencies, and learning from suboptimal data. The headline 1.62-fold D4RL comparison is unchanged; added experiments do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: Appendix G newly attributes prediction glitches without coarse-to-fine discretization to inadequate coverage of numerous action bins. Appendix F distinguishes demonstrations' benefit to learning speed from online interaction's benefit to final performance. The existing inference-latency limitation and proposed future remedies remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page URL, identifies datasets used for existing ablations and sensitivity tests, and documents DrQ-v2+'s critic, exploration, and configuration differences. Existing hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain. Conversely, Appendix C.3 removes v1's explicit statement that the RLBench baseline scores were taken from the CQN paper.

E1.justification: The same nine D4RL dataset/task combinations and 20 RLBench tasks remain. Appendix G adds a five-mode synthetic reward landscape beyond the original three-mode motivating example. Fully offline and demonstration-free online evaluations broaden data-access conditions on retained locomotion tasks, without adding another application domain.

E2.justification: The new offline comparison includes CQL, IQL, TD3+BC, Onestep RL, RvS-R, filtered BC, Decision Transformer, and DWBC. Most comparator scores come from cited papers, with selected DWBC results reevaluated. Appendix F also adds PPO to the online comparison. Existing main-experiment comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendix F introduce fully offline and fully online training protocols. Offline ARSQ and reevaluated DWBC use 10 evaluation trajectories; DWBC labels the top 5% of trajectories as expert. Appendix G introduces 2,000 training points and 1,000 error-evaluation points. Newly specified tasks for existing ablations are disclosures, not established protocol changes.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds a controlled analysis of Q-prediction and discretization errors, comparing independent decomposition, ARSQ without coarse-to-fine discretization, and full ARSQ. New D4RL learning curves examine convergence, while Appendix F compares learning with different data-access regimes. The earlier conditioning, backbone, and temperature analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports three seeds for existing demonstration-quality, RLBench, ablation, and sensitivity experiments, beyond v1's main D4RL disclosure. It adds error bars to previously unaccompanied auxiliary results and reports uncertainty in new tables. This establishes expanded reporting, not an increase in runs; uncertainty conventions remain unspecified.

E6.justification: New Table 1 reports an offline aggregate score of 741.1 for ARSQ versus 698.5 for CQL; Table 4 reports Q errors of 17.57, 0.50, and 0.16 for independent decomposition, ARSQ without coarse-to-fine discretization, and ARSQ. Online and convergence results are added. Existing Figure 5 revises bottom-30% ARSQ/CQN scores from 73.1/33.8 to 69.8/35.7, reducing the stated ratio from 2.2 to 2.0. Ablation and sensitivity values also change; Figure 4's headline results remain.

M1.justification: The written method specification is corrected: Equation (16) adds the temperature multiplier to log-sum-exp normalization, and Equation (18) squares the training residual. The architecture, conditioning scheme, and algorithms remain substantively unchanged. These formula corrections do not establish that the implementation changed.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify dimensional advantages, double value networks, and DrQ-v2+. A fully offline subsection and Appendices F–G extend the existing structure, while most original prose and organization remain. Affiliations, proceedings information, acknowledgements, and heading capitalization are also updated.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual evidence with offline-performance and Q-error tables, D4RL and online learning curves, and Q-landscape/error heatmaps. Existing diagrams and plots are redrawn or rescaled, with revised legends and appendix placement. The original demonstration-quality and 20-task RLBench figures are retained and renumbered, not newly introduced.

R1.justification: References and comparisons are added for offline methods including IQL, TD3+BC, Onestep RL, Decision Transformer, RvS, and DWBC. The central related-work discussion and positioning relative to CQN and autoregressive Q-learning remain stable. Numerous other reference changes are publication-metadata updates rather than new cited works.

T1.justification: The added temperature multiplier in Equation (16) repairs the mathematical normalization needed to satisfy the dimensional-advantage constraint. Theorem 4.3 and its Appendix A proof remain substantively unchanged; rewriting log-sum-exp equal to zero as an exponential sum equal to one is equivalent.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects important normalization and loss-specification errors and substantially strengthens empirical justification through offline/online evaluations and a controlled test of the proposed discretization mechanism. Broader seed disclosures and uncertainty reporting also improve assessability. These gains concern correctness and evidential support, not higher headline performance, which remains unchanged. Removing explicit RLBench baseline-score provenance and leaving uncertainty conventions undefined are drawbacks, but they do not outweigh the substantive improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ARSQ research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original ARSQ results and adds fully offline and fully online evaluations, reevaluated DWBC results, and a controlled Q-prediction error study.

before.justification: v1 reports original ARSQ experiments on D4RL and RLBench, component ablations, temperature sensitivity, and computational measurements. Some baseline results are explicitly attributed to earlier work.

results.title: Learning from Suboptimal Data in Continuous Control via Auto-Regressive Soft Q-Network

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement retain the same claims: adaptive allocation without knowing worker means, performance comparable to informed allocation, resource savings over greedy allocation, and the ATA-Empirical variant. The revised mathematical guarantees and additional experiments do not change these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 6.2 now explains ATA-Empirical's adaptivity through η²μ_i² and relates recovery of individual Orlicz-norm dependence to comparable α_i/μ_i ratios across workers. V1 presented individual-norm adaptation without this qualification. Appendix A.2 also adds an interpretation of the new results as robustness across timing distributions.

D1.justification: V2 supplies sampling formulas for the new timing distributions, CNN layer and parameter counts, the Adam learning rate, and the procedure for reusing prior bandit observations. The existing Python and Intel Xeon implementation disclosure moves to Appendix A; no code-access resource is added.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates synthetic quadratic optimization and timing simulations. V2 adds CNN training on CIFAR-100 and a distinct worker environment combining Exponential, Uniform, Half-Normal, Lognormal and Gamma timing distributions, substantially broadening task and environment coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparators remain GTA/Rennala SGD, OFTA, labelled FTA: Optimal in plots, and UTA. V2 extends the same comparator set to its new experiments. Adam is the CNN optimizer, not an added allocation baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix A.4 introduces a 160k-parameter CNN evaluated with Adam at learning rate 8×10^-5, B=23 and n=17, 51, 153. Appendix A.5 adds a controlled protocol using 0, 500,000 or 5,000,000 prior bandit iterations at n=51. These are new experimental designs; the retained synthetic settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix A.2 adds robustness tests across five timing-distribution families with matched means within worker groups. Appendix A.5 tests how prior timing observations reduce exploration costs, a benefit only discussed in v1. The original linear-noise and regret analyses are retained as A.1 and A.3.

E5.justification: The regret experiment still reports five simulation runs and standard-deviation bars: v1 Section 7.2/Figure 3 becomes v2 Appendix A.3/Figure 4. No new repeated-run counts, seed disclosures or uncertainty-reporting procedures accompany the added experiments.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the original plots are retained, including the regret plot renumbered from Figure 3 to Figure 4. New Figures 3, 5 and 6 report mixed-distribution behavior, CIFAR-100 loss versus runtime and worker time, and faster approach to OFTA with prior observations. These are additional outcomes, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Equations (7)–(8) change the confidence multipliers from 4eα and 4eξ to 2α and 2η. ATA uses a centered Orlicz-norm bound, while ATA-Empirical replaces standard-deviation/mean prior information with an Orlicz-norm/mean bound. These change confidence calculations, but the allocation objective, algorithm loop and RAS procedure remain intact.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative remain unchanged. The linear-noise and regret subsections move into a new experimental appendix, subsequent appendices are relabelled, and v2 adds acknowledgments and an impact statement. Heading capitalization, correspondence information and several explanations receive limited editing.

P2.justification: V2 adds three substantial multipanel figures for heterogeneous distributions, CIFAR-100 and prior observations. Existing Figure 2 and the regret figure move into the appendix, with the latter becoming Figure 4. Table 2 is widened and expands method labels. The new displays and redistribution substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Boucheron et al. for concentration results, Kingma and Ba for Adam, and Krizhevsky et al. for CIFAR. The related-work positioning is otherwise retained. Updated MindFlayer and Ringmaster publication information refers to works already cited in v1.

T1.justification: Assumption 3.1 changes to centered Orlicz norms. Theorem 4.2 replaces 1+η√ln(B) with 1+4ηln(B), with η redefined through Orlicz norms. Theorem 6.3 replaces the factor (1+η²)α_i² with η²μ_i². V1's variance-to-Orlicz lemma is removed, and v2 substantially revises concentration, maximum and regret proofs in Appendices D–E.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens theoretical and empirical support. Appendix E replaces v1's problematic variance-based maximum and norm arguments with explicit Orlicz-norm derivations, while Appendix A adds a real neural-network task and targeted robustness and exploration studies. These address important weaknesses of v1. The runtime guarantee becomes weaker, and centered versus uncentered norm definitions remain inconsistent, so the improvement is in support and validation rather than a stronger guarantee.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ATA research. Their main texts, equations, algorithms, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite additions and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those results and adds heterogeneous timing-distribution simulations, CIFAR-100 training results and experiments varying prior timing observations in Appendix A.

before.justification: V1 reports original task-allocation and SGD simulations, runtime and worker-time comparisons in Tables 1–2, and repeated regret simulations in Section 7.2.

results.title: ATA: Adaptive Task Allocation for Efficient Resource Management in Distributed Machine Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion expand the stated benchmark contribution from ten to fourteen datasets and from over 2,200 to over 2,700 models, explicitly listing eight classic baselines. The principal comparative conclusions remain; the encoder takeaway is refined to less informative graphs, including heterophilic ones.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes the original lower-homophily datasets from the newly evaluated strongly heterophilic graphs, refining its interpretation of encoder benefits. It adds memory-based deployment guidance and explains resource-driven exclusions from large-graph evaluation. Existing mechanism explanations and predictor-failure interpretations largely remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds H2GCN search ranges, GLEM EM/LoRA settings, heterophilic-data preparation, and a direct processed-data repository reference. Appendix D specifies large-graph features and resource constraints. Most existing implementation details remain, but the complete semi-supervised training-time breakdown is removed.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original ten datasets and evaluates Cornell, Texas, Wisconsin, and Washington, introducing strongly heterophilic webpage-classification coverage. Appendix D additionally evaluates ogbn-products, with 2,449,029 nodes and 47 product categories, substantially extending graph-scale coverage.

E2.justification: GLEM is added to the main accuracy and Macro-F1 comparisons, H2GCN to encoder comparisons, and GAT with LLM embeddings to the large-graph evaluation. Existing LLM comparators remain. DeepSeek-Chat becomes DeepSeek-V3 with identical scores; an actual backend change is not established.

E3.justification: Existing evaluation settings largely remain. Added experiments specify heterophilic train/validation/test splits of 10/10/80 and 60/20/20, and an ogbn-products protocol using Qwen2.5-3B embeddings and a reduced 221,309-node test set. Memory measurement during training and inference is added for Cora, WikiCS, and arXiv.

E4.justification: Section 5.1 now directly tests the encoder-benefit hypothesis on four strongly heterophilic graphs, including comparisons with H2GCN. Section 4.3 adds memory analysis, while the full semi-supervised training-time analysis is removed. Existing backbone-sensitivity, biased-prediction, and hallucination analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The four-run statement, existing ± reporting, and single-run exception for LLMIT on arXiv are retained. No new seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures appear. The new large-graph and memory tables provide point estimates.

E6.justification: Matched scores remain unchanged, but new GLEM results alter some rankings: semi-supervised Pubmed accuracy is 81.70%, above the previous winner LLMIT at 80.99%. v2 adds heterophilic, ogbn-products, and memory results and deletes v1 Table 17's timings. Its new Texas claim overstates GCN's gain: Table 5 shows 58.67 versus 55.20, a 3.47-point difference, rather than the stated 12%.

M1.justification: The existing encoding, TAPE, predictor, and zero-shot prompting procedures remain unchanged. Renaming LLM-as-Reasoner to LLM-as-Explainer does not change its operation. GLEM and H2GCN expand the evaluated comparisons rather than revise the proposed procedures.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title, consistently replaces Reasoner with Explainer, revises selected explanatory paragraphs, rewrites the impact statement, and adds acknowledgments and a large-graph appendix. The main section sequence and most existing prose are preserved.

P2.justification: v2 adds dedicated heterophily, large-graph, and memory tables; moves and expands the dataset-statistics table into the main text; and inserts GLEM rows into comparison tables. Figure 1 gains dataset and evaluation bands. The semi-supervised timing table is removed, while most other figures retain their appearance.

R1.justification: New citations include H2GCN, the heterophilic-data source, GRENADE, and GAugLLM. WebWalker is removed, and model-report references change to Qwen2.5 and DeepSeek-V3. The taxonomy and positioning relative to GLBench remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The graph definitions, mutual-information decomposition in Equation (1), and mathematical descriptions of TAPE and LLaGA are retained. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: The four strongly heterophilic datasets and H2GCN comparisons address an important weakness: v1 supported its heterophily conclusion using graphs with homophily above 55%. GLEM comparisons, million-node evaluation, and memory measurements further strengthen the benchmark's evidential and practical value. These gains outweigh the loss of the semi-supervised timing table and the new overstatement of GCN's Texas improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLMNodeBed study despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds heterophilic-graph comparisons, ogbn-products evaluation, GLEM results, and memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark experiments, backbone comparisons, prediction-error analyses, and computational timings in the main text and appendices.

results.title: When Do LLMs Help With Node Classification? A Comprehensive Analysis

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims about moment utilization, variance reduction, the variance-aware convergence framework, and superior convergence. Additional experiments support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 qualifies the theoretical speedup as applying primarily when variance dominates and explains why larger beta1 can help. Section 6.1 softens uniformly lower-gap language to generally faster convergence with competitive gaps, while Section 6.3 connects the new momentum results to the theory.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 replaces the Ackley objective specification with an explicit Cubic formula. Other implementation and hyperparameter disclosures remain unchanged. Appendix B.3 still describes SST-2 only and supplies no COPA-specific reproduction details.

E1.justification: Coverage expands to COPA causal reasoning alongside SST-2, and Cubic replaces Ackley among synthetic functions. Other application coverage remains. Levy was already evaluated in v1's Figure 1 and Appendix B.1 despite its inconsistent Rastrigin references in Section 6.1.

E2.justification: Figure 1 adds ZO-SGD and ZO-signSGD to ZO-RMSProp and ZO-AdaMM, substantially broadening the synthetic comparison from adaptive optimizers to include nonadaptive update rules. The adversarial-attack and LLM comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Figure 1 extends the reported synthetic optimization horizon from approximately 10,000 to beyond 50,000 iterations. Figure 3(d) introduces a controlled comparison of beta1 values 0.3, 0.6, and 0.9. Retained experiments' listed metrics and Appendix B hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 3(d) adds an analysis of how beta1 affects R-AdaZO training-loss convergence on OPT-1.3B and SST-2. This supplements the unchanged first- and second-moment sensitivity analyses on the Quadratic function in Figure 2.

E5.justification: Both versions report means over three independent runs for Figures 1 and 3, and means with standard deviations over five runs for Table 1. The added curves use the existing reporting practice; no new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Figure 1 adds baseline and Cubic results, removes Ackley results, and extends the synthetic trajectories. Figure 3 adds a reported 2.14× COPA speedup and momentum-sensitivity results. SST-2's 4.29× and 3.75× speedups and Table 1 remain unchanged. Longer synthetic horizons do not establish same-budget performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 retains the same gradient estimator, first-moment update, second moment based on squared first moments, and parameter update. The revised smoothing definition changes the theoretical analysis, not the optimization procedure.

P1.justification: The section organization and most prose remain intact. Changes include localized theoretical explanations, an expanded adversarial-task introduction, corrected cross-references and terminology, updated affiliations and publication information, and a short Impact Statement.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with additional comparator curves, changed function panels, extended axes, and removed speedup annotations. Figure 3 expands from two panels within one column to a full-width four-panel display. Figure 2 and Table 1 are relocated without substantive display changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to randomized smoothing by Duchi et al., ZO-signSGD, COPA, and RELiZO. It adds a short discussion of query-reusing linear interpolation and explicitly attributes randomized smoothing, while retaining the overall research positioning.

T1.justification: Equation (11) changes smoothing from the sphere to the ball, with corresponding proof revisions. Appendices A.7–A.8 revise mathematical reasoning, inequalities, dimension-dependent constants, and parameter choices. Appendix A.10 replaces the brief argument for Corollary 5.10 with supporting lemmas and a substantial derivation for the renamed Theorem 5.10.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects the foundational sphere-versus-ball smoothing mismatch and makes the previously abbreviated ZO-AdaMM convergence argument substantially more inspectable through Appendix A.10. Broader baseline comparisons, the LLM momentum test, and a clearer variance-dominant qualification strengthen validation and claim precision. These gains outweigh the lost Ackley coverage, although COPA-specific reproduction details remain missing.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same R-AdaZO research. Their main text, equations, figures, table, and Appendices A and B are readable and support reliable matching across revisions.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and reports additional synthetic comparisons, COPA fine-tuning results, and an LLM momentum-sensitivity experiment.

before.justification: Sections 6.1–6.3 report original synthetic optimization, MNIST adversarial attack, and SST-2 fine-tuning results in Figures 1–3 and Table 1.

results.title: Refining Adaptive Zeroth-Order Optimization at Ease

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the same claims: finite codebooks preserve generation quality, enable perceptual compression, and support compressed conditional generation with a posterior-sampling interpretation. Guidance and editing were already announced in v1. The new tokenization discussion is a perspective and future direction rather than a demonstrated core contribution.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive explanations concerning unreliable classifier gradients, random-subset selection for diversity, and the rate–perception–distortion interpretation of reduced prompt alignment. It discusses when editing's weaker structural preservation can be useful and interprets codebook indices as autoregressive image tokens. Existing limitations concerning the VAE, high bit rates, and incomplete theoretical understanding remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B and Table 1 disclose checkpoint identifiers, codebook sizes, timestep counts, matching-pursuit settings and normalization, and comparator configurations. Further additions specify caption generation and bit accounting, metric implementations, restoration sampler settings, and guidance/editing parameters. These substantially improve reproducibility; the project code/demo link was already present in v1.

E1.justification: v4 adds a concrete qualitative editing evaluation on modified-ImageNetR-TI2I (Appendix C.7, Figure 27), extending demonstrated coverage beyond v1's brief announcement of editing. The principal generation, compression, inverse-problem, and four face-restoration datasets were already specified in v1; additional face results and resolution settings do not constitute new datasets.

E2.justification: The main compression and restoration comparator sets are retained. The supplementary editing comparison adds DDPM inversion and full and mid-way DDIM inversion. Appendices C.5–C.6 also explicitly compare compressed guidance against standard CG and CFG, extending the reported comparisons without replacing the original baseline suite.

E3.justification: Newly reported evaluations introduce 768×768 compression, controlled timestep-selection comparisons, caption-conditioned compression at CFG scales 3 and 6, and compressed-guidance parameter sweeps. Generation evaluation expands to KID and DINOv2 distances, while text guidance adds CLIP alignment assessment. These substantially broaden evaluation design; newly disclosed configurations for retained experiments do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's codebook-size experiment and brief statement about prompts, v4 supplies direct analyses of ordinary versus adapted timestep reduction (B.4, Figure 15), caption conditioning (B.6, Figure 16), and guidance-strength/subset-size tradeoffs (C.5–C.6). These provide substantive evidence about design choices, sensitivity, and quality–fidelity tradeoffs.

E5.justification: Figure 8 newly displays shaded ranges around KID and DINOv2 kernel-distance curves, whereas v1's generation plots show unbanded estimates. The text does not define these ranges or report repeated-run counts or seeds, so their confidence level and estimation procedure cannot be determined.

E6.justification: The main results are retained, while the appendices add substantial quantitative and qualitative evidence. Table 8 newly reports CCG FID 13.669 versus standard CG values 31.548, 14.481, and 14.921 under its stated setup; Figure 26 reports lower prompt alignment for CCFG. Additional results cover 768×768 compression and the other face datasets. Tables 2–5 tabulate existing Figure 5 results rather than demonstrating new performance gains.

M1.justification: The central sampler, compression rule, and restoration procedures in Eqs. (5)–(12) remain unchanged. Appendix B.4 adds an explicit adapted alternative to timestep skipping: retain 1000 denoising steps but use singleton codebooks outside steps 400–899. The detailed compressed-guidance and editing descriptions mostly elaborate applications already announced in v1.

P1.justification: The main section order, abstract, and much of the exposition are retained. v4 repairs unresolved appendix references, expands selected explanations, adds an impact statement and organized supplementary sections, and updates the publication footer. This is limited editorial revision of the existing narrative despite substantial added scientific material.

P2.justification: v4 adds extensive visual evidence and tabulation: Figures 8–27 and Tables 1–8 include metric plots, comparison grids, configurations, numerical results, and editing examples. Tables 2–5 redisplay existing compression results. Existing Figures 6–7 move, and Figure 5 refines its encoder-decoder-bound labeling and layout.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a focused comparison with Liu et al. (2021), distinguishing its entropy-constrained optimal-transport formulation from DDCM's cross-modal conditioning. The appendices add relevant editing, classifier-robustness, and evaluation references. The broader positioning around discrete diffusion generation and zero-shot compression remains stable.

T1.justification: v1 states Proposition 6.1 and mathematical connections without supplying the referenced proofs. v4 adds a general-SDE proof argument in C.1, derives the approximate compression connection using Gaussian norm concentration in C.2, and develops the MMSE-based restoration objective in C.4.1. The proposition's main-text statement remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially remedies v1's missing supporting material: the appendices provide implementable configurations, mathematical arguments, and actual evaluations for previously announced applications, including unfavorable tradeoffs. This materially improves reproducibility and critical assessment while retaining the original evidence. Limitations remain: Figure 8's bands are undefined, and C.1 does not establish why rescaling the diffusion coefficient preserves the claimed posterior.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DDCM work and are readable, including figures and equations. v1 ends after its references despite unresolved supplementary references; v4 supplies Appendices A–C. This is a difference in the supplied documents, not an extraction gap.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and supplies additional quantitative and qualitative results, including compressed guidance and image editing.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation, image-compression, inverse-problem, and face-restoration experiments in Figures 3–7.

results.title: Compressed Image Generation with Denoising Diffusion Codebook Models

C1.justification: The central claims about subspace alignment, spectral initialization, and convergence remain. v2 adds an explicit introductory claim of competitive performance at nearly LoRA's time and memory cost, centers the contribution on spectral initialization, and drops the introductory claim of stronger guarantees through a modified gradient update.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the explanation of competing methods' limitations: LoRA-GA's weight offset introduces a biased target, its approximation neglects a quadratic step-size term, and LoRA-SB restricts subspace adaptation. Practical preconditioning guidance shifts from the earlier emphasis on high ranks toward robustness to poorly chosen learning rates. New results also receive interpretations concerning reasoning, knowledge retention, and stability.

D1.justification: Appendix G adds method- and dataset-specific optimized learning rates, batch sizes, scaling parameters, prompting information, and settings for the added experiments. v2 also reports training time and memory. Conversely, the earlier spectral-initializer tuning tables and explicit gradient-averaging implementation description are removed. These materially change the available reproduction information.

E1.justification: v2 adds MNIST transfer from odd to even digits and Alpaca instruction fine-tuning evaluated on MMLU general knowledge. GLUE, MetaMathQA/GSM8K, and Code-Feedback/HumanEval remain. These additions extend the represented domains and tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds PiSSA and LoRA-Pro to the GLUE comparison and LoRA-SB to synthetic comparisons. Multi-step full fine-tuning disappears from the corresponding GLUE and LLM benchmark tables, although it appears in the new MNIST experiment. Table 2's v2 'Full' row represents a single gradient update, not the removed full-fine-tuning baseline.

E3.justification: v2 narrows the main benchmark comparisons to rank 8, revises learning-rate searches and method-specific settings, and adds 8-shot chain-of-thought evaluation and a separate 395K-sample, four-epoch MetaMathQA experiment. The synthetic comparator experiment changes sample size, rank configurations, and target spectrum. QNLI's one-step full-update learning rate changes from 0.02 to 0.05.

E4.justification: v2 adds T5/MRPC alignment measurements, MNIST optimization trajectories, rank-8 approximations of one-step updates, SST-2 learning-rate robustness tests, and a neuron-norm ratio histogram. The earlier CoLA/MRPC rank-by-initialization/preconditioning ablations are removed. The initialization-variance analysis and pretrained-versus-adapted singular-value plots are retained.

E5.justification: Mean/standard-deviation reporting remains, including three-run GLUE results. v2 adds five-seed, 95% confidence intervals for learning-rate robustness and two-run means for the full-data math experiment. Its NLG Table 3 changes the stated run count from three to five, but Appendix Table 6 still lists three, leaving the actual count unresolved.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced, added, or removed. One-step QNLI accuracy changes from 69.13 to 76.64 alongside the changed learning rate. New results include LoRA-One's 47.24 on MMLU and 63.80 after four epochs on full-data GSM8K, plus resource measurements. Higher-rank benchmark and ablation entries disappear. Revised LoRA-One scores are not same-setting gains because the procedure and tuning change.

M1.justification: v1's primary algorithm uses unweighted singular vectors, offsets the pretrained weights, and applies preconditioned AdamW. v2 replaces it with singular-value-weighted initialization without that offset and ordinary AdamW; this procedure already appeared as Spectral (-) in v1 Algorithm 2. Spectral preconditioning is separately implemented as LoRA-One-P. The former primary implementation and mask-free nonlinear update are removed, so this exceeds renaming.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions, related work, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Algorithms/discussion and experiments become separate sections, linear convergence exposition moves into the appendix, and a new preconditioning appendix reorganizes the presentation. Proof sketches and the nonlinear exposition are substantially revised.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main text and substantially redesigns its displays: a new three-panel overview, restructured benchmark tables, resource-cost reporting, epoch comparisons, confidence-band plots, and a histogram. Earlier rank-ablation displays disappear; the toy trajectories are reduced and relocated, while the singular-value plots move to Appendix G.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning against recent LoRA theory, including Liu, Kim, and Xu et al., and connects the work to one-gradient-step feature-learning research. The previously acknowledged concurrent LoRA-SB work receives a substantive methodological critique and comparison. New analytical discussion also sharpens the distinction from LoRA-GA; these changes exceed bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 replaces the nonlinear orthonormality/orthogonality and absolute-shift assumptions with neuron-balance and relative-shift conditions. Appendix D replaces Hermite-based population-gradient arguments with angular ReLU-gradient analysis, changing initialization scaling and convergence bounds. The smoothed-gradient theorem and proof are removed, and linear alignment analysis is specialized to equal step sizes. The linear convergence results are retained in Appendix C.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the connection between theory and practice: the primary implementation follows the spectral construction, alignment is tested on T5, and stronger comparator coverage, learning-rate robustness tests, and measured resource costs directly examine central claims. These gains outweigh the loss of rank ablations and full-fine-tuning benchmark controls. The conflicting NLG run counts remain a material reporting weakness, and revised scores should not be interpreted as controlled improvements over v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LoRA-One research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, alignment and transfer experiments, and learning-rate robustness analyses in Section 6 and Appendices B and G. Some comparator results are explicitly attributed to prior work.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments, T5 evaluations on GLUE, LLaMA 2-7B fine-tuning results, and initialization/preconditioning ablations in Section 5 and Appendix F.

results.title: LoRA-One: One-Step Full Gradient Could Suffice for Fine-Tuning Large Language Models, Provably and Efficiently

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the central empirical contribution from transition prediction and state-of-the-art OPE to superior online MPC performance. This adds a substantial claim about practical control utility. The dataset, architecture, and original cross-environment transfer claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving environment stability, inadequate action sampling, and task-dependent transfer, including TDM's negative transfer in MPC. It also interprets Figure 9 as consistent scaling benefits, although its MPC panels show nonmonotonic returns and some subsets below scratch training. Existing bounded-prediction, calibration, and computational limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a stated code/data repository link and newly discloses UniTraj sampling weights in Appendix A.3/Table 3. Appendix B.5 documents MPC sampling, horizons, and noise settings; C.4 reports inference timing. These materially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the retained training recipe.

E1.justification: v2 adds online action selection through MPC: proposal-policy control on HalfCheetah, Hopper, and Walker2D, and random-shooting control on Hopper and Walker2D. This substantially extends task requirements beyond v1's prediction and policy evaluation, while retaining the original environments and UniTraj coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 14 adds MLP and TDM predictions to the Cart-2-Pole zero-shot comparison, where v1 showed TrajWorld against ground truth. New MPC comparisons also include proposal-policy or random-action references. The existing transition-prediction and OPE comparator sets are unchanged.

E3.justification: New MPC protocols use medium-replay training data, medium-level proposal policies, 128 candidate trajectories, environment-specific planning horizons and sampling noise (Appendix B.5). Section 5.5 adds subset-pretraining experiments with expert-data fine-tuning and evaluation across all data levels. These are additional protocols; retained prediction/OPE settings and training budgets are unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 9 newly tests pre-training quantity and composition using 1%, 10%, JAT-only, and full-UniTraj variants for prediction and MPC. Figures 12 and 14 add planner-choice and zero-shot baseline failure analyses. The original few-shot, attention, and dataset-removal analyses remain, including v1 Appendix C.6 as v2 C.7.

E5.justification: The established three-seed main evaluations, two-seed appendix studies, and mean/dispersion reporting are retained. New MPC results follow the existing three-seed practice. No changed run counts for retained experiments or new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedures are reported.

E6.justification: Existing OPE values are identical in v1 Table 5 and v2 Table 6, but substantial new results appear. For example, v2 Table 8 reports Hopper MPC returns of 1401±236 with pre-training versus 1090±225 from scratch. Figure 9a adds normalized prediction errors of 1.00, 0.73, 0.69, and 0.68 for no, 1%, 10%, and full pre-training. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over corresponding v1 scores.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 retain the same scalarization, discretization, embeddings, interleaved attention, prediction objective, and model inference. MPC applies the existing world models through downstream evaluation procedures. Newly disclosed sampling weights do not establish a method revision.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall section sequence are retained. v2 inserts MPC and sampling subsections, reorganizes the analysis discussion, adds local explanations and acknowledgements, and updates affiliations and publication text. This is a limited structural expansion rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial comparative displays for proposal-policy MPC, pre-training scale, random-shooting MPC, and zero-shot baselines (Figures 7, 9, 12, 14), plus sampling-weight and MPC-result tables. Existing architecture, prediction, OPE, and attention displays remain with renumbering and layout adjustments.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations on axial attention, video transformers, motion forecasting, and recent world models. Section 6 clarifies the transfer-focused use of two-dimensional attention, while Appendix D expands the comparison with Schubert et al. through data diversity and MPC settings. The overall research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The MDP and trajectory definitions, architecture and loss equations, prediction-distribution definitions, OPE formulas, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Neither version contains formal theorems or proofs, and the additional experiments introduce no new formal results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical validation by testing whether transferred dynamics support useful online action selection, an important uncertainty left by v1's prediction and OPE results. Matched MPC comparisons, additional ablations, zero-shot baselines, and sampling/access disclosures make the contribution more assessable and reproducible. Benefits are not universal: Table 8 shows environment-dependent outcomes, and Figure 9 contradicts the strongest scaling language. These qualifications limit the claims but do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UniTraj dataset and TrajWorld model. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds model predictive control experiments, pre-training scale analyses, and zero-shot baseline comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original zero-shot prediction, transition prediction, off-policy evaluation, and ablation results, including Figures 4–6 and Appendix C.

results.title: Trajectory World Models for Heterogeneous Environments

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: existing hallucination mitigation sacrifices recall, while training-free SPARC improves precision and recall with minimal overhead. New experiments support these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies background tokens as potentially carrying global context and discusses limitations of interpreting raw attention and unnormalized attention totals. It also adds interpretations concerning tuning and POPE instruction following. The existing limitation concerning early-caption hallucinations and CHAIRs is retained in Appendix F.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code repository link, RTX8000 hardware information, latency-measurement details and a float16 attention-state memory estimate below 40 KB. It also documents segmentation masks, gradient weighting, additional parameter ranges and the POPE comparator's scaling setting. Existing SPARC implementation settings remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds a supplementary POPE evaluation involving caption-conditioned object-presence questions and instruction following. The original detailed-captioning coverage on IIW-400, DOCCI and MS-COCO remains unchanged.

E2.justification: OPERA, VCD, VOLCANO and PAI remain the comparators in the retained caption-quality experiments. New efficiency and POPE comparisons reuse existing methods, including the previously evaluated naive attention-scaling approach; no comparator is added or removed within a retained experiment.

E3.justification: V2 substantially extends evaluation design with object-mask attention scoring on 5,000 COCO images, gradient-weighted and token-normalized diagnostics, latency measurement, and four-parameter sweeps on 500 DOCCI images for two additional models. POPE introduces caption-first prompting, accuracy restricted to instruction-compliant responses, and an instruction-following metric. Original captioning protocols are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component ablations, attention-sink and caption-diversity analyses, v2 adds semantic-region grounding measurements, saliency checks and token-count normalization (Table 5; Figures 12–13). Appendix C extends four-parameter CLAIR sensitivity studies to LLaVA-NeXT and Qwen2-VL, while Appendix E examines instruction following. These substantially broaden validation of the method's mechanism and sensitivity.

E5.justification: V2 newly reports timing measurements with ± terms in Table 6, although their statistical meaning and repetition count are unspecified. Both versions already report five repetitions for CHAIR and Q1–Q3 bands in Figure 5; no increase in those run counts is stated.

E6.justification: Headline Tables 1–4 and the original CHAIR results remain unchanged. Substantial additions include relevant-region attention of 17.85%, 15.50% and 19.17% for baseline, naive scaling and SPARC; baseline/SPARC latency of 30.37/31.21 ms per token; further parameter-sweep results; and conditional POPE accuracies of 82.01%, 81.45% and 83.13%. New diagnostic figures also report saliency and normalized-attention findings.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the same EMA-based relative activation score, token selection, cumulative selection counts and cached-value amplification, with unchanged Equations 1–9. The caption-first POPE setup extends evaluation without revising SPARC's attention-calibration procedure.

P1.justification: V2 locally rewrites Sections 3.2–3.3, organizes Section 5.3 with descriptive subheadings, and adds acknowledgements, an impact statement and a POPE appendix. Author information and some wording are corrected. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: The display set substantially expands with grounding and timing tables, cross-model sensitivity tables, POPE tables, and saliency and normalized-attention figures. V1 Tables 6–9 are consolidated into v2 Table 8 without changing their values. Existing plots are retained and renumbered where needed, alongside conference-style title formatting and running headers.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting attention interpretation, segmentation-based analysis and caption-based reasoning, including Darcet, Zhang, Ren, Ravi and Mitra. The anonymous visual-attention-sink citation becomes Kang et al., referring to the same work. The central positioning against hallucination mitigation and naive attention amplification remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The method equations, caption-similarity definition and CHAIR formulas are retained. V2's additional attention diagnostics introduce empirical measurements, without adding or revising formal assumptions, propositions, proofs or theoretical derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central mechanism and efficiency claims. Semantic-region measurements, saliency checks and token-count normalization address weaknesses in v1's reliance on raw and aggregate attention, while Table 6 supplies previously missing runtime evidence. Broader sensitivity studies further support assessment across models. POPE accuracy remains limited by compliance-based filtering, and timing uncertainty is insufficiently explained, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger validation of the paper's central arguments.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SPARC and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained material can be matched across appendix renumbering and table consolidation.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds grounding measurements, efficiency experiments, further sensitivity analyses and POPE evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original captioning experiments, human evaluations, attention analyses and ablations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Visual Attention Never Fades: Selective Progressive Attention ReCalibration for Detailed Image Captioning in Multimodal Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same claims: valid Bayes-assisted PPI, improved efficiency when predictions agree with the prior, robustness with heavy-tailed priors, and compatibility with power tuning. The principal contribution and its intended scope remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix S5.1 newly explains AlphaFold's above-nominal coverage in Figure 3 as conservatism introduced by the union-bound construction of the odds-ratio interval. Existing interpretations of prediction bias, horseshoe robustness, prior-scale choices, and computational limitations are retained.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository link and Appendix S5.2, identifying Python, ppi-py for baseline comparisons, and an Intel Core i7-11850H CPU. These are new reproducibility disclosures; the PDFs do not establish a change in the underlying implementation or hardware.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same biased/noisy prediction simulations and AlphaFold, Forest, Galaxies, Healthcare, Genes, and Census tasks. Section 5.2 now identifies AlphaFold explicitly as odds-ratio estimation, but that task and its construction were already documented in v1 Appendix S5.1.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the same comparator membership: classical inference, PPI, PPI++, their full-uncertainty variants where applicable, and the same FAB prior variants. Figures 1–3 and S6–S13 show no added or removed comparison methods.

E3.justification: The reported sample sizes, random labeled/unlabeled splits, bias and noise settings, nominal error level, and MSE/volume/coverage metrics are unchanged. Both versions use the same large-unlabeled-sample simplification. The new implementation subsection discloses details without reporting a revised experimental protocol.

E4.justification: The bias and noise sweeps, Gaussian-versus-horseshoe comparisons, example intervals in Figure S9, and Forest prior-scale sensitivity analysis in Figure S10 are retained. The Census analysis of bias and labeled sample size is also unchanged.

E5.justification: Experimental repetition counts and uncertainty-reporting practices are unchanged, including 1000 repetitions for the principal studies and 100 for Figures S10 and S12. Neither version adds seeds, confidence bands for experimental averages, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The corresponding experimental figures retain identical plotting content, including numerical curves, example intervals, and comparator rankings. The empirical findings in Sections 5 and S6 are unchanged; the added AlphaFold coverage explanation does not introduce new results.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1 and 2 correct the standard-error scaling for the unlabeled mean: Algorithm 1 introduces division by sqrt(N), and Algorithm 2 uses variance normalization N(N−1). This repairs the written finite-sample interval calculation. The rectifier estimator, priors, shrinkage mechanism, and power tuning remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized explanatory rewrites, clarifies the AlphaFold task, fixes grammar and cross-references, and adds implementation, code, and impact-statement text. The appendix proof organization changes locally, while the overall section sequence and narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: All thirteen figures and both algorithm boxes remain. Figure S5 is reduced in display size, several figures shift within the page flow, captions receive small edits, and the running title is removed. The plotted graphics themselves are unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds Efron (2011) for Tweedie's formula, replacing empty citations in Section 4.1 and Appendix S1.1. The renamed Cortinovis–Caron reference has the same arXiv identifier, and other bibliography updates concern existing works. The positioning relative to PPI and Bayesian PPI remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix S3 substantially revises the horseshoe convergence argument. V1 Lemmas S3.2–S3.3 are replaced by a horseshoe-specific lemma using uniform bounds and Hausdorff convergence, with classical normalized-interval convergence restricted to nonzero rectifiers. V2 separately establishes coverage at zero and discusses its random limiting region; the Gaussian proof also gains the missing zero case. The robustness corollary now concerns full-set convergence, and Section 3.1 corrects the control-variate variance-reduction condition.

improvement.justification: V1's horseshoe convergence lemma asserted classical normalized-interval behavior even at a zero rectifier using an insufficient pointwise argument. V2 restricts that conclusion, supplies a substantially fuller convergence proof, and establishes zero-case coverage separately. Together with the standard-error corrections in both algorithms and new implementation information, these changes substantially strengthen the paper's central theoretical support and the reliability of its stated procedure. The empirical evidence remains unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FAB-PPI by the same authors. Their main text, equations, algorithms, figures, and appendices S1–S6 are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix S6 retain the work's original simulation and real-data results, including estimation error, interval volume, and coverage.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix S6 report original simulations and evaluations on six real datasets, measuring estimation error, confidence-interval volume, and empirical coverage.

results.title: FAB-PPI: Frequentist, Assisted by Bayes, Prediction-Powered Inference

C1.justification: Although the abstract is unchanged, the introduction adds a demonstrated high-dimensional feasibility contribution, where v1 largely presented such applications as future potential. The conclusion also strengthens comparable performance to comparable or better performance. Listing the diffusion/Latent-SDE connection as a contribution mostly highlights content already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the horizon experiments as evidence of greater training stability and attributes part of the motion-capture advantage over ARCTA to state-dependent volatility, supplementing v1's posterior-context explanation. Appendix C.3 expands the applicability discussion. The established limitations concerning posterior flexibility and general diffusion terms remain essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, video data-generation and architecture references, the convolutional-encoder adaptation, and coefficients for the new synthetic systems. It also reports the video's training budget and single-GPU runtime. Most original GRU/MLP and optimization information is retained in Appendix D after moving from v1's Appendix B.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained Lorenz and motion-capture datasets, v2 evaluates 32 × 32 pendulum videos, a linear stochastic system, and stochastic Lotka–Volterra dynamics. Section 5.2 also changes the motion-capture description from 35 subjects to subject 35; unchanged splits and scores do not establish an actual cohort change.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains the same eight comparison methods. Adjoint sensitivity remains the competing training method in the added experiments. The Kalman-filter likelihood supplies an exact reference, while the Lotka–Volterra comparison ablates SDE Matching's volatility parameterization; it does not newly evaluate ARCTA.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include equal 20,000-iteration video training, a Kalman-filter likelihood reference for a specified linear system, gradient comparisons over horizons T = 1, 2, 5, 10, and controlled state-dependent versus state-independent volatility experiments. The retained motion-capture split and six-dimensional latent setting are unchanged.
