M1.justification: Section 3.1 revises the stated straight-through gradient update and moves alpha's weighting from the codebook term to the encoder commitment term. Cross-attention projections become explicitly modality-specific. The dual encoders, partitioned codebook, top-K quantization and token-packing framework remain. These are localized changes to the specified computation; the PDFs do not establish corresponding implementation changes or reruns of retained experiments.

P1.justification: Editing concentrates on the method explanations, terminology, captions and appendix headings. Hyperparameter sensitivity receives a separate subsection, QA is renumbered, and an interpretability subsection is added. Publication metadata and a conflict-of-interest statement are updated. The overall narrative structure and most introductory, related-work and concluding text remain.

P2.justification: The experimental displays are substantially revised: v3 adds Table 5, rebuilds Figure 5 around loss-weight and codebook-size sensitivity, replaces the old QA panel with the three-panel Figure 6, and adds the token-frequency Figure 7. Figure 3 is relocated and reduced from full-width to a single-column display. The architecture figures and principal EHR tables are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations for the additional QA datasets and models and for previously used resources including UMLS, MONDO and DrugBank. It also corrects RAW-EHR to RAM-EHR and adds retrieved-knowledge summarization to its description. The main positioning relative to vector-quantized tokenizers and structured EHR models remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–2 replace common d-by-d projection matrices with modality-specific matrices having dimensions compatible with the text and graph embeddings. The straight-through and codebook-loss expressions are also revised. These are limited mathematical corrections; the mutual-information objectives in Equations 6–9 and Appendix C task definitions remain, with no new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked controls isolating the shared and modality-specific packing losses and tested QA with only one LLM on one benchmark. v3's Table 5 directly tests those central components across all three EHR datasets, while Figure 6 broadens evidence for QA applicability across three models and benchmarks. Together with the revised training equations and corrected result descriptions, this substantially strengthens the paper's scientific support. New QA sample counts and uncertainty remain unspecified, and changed codebook-sensitivity curves are unexplained, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MEDTOK, and all pages, including Appendices A–C, are readable. Methods, equations, tables and figures can be matched across versions. Revised QA settings require separate treatment of those results but do not prevent a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains the original EHR experiments and reports additional loss ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, medical-QA comparisons and a token-interpretability case study.

before.justification: v1 reports original EHR prediction experiments in Tables 3–4, modality and codebook-size analyses, and LLaMA3.1-8B medical-QA results.

results.title: Multimodal Medical Code Tokenizer

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution outline, and central discussion retain the same claims: contamination can make conformal calibration conservative, and selective annotation can improve power with approximate type-I error control under stated conditions. The expanded experiments support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5 newly emphasizes the requirement that calibration and test inliers share an i.i.d. distribution. It also discusses label ambiguity, possible extensions using uncertainty information, and retaining uncertain points as inliers. These additions refine applicability and interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds implementation information for the new configurations, including the VGG-19 model source, SCALE’s activation-rescaling rule and 65% percentile setting, and the One-Class SVM RBF kernel. Existing split recipes, ReAct’s 90% threshold, and the method’s repository link remain.

E1.justification: The three tabular datasets and six visual-data pairings remain. However, v2 adds distinct scenarios with score-selected contaminants resembling inliers across the tabular datasets and changing test-time outlier populations on shuttle (Figures 16–20), substantially extending coverage beyond random contamination.

E2.justification: The comparison methods remain Standard, Oracle, Naive-Trim, and Small-Clean. LOF, One-Class SVM, ReAct/VGG-19, and SCALE/ResNet-18 are additional scoring configurations shared by Label-Trim and its comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluations using LOF and One-Class SVM on tabular data and ReAct/VGG-19 and SCALE/ResNet-18 on visual data. New protocols include contamination rates up to 15%, percentile-based outlier selection, and shuttle tests varying outlier percentile ranges while training/calibration outliers come from the 30th–100th percentiles. These supplement the retained original protocols.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained contamination, labeling-budget, significance-level, and KDDCup99 variability analyses, v2 tests sensitivity to scoring models, heavier contamination, harder contaminants, and test-time outlier shifts. Figures 13–20 substantially expand robustness evidence and reveal settings with weak detection power.

E5.justification: Both versions generally use 100 random data splits, retain 400-split KDDCup99 labeling-budget analyses, and report standard errors in visual-data tables. The added results follow the existing reporting practices; no new statistical estimation procedure or increased repeat count is documented.

E6.justification: Original numerical tables are retained, including v1 Tables 4–9 as v2 Tables 6–11. Substantial new results appear in Figures 13–20 and Tables 4–5 and 12–23. For example, at alpha = 0.01 and 5% contamination, the new ReAct/VGG-19 and SCALE/ResNet-18 evaluations report Label-Trim relative powers of 1.606 and 1.627, respectively, both with type-I error 0.009.

M1.justification: Section 3.3, Equation (4), and Algorithms 1–2 retain the same procedure: annotate the highest-scoring calibration points, remove confirmed outliers, and calibrate using the retained set. Additional scoring models test the existing model-agnostic procedure.

P1.justification: Most original exposition is retained, with grammatical corrections, added pointers to experiments, and expanded discussion. The former tabular and visual appendices become subsections B.2.1 and B.2.2 under Additional Experiments. These are limited narrative and organizational changes.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and repositions figures, tables, and algorithms. It adds the method schematic in Figure 2, robustness Figures 13–20, and fourteen new tables. Existing graphics are retained and renumbered, while table captions more explicitly identify scoring configurations.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting LOF, One-Class SVM, SCALE, and the VGG-19 implementation. Section 5 also connects the work to ambiguous-ground-truth research by Stutz, Javanmardi, and Caprio and colleagues. The main related-work positioning in Section 1.3 remains stable.

T1.justification: Proposition 2.1, Lemma 2.2, Assumption 2.3, Theorem 3.1, and Appendix A’s auxiliary propositions, mixture-distribution corollary, and proofs are substantively unchanged. The labeling-budget condition m <= alpha(n + 1) is retained.

improvement.justification: v1’s empirical support relied on one scoring configuration per data modality and random contamination. v2 substantially strengthens that support by testing alternative scorers, harder contaminants, heavier contamination, and shifted test outliers, exposing low-power regimes alongside successes. These tests address important questions about robustness while preserving the original evidence. The schematic and clearer limitations further improve the paper, although the theoretical guarantees remain unchanged and require matching inlier distributions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Label-Trim research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across the layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds evaluations with additional scoring models, harder contamination scenarios, and test-time outlier shifts.

before.justification: v1 reports original outlier-detection experiments on three tabular datasets and six visual-data pairings in Section 4 and Appendix B.

results.title: Robust Conformal Outlier Detection under Contaminated Reference Data

C1.justification: The abstract now explicitly claims state-of-the-art performance on language as well as vision tasks. A new introduction contribution asserts versatility across vision/language benchmarks and fully fine-tuned/LoRA models. This materially broadens the claimed applicability beyond v1's vision-only evidence, while retaining the original alignment and isotropic-merging contributions.

C2.justification: V2 develops activation preservation as an explanation for reduced interference, interprets similar Iso-C/Iso-CTS NLP performance as evidence that the common subspace is sufficient there, and explains when isotropic scaling matters within Iso-CTS. The conclusion replaces v1's vision-only limitation with the limitation that low-rank structure is not fully exploited; the potentially suboptimal Task Arithmetic common subspace remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: V2 supplies checkpoint sources, LoRA rank and reconstruction instructions, the language-model identity, and protocol references for the added evaluations. Existing vector-parameter averaging, the default common-subspace fraction, and the alpha table are retained. The same code URL remains, while v1's inconsistent statement promising a future release is removed; the PDFs do not establish a newly available resource.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates vision tasks only. V2 adds language-model merging on 7-task and 8-task subsets of the T0 mixture (Section 5.3, Table 3), substantially extending domain and task coverage. The original vision datasets are retained; the LoRA experiments reuse the existing eight vision tasks.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains its comparator set. New comparisons evaluate DARE-TIES, KnOTS-TIES, and KnOTS-DARE-TIES for LoRA (Table 2); Fisher Merging, RegMean, and MaTS for language models (Table 3); and additional vision baselines including PCB and CART (Table 4). These are evaluated comparators, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: V2 introduces rank-16 LoRA evaluations using KnOTS ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14 checkpoints, T5-Large-LM-Adapt language evaluations, and a separate vision comparison using Task Arithmetic checkpoints instead of the Consensus Merging checkpoints used in Table 1. Appendix D.2 also introduces mean L1 embedding distance as an interference measure. The retained Table 1 protocol and reported alpha choices are unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of embedding interference (Appendix D.2, Figure 7), the necessity of isotropic scaling within Iso-CTS (D.4, Figure 8), alignment across transformer layers (E.2, Figure 13), and whether the alignment–performance relationship persists on ViT-L/14 (E.3, Figure 9). The earlier interpolation, subspace-size, alpha-sensitivity, and single-task flattening analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or run-level uncertainty. The retained boxplots summarize variation across tasks rather than repeated runs. The revised Pearson correlation value changes a result, not the statistical reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Table 1 is numerically unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results: Iso-CTS scores 75.0/89.6 normalized accuracy for LoRA ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14 (Table 2), while Iso-C scores 75.6/83.3 absolute accuracy on the 8/7 NLP tasks (Table 3). Table 4 and the new analyses add further outcomes. Section 3.3 and Figure 3 revise the reported SAR–NAI correlation from 0.88 to 0.94. The added benchmark scores are not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and the core spectral merging operations remain unchanged. Section 5.2 adds a limited input adaptation for LoRA: reconstruct each task update as Delta W_t = B_t A_t before applying the existing merging procedure. No substantial algorithm redesign or new training objective is introduced.

P1.justification: Most introductory and methodological prose is retained. Local rewrites clarify cosine similarity and alignment terminology; Section 5 is reorganized around fully fine-tuned vision, LoRA, language, and analyses; and existing appendix material is redistributed under experimental details, experiments, and visualizations. Affiliations, publication text, and acknowledgements are also updated. These edits do not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 adds dedicated tables for LoRA, NLP, and alternative-checkpoint vision comparisons, plus figures for interference, isotropic-scaling ablation, larger-model correlation, and per-layer alignment. Existing NAI plots have revised axes and Figure 3 has revised labeling. Earlier appendix plots and the alpha table are retained and relocated or renumbered, rather than removed.

R1.justification: V2 adds a substantive distinction between static and dynamic merging, contrasting Twin-Merging and EMR-Merging and explicitly limiting its scope to static merging. References supporting the additional merging comparisons, language evaluations, interference analysis, and complexity analysis substantially expand the literature coverage. The updated publication details for TSV and KnOTS refer to works already cited in v1.

T1.justification: V2 adds theoretical appendices absent from v1: a spectral derivation of effective rank, a projection-based SAR monotonicity argument, an activation-interference decomposition, and a variance argument explaining underrepresented tasks (Appendix A). Appendix B adds an asymptotic SVD-cost comparison of Iso-C, Iso-CTS, and TSV-M. These additions go substantially beyond restating the existing method equations.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's explicit vision-only limitation with language experiments and adds LoRA evidence and broader baseline comparisons. The new Iso-CTS scaling ablation and interference measurements more directly test the proposed mechanism, while the theoretical appendices clarify its rationale and computational cost. These gains substantially strengthen generality and explanatory support while preserving the earlier evidence. The interference argument remains approximate and uncertainty reporting is still absent, but these limitations do not outweigh the improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Iso-C/Iso-CTS research, with readable text, equations, algorithms, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Shared content can be matched reliably despite the expanded experiments and reorganized appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds LoRA and language-model evaluations, additional vision comparisons, interference measurements, and component ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original model-merging results on 8, 14, and 20 vision tasks in Table 1, together with original alignment analyses and ablations in the main text and Appendix B.

results.title: No Task Left Behind: Isotropic Model Merging with Common and Task-Specific Subspaces

C1.justification: The central contribution remains three lossless methods requiring no additional training. v2 specifies headline speedups of up to 2.8× for SLEM and 1.7× for TLI, and drops v1's claim that TLI outperforms SLEM on average. It also adds a claim that Hugging Face maintainers found both methods most effective among previously supported speculative-decoding algorithms.

C2.justification: The limitations discussion newly identifies architecture and training differences as factors affecting acceptance rates and points to benchmark failures with insufficiently fast or accurate drafters. It replaces v1's explicit qualification about optimized homogeneous SD potentially outperforming the proposals with greater emphasis on benefits even when homogeneous alternatives exist.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a benchmarking-repository address, identifies GPU types and counts for benchmark configurations, and states a generation range of 128–512 new tokens per prompt. It also reports completed TLI integration into Transformers, which was pending in v1. These substantially expand reproducibility and access information, although the repository itself was not inspected.

E1.justification: The Stack code-generation evaluation in v1 Table 7 is absent from v2. CNN-DailyMail, SCROLLS, and HumanEval remain, preserving summarization, long-context, and code-generation coverage. Added model families do not introduce new tasks or datasets.

E2.justification: Autoregressive decoding and Hugging Face's standard speculative decoding remain the comparison algorithms. Both are retained in the corresponding Gemma benchmarks, and the added DeepSeek benchmarks reuse these baselines. New target and drafter choices expand model configurations rather than introduce another competing decoding method.

E3.justification: v2 substantially revises the benchmark configuration matrix, adding DeepSeek distilled targets and drafters and comparisons across GPU setups, while removing standalone Llama throughput configurations. It drops the 1e-07 temperature condition, separates SLEM at temperature zero from TLI at temperature one, and adds explicit AR-relative speedups. The 30-prompt averaging protocol remains.

E4.justification: The task-conditioned vocabulary-overlap diagnostic expands from selected pair/task examples in v1 Table 6 to comparisons across datasets and additional model pairs in v2 Table 10. The token-decomposition complexity study, Figures 1–3, and tokenizer-injectivity experiment are retained. No new component-ablation study is introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions average benchmark results over 30 prompts without reporting repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The descriptive statistics and density estimation for token-decomposition counts are unchanged. Additional benchmark rows do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive DeepSeek results and replaces many existing benchmark values. For example, Mixtral/CNN-DailyMail at temperature zero reports AR/vicuna throughput of 10.2/9.9 tokens per second in v1 Table 7 versus 7.8/16.4 in v2 Table 1. These are revised reported results, not established same-setting gains, because v1 omits hardware details. Phi-4/SCROLLS values are retained, while task-specific overlap results are expanded.

M1.justification: Appendix B corrects Algorithm 5, which Algorithms 1 and 4 invoke: the final token uses the residual distribution only after rejection; otherwise it is sampled directly from the target. v1 always specified residual sampling. The core SLEM, SLRS, and TLI mechanisms remain unchanged; this establishes a pseudocode correction, not an implementation change.

P1.justification: v2 revises the contributions, empirical-results narrative, and limitations; standardizes algorithm terminology; and reorganizes appendices into separate speedup, vocabulary, and proof sections. It also changes the author list and adds acknowledgments and an impact statement. Most technical exposition and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: The benchmark presentation is substantially redesigned into separate SLEM and TLI tables, with explicit method, hardware, and speedup columns and multipage appendix tables. The task-specific overlap table is greatly expanded. Figures 1–3 retain their content but move with the reorganized appendices; these are relocations, not new figures.

R1.justification: v2 adds supporting references for models and datasets, including Phi, Mixtral, Vicuna, Gemma 2, CodeLlama, HumanEval, and SCROLLS. The positioning relative to prior speculative-decoding research remains largely unchanged. Publication updates and duplicate entries for existing works do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix B corrects standard SD's stated guarantee from identical outputs to equality in distribution and removes the assertion that its expected acceptance rate is at least that of autoregressive decoding. The named theorems, vocabulary assumptions, token-composition lemma, and proofs otherwise retain their mathematical substance; appendix moves and lemma renumbering add no theory.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects Algorithm 5's missing all-accepted sampling case and substantially improves experimental auditability through hardware disclosures, generation details, and a benchmark-code reference. Its broader comparisons report both speedups and slowdowns, giving a stronger basis for assessing practical applicability. Removing The Stack and near-zero-temperature results reduces coverage, and headline claims remain imperfectly synchronized with the tables, including TLI's stated 1.7× maximum versus 2.04× in Table 7. These drawbacks do not outweigh the gains in correctness and experimental transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same heterogeneous-vocabulary speculative-decoding work. Their text, algorithms, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison. The publication agreement appended to v2 adds no research evidence.

after.justification: v2 reports expanded decoding benchmarks and vocabulary-overlap measurements, while retaining the original tokenizer and token-decomposition analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original decoding benchmarks, vocabulary-overlap measurements, tokenizer-injectivity tests, and an empirical analysis of token-decomposition complexity.

results.title: Accelerating LLM Inference with Lossless Speculative Decoding Algorithms for Heterogeneous Vocabularies

C1.justification: V1 attributes TDD-Bench-Verified to the authors' prior work. V2 presents it as a contribution of this paper in the abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion. This substantially expands the claimed contribution scope, while retaining the central Otter performance and SWE-patch-validation claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations connecting test modification to available context, comparative performance to execution feedback and output-format demands, and ensemble gains to prompt diversity rather than ranking alone. It also discusses limits to scaling and improving already-ranked leaderboard patches. The original limitations concerning Python coverage, single-test generation, and unreliable SymPy coverage remain unchanged.

D1.justification: New Section 5 substantially improves benchmark documentation: it specifies the evaluation harness, execution of contributed tests, filtering from 500 to 449 instances, and coverage computation. These are disclosures about the retained benchmark, not evidence of changed construction. V2 also identifies GPT-4 for Table 3 comparators and explicitly states that generated tests are available through the existing repository.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 449 TDD-Bench-Verified instances across 12 Python repositories and 276 SWT-Lite instances. V2 Section 6.7 adds a downstream task: selecting among patches from the top three leaderboard systems using CodeT ranking, extending the earlier patch-filtering application.

E2.justification: The six external comparison methods in Table 3 and the 22-system patch-filtering roster remain unchanged. V2 Table 10 expands the internal ensemble comparison with greedy/high-temperature and heterogeneous/high-temperature mixtures. Newly discussed EvoCoder and CodeMonkeys are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V2 adds one-to-five-candidate scaling, temperature-1.0 sampling, mixed ten-candidate evaluation, and a one-attempt planner control. The original principal evaluation settings remain unchanged. Section 6.4 also revises the stated inputs of two comparison methods from a golden patch to a proposed patch; this changes the reported setting without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands analysis beyond v1's component-removal and contamination studies. Table 2 separately tests plan refinement and action validation; Table 6 diagnoses outcomes by test modification, execution failure, and localization correctness. Appendices C–E add ensemble scaling, temperature-versus-prompt comparisons, oracle-ranking analysis, and hallucination-replacement diagnostics.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run uncertainty estimates. Table 10's multiple generated candidates and their average performance describe ensemble sampling, rather than replications estimating experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: The headline Otter and Otter++ results remain unchanged, but substantial new results accompany the added analyses and Table 1 coverage column. For example, Table 10 reports 166 versus 146 Top-1 successes for heterogeneous prompts versus high-temperature sampling. Table 1 corrects the GPT-4o zero-shot count from 99 to 84 while retaining 18.7%. Section 6.7 additionally reports a sparsely documented 2% patch-ranking improvement.

M1.justification: The localizer, self-reflective planner, test generator, import repair, and five-prompt Otter++ selection procedure are unchanged. The appendix prompts are retained verbatim apart from numbering. Added experimental variants do not replace the proposed pipeline.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the relative order of retained sections remain intact. V2 inserts a dedicated benchmark section and three analysis appendices, makes localized wording corrections, and expands related-work, comparison, and impact explanations. The revision mainly adds material rather than extensively rewriting the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adds benchmark-filtering and evaluation-harness diagrams, plus four analysis tables. Table 1 gains a coverage column, and Table 2 gains component grouping and additional ablation rows. Existing graphical content and prompt figures are retained, with substantial resizing, relocation, and surrounding layout changes.

R1.justification: V2 removes the Ahmed et al. benchmark reference and changes TDD-Bench-Verified from prior work into a present-paper contribution, materially revising research positioning. It also adds substantive discussions of EvoCoder, CodeT, CodeMonkeys, and SWE-Bench+, including their relationship to Otter and its evaluation.

T1.justification: V1 only describes tddScore as blending fail-to-pass performance with coverage. V2 Section 5.3 adds explicit mathematical definitions of dataset aggregation, fail-to-pass correctness, and adequacy over added and deleted lines. This formalizes the custom metric already used in v1; it does not establish a changed metric or introduce proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens auditability and evidence for the central design choices. It makes the previously only briefly described benchmark evaluation and score self-contained, isolates refinement and validation within the novel planner, and quantitatively tests heterogeneous prompting against temperature sampling. It also fixes the inconsistent zero-shot count. The new 2% patch-ranking claim remains underspecified, but the stronger documentation and targeted validation provide substantial benefits independently of that claim.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Otter research work. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and retained methods, tables, figures, and prompts can be matched reliably across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds planner ablations, sampling comparisons, test diagnostics, and a patch-ranking experiment.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments with GPT-4o and Mistral-large, evaluations on TDD-Bench-Verified and SWT-Lite, component ablations, and filtering of patches from 22 SWE systems.

results.title: Otter: Generating Tests from Issues to Validate SWE Patches

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and concluding account retain the same sequence-level ordered-coverage contribution and reported 4.5x/6.6x headline improvements. The added experiments support and extend evaluation without redefining these central claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of encoder dependence and possible reasons for GAIfO and LIV underperformance. Section 7 replaces v1's explicit failure condition involving unrealizable subgoals with a broader task-misspecification caveat, and replaces identifying realizable subgoals as future work with incorporating language subgoals. Existing temporal-ordering and pretraining explanations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents default object-position randomization and distinct training/evaluation seeds, identifies the added baselines' input differences, and supplies backbone sizes and timing-workload details. The abstract replaces the direct code-repository pointer with a project-website pointer; this does not establish a change in actual code availability. Most existing implementation details are retained.

E1.justification: The same ten Meta-world and four Humanoid tasks remain. v2 adds an image-observation policy condition on five existing Meta-world tasks, extending evaluation beyond v1's state-input policies. Increased demonstration counts are experimental-setting changes rather than new task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds two substantially different comparator families on five Meta-world tasks: adversarial imitation through GAIfO and language-conditioned rewards through LIV. Existing comparators remain. GAIfO receives state demonstrations and LIV receives text goals, so these additions broaden comparison scope without providing identical-input comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 adds protocols varying demonstration count and speed composition, visual backbones, and policy observation modality. Its latency experiment uses 100 rollouts per method, demonstration length 100, and learner lengths 100 and 300. The original training budgets and Table 3 hyperparameters remain unchanged; newly documented randomization does not establish a change to existing experiments.

E4.justification: Sections 5.6–5.8 and Appendices C.4–C.6 add substantial analyses of demonstration scaling, mixed-speed demonstrations, Meta-world encoder sensitivity, dependence on state versus image policy inputs, and runtime scaling. The earlier temporal-misalignment, pretraining, Humanoid encoder, and qualitative failure analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 5.1 newly states that training and evaluation seeds differ. This adds seed documentation without establishing additional runs. Existing three-run analyses and mean/standard-error reporting remain; the additional result tables continue that reporting practice rather than introducing significance tests or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Numerical entries in Tables 1–5 are unchanged. Figure 6 and Tables 6–9 add substantial results: ORCA reaches 1.10 normalized return with 20 same-speed demonstrations, the image-policy comparison reports 0.76, and 100-frame reward computation takes 56.9 ms. Additional baseline and encoder results also appear. These are newly reported comparisons and settings, not version-to-version improvements on the original tests.

M1.justification: Section 5.6 introduces a multiple-demonstration adaptation: compute ORCA rewards separately for each video and take their maximum at each timestep, as defined in Equation 7. The original single-video recurrence, reward, pretraining procedure, and Humanoid confidence scaling remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 adds an appendix contents list, moves implementation material from v1's C.1–C.3 into B.4–B.6, and separates additional results into reorganized subsections. Local wording, headings, and publication text are revised. The main narrative and most existing prose remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds the multiple-demonstration chart in Figure 6 and Tables 6–9 for the new comparisons. It expands captions, relocates and resizes existing figures and tables, and adjusts some diagram annotations. The established layouts and most existing graphical content are preserved.

R1.justification: Related work adds a focused comparison with demonstration-conditioned policies requiring action labels, citing works such as Duan, Jain, and Palo and Johns. New references also support GAIfO, LIV, and encoder variability. The central positioning against frame-level optimal transport remains; publication and citation-year updates otherwise refer to retained works.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 adds an O(T times demonstration length) runtime claim and a lower-bound comparison with methods requiring a full frame-distance matrix. The ordering and coverage propositions, Appendix A proofs, and counterexamples retain their substance. Explicit trajectory arguments added to reward notation do not change those proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's state-input policies and fixed Meta-world encoder through image-policy and backbone comparisons, while testing demonstration scaling and computational cost. These additions address important uncertainties about applicability and practical performance. The experiments remain on limited task subsets, some baseline inputs differ, and the revised limitations lose a specific failure caveat, but the broader empirical scrutiny provides a clear net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ORCA research. All 24 pages of v1 and 28 pages of v2, including Appendices A–C, are readable. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable matching across the appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds multiple-demonstration, baseline, visual-encoder, image-policy, and runtime results.

before.justification: v1 reports original Meta-world and Humanoid experiments, including benchmark returns, training curves, temporal-misalignment tests, and pretraining analyses.

results.title: Imitation Learning from a Single Temporally Misaligned Video

C1.justification: The central contributions remain scalable two-stage tabular ICL, distribution-aware embeddings, handling up to 500K samples and 500 features, and performance comparable to TabPFNv2 with faster inference. Updated benchmark counts and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for TabPFNv2's greater ensemble benefit, acknowledges curriculum-related degradation on some small datasets, and identifies possible disadvantages from mean imputation and withholding categorical metadata from TabPFNv2. The RoPE permutation-invariance limitation was already discussed in v1 and is additionally emphasized in v2's conclusion.

D1.justification: The abstract newly reports availability of pretraining code, extending the previously advertised inference code and pretrained weights. Appendices E.1, E.3, and G add explicit learning-rate parameters, hierarchical-node data and target handling, and RF settings. Reported pretraining time changes from two weeks to 20 days, substantially expanding information about reproducing training and extensions.

E1.justification: Both versions use TALENT classification datasets, the same synthetic-data families, and the same large-table memory scenarios. Development datasets excluded from v2's main aggregate remain evaluated in Appendix F, and the new analyses reuse existing coverage. Aggregate membership changes concern the evaluation protocol.

E2.justification: Figure 5 and Appendix I add TabM, LoCalPFN, and TuneTables to reported comparisons; LoCalPFN and TuneTables enter only accuracy rankings. Appendix G additionally evaluates TabPFNv2-RF, substantially strengthening the comparison with scalable alternatives on large datasets.

E3.justification: Reported stage-one pretraining increases from 100K to 160K steps and changes from warmup/cosine decay to cosine restarts. v2 introduces a 20K-step prior ablation, ensemble-size sweeps, and RF experiments with four-member foundation-model ensembles and adaptive pruning. It also excludes development datasets from the main aggregate. The stated counts remain inconsistent: removing 15 from 188 does not yield 171, and 116 small plus 53 large datasets totals 169.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained RoPE case study, metafeature analyses, and memory experiments, v2 adds tests of tree-based SCMs and curriculum stages in Section 5.3 and Figures 9–10/E.2. Appendices G and H add RF-extension analysis and ensemble-size sensitivity, substantially expanding examination of design choices.

E5.justification: Both versions report bootstrap medians with 10%/90% intervals for metafeature fits and Wilcoxon–Holm tests at significance level 0.05 for rank diagrams. The additional results do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation practice, seed disclosure, or repeated-run count.

E6.justification: Aggregate accuracy ranks for TabICL/TabPFNv2 change from 6.28/6.32 in v1 Figure E.1 to 6.95/7.17 in v2 Figure I.1. These use changed cohorts and comparators, so they are not same-setting performance changes. New results include curriculum-stage ranks of 11.40, 7.46, and 6.95, RF-extension outcomes, ensemble-size effects, and per-dataset scores in Table F.1.

M1.justification: Appendix G adds the TabICL-RF adaptation, combining tree partitioning, localized ICL predictions, and validation-based adaptive pruning. The main three-transformer architecture, synthetic-data generators, and hierarchical classification procedure remain unchanged; Appendix E.3 elaborates the existing hierarchy.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted prose edits, renames Section 2.3, expands explanations and limitations, and adds subsections within the existing narrative. Appendices are reorganized and renumbered, but most retained exposition and the main section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 9–10, E.2, G.1, and H.1 and Table F.1, substantially expanding the visual evidence. It also expands baseline displays, redraws the stage-one learning-rate panel, and revises architecture labels and figure placement. The synthetic-data and memory plots are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds Grinsztajn's 2024 thesis as explicit inspiration for tree-based SCMs; v1 acknowledged his contribution without citing that work. New Appendix A consolidates and extends comparison with TabPFNv2 across architecture, label fusion, pretraining, and scalability, while the broader research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: New Section 3.5 derives componentwise complexity and distinguishes TabICL's O(nm^2 + n^2) cost from TabPFNv2's O(nm^2 + n^2m). Appendix B correspondingly revises v1 Appendix A's shared attention-cost motivation. This is a focused analytical addition rather than a new theoretical framework.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct ablation support for its tree prior and curriculum; v2 adds these tests, ensemble sensitivity, and a stronger TabPFNv2-RF comparison. Separating development datasets, adding explicit complexity analysis, and reporting pretraining-code availability further strengthen evaluation and reproducibility. Unreconciled dataset counts weaken protocol clarity, but the substantial gains in validation and transparency outweigh this limitation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TabICL research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, and added material.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results and adds tree-prior and curriculum ablations, ensemble-size experiments, and random-forest extensions.

before.justification: v1 reports original TabICL classification results, runtime and memory measurements, and empirical analyses of learned representations.

results.title: TabICL: A Tabular Foundation Model for In-Context Learning on Large Data

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: explaining Prior Guidance through score alignment, controlling log-density through deterministic guidance, and extending control to stochastic sampling. New experiments support these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V2 discusses finite-step accuracy and the additional sampling required under stronger stochastic noise. It also explains Prior Guidance's weakening control as noise reduces information from the initial latent, and notes that NIQE favors lower-detail images. These add practical qualifications to the retained interpretations.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository link and documents implementation details for the new experiments, including Euler integration, moving-average finite-difference estimation of quantile derivatives, and early/late noise schedules. The existing JAX score-alignment listing is unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions cover CIFAR-10, ImageNet at 64 and 512 resolution, Stable Diffusion text-to-image generation, and synthetic Gaussian mixtures. The additions evaluate retained coverage; classifier-free guidance changes the model configuration rather than the dataset or task.

E2.justification: V2 adds Prior Guidance to the early/late stochastic-noise comparison in Figure 19 and regular samples as a reference in the NIQE comparison in Figure 20. The existing FLIPD comparison remains unchanged. LPIPS and SSIM are discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols include deterministic and stochastic sampling-step sweeps, quantile-estimation sample counts from 16 to 1024, noise strengths of 0.1, 0.5, and 0.9 times the diffusion strength, and a 1024-step reference likelihood estimate. V2 also adds classifier-free-guidance evaluation and NIQE scoring. These substantially expand evaluation without replacing the retained protocols.

E4.justification: Appendices E and H newly test whether requested likelihoods are reached and how discretization, quantile-estimation sample size, and stochastic noise affect accuracy. Appendices J–L add guidance-strength analyses, classifier-free-guidance compatibility, stochastic Prior Guidance comparisons, and perceptual-quality analysis.

E5.justification: Figure 19 newly specifies two starting seeds, four stochastic samples per seed, and shared inner-loop seeds across runs. New quantitative plots include error bars, although their statistical meaning is not defined. The retained normality tests and reported plus/minus values are unchanged.

E6.justification: V2 adds target-versus-obtained likelihood results, reporting correlations above 99% even with 32 deterministic Euler steps, and shows greater sampling requirements under stronger noise. Figures 16–20 add measured detail, likelihood, and NIQE trends. Existing results, including 97%/100% score alignment and 84% versus 29% detail correlations, are retained; these are additional results rather than same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: Prior Guidance, score-alignment verification, deterministic Density Guidance, and the stochastic projection and drift corrections are retained. The new experiments apply existing procedures; the Rayleigh-quotient shorthand does not change the stochastic method.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain largely unchanged. V2 adds short experimental appendices and acknowledgements, updates cross-references, makes limited wording edits, and renames Appendix D from likelihood steering to Density Guidance.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the appendix displays with multi-panel convergence plots, paired image-and-metric comparisons, stochastic sampling grids, and NIQE plots and examples in Figures 12 and 15–20. Existing figures are largely retained, with some relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds Skreta et al. to the attribution of generalized density tracking and cites NIQE, LPIPS, SSIM, and a diffusion super-resolution application when motivating perceptual evaluation. The main research positioning is retained; the Karczewski citation's year update refers to the same work.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 corrects the forward Gaussian kernel's covariance from sigma_t I to sigma_t^2 I. The score-alignment proofs, Gaussian-mixture theorem, and density-guidance derivations otherwise remain intact. Rewriting the stochastic derivation using the existing Rayleigh quotient introduces no new theoretical result.

improvement.justification: V1 supplied theoretical guarantees and qualitative detail control but lacked direct quantitative validation of reaching requested likelihoods. V2's Appendices E and H address that central evidence gap and expose discretization and noise dependence; additional detail and perceptual comparisons strengthen practical validation. Together with documented code access, this substantially improves the paper's empirical grounding. Undefined error bars and NIQE's preference for smoother images still limit statistical and perceptual conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Density Guidance work. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds quantile-matching accuracy experiments, quantitative guidance comparisons, and NIQE evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original score-alignment measurements, image-detail correlations, generated-image comparisons, and Gaussian-mixture and image-data analyses.

results.title: Devil is in the Details: Density Guidance for Detail-Aware Generation with Flow Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's central findings, and conclusion retain the same principal claims: finetuning and forgetting are predictable from model size, available target data, and injection fraction, and approximately 1% pretraining-data injection mitigates forgetting. The added experiments support these claims without redefining their central scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning corpus memorization, data diversity versus parameter proximity, and small models' suitability for sequential adaptation. It develops the rewarming explanation with measurements and discusses practical downstream effects, explicitly acknowledging near-chance MMLU performance. These extend v1's narrower capacity and regularization discussion.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the existing training duration as 13–5200 epochs and adds instruction-tuning implementation details: mask storage in the sixteenth token-ID bit, bitwise extraction, and instruction delimiters. It also specifies anchored regularization strengths and discusses learning-rate-dependent weight decay. Core architecture, hardware, and training disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained language-modeling domains, v2 actually evaluates instruction finetuning on OpenHermes and downstream question answering on ARC-Easy and MMLU. These substantially extend both the represented data and task requirements.

E2.justification: Appendix A adds Anchored AdamW with regularization strengths 0.01, 0.10, and 1.00 to the Github comparison against Adam with and without data injection. A toy optimization example also compares Adam, AdamW, and Anchored AdamW. Existing scaling-law alternatives and the pretraining optimizer comparison are retained.

E3.justification: The original experimental grid is retained, but substantial new protocols are added: D = 10N pretraining on Freelaw, instruction-masked OpenHermes training with 189K–1,890K tokens, and zero-shot accuracy evaluation for Medium, Large, and XL models. Table 3 additionally measures baseline losses at the finetuning learning rate to account for rewarming.

E4.justification: v2 adds controls testing parameter anchoring as an explanation for data injection's benefits, robustness to a shorter pretraining budget, and explicit measurement of rewarming effects. These extend the original learning-rate, replay-data-size, and scaling-law analyses. The earlier extrapolation experiment is retained and relocated, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix B introduces z-score significance testing at the 99% threshold for ARC-Easy accuracy differences, marking nonsignificant comparisons. The existing practice of reporting scaling-law errors over 128 bootstrap repetitions remains unchanged; no increase in repeated training runs is reported.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises forgetting coefficients and average MRE from 0.49% to 0.40% under the revised predictor; finetuning and retained extrapolation results are unchanged. New results cover rewarming, Anchored AdamW, D = 10N, OpenHermes, and downstream accuracy. OpenHermes table MREs are 0.59% and 0.29%. The retained weight-decay plot also swaps Adam/AdamW labels, changing the attribution of its results.

M1.justification: The main data-injection procedure and model architectures remain unchanged. v2 refines the forgetting predictor by using a rewarmed baseline without the fitted offset E. Appendix A also introduces Anchored AdamW as an alternative and adapts finetuning to exclude instruction tokens from the loss.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and section organization are retained. v2 adds explanatory paragraphs, acknowledgments, and a practical-consequences appendix, moving coefficient estimation from Appendix B to C. These are localized expansions rather than an extensive rewrite or wholesale reorganization.

P2.justification: v2 adds five figures covering optimizer behavior, pretraining-budget robustness, instruction tuning, and downstream performance, plus rewarming, OpenHermes, and significance tables. Table 2 loses its forgetting-offset column. The extrapolation table and cost-of-forgetting plot are relocated, and the retained weight-decay figure's optimizer legend is swapped.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting instruction tuning, OpenHermes, ARC, MMLU, loss-to-loss scaling, and weight decay. It more explicitly distinguishes data-scarce finetuning from continual pretraining and qualifies the argument favoring smaller models on inference-cost grounds. The main related-work positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Equations 1 and 7 remove the additive E term and redefine the baseline using the rewarmed model, changing the mathematical specification of forgetting. Appendix A adds the anchored quadratic regularizer. The scaling-law fitting derivation is otherwise unchanged, moving from Appendix B to C; no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's loss-based evidence at one pretraining budget: it tests downstream accuracy, instruction tuning, budget robustness, and an alternative regularizer. Measuring rewarming also improves the interpretation of the central forgetting model. Some conclusions remain too broad, particularly claims of consistent ARC-Easy benefits despite many nonsignificant comparisons, while MMLU remains near chance. These limitations constrain the practical conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and explanation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching authors, objectives, core experiments, and substantial shared content. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds rewarming measurements, optimizer comparisons, instruction finetuning, pretraining-budget robustness tests, and downstream evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining and finetuning experiments, 1500 finetuning runs across 12 domains, fitted scaling laws, extrapolation results, and ablations.

results.title: Scaling Laws for Forgetting during Finetuning with Pretraining Data Injection

C1.justification: The abstract, five introduction contributions, and central conclusion retain the same claims: math PRMs generalize poorly beyond mathematics, and synthetic multi-domain supervision produces a broadly effective VersaPRM with released data, code, and models. The additions principally support and qualify these existing headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets held-out-domain performance as evidence beyond broader training coverage and acknowledges some benefit from learning the question format. Appendix F adds explanations of factual, arithmetic, and answer-consistency failures; Appendix G.2 proposes score-induced bias as an explanation for unsuccessful refinement. Section 7 also raises possible preference for Llama-family generators, substantially expanding applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 supplies prompts and operational details for rewriting, ablated labeling, open-ended generation and grading, and refinement, plus the 0.4 self-filtering threshold. It newly discloses AWS Bedrock batch inference and generation/labeling cost below $100. Original training hyperparameters and access information remain unchanged. Reproducibility is locally limited by Figure 15 listing a ground-truth answer despite describing its omission.

E1.justification: The original training sources and 14-domain MMLU-Pro coverage are retained. Appendix G.1 adds a limited but distinct task: answering 116 existing law questions with their answer choices removed. This extends evaluation beyond multiple choice, while the held-out-domain experiments change training splits within existing domain coverage.

E2.justification: The main math-PRM comparator suite is retained. Appendix B.5 newly evaluates Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct directly as a step judge, with reported comparisons in Figures 16–17. Those comparisons also include new self-filtered, rewrite-augmented, and prompt-ablated VersaPRM variants.

E3.justification: v2 enlarges the manual label audit from 30 to 64 questions and specifies a 30-question subset for the simplified-prompt audit. New evaluation designs include five domain-holdout controls, open-ended law questions graded by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, and one-step refinement evaluated by average Pass@1 over 1,754 questions. The established main benchmark protocol remains intact.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's counterfactual, training-configuration, and aggregation analyses, v2 adds domain-holdout tests, rewrite augmentation, self-filtering, an end-to-end labeling-prompt ablation, manually analyzed successes and failures, and iterative refinement. These investigate transfer, supervision quality, robustness, and failure conditions. Counterfactual augmentation is retained and incorporated into expanded comparisons, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 newly reports 95% confidence intervals for manual annotation agreement: 0.69–0.89 for CoTs labeled correct and 0.63–0.79 for those labeled incorrect. v1 reported point estimates alone. This is a localized addition to uncertainty reporting, concerning label quality rather than repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 4 retain their numerical results, but v2 adds extensive holdout, augmentation, judge-baseline, open-ended, failure-case, and DeepSeek-R1 Philosophy results. The enlarged audit reports 80%/71% agreement instead of 83%/70% on the smaller sample. The new refinement experiment reports Pass@1 of 51% without refinement, 45% with VersaPRM, and 44% with Qwen-2.5-Math-PRM.

M1.justification: The final VersaPRM architecture, loss, initialization, and fine-tuning procedure remain unchanged. v2 adds experimental procedural extensions: meaning-preserving rewrite augmentation, self-filtered retraining, and one-step refinement using PRM scores as feedback (Appendices B.2–B.3 and G.2). These supplement the existing method without replacing its central pipeline.

P1.justification: The main seven-section narrative and much existing prose remain intact. Revisions concentrate on related work, the DeepSeek discussion, future directions, and explanatory passages. Existing counterfactual material is regrouped into Appendix B, and an appendix roadmap is added; much remaining appendix movement is renumbering rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds held-out-domain plots, a Philosophy panel to the DeepSeek figure, expanded ablation grids, open-ended results, prompt displays, and highlighted error examples. Most existing plots are retained. Figure 2 removes the ground-truth input box despite its continued use in the text, and Figure 17's legend says Best of N although its caption identifies WMV.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning through CoT's domain-dependent benefits, compute-optimal training, teacher–student distillation, and Constitutional AI, adding works by Sprague, Hoffmann, Hinton, Gu, Bai, and others. New appendices also connect filtering and refinement to relevant prior research. The original math-PRM literature remains represented.

T1.justification: The PRM definition, aggregation formulas, and inference equations in Section 3 are retained. Beam-search and MCTS pseudocode match across v1 Appendix B and v2 Appendix C. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central generalization claim through held-out-domain controls and comparison with the 70B labeler used directly as a judge. The larger audit with confidence intervals, downstream labeling ablation, and candid failure and negative-refinement results also improve assessment of reliability and applicability. Open-ended evidence remains preliminary and LLM-graded, and new prompt/legend inconsistencies are drawbacks, but these localized issues do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VersaPRM and retain the same core pipeline, datasets, and principal experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds held-out-domain evaluations, further ablations, open-ended questions, error examples, and iterative-refinement results.

before.justification: v1 reports original PRM training and evaluation results, reranking and search experiments, training ablations, and a manual audit of synthetic labels.

results.title: VersaPRM: Multi-Domain Process Reward Model via Synthetic Reasoning Data

C1.justification: The abstract and three principal contributions retain the same necessity bound, conditional accuracy/interpretability guarantees, and empirical accuracy/runtime claims, including the CUB-200 exception. The added introductory overview restates the framework's contribution.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the component-removal results as accuracy versus explanation-length or embedding-drift tradeoffs and uses radius saturation to support choosing 0.1. Its Impact Statement also identifies practical hyperparameter tuning as underexplored. Existing dictionary-rank and concept-set limitations are retained.

D1.justification: Figures 7–8 disclose numerical ranges for the new hyperparameter studies, including radius values from 0 to 0.3 and CIFAR-10 thresholds from 0.10 to 0.16. Existing algorithm pseudocode, code-access information, hardware descriptions, and runtime disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet, Places365, and the same synthetic generative-model settings. The added analyses vary components and hyperparameters within retained coverage.

E2.justification: CLIP-IP-OMP and lf-CBM remain the external comparators. V2 adds variants without dispersion or projection in Figure 6 and includes the frozen-concept baseline in five qualitative comparisons, Figures 24–28, where v1 presented CCR examples alone.

E3.justification: V2 introduces component-removal controls and threshold/radius sweeps, including maximum embedding deviation as a diagnostic. Figure 2 now reports CIFAR-100 and CUB-200 curves through 500 rather than 1,000 iterations, although whether training itself was shortened is unspecified. The main concept-set and explanation-length matching procedures remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's refinement-versus-frozen-baseline comparison, v2 adds before/after dispersion heatmaps, separate dispersion and projection ablations, threshold and radius sensitivity studies, and paired baseline explanation examples. Figures 5–8 and 24–28 substantially expand investigation of component roles, parameter sensitivity, and qualitative behavior.

E5.justification: V1's Figure 2 does not specify repeated runs or report variability. V2 newly reports five runs for CCR and its frozen-concept baseline across all five benchmarks, plotting means with minimum–maximum bands. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting, without establishing an increase over v1's undisclosed run count.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial diagnostic and sensitivity results. Figure 6 shows higher accuracy after removing either component, with longer explanations without dispersion and maximum embedding drift around 0.6 without projection versus 0.1 with it. New Figure 28 correctly predicts a bus interior that CCR misclassifies in retained Figure 23. Figure 2 now presents five-run summaries; Table 1 and the main benchmark rankings remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–4 retain the same constrained refinement, surrogate estimator, hard thresholding, linear classifier, dispersion, and projection procedures. The new experiments investigate existing components rather than introduce a revised method.

P1.justification: V2 adds an introductory roadmap and an Impact Statement, inserts ablation and hyperparameter subsections, and renumbers the earlier interpretability appendix from D.3 to D.5. Cross-references are corrected, while most existing prose and the overall scientific narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout. Figure 2 is redrawn with uncertainty bands and revised axes, and Figures 5–8 and 24–28 add substantial visual material. Earlier case-study figures are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds Zhou et al. (2018), Interpretable Basis Decomposition for Visual Explanation, and explains more explicitly why Chattopadhyay et al. (2024) provides the chosen theoretical testbed. Appendix A's substantive positioning is otherwise retained; most citation changes are stylistic.

T1.justification: The assumptions, definitions, bounds, convergence guarantees, and Appendix C proofs are mathematically retained. V1's Theorems 2–4 correspond to v2's Theorems 2.6, 3.3, and 3.4; numbering, typesetting, and corrected cross-references do not alter their substance.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical substantiation by addressing v1's unreported run variability and missing component and hyperparameter analyses. Figures 2 and 5–8 make the accuracy, explanation-length, and embedding-drift tradeoffs much more assessable. Paired baseline examples improve transparency, although Figure 28 complicates the retained attribution of the bus-interior failure to concept-set inadequacy. This localized interpretive tension does not outweigh the substantial gains in validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CCR research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, with retained material identifiable despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains the original empirical evaluations and adds component ablations, hyperparameter studies, embedding-correlation analyses, and baseline prediction examples.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-classification results in Figure 2, synthetic convergence experiments in Appendix D.1 and Figure 4, and qualitative prediction examples.

results.title: Enhancing Performance of Explainable AI Models with Constrained Concept Refinement

C1.justification: The central contribution, 30-task scope, and up-to-25% improvement claim remain. The introduction changes the claimed number of tasks with more than 4% improvement from 15 to 17, while the abstract and conclusion qualify superiority as applying to the vast majority of tasks. The counts correspond to rounded gains of at least 4%, leaving the strict threshold wording imprecise.

C2.justification: V2 substantially develops the mechanism explanation around repeated bridge information and underrepresented source signals. Appendix C newly attributes gains primarily to atomic routes rather than attention. Appendix D adds schema-level scalability arguments, a self-loop remedy, and compatibility discussions for advanced aggregators and temporal encodings. Existing prediction-head limitations are retained.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-availability statement and repository link in the abstract, explains how training tables provide labels and timestamps, and documents schema-level route computation and positional-encoding implementation. These add access and implementation information without establishing changes to the existing data-processing pipeline.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same seven RELBENCH databases and 30 tasks. Appendix A retains the dataset and task descriptions. The new ablations and positional-encoding experiment reuse existing coverage, including the existing rel-stack self-loop setting.

E2.justification: V1 compares against LightGBM and heterogeneous GraphSAGE. V2 retains these comparisons and adds evaluated GAT and GIN baselines across all 30 tasks in Tables 5–7, substantially broadening the GNN comparison. GraphSAGE corresponds to the existing Hetero-GNN baseline.

E3.justification: The main temporal splits, Table 4 sample counts, metrics, prediction heads, and losses remain unchanged. New experimental configurations include a controlled GraphSAGE-style aggregation variant without attention and the supplemental positional-encoding configuration on two rel-stack classification tasks.

E4.justification: V1 contains no component ablation. V2 Appendix C adds an attention ablation across all 30 tasks to distinguish atomic-route benefits from attention benefits. Appendix D additionally tests a positional-encoding remedy for the previously discussed self-loop limitation.

E5.justification: Both versions report main results averaged over five seeds. V2 introduces no new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, variability estimates, or significance-testing procedures; the additional appendix results do not establish a changed uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 5–7 add GAT, GIN, and no-attention results across all 30 tasks. Six existing RelGNN scores change: study-adverse MAE becomes 44.461 instead of 44.681, and five recommendation entries change, including rel-amazon user-item-rate MAP from 0.87 to 0.92 and rel-stack user-post-comment from 13.76 to 14.00. Appendix D also reports a 2% improvement on both rel-stack classification tasks without absolute scores.

M1.justification: The core atomic-route, fusion, attention, and aggregation procedure in Equations (1)–(7) is retained. Appendix D adds an implemented schema-graph relative positional encoding that modifies messages by adding a learned, scaled positional term to address self-loops.

P1.justification: The introduction, preliminaries, structural motivation, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. The former Method section is split into topology and architecture sections, meta-path background moves to related work, and experiments gain explicit setup, results, and limitations subdivisions. Appendices C–D extend the document structure.

P2.justification: V2 restyles the structural diagrams and revises the RDL illustration. V1 Figures 4–9 are consolidated into a six-panel Figure 4, preserving their dataset coverage. Three new ablation tables add substantial comparative displays with best and second-best highlighting.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion of HiGPT and citations covering positional encodings, GAT, GIN, advanced aggregators, and temporal encodings. The central positioning against conventional heterogeneous GNNs and alongside prediction-head improvements remains. The meta-path discussion is largely relocated from preliminaries to related work.

T1.justification: V2 explicitly defines the directed schema graph and adds the Laplacian-based mathematical construction of relative positional encoding and its message update in Appendix D. The principal message-passing equations remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V1 left the central benefit of atomic routes confounded with its use of attention. V2 substantially addresses this deficiency through the aggregation-matched ablation and GAT/GIN comparisons across 30 tasks in Tables 5–7, strengthening evidence for the main contribution. Clearer structural explanations also help. Appendix C overstates universal superiority—GIN beats RelGNN on study-adverse—and the positional-encoding result remains underspecified, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RelGNN research. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including material reorganized or expanded in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark results and adds component ablations, additional baseline results, and a positional-encoding experiment in Appendices C–D.

before.justification: V1 Tables 1–3 report original RelGNN classification, regression, and recommendation results across 30 RELBENCH tasks.

results.title: RelGNN: Composite Message Passing for Relational Deep Learning

C1.justification: The introduction adds a substantive contribution: annealed fine-tuning followed by hard-sort inference is claimed to produce exact doubly-stochastic matrices, reduce complexity from O(N^2) to O(LN log N), and improve Cats and Dogs accuracy. This extends the original efficiency contribution beyond parallel soft sorting; the other principal claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly distinguishes approximate double stochasticity during soft-sort training from exact hard-sort inference. It adds limitations concerning strictly causal/autoregressive attention and memory growth with slice count, interprets the slicer ablation, and qualifies the soft-sort runtime advantage to Sinkformer with S>3. These materially clarify applicability and efficiency.

D1.justification: V1 promises code release upon acceptance; v2 supplies an implementation repository address. V2 documents the 40-epoch annealing schedule, decay factor 0.8, and TweetEval implementation and hyperparameters. Most previous implementation details and appendix hyperparameter tables are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds TweetEval sentiment classification, extending sentiment evaluation from movie reviews to tweets. All previous datasets and tasks remain; the MNIST patch-size experiment moves to Appendix A.2.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparators remain Transformer, DiffTransformer, and Sinkformer, including on TweetEval. Changed Sinkhorn iteration counts concern experimental settings, while sorting and slicer variants are internal ablations.

E3.justification: V2 adds a 40-epoch annealing protocol and separate sharpened-soft and hard-sort evaluations across the existing Cats and Dogs data fractions. It also introduces a slicer experiment varying L over 1, 8, 32, 64, and 128 and inverse temperature over 0.1, 1, and 10. Runtime comparisons replace Sinkformer S=50 with S=3. Existing task-training schedules remain documented unchanged.

E4.justification: New comparisons test the effects of annealing and hard-sort inference (Table 1), and whether learnable, frozen, or axis-aligned slicing performs better as slice count and inverse temperature vary (Table 6). These substantially expand evidence about core design choices. The previous data-scarcity and MNIST patch-size analyses remain.

E5.justification: Retained experiments preserve their run counts and reporting practices: three-run means and standard deviations for Cats and Dogs, four-run ModelNet40 and translation summaries, and ten-run runtime averages. New ablations extend the existing mean-and-standard-deviation practice without introducing confidence intervals, significance tests, or an explicit increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds TweetEval, slicer-grid, and hard-sort runtime results. Its expanded Cats and Dogs table reports 80.61% sharpened-soft and 81.23% hard-sort accuracy at full data after additional fine-tuning, alongside the retained 79.47% initial result; these are different training conditions. IMDb Sinkformer median accuracy changes from 85.40% to 85.39%, and Transformer worst accuracy from 85.30% to 85.20%. ModelNet40, translation, and MNIST results remain.

M1.justification: V2 adds temperature-annealed fine-tuning followed by replacement of soft sorting with hard sorting at inference (Section 4.4). This changes the training and inference procedure and introduces an exact-permutation variant; the original soft-sorting pipeline in Algorithm 1 remains.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition is retained, with localized wording and terminology clarifications. V2 introduces sorting and slicer subsections, adds Limitations and Impact Statement sections, and moves the MNIST discussion into Appendix A.2. The overall introduction–background–method–experiments structure remains.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout. V2 restructures the Cats and Dogs table into baseline and sorting-mode groups, adds TweetEval and slicer tables, revises runtime plots and legends, and relocates the MNIST figure. Existing figures, tables, and the algorithm are extensively resized and repositioned.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to TweetEval and Constrained Sliced Wasserstein Embedding, the latter supporting discussion of learned slicing. The broader positioning relative to Sinkformer, ESP, soft sorting, and differential attention remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 corrects Equation 4 by adding the missing 1/p power, writes the transport map with F_mu(x), and specifies absolute continuity rather than continuity. It also introduces the mathematical observation that lower-triangular doubly-stochastic attention reduces to the identity. The main ESP construction remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central attention design through sorting-mode and slicer ablations, clarifies approximate versus exact double stochasticity, and documents important causal and memory limitations absent from v1. Code-access information further improves reproducibility. The extra 40 fine-tuning epochs limit comparisons with unchanged baselines, and broad efficiency wording remains in the conclusion and Appendix A, but the additional design evidence and clearer applicability address important weaknesses in v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ESPFormer and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C. Retained content can be matched across formatting changes, renumbering, and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds TweetEval evaluation, sorting-mode comparisons, and slicer ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification, sentiment-analysis, translation, and runtime experiments, including ESPFormer results and supplementary analyses.

results.title: ESPFormer: Doubly-Stochastic Attention with Expected Sliced Transport Plans

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: generalized anisotropic smoothness, connections to clipping and adaptive updates, and convex/nonconvex convergence guarantees. V2's explicit exclusion of momentum and moving averages clarifies restrictions already present in v1's examples.

C2.justification: V2 discusses when the new norm-coercivity requirement is mild or avoidable and clarifies applicability of the isotropic convergence assumptions. The conclusion adds extension to additive nonsmooth objectives as a research direction and explains that it is not straightforward.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code-repository link absent from v1, documents the MNIST network widths, activations, loss, subset size, and full-gradient updates, and lists parameter choices in Figure 4. It also explicitly states the stepsize mapping used for the existing quartic experiment.

E1.justification: V2 adds neural-network training on MNIST, extending coverage from a quartic toy objective and synthetic phase retrieval to learning from image data. The original tasks remain; the logistic-loss appendix is theoretical in both versions.

E2.justification: The retained phase-retrieval comparison still includes GD, β-GD, and gradient clipping. The citation attached to β-GD changes from v1's reference [9] to Chen et al. (2023), while the plotted comparator remains. The new MNIST experiment reuses gradient clipping rather than introducing another baseline.

E3.justification: The added MNIST experiment introduces a specified fully connected ReLU network, cross-entropy loss, 600 training examples, full-gradient updates, and training-loss plots over 250 iterations. Existing phase-retrieval dimensions, data generation, and method parameters remain unchanged. Explicit quartic stepsize formulas clarify previously documented settings.

E4.justification: Figure 4 adds a parameter-sensitivity study with three paired stepsize/clipping-parameter configurations for each of two preconditioners and gradient clipping. The quartic parameter sweep and 100-instance phase-retrieval robustness comparison already existed.

E5.justification: V1 displays individual phase-retrieval trajectories across 100 random instances. V2 reports their mean with one-standard-deviation bands on a logarithmic plot and explicitly describes this reporting practice. The stated number of instances remains 100.

E6.justification: Figure 4 adds a complete set of neural-network training-loss trajectories showing different transient behavior and final losses across parameter choices. Figure 2 also contains small trajectory changes while retaining its convergence trade-off. The existing phase-retrieval ranking is retained, with aggregate results replacing the individual-run display.
