M1.justification: The update in Equation (2), reference-function families, and connections to memoryless adaptive methods and clipping remain unchanged. Renaming separable reference functions as anisotropic and explaining equivalent clipping parameters do not change the algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain intact. V2 clarifies terminology and explanations, renames separable reference functions, reorganizes Appendix D, removes the contents and classification front matter, and adds acknowledgements and an impact statement.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and references, relocating and resizing existing displays. It adds Figure 4 and a smoothness-constant summary in Table 2. Figure 3 replaces individual trajectories with mean curves and shaded uncertainty bands; Figure 2 uses equivalent reciprocal-parameter legend labels.

R1.justification: V2 adds connections to accelerated methods through Kim et al. (2023) and anisotropic prox-regularity and proximal interpretations through Laude (2021), alongside new proof and MNIST references. It corrects the phase-retrieval source attribution and removes the Topics in optimal transportation reference. The overall research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Definition 2.4 replaces a non-strict spectral bound with a strict bound plus norm-coercivity. Proposition 2.6 replaces general strong monotonicity with injectivity, supported by a new global-homeomorphism proof; the monotonicity argument survives under a symmetry assumption in Proposition D.2. Proposition 2.9 correspondingly uses injectivity. V2 also removes the convexity restriction from Proposition 2.2's conjugate statement, adds Corollary 2.11 and Proposition D.1, and revises logistic-loss and clipping derivations in Appendix D.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is repairing a central theoretical gap: v1's Appendix B.4 infers monotonicity from eigenvalue bounds on generally nonsymmetric matrix products. V2 restricts that argument to symmetric products and develops the general sufficiency argument through injectivity with explicit additional assumptions. The code link, statistical summaries, and MNIST experiment also improve reproducibility and empirical support. Newly added Corollary 2.11 appears to reverse the required scaling, stating δL1 rather than L1/δ; this local defect remains, but does not outweigh the substantial repair to the main argument.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison despite substantial theoretical revisions and different layouts.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, and Section 4.3 and Figure 4 add original neural-network training results on a 600-example MNIST subset.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.2 and Figures 2–3 report original optimization experiments on a quartic objective and synthetic nonconvex phase retrieval, including 100 random problem instances.

results.title: Nonlinearly Preconditioned Gradient Methods under Generalized Smoothness

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: self-supervised context-ablation rewards improve fine-grained citations through best-of-N sampling and preference optimization. The headline improvement of up to 5.3 citation-F1 points remains unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the interpretation that ContextCite SFT reduces answer correctness with one of approximately preserved correctness, following revised baseline scores. It adds substantive discussion of the mismatch between contributive training and corroborative evaluation, qualifies ALCE comparisons by training conditions, interprets latency tradeoffs, and explicitly limits applicability to models exposing output probabilities.

D1.justification: v2 adds a SelfCite source-code link, specifies NLTK segmentation of ContextCite responses, documents the NLI model and its capped sentence-ablation procedure, and supplies latency hardware settings. Appendix A's original training recipe is largely unchanged; these additions mainly expand reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: v2 adds ALCE evaluation on ASQA and ELI5 (Appendix F, Table 8), extending sentence-level long-context evaluation to chunk-level citation tasks under a training-to-evaluation distribution and format mismatch. Existing LongBench-Cite coverage and training datasets are retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds SimPO with NLI rewards, a controlled alternative initialized from LongCite-8B. The new ALCE comparison includes prompted Llama-2-13B-chat and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and reported results from Huang et al. (2024), with the latter explicitly distinguished by its in-distribution training. The Claude Citations comparison already existed in v1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces zero-shot ALCE evaluation using NLI-based citation metrics, ASQA exact-match recall, and ELI5 correctness. It also adds a controlled reward comparison and a latency protocol using eight A100 GPUs, batch size one, and model parallelism. These are additional protocols; the original LongBench-Cite settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether SelfCite's reward improves on an NLI reward with the training pipeline held fixed, whether sentence-level training transfers to chunk-level ALCE tasks, and how sampling versus reranking contributes to latency. Existing reward, length-balancing, training-size, iterative-training, and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run performance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both retain the same candidate-diversity statistic: 4.8 unique candidates per statement on average, with standard deviation 3.2. The added experiments do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds NLI-baseline results (75.0 average citation F1), ALCE results, and latency measurements, while retaining the original SelfCite Table 1 scores. Table 2 changes Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct average correctness without citations from 60.2 to 68.9 and with citations from 71.7 to 63.3. Table 4 changes the 8K-training F1 from 64.4 to 65.9 and citation length from 195.2 to 158.1. These reported revisions do not establish across-version model improvements.

M1.justification: The context-ablation reward, citation-only best-of-N sampling, SimPO optimization, and length balancing remain unchanged. Expanded Algorithm 1 incorporates the 384-token filter already stated in v1's prose and clarifies candidate indexing; it does not establish a new procedure.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify citation resampling, simplify the SimPO rationale, and revise results interpretation and limitations. v2 adds an Impact Statement, a latency subsection, and Appendices E–G, moving the existing qualitative appendix to H. The overall narrative and main section order remain intact.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column report to a two-column conference layout with different front matter, headers, and figure/table placement. v2 adds latency, ALCE, and prior-method comparison tables and expands Table 1. Existing figures and qualitative tables are retained but resized or relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds Mudgal et al. (2024) to motivate best-of-N evaluation and expands positioning through Appendix G/Table 9, comparing citation granularity, generation passes, preference optimization, context capacity, and supervision. Most compared works and the central self-supervised positioning were already present in v1.

T1.justification: The necessity/sufficiency reward derivation and Appendix B's ContextCite surrogate-model and citation-extraction mathematics remain substantively unchanged. Algorithm clarification and explicit restatement of the reward sum introduce no new theoretical result or mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the reward's distinctive value: the controlled NLI comparison reports 75.0 versus SelfCite SimPO's 77.9 average F1, while ALCE transfer tests and latency measurements address generalization and practical cost absent from v1. Clearer applicability limits and code-access information also help. Some new prose overstates superiority: Appendix F's claim that LongCite beats prompting conflicts with the ELI5 citation scores in Table 8. This localized weakness does not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SelfCite. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial layout changes and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds an NLI-reward baseline, ALCE evaluations, and latency measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original SelfCite experiments on LongBench-Cite, including best-of-N sampling, SimPO training, ablations, iterative optimization, and a Claude Citations comparison.

results.title: SelfCite: Self-Supervised Alignment for Context Attribution in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and principal conclusion retain the same claims: semantic motion guidance and text-aligned 2D completion improve test-time pose estimation, including more than 12% PA-MPJPE reductions on 3DPW and 3DHP. Added evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains resilience to erroneous labels through the alignment regularizer being constrained by 2D projection supervision. It adds an interpretation of EMA sensitivity and identifies motion blur and residual directional ambiguity as unresolved issues. Earlier limitations concerning motion timing and MotionCLIP generalization remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B supplies substantial previously unavailable labeling details: GPT-4o identity, prompts, dictionary constraints, downsampling, CLIP consistency checking at 0.3 and manual correction. Section 5.2 also specifies the OpenPose confidence threshold of 0.3. Conversely, Section 4.1 drops v1's explicit stride-1 specification without stating a replacement.

E1.justification: Human3.6M training and 3DPW, 3DHP and EgoBody evaluation remain unchanged. Section 5.5 adds an explicit semantic-input failure scenario, evaluating pose adaptation with incorrect VLM labels versus correct oracle labels. No new dataset or domain is introduced.

E2.justification: The matched benchmark comparisons retain their baselines. The motion-discriminator and unpaired-local-pose alternatives in v1 Table 3 reappear in v2 Table 4 with clarified names and unchanged results. Added runtime and qualitative comparisons use existing comparators.

E3.justification: Existing backbones, pose metrics and training settings are retained. New analyses introduce a 5,000-frame labeling audit, incorrect-label/oracle/no-adaptation controls, per-frame runtime evaluation and an EMA grid from 0.75 to 0.95. The newly specified OpenPose threshold documents an existing setting rather than establishing changed preprocessing.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands analysis beyond the retained component and fill-in ablations. C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the same central contributions: a differentiable variational family covering tree space, a closed-form density, no required MCMC subroutines, and competitive inference using fewer gradient evaluations. The added evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Appendix B.3 identifies underestimation for tree lengths of eight or greater and suggests a mismatch between approximately exponential long-branch posteriors and log-normal pairwise distributions. The computational discussion newly attributes observed near-linear VIPR scaling to likelihood evaluation and explains VBPI's scaling through SBN normalization and parameter growth. These materially extend the earlier limitations and mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds VIPR code and diagnostic-histogram access information, a more specific rooted-VBPI implementation reference, the MS simulation command, and runtime hardware details. E1.justification: The original twelve genomic datasets are retained. Section 4.4 and Appendix B.3 add two synthetic evaluation regimes: neutral coalescent/infinite-sites MS datasets and Kingman/Jukes-Cantor datasets with known generating trees. This substantially extends evaluation beyond observed genomic data and their subsets.

E2.justification: Appendix B.1 adds a limited quantitative comparison with cubeVB's restricted tree-space coverage, previously discussed qualitatively. E3.justification: The runtime study replaces COVID-19 subsets containing 3–72 taxa with simulated datasets containing 8–512 taxa and 1,000 sites. It changes the stopping rule from 1,000 iterations to five minutes or 1,000 iterations, whichever occurs first. New protocols also specify MCC-based cube-space assessment and known-tree checks using ten eight-taxon simulations, 10,000 optimization iterations, and 10,000 posterior samples.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of posterior mass excluded by cube space, pairwise Hamming-distance characteristics, and recovery of known tree lengths and likelihoods. The revised scaling study also measures parameter counts. These investigate representation coverage, approximation failures, and computational bottlenecks beyond v1's posterior summaries and convergence plots.

E5.justification: Appendix B.4 newly identifies the parenthesized uncertainties as standard errors estimated using 100 bootstrap samples. The numerical uncertainties and existing chain/restart counts are retained, so this establishes improved reporting rather than additional experimental replications.

E6.justification: v1 Tables 1–2 are numerically preserved in v2 Tables 6–7, and all twelve appendix convergence traces are retained. Substantial new results include 15.2–99.9% of sampled trees lying outside the assessed cube space, parameter-count comparisons, and long-tree underestimation. The replacement runtime study reports approximately linear VIPR scaling instead of the earlier approximately quadratic behavior, under different experimental conditions.

M1.justification: The independent log-normal distance distributions, single-linkage tree construction, closed-form density, and LOOR, reparameterization, and VIMCO estimators remain unchanged. Algorithm input declarations and redistributed explanations clarify the existing procedure.

P1.justification: The six-section narrative remains recognizable. v2 copyedits prose, folds the notation subsection into Background, redistributes gradient explanations between Section 3.3 and Appendix C, reorganizes Appendix B into named subsections, and adds an Impact Statement.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout, redraws Figure 1, and merges the earlier DS1 and COVID figures into a six-panel Figure 2. It presents simplified benchmark tables in the main text and preserves complete versions in the appendix, while adding coverage, dataset-characteristic, parameter-count, and simulation displays and replacing the timing visualization.

R1.justification: The introduction adds ARTree and discussion of RAxML, neighbor-joining, and Phyloformer, distinguishing non-Bayesian reconstruction from marginal-likelihood estimation. Simulation references are also added. These broaden the context while retaining the original positioning against SBN-based inference and restricted matrix representations.

T1.justification: Proposition 1, its Appendix A induction proof, the objectives, and the gradient-estimator formulas remain mathematically unchanged after matching relocated equations. Expanded Kingman-process explanations and the explicit reference to the Leibniz integral rule explain existing mathematics.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny through controlled scaling experiments, quantitative support-coverage checks, and known-tree diagnostics exposing a concrete approximation failure. These address important gaps in evaluating computational behavior and applicability, while preserving the original proof and benchmark results. Bootstrap and implementation disclosures improve auditability. Figure 6 retains an inconsistent COVID-19 caption despite describing simulated-data results, but this reporting flaw does not outweigh the validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VIPR research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those inference results and reports additional simulations, tree-space coverage measurements, dataset statistics, and computational scaling results.

Figure 1 is relocated and captions are revised; the appendix stimulus examples are retained with new numbering.

Tables 9, 11, and 12 add further ablation and baseline outcomes.

T1.justification: Appendix H adds a formal discrete ALLDIFFERENT violation-degree function and connects it to the existing penalty-design rationale. improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1 by testing output-function choices, direct optimization, competing heuristics, and runtime sensitivity, while examining scalability on much larger MAXCUT instances. These additions strengthen evidence and transparency, including unfavorable comparisons, although uncertainty reporting remains limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ConsFormer research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison; v2 retains Appendices A–D and adds E–I.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds original MAXCUT, multi-start, output-function, baseline, and direct-gradient-descent experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original ConsFormer experiments on Sudoku, graph coloring, and nurse scheduling, including performance comparisons and ablations in Section 4.

results.title: Self-Supervised Transformers as Iterative Solution Improvers for Constraint Satisfaction

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory findings, and substantive conclusion retain the claims that heterogeneity and uniqueness constrain alignment and that alignment does not universally predict performance. The new experiments support the existing practitioner implications rather than redefine these central claims.

C2.justification: Section 5.1 replaces the interpretation that high corruption undermines the performance-capacity relationship with an account of flattening alignment-performance slopes while larger language models still perform better. Section 6.2 and Appendix D.7 add task-specific interpretations connecting alignment-performance slopes to the usefulness of explicit alignment.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 supplies the GPT-4o caption-generation prompt. Appendix A.4 documents MM-IMDb linear-probe tuning, 100-epoch probe training, and 30-epoch CLIP fine-tuning with learning rates, cosine scheduling, and warmup. Appendix A.1 newly discloses an alignment batch size of 512. These substantially extend procedural documentation; the code URL is unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds MM-IMDb movie-genre prediction, including 23 binary tasks and fine-tuning experiments on 10 classes under scarce labels. It also replaces corrupted Wikipedia image-text inputs with semantically modified captions paired with unchanged images, materially changing the evaluated input conditions. The earlier synthetic and five MultiBench datasets remain.

E2.justification: The new MM-IMDb comparison evaluates supervised-only fine-tuning against combined supervised and CLIP training in Figure 10. Appendix D.3 adds randomly initialized network controls. The original pretrained vision and language model families are retained.

E3.justification: Wikipedia experiments replace random character deletion and Gaussian pixel substitution with GPT-generated semantic caption changes at 10–100% uniqueness. New protocols vary alignment metrics, alignment batch sizes of 256/512/1024, and the first encoder's depth. MM-IMDb uses 1024 examples per train/validation/test split and an explicit-alignment loss-weight sweep. Correlation metrics also change predominantly from Pearson to Spearman.

E4.justification: Appendices D.1–D.3 add tests of alignment-metric and batch-size sensitivity, deeper first-modality encoders, and randomly initialized networks. These examine measurement robustness, architectural dependence, and the role of training beyond v1's analyses. Figure 10 additionally tests sensitivity to explicit-alignment strength across movie genres.

E5.justification: Most plotted association estimates change from Pearson r to Spearman rho. The original five synthetic-data seeds and three MultiBench seeds remain unchanged; an increase in repeated runs is not documented. Figures 24–26 introduce a reporting inconsistency: plot labels use rho while captions still specify Pearson.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises retained correlations, including AVMNIST vision/audio values from 0.944/0.974 to 0.887/0.723. The replacement vision-language experiment reports Figure 8 slopes of 0.112, 0.071, and 0.024 at uniqueness levels 10, 50, and 90. Numerous robustness and MM-IMDb findings are added. Changed inputs and correlation metrics prevent interpreting these revisions as matched-setting performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: The original synthetic construction and independent unimodal encoders remain. Section 6.2 adds a bounded algorithmic application: fine-tuning CLIP encoders with L = L_sup + w L_CLIP, with supervised predictions from language embeddings. This introduces an explicit-alignment training objective without redesigning the original framework.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. Local revisions update the experimental setup and Section 5.1, subdivide Section 6, and reorganize the appendices around additional analyses. A forward-looking conclusion paragraph moves into the Impact Statement, and affiliation and proceedings information are updated.

P2.justification: Figure 6 replaces heatmaps with scatterplots against encoder depth minus transformation depth. V2 adds the MM-IMDb displays and extensive metric, batch-size, depth, and initialization panels. Previously separate vision-language figures are consolidated into Figures 27–28, and Figure 2 gains explanatory labels. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 adds Arevalo et al. (2017) for MM-IMDb. The alignment literature and positioning relative to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis remain substantively unchanged. Consolidating duplicate MultiBench references does not remove a distinct prior work.

T1.justification: The alignment equations, synthetic-data definitions, independence assumptions, and illustrative prediction tables are retained. The bijection assumption is rephrased without changing its substance. No new theorem, proof, or theoretical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1's empirical support through measurement-sensitivity and initialization controls in Appendices D.1–D.3 and a direct test of explicit-alignment weighting in Section 6.2. The documented semantic-caption manipulation also makes the intended intervention more interpretable than character/pixel corruption. These additions substantially strengthen robustness assessment and practical relevance. The Pearson/rho caption inconsistency in Appendix D.4 is a limited reporting drawback.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained content can be matched despite substantial appendix expansion and figure renumbering.

after.justification: V2 reports these empirical investigations with revisions, plus original robustness experiments, random-initialization controls, and MM-IMDb classification and fine-tuning results.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-data, vision-language, and MultiBench experiments in Figures 4–9, Table 1, and Appendix D.

results.title: Understanding the Emergence of Multimodal Representation Alignment

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion redefine the central contribution from transferring image VLMs into zero-shot video captioning to extending both image and short-video models beyond their temporal windows for long-video captioning. Performance and efficiency claims now center on LLM-based consolidation, changing the claimed applicability and contribution framing.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges that initial VLM counting and identification hallucinations propagate through consolidation. It adds interpretations of the k precision–recall trade-off and InternVL2.5's temporal-modeling benefits. Appendix A also strengthens the superiority interpretation to all evaluation metrics, although Table 8 still gives Mistral summarization higher METEOR than SGVC.

D1.justification: New disclosures include the 235M-parameter model, BERT-base and decoder-only T5-base, frame-sampling counts, k and tau defaults, paragraph repetition penalty, A6000 measurement hardware, and CPU graph merging. v1's explicit randomized LLaVA decoding recipe is omitted. Prompt templates and principal optimizer settings remain unchanged; these disclosures do not establish corresponding changes to earlier experiments.

E1.justification: v2 adds MSVD evaluation alongside retained MSR-VTT and ActivityNet Captions evaluations. The graph-to-text training sources remain the same. Long-video paragraph captioning already appeared in v1, so the revised long-video emphasis does not establish a newly added task.

E2.justification: v2 adds VidIL without reference exemplars, evaluates VidIL and Video ChatCaptioner on ActivityNet, and adds GPT-4o mini summarization. It removes ActivityNet comparisons with MFT, PDVC, Vid2Seq, and Streaming GIT, and drops DeCap-CC3M from MSR-VTT. Most other earlier MSR-VTT comparators remain in Appendix A, Table 8.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from LLaVA-based captions to comparisons across BLIP, BLIP2, and InternVL2.5 configurations, extending the existing same-caption summarization controls. Paragraph fine-tuning is reported as 400 rather than 500 iterations. New protocols measure per-video inference time and peak memory and vary graph hyperparameters; the retained captioning metrics and dataset splits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The 4–12-frame ablation in v1 Table 3 is removed. v2 instead tests prioritized-subgraph size k and matching threshold tau in Tables 6–7, adds computational-cost analysis, and presents explicit counting and object-misidentification failures in Appendix C. Additional qualitative examples expand the diagnostic evidence beyond relocated examples.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repetition counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial benchmark, backbone, efficiency, and sensitivity results while removing the earlier frame-count and supervised ActivityNet results. In retained LLaVA-based MSR-VTT entries, SGVC FBERT changes from 0.484 to 0.497 and Mistral summarization FBERT from 0.416 to 0.414 without explanation (v1 Table 1; v2 Table 8). New-backbone results do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The caption-generation stage extends from individual frames processed by image VLMs to either frames or short clips, including an implemented InternVL2.5 configuration. This broadens the input procedure, while Hungarian object matching, graph consolidation, prioritized subgraph extraction, and the graph-to-text training objective remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around long-video captioning. Method and experiment subsections are reorganized, analysis gains separate efficiency and hyperparameter discussions, and appendices are reordered and expanded. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond additions of scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with a graph-to-text attention-mask illustration. Results are reorganized into backbone- and dataset-grouped tables, with new efficiency and sensitivity displays and an expanded appendix comparison. Qualitative figures are enlarged, rearranged, and supplemented; several earlier examples and the prompt tables are retained through relocation.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially repositioned around long-video consolidation, adding memory-based and recursive approaches such as memory consolidation, MovieChat, Video ReCap, and LongVLM, alongside newer video models and BLIP/BLIP2. This replaces the earlier paragraph-captioning-centered discussion and changes the comparison with prior research beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The scene-graph definitions, cosine/Hungarian matching, attribute union, next-token objective, and BERTScore mathematics retain their substance. Graph-update notation is shortened into Algorithm 1 and equations are renumbered, without a new theoretical assumption, derivation, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 claims efficiency and backbone flexibility without measured costs or evaluation across multiple backbones. v2 substantially strengthens this evidence through image/video backbone comparisons, stronger ActivityNet comparators, and measured memory and runtime in Table 5. Hyperparameter studies and explicit failure cases also improve assessability. Removing the frame-count ablation and supervised comparisons loses useful context, while unexplained BERTScore revisions and overbroad superiority wording weaken reporting. These drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial improvement in support for the paper's central claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SGVC research, retaining its graph-consolidation pipeline and principal benchmarks despite a revised title and emphasis. All 13 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v2, including equations, tables, figures, and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original SGVC results on MSR-VTT, MSVD, and ActivityNet Captions, computational measurements, hyperparameter studies, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original SGVC results on MSR-VTT and ActivityNet Captions, a frame-count ablation in Tables 1–3, and qualitative outputs.

results.title: Fine-Grained Captioning of Long Videos through Scene Graph Consolidation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: learning a manifold optimizer from noisy samples, combining first- and zero-order traversal, and obtaining favorable denoising–complexity tradeoffs. The conclusion retains the qualification that theoretical guarantees assume an ideal learned graph.

C2.justification: Appendix G adds substantive qualifications: tested autoencoders can achieve higher accuracy, image outputs exhibit pixelation and color artifacts, and radius tuning may extend the method's accuracy range. The new ablation also supports the proposed division of roles between first- and zero-order steps. Existing limitations concerning guarantees for learned landmarks remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, explicit streaming-average and affine-projection formulas in Appendix E, autoencoder architectures and Adam learning rate, and image preprocessing details. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Some ambiguity remains: G.1 describes a two-dimensional bottleneck, whereas Table 2 includes wider bottlenecks; code availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic manifolds and generated gravitational waveforms. v2 retains this coverage and adds patch denoising using 300 ImageNet images and a single DIV2K image (Appendices G.2–G.3), substantially extending the domain and introducing a single-image learning scenario.

E2.justification: v1's quantitative comparison uses nearest-neighbor search. v2 retains it and adds 15 autoencoder configurations (Figure 13, Table 2), plus first-order-only traversal and zero-order search over all graph edges (Figure 18). These substantially broaden the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: The gravitational-wave test set increases from 5,000 to 20,000 samples, while training remains at 100,000. New image protocols use 8 × 8 × 3 patches, Gaussian noise with sigma 0.1, and 890,000 or 170,000 training patches with strides 8 or 4. v2 also introduces autoencoder configurations and controlled component-ablation procedures. The retained hyperparameter table relabels the neighbor-radius entries from R_nbrs to R_nbrs squared.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained radius comparison and network visualizations, Appendix G.4 adds a controlled ablation testing why gradient steps and zero-order tunnels should be combined. Appendix B.2 adds a noisy-versus-denoised waveform case, and G.2–G.3 provide image and patch case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The larger test set changes evaluation size, while the theoretical probability bounds concern mathematical guarantees rather than empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Figures 8–9 show revised gravitational-wave curves, with Figure 9 using the enlarged test set. v1 Table 1's exact landmark counts, computational costs, and MSEs are removed. v2 adds autoencoder outcomes, image-denoising curves and examples, and ablation findings showing low computational cost but high error for first-order-only traversal. These are added or replaced results; the revised curves do not establish a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the online graph-learning and mixed-order traversal framework. However, Appendix D revises the stated tangent-space update: Algorithms 4–5 replace inputs x_i with landmark-centered inputs x_i - q_M and formulate the update through eigenvalues of the second-moment matrix. This is a localized revision to the documented procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence remains intact, with mostly local condensation, terminology and notation edits, and revised explanations. Appendix D's exposition is reworked and Appendix E collects additional algorithm explanations. Author information, publication text, and acknowledgements are also updated.

P2.justification: v2 adds waveform, autoencoder, image-denoising, and ablation displays in Figures 10 and 13–18, plus an architecture table. Figures 8–9 are redrawn with revised sizing, axes, and legends. The original numerical results table is removed; the original hyperparameter table becomes Table 1, and the retained torus and sphere figures become Figures 11–12.

R1.justification: v2 adds Gong et al. (2010) and extends the nearest-neighbor efficiency critique to empirical manifold-denoising methods. It also adds the DIV2K dataset reference, Agustsson and Timofte (2017). The broader positioning relative to manifold estimation, Riemannian optimization, and graph search is retained.

T1.justification: Theorem A.1 aligns its zero-order-edge assumption with the existing main theorem and adds a covering argument bounding the required degree. Its complexity bound changes the covering radius from tau_M/80 to tau_M/160. Appendix D also replaces the SVD-based derivation with centered second-moment reasoning. The principal denoising rate and phase-analysis results remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central efficiency argument: v1 compared chiefly against nearest-neighbor search, while v2 adds learned baselines and an ablation directly testing the mixed-order design. The added covering argument strengthens justification of the complexity bound, and implementation documentation improves. Removing the exact results table reduces auditability, and the new image evaluations and autoencoder specifications remain limited, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains in supporting evidence and technical clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same manifold-denoising framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 reports gravitational-wave experiments and adds original autoencoder comparisons, natural-image denoising experiments, and component ablations in Appendix G.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-manifold simulations and gravitational-wave denoising experiments, including training curves and numerical accuracy–complexity comparisons in Figures 8–9 and Table 1.

results.title: Fast, Accurate Manifold Denoising by Tunneling Riemannian Optimization

C1.justification: Both versions claim pixel-level horizontal/vertical alignment, effective retrieval across seven tasks, competitive fine-tuning on five of six tasks and waveform generation from pixel embeddings. Rewording and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 explicitly qualifies median composites as more informative than single-date images but less informative than full time series. H.10 attributes their advantage to more stable, representative reflectance patterns. These refine the temporal-information interpretation; the existing limitations concerning static inputs and geographic/year specificity remain.

D1.justification: Section 4 adds a code-repository link absent from v1, and Table G1 explicitly lists the selected neighbor count for each task. Most architecture, optimizer, hardware and diffusion settings are carried over from v1 Appendix D to v2 Appendix E.

E1.justification: The seven tasks and core French datasets are retained. Appendix H adds cross-year evaluation for 2019 and 2021, pooled 2019–2021 pretraining, single-sensor inputs and single-date imagery scenarios. These extend temporal and input-condition coverage within the existing domains.

E2.justification: Fine-tuning comparisons expand from AnySat and CROMA to include DOFA, DeCUR and SatMAE in Tables 2 and G2. Table 1 also adds canopy-height comparisons with Liu et al. (2023), Tolan et al. (2024) and Lang et al. (2023), alongside Schwartz et al. (2023). These are reported comparisons, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes comparator pretraining from 200K to 250K steps and DUNIA fine-tuning from the last two neighborhood-attention layers to the last layer. Added protocols vary input size, retrieval database size, neighbor count and temporal training/evaluation design. These reported revisions do not establish that retained results were rerun. Table G2 also changes the PASTIS sample count from 300 to 300K images, an unexplained inconsistency with the stated dataset size.

E4.justification: The five original ablations are retained as H.1–H.5. New sections H.6–H.10 examine retrieval overhead, input-size sensitivity, temporal stability, sensor contributions and median composites versus single-date inputs. Appendix D adds a t-SNE comparison of pixel and patch embeddings, and Appendix I expands qualitative map examples.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added evaluations continue to report point estimates without introducing uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial comparator and supplementary results. For example, Table H11 reports PASTIS wF1 of 42.3 with single-date inputs versus 77.0 with median composites; Table H6 reports DUNIA runtimes of 4.22/4.80 seconds versus 177.37 for AnySat. Existing principal DUNIA table values are retained or rounded, while smaller-data results move to Appendix G; these do not demonstrate new same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The dual-decoder architecture, waveform and multitemporal autoencoders, Zero-CL/VICReg alignment, reconstruction losses and diffusion generator remain unchanged. Matching the appendices confirms that expanded architectural explanations do not introduce new method components; the fine-tuning revisions concern evaluation settings.

P1.justification: Section 3 receives a rewritten, multi-paragraph architectural overview, and related work gains a dedicated EO subsection. Existing appendix material is substantially reorganized: objectives and waveform generation become separate sections, experimental settings move, and reduced-label evaluations receive their own section. Terminology and prose are also edited throughout.

P2.justification: Figure 2 becomes a simplified architecture diagram while the detailed diagram moves to Figure A1. v2 adds Figure D1 and Tables H6–H11, restructures Tables 1–2 with smaller-data results in G1–G2, and expands the original combined map figure into Figures I1–I3. The four waveform-example figures remain unchanged apart from presentation and numbering.

R1.justification: A dedicated Section 2.2 substantially expands domain-specific positioning by discussing masked-reconstruction and contrastive approaches for Earth observation, including SatMAE, SatMAE++, DOFA, CROMA, DeCUR and AnySat. Additional canopy-height literature also broadens the context beyond v1's primarily general contrastive and multimodal review.

T1.justification: The alignment losses, diffusion formulations and radar-normalization equation are retained after appendix relocation and equation renumbering. The decoder-channel index correction in Section 3.1 agrees with the formula already present in v1 Appendix A.1. No substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens comparative validation and the justification of practical design choices through broader baselines and targeted temporal, sensor, compositing and runtime tests. Clearer architectural diagrams and code-access information also improve usability. Table G2's inconsistent PASTIS count and unexplained setting revisions limit reproducibility, but these localized problems do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and explanation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DUNIA and provide readable main texts, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds comparator evaluations, runtime measurements, temporal tests and input-sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval, fine-tuning and waveform-generation results across seven Earth-observation tasks, alongside architectural ablations and qualitative examples.

results.title: DUNIA: Pixel-Sized Embeddings via Cross-Modal Alignment for Earth Observation Applications

C1.justification: The abstract and principal framework contributions remain unchanged. Introduction contribution 3 expands the empirical claim to multiple-choice question answering and explicitly claims best-calibrated coverage across boosting trees, neural networks, and LLMs.

C2.justification: Section 3 adds an explanation attributing the faster convergence analysis to concentration of weighted coverage rather than pinball loss. Section 5.3 interprets conservative conformal's comparable MCQA coverage deviation as requiring larger prediction sets. Existing experimental interpretations and computational limitations remain.

D1.justification: Section 5.3 identifies the source and restricted availability of the logged model probabilities. Appendix C.3 lists the 16 subjects and their exact nine-basic/seven-advanced grouping. Existing implementation details in Appendix C are retained; MCQA calibration sample counts and splits remain unspecified.

E1.justification: Section 5.3 adds multiple-choice question answering on a 16-subject MMLU subset using LLaMA-13B predictions, with subjects grouped into basic and advanced categories. This substantially extends coverage beyond income regression and toxicity classification, which are retained.

E2.justification: The corresponding ACSIncome and CivilComments experiments retain their comparator sets. The new MCQA experiment reuses split and conservative conformal prediction; no new comparison method is introduced.

E3.justification: The added MCQA configuration uses logged four-choice probabilities from LLaMA-13B, APS scores, and a 40% subject-accuracy threshold for grouping. Existing experiments retain their stated splits, sample budgets, preprocessing, models, and evaluation metrics.

E4.justification: The analyses varying group counts on ACSIncome and calibration sample sizes on CivilComments are unchanged. The MCQA addition reports aggregate benchmark outcomes without introducing a separate ablation, robustness test, or error analysis.

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly reports distributions across ten one-shot prompts for MCQA. The existing experiments retain their 100 reshuffled runs and associated distribution and standard-deviation reporting. This does not establish increased replication of the earlier experiments.

E6.justification: Figure 5 adds results for a new task: Kandinsky (FY) has lower group-average coverage deviation than split conformal and comparable deviation to conservative conformal, with smaller prediction sets. The six original ACSIncome and CivilComments plots and their findings are unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the same quantile-regression objectives, randomized scores, prediction-set construction, and test-time alternative. Explicit randomness notation and the MCQA application do not change the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v2 clarifies training-conditional versus marginal coverage, makes calibration conditioning and randomness explicit, adds a proof sketch and MCQA subsections, and updates an author affiliation. The overall section organization and most existing prose are retained.

P2.justification: v1's six-panel Figure 3 is split into four-panel Figure 3 and two-panel Figure 4, with revised captions and placement. v2 adds the two-panel MCQA Figure 5. The original plot contents and the two introductory artwork figures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused discussion of Blot et al. on joint covariate-label groups and Plassier et al. on joint distribution shifts, distinguishing its guarantees from theirs. A footnote distinguishes Brunekreef et al.'s same-named segmentation method. MMLU, MCQA, and LLaMA references are also added.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1 replaces weight sup-norm scaling with coefficient L1-norm scaling under a normalized basis and changes log(4/delta) to log(4d/delta). Appendix A.1 separates a fixed-weight result into Lemma A.1 and adds a union-bound proof for the uniform guarantee. Corollaries 3.2–3.4 and their proofs are updated accordingly. Corollary 3.5 changes from a simultaneous guarantee over target distributions to a high-probability guarantee for each fixed target distribution.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is addressing the unsupported fixed-weight-to-uniform step in v1's central proof. Lemma A.1 and the new union-bound argument support appropriately revised guarantees, including corrected target-distribution quantifiers. Although the resulting bounds are weaker, their justification is materially stronger. The MCQA evaluation and more precise research positioning add useful support, despite sparse calibration details for the new experiment. Repairing the central theoretical argument constitutes a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Kandinsky Conformal Prediction. Their main text, algorithms, equations, figures, references, and appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original conformal-prediction evaluations using previously logged LLaMA-13B outputs on an MMLU subset in Figure 5.

before.justification: v1 reports original conformal-prediction experiments on ACSIncome and CivilComments, including coverage and prediction-set-size results in Figure 3.

results.title: Kandinsky Conformal Prediction: Beyond Class- and Covariate-Conditional Coverage

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: efficient function-space learning-rate measurement, analysis of optimizer dynamics, and FLeRM transfer across width, depth, initialization scale, and LoRA rank. The new experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: C.7 proposes overfitting as the explanation for imperfect ResMLP test-loss alignment, contrasting the single-epoch transformers. C.11 attributes noisy SGD curves to using SGD with transformers, supported by the smoother ResMLP experiment. These add specific interpretations without replacing the earlier conclusions.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses roughly 814M parameters for the retained widest transformer, explains cosine-schedule transfer through base-model learning-rate ratios, and supplies settings such as momentum 0.9 and AdamW weight decay 0.1. The original model/data details and code-access link remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIFAR-10, Wikitext-103, Cold French Law, and MathPile for the same classification and language-modeling tasks. The added test-loss evaluations and model/optimizer sweeps retain this data and task coverage.

E2.justification: The width-transfer comparisons expand beyond standard Adam to momentum SGD, SignSGD/Signum, AdamW, Adamax, and Adagrad, each compared with its FLeRM counterpart (Figures 20–25). Figure 15 also newly compares the Kronecker estimator against IID and no-assumption estimators.

E3.justification: The original experimental settings are retained, but Appendices C.7–C.11 introduce test-loss evaluation, cosine scheduling, affine layernorm parameters, simultaneous width/depth scaling, and alternative optimizer settings. Figure 15 adds a first-training-step estimator evaluation using 10,000 batches.

E4.justification: v2 retains the periodic-update, equal-rate, and LoRA analyses and substantially expands diagnostics. New analyses examine covariance assumptions, generalization, sensitivity to schedules and layernorm configuration, joint scaling, optimizer robustness, and the effect of readout-specific variance reduction (C.6–C.11 and Appendix D).

E5.justification: Figure 15 newly reports empirical estimator bias and variance over 10,000 batches. This characterizes estimator variability rather than independent training-run uncertainty. The eight-seed base-model averaging and single-seed LoRA calibration remain unchanged, and the new performance plots do not add confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Figures 1–14 retain their results, while Figures 15–26 add substantial findings: the Kronecker estimator trades some bias for reduced variance, test-loss optima align more closely with FLeRM, additional optimizer/configuration comparisons support transfer, and readout-specific estimation reduces ResMLP curve noise. These are additional results under their stated settings.

M1.justification: Appendix D adds a readout-specific estimator exploiting independence between output rows and bias entries, evaluated in Figure 26. The core FLeRM procedure remains. Algorithm 1 also corrects its learning-rate ratio to base/current, agreeing with Equation 19 already present in v1; this does not establish that the original implementation changed.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain largely unchanged. Limited edits clarify time-indexed matching and matrix dimensions, repair wording, and update publication footnotes. Acknowledgements and an impact statement are added, while new scientific material is organized into C.6–C.11 and Appendix D.

P2.justification: Figures 15–26 substantially expand the visual evidence with bias/variance bars and additional generalization, robustness, and estimator-comparison plots. Figures 1–14 retain their designs, with appendix figures relocated. Some new labeling is inconsistent, notably Figure 25's transformer plot label versus its ResMLP caption.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds Chizat and Bach, Sirignano and Spiliopoulos, and a comparison with Chizat and Netrapalli's feature-speed approach. It also softens the Everett discussion from violated alignment assumptions to difficulty choosing appropriate assumptions. The overall research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds a localized mathematical extension: it derives readout-row and bias independence, corresponding simplified estimators, and equivalence of IID and diagonal assumptions for estimating the summed bias variances (Equations 29–35). The general Kronecker and tensor-normal derivations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps in v1 through direct estimator bias/variance measurements, held-out losses, and robustness checks beyond constant-schedule Adam. It also corrects the pseudocode ratio and derives a tested readout-specific refinement. These additions substantially strengthen the evidence and reproducibility; minor new caption and labeling inconsistencies do not outweigh those gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Function-Space Learning Rates by the same authors and are readable, including their appendices. The original methods, experiments, and figures can be matched reliably to the retained material in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds estimator diagnostics, test-loss results, and experiments with additional training configurations and optimizers.

before.justification: v1 reports original learning-rate and training-loss experiments on ResMLPs, transformers, and LoRA adapters in Section 4 and Appendix C.

results.title: Function-Space Learning Rates

C1.justification: The abstract, three contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same substantive claims: gradient-based discovery of refusal directions, multidimensional refusal cones, and multiple representationally independent refusal mechanisms. The added experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds a causal argument based on compositional improvements, interprets the over-refusal curves as a better safety/helpfulness trade-off, and revises retain-loss guidance around capability preservation. These extend the existing interpretation rather than replace it; Section 7's limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The expanded asset table supplies access links and licenses for the newly evaluated datasets, and Table 4 explicitly identifies TruthfulQA MC2. Core implementation, optimizer, loss weights, direction-selection instructions, and the code-access address are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on the StrongREJECT dataset and SORRY-BENCH, benign over-refusal testing with XSTest, and capability evaluation on ARC-Challenge, GSM8K, and MMLU. StrongREJECT previously appeared as the judge rather than an evaluated prompt dataset. Existing training datasets, JailbreakBench, and TruthfulQA remain.

E2.justification: DIM remains the principal comparator. v2 adds no-intervention baselines to the JailbreakBench and RepInd comparisons, introduces DIM into the retain-loss trade-off plot, and reports a multiple-DIM-direction control for compositional ablation.

E3.justification: Core training splits and Table 3 hyperparameters remain unchanged. New protocols include an addition/ablation weight sweep with complementary weights, simultaneous top-k ablation, and an activation-strength sweep for safety versus over-refusal. The retain-loss analysis replaces validation-KL comparisons with average capability-score changes, and RepInd evaluation expands beyond Gemma 2 2B.

E4.justification: v2 adds component-loss ablations, compositional tests of independent directions, orthogonality analyses across models, and safety/over-refusal trade-offs. It substantially revises the retain-loss sensitivity analysis. Conversely, v1 Figure 12's experiment on cones with representationally independent basis vectors is removed.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 15 explicitly reports means and standard deviations over five runs per retain-loss weight. Its v2 replacement presents scatter points without the corresponding run-count or uncertainty explanation. The new loss-balance plot also leaves its error bars undefined; existing cone-sampling and RepInd candidate-count disclosures remain.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial benchmark and mechanistic results while retaining Table 1 and Figure 2's original results. Its new Figure 8 reports compositional-ablation ASR increasing from 0.423 with one direction to 0.816 with five, versus 0.786 for DIM. Additional results appear in Tables 4–5 and the expanded appendices; the original RepInd-cone results disappear.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and the ablation, addition, retain, and RepInd objectives remain unchanged. Simultaneous ablation of multiple directions is introduced as a mechanistic experiment, without revising the proposed optimization algorithms.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose are preserved. v2 reorganizes the previously combined experimental appendix into topic-specific sections, expands selected related-work and RepInd explanations, and updates affiliation and publication text.

P2.justification: v2 adds consolidated benchmark tables and several new plots, expands Figure 7 into a comparison across models, and replaces the two-panel retain-loss figure with a Pareto scatter plot. The RepInd-cone figure is removed. Many other figures are identical apart from relocation, resizing, or numbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds an over-refusal literature paragraph and distinguishes its gradient-based discovery approach from concurrent independent-direction research by Pan et al. Additional benchmark references accompany the evaluations. The central positioning relative to Arditi et al. and representation engineering remains intact.

T1.justification: The refusal properties, cone definition, representational-independence criterion, and mathematical objectives are retained. v2's recursive notation for ablated activations explicitly describes the already specified intervention across layers; it does not introduce a different criterion, substantive derivation, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for generalization and complementary refusal mechanisms through additional benchmarks, evaluations across models, component ablations, and compositional interventions. These address v1's reliance on JailbreakBench and TruthfulQA for the main performance comparison and Gemma 2 2B for RepInd evidence. The gains outweigh the removed RepInd-cone analysis and weaker run reporting. Some reporting inconsistencies remain: for example, v2 Table 4 gives a 2.5-point TruthfulQA loss for Qwen 2.5 14B, while Table 1 implies 2.9.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RDO, refusal-cone, and representational-independence research. All 18 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison without material reading gaps.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark evaluations, loss ablations, compositional interventions, and over-refusal experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original jailbreak evaluations, TruthfulQA results, refusal-cone experiments, and analyses of independent directions and adversarial suffixes.

results.title: The Geometry of Refusal in Large Language Models: Concept Cones and Representational Independence

C1.justification: The two-mechanism, task-design and critical-learning-rate contributions remain. v2's introduction strengthens the empirical contribution from extracting scaling laws to explicitly claiming quantitative agreement with theoretical predictions within error bars. This refines the central validation claim without changing the research objective.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly cautions that the toy mechanisms are non-exhaustive and discusses transient, high-dimensional alternatives, refining v1's approximate-bound framing. It also drops v1's interpretation that adding a post-reaction period yields more efficient scaling, instead emphasizing agreement with theoretical ranges and changes in mechanism selection.

D1.justification: v2 adds extensive implementation and reproduction information: Euler updates, weighted MSE, optimizer settings, initialization, training schedules, parameter grids, hardware and figure-specific configurations (S3–S4). It states that code and model data are available through GitHub and Zenodo, replacing v1's release promise. Newly disclosed training details do not establish that previously unspecified settings changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate delayed activation, delayed cue discrimination with and without post-reaction periods, and a no-delay cue-response control. v2's larger time constant and expanded parameter sweeps concern model configurations within these retained tasks, rather than new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates additional external baseline methods. Slow-point and limit-cycle mechanisms remain the principal comparisons; LSTMs, GRUs, Transformers and newly discussed alternative approaches are cited rather than experimentally benchmarked.

E3.justification: The empirical evaluation pipeline changes substantially. v2 normalizes reaction reliability by total output, revises success/failure criteria and training-window definitions, and replaces modified-ReLU cutoff estimation with exponential-saturation or sigmoid fits (v1 S2 versus v2 S3.4). It also extends the plotted rank-2 delay sweep and adds experiments with tau = 20 ms.

E4.justification: v2 adds a time-constant robustness study (Fig. S5), mechanism-discrimination diagnostics and a direct empirical test of slow-point scaling (Fig. S3), and representative successful and failed trajectories (Fig. S4). The existing no-delay ablation gains a quantitative scaling analysis in Fig. S6; it is not a newly introduced task.

E5.justification: Rank-2 repetitions increase from 10 to 100 networks per condition (v1 Fig. 4C; v2 Fig. 3C). v2 also tabulates seed counts and newly specifies covariance-based Monte Carlo estimation of 95% confidence intervals. v1 already reports regression uncertainties and Fisher tests with Bonferroni correction, so statistical reporting is expanded rather than introduced.

E6.justification: Without/with post-reaction periods, v1 Fig. 6 reports slopes of -2.40 ± 0.36 and -1.57 ± 0.18; v2 Fig. 4 reports decay-exponent magnitudes of 2.72 ± 0.07 and 2.65 ± 0.23. v2 additionally reports slow-point scaling of 4.05 ± 0.10 and no-delay scaling of 0.38 ± 0.02. These are revised or added results under changed analyses and expanded experiments, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The RNN architectures and ghost/limit-cycle toy models are retained. However, the auxiliary mechanism-classification procedure changes from firing-rate dispersion (OM, v1 S2.2) to a spectral-power ratio computed from correlations of principal components (MDI, v2 S3.4.1). This revises an analysis component without replacing the central models.

P1.justification: The introduction and discussion are extensively rewritten around three explicit research questions, with machine-learning motivation moved forward from the discussion. The separate conclusion is absorbed into concluding remarks, results gain explanatory subheadings, and the appendix is reorganized into background, theory, experimental methods and reproduction sections.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout and substantially restructures the figures. Fig. 1 combines revised mechanism diagrams with task illustrations; Fig. 2 contracts from five cases to three; v1 Fig. 3 moves to Fig. S1; theoretical and empirical phase diagrams are consolidated into Fig. 4. New diagnostic/control panels and Table S1 further expand the presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted literature on activity-silent and synaptic memory, reservoir/transient dynamics, universal approximation and low-dimensional computation. These additions broaden context and qualify applicability while retaining the principal connections to earlier ghost-model, low-rank RNN and sequential-memory research.

T1.justification: The central ghost and limit-cycle derivations and scaling exponents are retained, moving from v1 S1 to v2 S2. Limited mathematical changes include the revised reliability definition and replacement of OM with the formally defined MDI (v2 Eqs. S37–S38); no new central scaling theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the connection between theory and evidence through direct slow-point scaling tests, mechanism diagnostics and a time-constant control. Its expanded methods and stated code/data access also address important reproducibility gaps in v1. Some inconsistent figure references and parameter descriptions in S4 limit reproducibility, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RNN short-term memory study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures and appendices are readable, allowing reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments with approximately 80,000 RNNs, including revised scaling analyses, mechanism diagnostics and additional control experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original toy-model simulations and experiments with over 35,000 RNNs, including mechanism distributions, scaling fits and a no-delay control.

results.title: Dynamical phases of short-term memory mechanisms in RNNs

C1.justification: Although v1 already describes GRADMM as privacy-preserving, v2 strengthens this into an explicit differential-privacy contribution. Its abstract and introduction now claim privacy guarantees alongside convergence and performance guarantees, and its conclusion emphasizes matching noisy target gradients. Readability and transferability claims are retained.

C2.justification: v2 interprets gradient alignment and distribution similarity as explanations for performance, distance histograms as evidence against copying, and membership-inference results as privacy evidence even without DP. It newly qualifies effectiveness as dependent on real-example diversity and hypothesizes that privacy noise can improve generalization when only five real examples are available.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, documents privacy parameters and attack procedures, and explains that synthetic examples are generated independently. The independent-generation remark is additional documentation rather than an established procedural change. Existing optimization settings, hardware information and Appendix B prompts are retained; repository contents cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Appendix D and Figure 7 extend the existing data-scarce sentiment-classification evaluation to IMDB and a reported Sentence polarity benchmark. Section 5.3 also adds an SST-2 membership-inference test. The PDFs do not clarify whether Sentence polarity represents distinct data from the retained Rotten tomatoes benchmark.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain zero-shot generation, few-shot generation, Herding, K-center and Random comparisons. Added diagnostics reuse existing comparators or real data; different privacy settings are variants of GRADMM rather than newly introduced comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds privacy-controlled evaluations using epsilon values 0.05, 4 and infinity, delta 0.0001 and clipping threshold 1, plus normalized-gradient, FID and nearest-example-distance measurements. Its new membership-inference protocol selects a threshold on 100 members and 100 non-members, then evaluates another balanced group. Existing fine-tuning budgets and checkpoint-selection rules remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Sections 5.3–5.4 and Appendix D add gradient-error trajectories, distribution matching measured by FID, nearest-training-example distance histograms, membership-inference attacks and privacy-budget sensitivity. These examine gradient alignment, representativeness, copying and privacy–utility tradeoffs. The original projection, last-layer and filtering ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v1 gives point accuracies without uncertainty or repeated-run information. v2 adds ± values throughout Table 1, shaded uncertainty bands in Figure 1, and membership-inference averages over 10 runs. Classification run counts and the meanings of the ± values and bands remain unspecified; an increase in runs for existing experiments is not established.

E6.justification: Table 1 and Figure 1 contain revised results and new private-GRADMM results. For example, five-example SST-2 accuracy changes from 87.0 to 86.5±0.5 for non-private GRADMM, with 84.2±0.1 newly reported for epsilon 0.05. v2 also adds privacy, FID, gradient and benchmark outcomes. Table 2 and the original ablation values remain unchanged. The revised Table 1 supports the text's 13.1-point maximum advantage, although its caption retains 10.4%.

M1.justification: New Section 4.5 extends GRADMM with per-example gradient clipping and Gaussian noise added to the averaged target gradient. Algorithm 1 incorporates privacy parameters into optimization. This changes the gradient-matching procedure, while retaining the ADMM updates, top-k projection and filtering.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted abstract, introduction and conclusion edits, inserts privacy and analysis subsections and Appendix D, and adds an impact statement and acknowledgements. It also updates affiliation and publication text and shortens some baseline explanations. Most existing prose and the overall narrative organization are retained.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains a privacy-setting column and uncertainty displays, and Figure 1 gains private-GRADMM curves and shaded bands. v2 adds the FID table and substantial new plots in Figures 2 and 7–10. Existing ablation tables, sample-text figures and prompt figures are retained with relocation or renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting differential privacy, noise calibration, membership inference, noise-related generalization and IMDB, while removing the Dubey et al. Llama reference. Section 2 also removes the blanket statement that dataset distillation preserves privacy. The broader positioning against existing text-distillation and generation approaches remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4.5 extends the formal scope to differential privacy, specifying piecewise noise calibration in epsilon and delta and invoking composition to claim an (epsilon, delta)-DP guarantee. The convergence assumptions, Lemma 4.1, Theorem 4.2, Corollary 4.3 and their Appendix A proofs remain unchanged; no separate privacy proof is added there.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's weakly supported privacy assurances by supplying an explicit clipping-and-noise mechanism, privacy settings and attack evaluations. New gradient and distribution analyses directly test important explanations for the method's effectiveness, while uncertainty reporting improves assessment of the main results. The privacy argument remains brief, statistical definitions are incomplete and Table 1 has a stale caption, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gain in evidential support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GRADMM, with matching core methods, experiments and appendices. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison; the convergence proofs, prompts and generated examples can be matched across renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds differential-privacy evaluations, membership-inference results, gradient and distribution analyses, and additional benchmark results.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments, cross-model transfer results, component ablations and generated-text examples in Section 5 and Appendix C.

results.title: Synthetic Text Generation for Training Large Language Models via Gradient Matching

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the demonstrated acceleration scope from models up to 1.1B on two datasets to models up to 2B with C4 included. The central sharpness ordering, Blockwise LR contribution, near-2× acceleration claim, and Adam-mini memory-saving claim remain intact.

C2.justification: Section 6.1 newly interprets widening performance gaps on MiniPile/OpenWebText and approximately parallel C4 curves as suggesting benefits may persist at larger scales. It also connects lower pre-training loss with downstream usefulness. Existing mechanism explanations and future-work limitations remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly supplies a project-code link and substantially expands reproducibility documentation: 2B/C4 architecture and learning-rate tables, the C4 tokenizer and token budget, Lion learning-rate/weight-decay tuning, and WSD timing. Original hardware and retained experiment settings remain documented; the additions principally specify the new experiments.

E1.justification: v2 adds C4 pre-training alongside OpenWebText and MiniPile. It also introduces downstream evaluations on ARC-E, ARC-C, PIQA, HellaSwag, OBQA, WinoGrande, and SCIQ, substantially extending coverage beyond pre-training loss and sharpness measurements.

E2.justification: Lion becomes an evaluated comparator in v2 Figure 7, which compares vanilla Lion with Lion using Blockwise LR. The existing AdamW and Adam-mini comparisons remain; the comparator expansion is limited to this additional optimizer.

E3.justification: Existing OpenWebText/MiniPile protocols are retained. New settings include a 2B model, C4 training with sequence length 256, batch size 512 and approximately 20 training tokens per parameter, and zero-shot downstream evaluation using lm-evaluation-harness. Appendix A.3 additionally specifies Lion tuning and a WSD schedule with a stable phase through 66.7% of training followed by decay to zero.

E4.justification: v2 adds an explicit comparison of benefits across model scales in Figure 5, optimizer/scheduler robustness experiments with Lion and WSD in Figure 7, and sharpness evolution under Lion in Figure 11. These substantially extend the original block ablations, ratio sensitivity, and layer/parameter analyses, which are retained.

E5.justification: v2 introduces no new seed information, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures. Additional performance results retain the existing point-result reporting approach.

E6.justification: v2 adds 2B and C4 loss results, Lion/WSD outcomes, and seven downstream comparisons. The new 2B panel reports a 2.31× speedup; new Table 1 reports WinoGrande scores of 55.17 for AdamW versus 59.83 for Blockwise LR. These are additional experiments, not revised v1 measurements. The original ablation values remain unchanged in v2 Table 2.

M1.justification: The block grouping, sharpness estimator, learning-rate adjustment rule, default ratios, and switch after warmup remain unchanged. Lion and WSD experiments apply the existing strategy without introducing a new Blockwise LR component or adjustment procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 expands Section 6.1, broadens the headings and content of Section 6.3 and Appendix A.3, adds an Impact Statement, removes the appendix contents list, and updates publication and affiliation text.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and references, extensively resizing and repositioning displays. It adds scaling, Lion/WSD, and Lion-sharpness figures plus downstream and C4 tables. Figure 4 replaces its duplicated 1.1B panel with a 2B panel; the 1.1B result remains in Figure 1.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Raffel et al. for C4/T5, Hoffmann et al. for compute-optimal training budgets, and Zhao et al.'s optimizer study for experimental settings. The positioning relative to earlier Hessian analyses and optimization methods remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, sharpness estimator, Theorems 4.1–4.3, and their complete Appendix B proofs are substantively unchanged. The new empirical scaling comparisons introduce no additional theorem or derivation.

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrated pre-training loss improvements without testing downstream usefulness or an alternative learning-rate schedule. v2 addresses these substantive validation gaps through seven downstream tasks and Lion/WSD experiments, while adding C4, larger-model evidence, and reproducibility information. These additions substantially strengthen evidence of practical utility and generality. Run-to-run uncertainty remains unreported, but the retained method, proofs, and original results are not weakened.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sharpness disparity principle and Blockwise LR method. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–B are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds larger-model and C4 results, downstream task evaluations, and Lion/WSD experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-2/LLaMA training results, sharpness measurements, block ablations, learning-rate sensitivity experiments, and Adam-mini comparisons.

results.title: The Sharpness Disparity Principle in Transformers for Accelerating Language Model Pre-Training

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the stated contribution from identifying mechanisms for rule induction in one Llama model to evidence across three reasoning tasks and multiple model families. V2 explicitly claims robust support in Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, and Llama-3.1, while qualifying the evidence for GPT-2.

C2.justification: V1 interprets token information in head outputs as approximate symbolism; v2 argues that invariant variables can nevertheless occupy subspaces. V2 also adds a binding account, separates local function-vector computation from aggregation, discusses scale dependence and task specialization, and proposes post-retrieval MLP transformations for non-identity relations.

D1.justification: V2 specifies bfloat16 loading, model-specific GPU use, patching before the head-output projection, detailed component and position choices, verbal-data generation and filtering, and probe splits. A named planned code/data repository replaces the generic release-on-acceptance promise; the PDF does not establish that release has occurred.
