E1.justification: V1 evaluates ABA/ABB identity rules. V2 adds successor/predecessor letter-string analogies and synonym/antonym verbal analogies (Appendix C.5). It also uses length-four rules AABA, ABCB, and ABCC to distinguish representational hypotheses (Appendix B.4), substantially extending task requirements.

E2.justification: Figure 5 adds random-head ablation alongside the retained control that ablates low-scoring heads in the same layers. Standard induction-head and function-vector comparisons remain, with an additional function-vector variant evaluated at in-context example positions (Table 1).

E3.justification: Reported causal-mediation sampling changes from 20 prompts to 100 per direction, 200 total; ablation sampling changes from 20 to 40 prompts. Figures 3–4 replace top-10 head selection with statistically significant heads. V2 also adds 13-model, 1–10-shot evaluation, task-specific analogy scoring, and token-disjoint probe splits.

E4.justification: V2 adds component-level RSA, a test distinguishing positional from previous-variable representations, position-specific function-vector analyses, random ablation controls, and within/between-task comparisons. Appendix C additionally tests MLP involvement, decoding on unseen tokens, and differences between correct and error trials. These substantially deepen tests of the proposed mechanism.

E5.justification: V2 introduces 5,000-permutation testing with family-wise error control for causal-mediation scores, replacing simple zero-clipping in Figure 2. It adds 95% binomial confidence intervals, standard deviations over 10 random-ablation runs, and significance tests for correlations and error analyses. The original four-seed prefix-matching procedure remains.

E6.justification: The reported two-shot identity-rule accuracy remains 95%, but symbolic-induction correlations change from 0.13 to 0.11 with standard induction scores and from 0.82 to 0.86 with function-vector scores. V2 adds extensive model and analogy results, plus decoding accuracies of 98.63% and 98.10% (Table 6). Revised existing measurements accompany changed analysis settings.

M1.justification: The core symbol-abstraction, symbolic-induction, and retrieval mechanism and causal-patching Algorithm 1 are retained. The new binding discussion and post-retrieval MLP account elaborate the interpretation of existing transformer components; they do not document a redesigned model or inference algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section order and much existing prose remain. V2 revises the abstract, introduction, and final discussion, clarifies causal-mediation explanations, adds a Binding subsection and Impact Statement, and extends the appendix organization. These are targeted narrative changes rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 redraws heatmaps, changes color scales and significance displays, and adds random-ablation curves with uncertainty bars. New patching schematics, model comparisons, analogy displays, and seven tables substantially expand the presentation. V1's appendix Figures 6–7 are retained as v2 Figures 10–11.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused connections to concept vectors, symbolic circuits in synthetic-task models, external-memory binding, and function-vector development. The central positioning relative to abstractors and emergent symbolic computation remains. Numerous other reference changes update publication metadata rather than introduce different works.

T1.justification: The context constructions and causal-mediation equations retain the same mathematical content. Neither version supplies a theorem or proof that is subsequently revised. The added binding discussion is conceptual, while permutation testing and representational hypotheses support empirical analyses.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's limited validation on one model and one simple task. Broader evaluations, controlled head selection, random ablations, token-disjoint decoding, and error analyses strengthen the central evidence. GPT-2 exceptions and task-specific differences also clarify applicability. Broad necessity claims remain stronger than the tested scope, but the empirical and reproducibility gains substantially improve overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and three-stage symbolic mechanism. The text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical analyses and reports additional model evaluations, analogy experiments, decoding results, and error analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original identity-rule task performance, causal interventions, attention analyses, representational similarity analyses, and ablations in Llama3-70B.

results.title: Emergent Symbolic Mechanisms Support Abstract Reasoning in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central claims about one-step recoverability, imitation learning, and generator/verifier training. Introduction contribution 3 expands the claimed empirical superiority from MBPP and HumanEval to include CodeContests, without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 refines the mechanism explanation around jointly using relabeling and both verifier scores, replacing v1's preference for learned-only relabeling over dataset concatenation. It attributes some RFT weaknesses to incorrect intermediate actions and missing successful trajectories, and interprets the POMDP experiment as evidence of feedback use. The stated conclusion limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the oracle/learned reward weights, K = 3 for RFTLV, and more explicit baseline training construction. Appendix C documents first-code-block parsing, revised prompts and sequence length, and CodeContests prompt/input-output examples. Existing hardware, other tabulated training hyperparameters, inference software, and code-access link are retained.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained MBPP and HumanEval tasks, v2 actually trains and evaluates on competitive-programming CodeContests. It also introduces MBPP (POMDP), removing sample tests from prompts to change the information available to the agent. These substantially expand task coverage and input conditions.

E2.justification: STaR/Multi-STaR largely match the renamed single-/multi-turn RFT baselines. However, v2 Table 2 adds RFT and learned-verifier-selected RFTLV to the relabeling comparison. The base-trained verifier comparator in v1 Figure 4 is removed from the corresponding inference-scaling experiment.

E3.justification: The reported generator sequence limit changes from 8192 to 4096, and the prompt changes from code-only output to requesting reasoning before code. Added protocols include six-turn evaluation after three-turn training, Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct, and CodeContests with 1000 training and 165 test problems. Appendix B.2 adds 35×/80× test expansions; MBPP+ also has 30% fewer problems.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the verifier-only relabeling study with a five-way comparison separating verifier choice from one-step relabeling. It adds a hidden-prompt-test control and evaluation beyond the training horizon to investigate feedback use. Conversely, the on-policy versus base-trained verifier analysis is removed. The BCE/BT comparison and qualitative example are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed counts, repeated-training-run statistics, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both retain the same multiple-sample evaluation description for the verifier-loss comparison; the additional results do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Main comparison scores and scaling curves are revised. For example, Table 1's 8B HumanEval BoN ranking changes from Multi-STaR 63.2 versus µCODE 62.2 to RFT 62.8 versus µCODE 63.8. v2 adds CodeContests, Qwen, and expanded-test results. These are not controlled across-version gains because methods/settings changed. v2 also inconsistently reports 1B HumanEval RFT BoN as 34.1 in Table 1 and 36.5 in Tables 2–3.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Equation 4 change expert-label selection from maximizing the learned verifier alone to maximizing R(x,y) + 0.1 Rϕ(x,y). This is a localized procedural refinement: v1's combined-verifier ablation concatenated separately relabeled datasets instead. The iterative framework, verifier losses, and inference procedure remain.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially rewritten and reorganized: setup/results are recast, analysis headings become research questions, verifier and feedback analyses change order, and the qualitative discussion receives its own subsection. The appendices are reorganized into proofs, additional results, and technical details. STaR terminology changes to RFT.

P2.justification: The relabeling bar chart is replaced by a structured ablation table; the feedback plot expands from two three-turn panels to three six-turn panels; and the scaling plot loses its comparator curve. Table 1 gains a CodeContests column, and two appendix result tables are added. The qualitative illustration is retained and relocated; the BCE/BT plot receives axis-layout refinements.

R1.justification: The distinct prior works and substantive related-work positioning are retained. The additional AlphaCode preprint entry corresponds to the already cited Science article. Renaming the rejection-finetuning baselines and changing citation suffixes do not establish a substantive positioning change.

T1.justification: Definition 3.1 changes A* ≤ 1 to −1 ≤ A* ≤ 0, with the corresponding correction in Appendix A.1. This supplies the absolute-magnitude bound needed by the proof's Hölder-inequality step. Theorem 3.2 and the remaining proof structure are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central mechanism: Table 2 separates relabeling from verifier choice, while Figure 2 tests feedback dependence by withholding prompt tests and extending the evaluation horizon. CodeContests, Qwen, and denser private tests address v1's narrow validation. The corrected advantage bound also repairs a specific proof assumption. These gains outweigh the removed verifier-training analysis, although reporting needs reconciliation: RFT scores disagree across tables, and Section 3.1 retains the old selection rule despite the updated Algorithm 1 and Equation 4.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same µCODE research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on MBPP, HumanEval, and CodeContests, plus feedback analyses and appendix results using Qwen and expanded private tests.

before.justification: v1 reports original µCODE experiments on MBPP and HumanEval, including baseline comparisons, verifier ablations, inference scaling, and a qualitative example.

results.title: Multi-Turn Code Generation Through Single-Step Rewards

C1.justification: Both versions retain the same central contributions: anchored bidirectional generation, the protein-conditioned RNA-BAnG architecture and favorable synthetic and RNA-generation comparisons. The conclusion's added 'during inference' clarifies an already established scope; the new experiments support rather than redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive boundaries concerning uncertain motif spacing, domain/IDR preprocessing and homology-based scoring of designed sequences. It replaces v1's geometric-attention nonconvergence assertion with an interpretation based on measured performance differences. It also qualifies presumed dissimilarity to RNAFLOW's training data instead of asserting zero similarity.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code/model release; v2 states that code and weights are available at a specified repository. v2 also adds DeepCLIP parameter-count and checkpoint-selection details, plus reproducible MAFFT/MOODS settings and motif-construction instructions. Existing model dimensions, training budgets and hardware disclosures remain.

E1.justification: Appendix B.4 adds DualBindMix and DualBindMix Random, requiring simultaneous motifs; its DualBind row matches the existing DoubleBind task. Domain/IDR-trimmed protein scenarios are also added. Biological training sources and the main 71-sample test set remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Corresponding generation comparisons retain autoregressive generation, iterative/IAnG variants, random sampling, GenerRNA and RNAFLOW. Newly used sequence-alignment and motif-search tools serve as evaluators, without changing the generation baseline sets.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends evaluation protocols with BLASTN similarity scoring and MAFFT/MOODS motif scoring, including sigmoid transformation and a separate 0.4 haRNA threshold. Added experiments test sequence lengths of 100, 200 and uniformly sampled 40–50 tokens, motif spacing, component removal and protein preprocessing. Existing main training and test settings are retained.

E4.justification: Appendices B.4 and F.2–F.5 add length and motif-spacing sensitivity tests, geometric-attention and cross-attention-position ablations, protein-preprocessing case studies and alternative-scoring checks. These substantially expand analysis beyond v1's threshold sensitivity, structural-confidence and training-similarity analyses, which are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix F.5 newly specifies Pearson correlation to quantify agreement between DeepCLIP and motif-based scoring. Existing diversity/novelty uncertainty summaries remain unchanged, and no repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their values, but substantial results are added. Table B.3 reports both-motif proportions of 0.97 with fixed spacing and 0.05 with random spacing. Appendix F.5 reports motif-scoring areas of 0.49 for RNA-BAnG and 0.40 for random generation, with cross-scorer correlation 0.64. Additional results include comparator performance curves, ablations and preprocessing outcomes.

M1.justification: The described two-anchor generation procedure, attention architecture and two-stage training objective remain unchanged. Component removal and protein preprocessing appear as additional experiments, without replacing the proposed model or its standard inference procedure.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites expand the generation explanation, condense tokenization details and reorganize the evaluation-protocol discussion. Appendix F gains descriptive subsections, and an Impact Statement is added. The main narrative and section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables B.2–B.3 and Figures F.1 and F.4–F.8 for the expanded analyses. It merges the two architecture diagrams into Figure A.1, redraws Figure 1 and relocates several displays. The original per-sample score distributions are retained as Figures G.1–G.2 rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for MAFFT, MOODS and position-weight-matrix background: Katoh and Standley, Korhonen et al., Stormo et al., and Schneider and Stephens. The broader positioning against existing RNA-generation methods remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 1 introduces separate left/right lengths and explicit conditioning contexts. Their indices are not equivalent to v1: the first left token now conditions on x1 as well as x0, although Figure 2 generates x1 later. This introduces a local inconsistency with the retained generation order. Algorithm A.1 is unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through component ablations, alternative scoring that checks reliance on DeepCLIP, and stress tests exposing a multi-motif failure boundary. Reported code/weights availability also improves reproducibility. These gains address important evidential gaps in v1 and outweigh the localized conditioning-index inconsistency introduced in Equation 1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BAnG/RNA-BAnG work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds synthetic stress tests, component ablations, preprocessing case studies and alternative scoring analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic generation experiments and protein-conditioned RNA evaluations, including baseline comparisons, diversity and novelty results.

results.title: BAnG: Bidirectional Anchored Generation for Conditional RNA Design

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the reported validation claim from 46 simulated environments to 48 simulated environments and two real-robot tasks. Criticism of existing acceleration methods becomes more qualified. The central training-free, solver-compatible, multimodality-preserving acceleration claims and headline 2-7x range remain.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the matched-step comparison as evidence of benefits in low-step regimes and the robot/RDT experiments as evidence of broader practical applicability. It also interprets Consistency Policy's PushT trajectory bias as mode collapse. The existing smooth-versus-complex motion explanation and limitation requiring task-specific parameter tuning remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A and the new experiment captions add robot and camera specifications, training budgets, demonstration counts, horizon/buffer settings, and implementation or checkpoint locations, including sources for retained experiments. Some earlier Kitchen dataset details are omitted. Reproducibility remains imperfect: Table 5 specifies 37 grasping demonstrations, whereas Appendix A states 50 for each robot task.

E1.justification: V2 adds physical-robot dexterous grasping and square-stick insertion, ManiSkill2 PickCube and PushCube evaluations, and a symmetric PushT multimodality scenario. The earlier RoboMimic, Kitchen, BlockPush, and MetaWorld coverage remains, including results moved into Appendix E.

E2.justification: SDP(DDPM), previously discussed without reported comparisons, is evaluated in RoboMimic and the new robot experiments. Consistency Policy becomes a directly evaluated comparator in PushT Figure 3. The RDT experiment also compares DPMSolver++ with and without Falcon. Earlier comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds a comparison matching reduced-step DPMSolver's sampling budget to Falcon, measured runtime and CPU/GPU-memory evaluations, and a five-step DPMSolver++ configuration for RDT. Reported DDIM+Falcon thresholds also change: Transport ph from 0.005 to 0.001 and ToolHang ph from 0.01 to 0.003 (v1 Table 9; v2 Table 10). These are setting revisions, not merely additional disclosure.

E4.justification: V2 adds a matched-step control testing whether Falcon's advantage exceeds simply reducing solver steps, a PushT trajectory-diversity comparison with Consistency Policy, and threshold sweeps on Transport ph and ToolHang ph in Appendix E.2. The original threshold, exploration, selection-mechanism, BlockPush, and starting-point analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V2 specifies 20 rollouts for the new robot comparisons and 20 sampled trajectories for PushT. Conversely, the retained BlockPush multimodality result loses v1 Section 4.5's explicit 200-episode description. Mean-and-standard-deviation reporting and MetaWorld's 50-seed information remain; no new confidence intervals or significance tests appear.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial comparative, robot, RDT, and ablation results. Robot Tables 5-6 report Falcon matching DDPM's 100% and 90% success with 3.07x and 2.86x runtime speedups. Existing DDIM+Falcon Transport ph success changes from 0.74 to 0.81 while speedup falls from 1.71x to 1.57x; ToolHang ph changes from 0.51 to 0.54 and 1.92x to 1.61x. These accompany revised thresholds, so they are replaced-setting results. Kitchen, BlockPush, and MetaWorld results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Reference actions, one-step estimation, threshold-based selection, latent-buffer management, exploration, and partial denoising remain unchanged. Algorithms 1-3 retain the same procedures. Applying Falcon to RDT introduces another evaluated model, without a documented change to Falcon's algorithm.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: detailed environment descriptions move to Appendix A, Kitchen analysis moves to E.3, and BlockPush multimodality material is consolidated in E.4 while PushT takes its main-text role. The abstract, introductory comparison paragraphs, and preliminary explanations are revised, with corresponding appendix restructuring.

P2.justification: V2 adds PushT trajectories, robot execution sequences and hardware images, RDT demonstrations, supplementary threshold plots, and comparison tables. The original three-part ablation figure is split into Figures 4 and 7, and Kitchen/BlockPush displays move to the appendix. These substantially change the visual presentation beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including ManiSkill2, IBC, 3D Diffuser Actor, progressive distillation, and PFDiff. It corrects the ManiCM attribution, clarifies Consistency Policy's relationship to consistency trajectory models, and expands discussion of SDP's schedules and memory requirements. Falcon's overall positioning as a training-free alternative remains.

T1.justification: Proposition 3.1, Remark 3.2, and the solver derivations retain their mathematical content. V2's new Equation 6 displays the posterior expectation already defined in v1's prose, and Equation 4 rewrites the same loss equivalently. No substantive assumptions, proofs, or theoretical results are added.

improvement.justification: V1's practical acceleration evidence relies on simulation and NFE as a timing proxy. V2 substantially strengthens this foundation with physical-robot latency measurements, direct SDP comparisons, and a matched-step DPMSolver control addressing whether fewer solver steps alone explain the benefit. RDT evaluations broaden the demonstrated applicability. New reporting inconsistencies, particularly the 37-versus-50 demonstration counts and the grasping CPU-memory mismatch between prose and Table 5, limit reproducibility but do not outweigh these substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Falcon. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and the methods, equations, tables, and figures can be matched despite substantial additions and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains original simulation results and adds physical-robot experiments, RDT evaluations, baseline comparisons, and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation evaluations, success rates, computational costs, multimodality analyses, and ablations, including detailed MetaWorld results in Appendix C.

results.title: Falcon: Fast Visuomotor Policies via Partial Denoising

C1.justification: The abstract and three introductory contributions retain their meaning. V2 extends the concluding account to Pokémon and changes iterative reward refinement from a future possibility into a claimed demonstrated reduction of out-of-distribution errors. It also removes the introduction's blanket assertion that prior approaches fail to transfer knowledge to novel states.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's occlusion and initial-data limitations, v2 explains how unseen regions undermine semantic rewards and leave exploration dependent on uncertainty. It interprets Pokémon behavior as influenced by the Brock-specific prompt, favoring Squirtle training over collection diversity, and explains refinement as correcting that distributional limitation. These materially expand the account of applicability and behavioral tradeoffs.

D1.justification: V2 explicitly provides a code-and-VLM-MOTIF-checkpoint link and documents Pokémon implementation details, including PokeGym version, observations, actions, frame skipping, reward modifications, starting checkpoint, hyperparameters, and annotation prompts. It also specifies the additional annotation data and continuation procedure. Most existing implementation and computational-cost disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds Pokémon Red, covering navigation, battles, Pokémon collection, and progress toward the first Gym. It retains MiniHack and Robodesk and adds the half-open-drawer task used in Robodesk downstream evaluation. This substantially broadens the evaluated environments and task requirements.

E2.justification: The original comparison sets are retained. V2 adds a from-scratch DreamerV3 control for Robodesk block-pushing (Figure 22) and evaluates a task-reward-augmented Plan2Explore comparator in Pokémon Red. These are limited extensions of existing comparator families.

E3.justification: New protocols include 750k-step Pokémon comparisons with extrinsic rewards, a large RSSM, scheduled episode lengths, and map/battle metrics. Robodesk downstream evaluation uses models pretrained through 1M exploration steps. The refinement study adds 50k annotated pairs and 200 continuation episodes with original-reward and longer-running Plan2Explore controls. These additions do not establish reruns of the retained experiments.

E4.justification: V2 retains the original ablations and adds substantial Pokémon analyses: exploration allocation across catching, leveling, and navigation (E.8), concrete reward failures in unseen locations, and a controlled continuation examining reward refinement versus longer training (E.9; Figures 26–27). These investigate additional mechanisms and failure conditions.

E5.justification: V2 adds explicit five-seed reporting for Pokémon and ten-seed reporting for Robodesk downstream learning. It also identifies the refinement demonstration as one continued SENSEI seed with a selected Plan2Explore seed, without aggregate uncertainty. Existing experiments retain their seed counts and standard-error or standard-deviation conventions; no increased replication of those experiments is established.

E6.justification: V2 adds Robodesk learning curves showing faster learning with SENSEI-pretrained models, with incomplete success on Lift-Ball (Figure 21). Pokémon results show stronger navigation and leveling, but greater catching diversity for Plan2Explore. The single-seed refinement study reports two Gym victories, first occurring around 1.8M steps. These are new results under added settings, not improvements to the retained MiniHack or Robodesk exploration scores.

M1.justification: V2 substantially extends the fixed, task-free pipeline with task-conditioned VLM comparisons and extrinsic-reward integration (Section 4.4; Appendices A.1 and D.4). It also implements a second annotation and distillation round using SENSEI-collected observations (E.9), which v1 only suggested as future work. The underlying RSSM, distillation architecture, and switching mechanism remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 locally condenses the introduction, related work, captions, and discussion while retaining most existing prose and the main section sequence. Prompting becomes Appendix D, extended results move to E, and computation becomes F. These are limited editorial and organizational changes alongside the added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual presentation with Pokémon maps, screenshots, progress plots, distributions, refinement comparisons, and Robodesk downstream curves. Figure 4 gains a Pokémon trajectory, Figure 7 becomes narrower, the hyperparameter table gains a Pokémon column, and the previously separate left-camera illustration is merged into Figure 9. Existing analyses are also relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds Pokémon-related references to Pleines et al., Suarez, and Whidden, and positions its screen-only observations against previous Pokémon agents (C.3). It narrows the introductory criticism of prior methods' transfer capabilities. The broader positioning relative to MOTIF, Plan2Explore, and RL-VLM-F remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 revises the mathematical reward definition in Equation 8 by adding an extrinsic-reward term controlled by chi, distinguishing task-free and task-based exploration. The existing dynamics and switching equations remain unchanged; neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important evidential gap: downstream usefulness, previously demonstrated only in MiniHack, is now tested across robotic tasks with ten-seed results (Figure 21). Pokémon evaluations and explicit reward-failure analyses further strengthen understanding of the method's capabilities and limits, alongside improved reproducibility documentation. The goal-specific Pokémon prompt and single-seed refinement success constrain generalization, but the broader controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SENSEI research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and reports additional Pokémon Red evaluations, Robodesk downstream learning, and second-generation reward-refinement results.

before.justification: V1 reports original MiniHack and Robodesk experiments, downstream task learning, and ablations of semantic rewards, annotation sources, and exploration weighting.

results.title: SENSEI: Semantic Exploration Guided by Foundation Models to Learn Versatile World Models

C1.justification: The six stated contributions and headline claims remain. The abstract qualifies the earlier suggestion that symmetry is unaccounted for to being often inadequately addressed. Section 3.1.4 adds a 24% S.U.N. advantage claim for the new large-sample comparison and removes the claim that WyFormer alone demonstrated generation up to 52 atoms per unit cell.

C2.justification: v3 Appendix H.1 adds a substantive qualification about comparing stability scores obtained with different DFT workflows. The earlier warning that Materials Project relaxation settings are too coarse is removed, and nonconvergence is described as instability for S.U.N. accounting rather than proof of unrealistic structures. The central entropy, novelty and stoichiometry limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-access link, generation/training/forward-pass pseudocode, Spglib preprocessing information, VASP version and workflow identifiers, and an identifiable DFT hull file. Appendix E expands timing details and discloses disabling atom-type inference in the DiffCSP++ integration. Existing model hyperparameter lists are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use MP-20, its binary/ternary subset, MPTS-52, AFLOW and 3DSC for the same generation and property-prediction tasks. The larger DFT sample and new ablations remain within this coverage.

E2.justification: SymmCD changes from a cited work in v1 to an evaluated comparator in v3 Tables 1, 2 and 7. Table 12 also introduces a letter-based WyFormer generation control. The established external generators, property predictors and WyLLM comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v3 replaces the stated custom high-precision DFT workflow with a Materials Project double-relaxation/static workflow and changes the DFT reference hull. It adds a 10,000-structure evaluation with CHGNet pre-relaxation, a zero-meV stability threshold and train-only novelty reference, alongside the 105-structure evaluation. It also compares single versus double relaxation and specifies uniform 1,000-structure subsampling for Table 7 COV-P.

E4.justification: v3 adds a generation ablation comparing Wyckoff letters with site symmetry plus enumeration, tests the previously proposed harmonic-cluster generator, analyzes energy variability across random initializations, and evaluates sensitivity to DFT workflow. These substantially extend v1's retained property-encoding, LLM and diversity analyses.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 8 newly reports energy standard deviations across six pyXtal initializations for 1,000 representations, including a mean standard deviation of 0.14 eV/atom. Six initializations were already specified in v1; this is new variability reporting, not an increased run count. The p = 0.1 significance convention is retained.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises the 105-structure S.U.N. rates, including WyFormer/CHGNet from 6.9% to 23.1% and WyFormerDiffCSP++ from 12.8% to 22.2%, under revised DFT settings. v3 adds 10,000-structure S.U.N. results of 3.83% and 4.14% for different relaxation protocols, SymmCD and ablation results, and WyLLM stability scores. Table 7 also revises COV-P values; Tables 3–4 property-prediction scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The Transformer architecture, element/site-symmetry/enumeration representation, autoregressive cascade, augmentation and structure-generation routes are retained. The new pseudocode documents the existing procedure. Harmonic-cluster generation was already proposed in v1 Appendix P; v3 adds its evaluation.

P1.justification: Method exposition is substantially expanded and reorganized: spherical harmonics move from an appendix into Section 2.1.1, tokenization explanations are rewritten, and Appendix B expands into three algorithms. The abstract, evaluation narrative, DFT description and inference-speed discussion are also revised, beyond routine copyediting.

P2.justification: The tokenization diagram is redrawn, and the training diagram is redesigned and moved into the main text. v3 adds a generation flowchart, initialization-variability histogram and Wyckoff-position comparison display. Table 1 gains explicit protocol columns, Table 11 gains stability columns, and a generation-ablation table is added. Many earlier plots are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: The principal positioning against diffusion models and earlier Wyckoff representations is retained. v3 adds references concerning spherical-harmonic descriptors, Wyckoff augmentation, Spglib, atomate2, pymatgen and Matbench Discovery, while removing Dudarev and Monkhorst–Pack citations associated with the old DFT description. The MatterGen publication update refers to the same work.

T1.justification: The harmonic-descriptor formula is corrected between v1 Appendix C and v3 Section 2.1.1: v1 repeats h^(1) and takes an imaginary part after a real-part operation, whereas v3 concatenates real and imaginary parts using both h^(1) and h^(2). The remaining harmonic derivation is largely relocated, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's central stability comparison relied on 105 structures per method and explicitly could not distinguish leading models. v3 substantially strengthens evaluation through the larger DFT study, explicit protocol-comparability analysis, SymmCD comparison and direct generation ablations. Code-access information and expanded procedural documentation also improve reproducibility. Reporting remains imperfect—Table 6 retains old S.U.N. rates despite Table 1's revisions, and several cross-references are incorrect—but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WyFormer study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds a 10,000-structure DFT evaluation, SymmCD comparisons, generation ablations and initialization-variability measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original crystal-generation and property-prediction experiments, with additional timing, representation-ablation, LLM and token analyses in the appendices.

results.title: Wyckoff Transformer: Generation of Symmetric Crystals

C1.justification: The abstract's opening problem statement narrows from positive semidefinite to positive definite matrices. The principal contributions—memory-constrained determinant computation, determinant scaling laws, FLODANCE extrapolation, and the approximately 100,000-fold speedup claim—remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: New discussion interprets numerical discrepancies as arising from input-matrix precision, explains the fitting-window cost/accuracy tradeoff, and discusses robustness and applicability beyond NTKs. The earlier assertion that large-scale double-precision computation is infeasible is replaced by a reported feasible computation. Existing burn-in and numerical-conditioning caveats remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 substantially clarifies the precision pipeline: 32-bit network training, separate NTK formation/storage precisions, and 64-bit determinant calculations across methods. v2 also documents the GH200 computation and its 244-hour duration, Matérn construction parameters, and how LDL permutations and diagonal outputs feed FLODANCE. Existing detkit and imate access information is retained.

E1.justification: Appendix G.2 adds one synthetic spatial Gaussian-process setting using a multi-output Matérn kernel: 10,000 two-dimensional locations with ten outputs each. Existing CIFAR-10 and MNIST coverage remains. This extends evaluation beyond neural kernels without changing the determinant-estimation task.

E2.justification: New Appendix E.5 explicitly evaluates MEMDET against NumPy's slogdet and eigh, including Table E.4 and Figure E.4. The main approximation comparator set—SLQ, block diagonal, pseudo-NTK, and direct computations at different precisions—is retained.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 replaces the stated 32-bit large-scale NTK reference with 64-bit matrices. Table 2 changes from normalized log-determinant estimates to percentage relative errors with unnormalized reference values. Added experiments introduce random-subsampling, fitting-window, block-count, and Matérn-kernel protocols; the newly disclosed precision pipeline is separately a documentation change.

E4.justification: v2 adds numerical agreement and block-count stability checks for MEMDET in Appendix E.5, plus FLODANCE sensitivity to random subsampling and fitting-window size in Figures G.2–G.3. These substantially extend validation beyond v1's runtime/memory analysis and global-fit demonstration. The latter is retained as Figure G.1 from v1 Figure H.1.

E5.justification: Figure G.2 introduces uncertainty analysis across 15 independent subsamples, reporting ensemble means, standard deviations, normalized standard deviations, and prediction-error variability. Existing reporting across five trained networks and ten profiling repetitions remains; these counts are not reported as increased.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces numerical results and changes rankings: pseudo-NTK is closest for ResNet18 in v1, whereas v2 reports 122.95% error for pseudo-NTK and 2.9% for the best FLODANCE configuration. Figure 5's ResNet9 endpoint error changes from 0.05% to 0.2% alongside the reference-precision change, so this is not a same-setting deterioration. Table 1 revises MEMDET from 8.8 days/$364 to 13.8 days/$601. Additional accuracy, sensitivity, Matérn, and runtime results are reported.

M1.justification: FLODANCE Algorithm 1 and MEMDET's LU, LDL, and Cholesky algorithms retain their computational steps; Algorithms C.1–C.3 become D.1–D.3. Expanded precision and permutation explanations and application to another kernel do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and argument remain intact, with targeted introductory, notation, derivation, and implementation rewrites. Appendices are consolidated: MEMDET implementation and ordering are grouped in D, and scaling-law background, proofs, and parameterization in F. A nomenclature section and expanded appendix roadmap improve navigation.

P2.justification: v2 adds notation, accuracy, complexity, and runtime tables, together with new numerical-stability, sensitivity, and Matérn figures. Table 2 is restructured around relative errors, and Figure 5 has revised curves, axes, and precision labeling. The earlier global-fit figure moves from H.1 to G.1 with updated plots; existing algorithm diagrams are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds NTK-related references including Hodgkinson et al. (2025) and Wilson et al. (2025), and spatial-statistics references supporting the Matérn experiment. The numerical-linear-algebra positioning remains largely unchanged. Publication updates for existing works, such as Bahri et al. and Barzilai and Shamir, are not new citations.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 corrects the covariance kernel's codomain from scalar to matrix-valued, and the Lemma 1 proof corrects the cross-covariance block dimension to (n−1)d by d. Table H.1 adds comparative complexity formulas. The central assumptions, lemma, LLN/CLT proposition, and substantive proof arguments remain.

improvement.justification: v1's flagship large-scale experiment used 32-bit matrices despite emphasizing precision problems. v2 supplies 64-bit references and independent numerical checks, addressing an important weakness in the accuracy evidence. Subsampling and fitting-window tests, non-neural kernel evaluation, and clearer precision documentation substantially strengthen reliability and applicability. Some new summaries overstate their evidence—for example, Appendix E.5's stated error range excludes the 1.7×10−6 MobileNet entry in Table E.4—but these reporting defects do not outweigh the validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MEMDET and FLODANCE research. All 30 pages of v1 and 38 pages of v2, including appendices, equations, tables, and figures, support comparison. Relocated algorithms, proofs, and analyses can be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original NTK experiments and adds numerical accuracy checks, subsampling and fitting-window analyses, Matérn-kernel experiments, and runtime comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original NTK determinant experiments on CIFAR-10 and MNIST, approximation comparisons, and empirical memory and runtime measurements in Appendix E.

results.title: Determinant Estimation under Memory Constraints and Neural Scaling Laws

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: fully Bayesian tree-kernel inference, efficient sampling, explicit predictive uncertainty and competitive Bayesian optimization. The added introductory motivation does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies wall-time as BARK's main limitation and recommends alternatives for cheap or fast evaluations, extending v1's narrower sampling-cost discussion. It replaces the explanation that GP-RBF performs worse under continuous relaxation with a more qualified competitiveness statement. New discussions explain nonstationarity, categorical correlations and settings favoring smooth GP kernels.

D1.justification: v2 names BoTorch's optimize_acqf_mixed_alternating routine and newly explains that the unchanged BART grid size was chosen to match BARK's optimization wall-time. Hardware, software versions, code access, sampling settings and solver parameters remain. The new parameter-summary table consolidates previously stated values.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original datasets and tasks, adding smooth continuous optimization benchmarks, Hartmann (6D) and Styblinski-Tang (10D), and continuous, ordered-discrete and categorical toy regression examples. These extend the existing regression and optimization coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds GP-RBF to the retained four-dataset regression comparison through Table 7 and compares alternating and enumerated GP-RBF variants together on XGBoostMNIST in Figure 6. The other main BO comparator families remain.

E3.justification: The reported GP-RBF optimization protocol changes substantially: v1 uses continuous relaxation with one-hot categorical encoding when enumeration is infeasible; v2 uses alternating continuous optimization and discrete local perturbations. This affects central benchmark comparisons. v2 also adds per-iteration fitting, acquisition-optimization and total-time measurements; the existing BO initialization and iteration budgets remain.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds diagnostic experiments examining nonstationary function modeling and predictions for unseen categories. Section 7.4 and Appendix F.2 substantially extend the earlier posterior-sampling timing comparison to BO fitting and optimization costs across methods and benchmarks. Existing depth-prior, sample-count and kernel-approximation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions already report BO medians and interquartile ranges across 20 runs, regression means and standard deviations, and the same sensitivity-study run counts. v2's expanded Figure 5 caption restates existing uncertainty reporting; added result rows do not introduce a new statistical procedure.

E6.justification: Figures 5–6 replace GP-RBF results under the revised optimizer, putting it ahead of BARK on DiscreteAckley, DiscreteRosenbrock and CCOBench; these are not same-protocol gains. v2 adds continuous-benchmark, toy-regression and runtime results, plus GP-RBF regression scores—for example, Student Performance MSE 1.00 versus BARK's retained 0.73. Original Table 1 and posterior-sampling timing values are unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed BARK procedure is unchanged: forest-agreement kernels, MCMC inference, marginalization over leaf values, domain-uniform splits, low-rank updates and integrated-UCB optimization remain. Added explanations and the revised GP-RBF baseline optimizer do not change BARK.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are preserved. v2 adds introductory motivation, targeted experimental explanations, a wall-time subsection and an impact statement, while expanding and reorganizing appendix headings. This is a limited narrative revision rather than an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial displays: toy-regression and continuous-BO figures, runtime panels, a related-work matrix, a parameter-summary table and a GP-RBF regression table. The XGBoostMNIST runtime panels appear in both the main text and appendix. Figure 1 is enlarged, Figures 5–6 receive layout and legend changes, and existing appendix figures are relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds Wan et al. (2021) when discussing alternating optimization and Surjanovic and Bingham (2013) for the continuous benchmarks. New Table 2 systematically compares largely previously cited methods by surrogate, optimizer and domain support, refining rather than redefining BARK's research positioning.

T1.justification: The kernel equations, computational derivations, posterior-sampling ratios, Laplace-limit proof, approximation-failure argument and optimization formulation are retained. v1 Appendices E–G correspond to v2 Appendices H–J; their relocation does not add theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the central empirical comparison with a more capable mixed-space GP-RBF optimizer, GP regression comparisons and smooth-function tests. New runtime evidence and explicit applicability limits make the performance claims more balanced and practically informative. These address important weaknesses in evaluating BARK's advantages and costs. Table 7's mistaken BART caption, despite clearly labeled BARK columns, is a limited clarity defect against these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BARK research. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables and figures; relocated material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds toy regression experiments, continuous optimization benchmarks, GP-RBF regression comparisons and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original regression results, synthetic and applied Bayesian optimization experiments, posterior-sampling timings and sensitivity analyses.

results.title: BARK: A Fully Bayesian Tree Kernel for Black-box Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: language-guided cross-domain forecasting, TCP-based alignment, TimePPO mitigation of autoregressive error, and strong benchmark and zero-shot performance. Added evidence does not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation: it links final-step accuracy to sequence-wide return optimization, attributes GPT-2's shortfall to instruction following, and explains output-length and masking trade-offs. It also argues for applicability with limited fine-tuning data and TE-only updates. These mechanism and applicability discussions were absent from v1.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 supplies exact instruction and background paraphrases for the new prompt tests. Figure 8 newly discloses attention softmax renormalization after hiding system and special tokens, and Table 1 changes the source attribution for borrowed results from TimesNet to iTransformer. Existing hardware, optimizer, principal hyperparameters, and code-access information remain.

E1.justification: The same nine datasets remain represented. Appendix C.1 extends zero-shot evaluation beyond Traffic and Illness to held-out Weather, Electricity, and ETT targets. This broadens the tested domain-transfer scenarios without introducing a new dataset family.

E2.justification: v2 adds TimesFM as an evaluated external comparator in Table 14. The comparator sets in the original main benchmark and Traffic/Illness zero-shot comparison remain unchanged. iTransformer becomes a cited source of baseline results, rather than an additional evaluated method.

E3.justification: The original benchmark settings remain, but v2 adds restricted-source pre-training protocols, backbone and prompt controls, final-segment error metrics, 5–20% fine-tuning data conditions, component-freezing experiments, and mask-rate/output-length grids. These substantially extend evaluation design. One new transfer protocol is inconsistently documented: Appendix C.1 names ETTh2, whereas Table 13 labels ETTm2.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained TCP/reward ablations and alpha/tau analyses, v2 tests GPT-2 and linear backbones, prompt paraphrases, beta/eta sensitivity, and final-step error accumulation. Appendix C adds transfer analyses, fine-tuning data-volume and component controls, and joint masking/output-length sensitivity. These address several previously untested questions about mechanism, robustness, and adaptability.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty intervals. Reported averages aggregate forecasting horizons; the additional experiments do not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial numerical evidence in Tables 5–6, 8, and 13–17 and Figure 6. Original benchmark scores and retained appendix results are unchanged. Table 1 revises several win counts: fine-tuned LangTime changes from 49 in v1's table and 50 in its accompanying prose to 45 in both locations in v2.

M1.justification: The architecture, TCPs, and repeat-based TimePPO procedure remain. However, Equation (8) changes the maximized objective from adding a squared-error term to subtracting the Huber prediction loss. This substantively revises the stated alignment penalty, although the PDFs do not establish whether implementation or training runs changed.

P1.justification: There are targeted rewrites of the introduction and model-analysis explanations, expanded captions, and new acknowledgements and an impact statement. Appendix B gains ablation details, while new Appendix C subsections precede the retained full results and cases. The original narrative and main section order largely remain.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn to separate temporal extraction, multitask pre-training, and TimePPO fine-tuning. v2 adds nine tables and a beta/eta sensitivity figure, expands explanatory captions, and rearranges the experimental displays. Existing detailed result tables and forecasting cases are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for TimesFM, Chronos, GPT-2, linear forecasting, iTransformer, and additional forecasting research. Appendix C.1 adds positioning against large-scale time-series foundation models. Section 2's central account of prior alignment methods and RLHF remains essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 corrects the small-error branches of both Huber definitions by restoring squared residuals in Equations (9)–(10). Equation (8) also corrects the penalty direction under maximization. These are limited mathematical corrections; no new theorem, proof, or formal guarantee appears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the roles of the LLM backbone and TimePPO through backbone controls, final-step error evaluation, and additional transfer and fine-tuning studies absent from v1. Correcting the maximized objective's penalty sign and the Huber formulas also improves mathematical consistency. These gains outweigh the new ETTh2/ETTm2 labeling inconsistency, although neither version quantifies run-to-run uncertainty.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LangTime and TimePPO. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete Appendices A–C support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds backbone controls, prompt-variation experiments, error analyses, transfer comparisons, and fine-tuning sensitivity studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments, fine-tuning comparisons, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and zero-shot evaluations on Traffic and Illness.

results.title: LangTime: A Language-Guided Unified Model for Time Series Forecasting with Proximal Policy Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: approximate continuous MEC through cooperating diffusion models, avoidance of prescribed cross-domain geometric costs, bidirectional generation, and effectiveness in alignment and translation. The expanded experiments primarily support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 attributes CelebA-HQ performance partly to its larger training set and interprets guidance as balancing fidelity with mutual-information maximization. These extend v1's general quality–fidelity discussion. The single-cell interpretation also now emphasizes consistency across PBMC and BM.

D1.justification: v2 adds a stated public source-code location, PBMC/BM preprocessing and training details, and CelebA-HQ pretrained-model sources and hyperparameters. Conversely, v1's layer-by-layer SNARE-seq MLP table and specific 2,000-step pretraining/350-step conditional-training recipe disappear rather than moving with the retained experiment.

E1.justification: v2 adds PBMC RNA–ATAC alignment, bone-marrow RNA–protein alignment, and CelebA-HQ male/female image translation, extending biological populations, modality combinations, and image domains. SNARE-seq remains in Appendix B.1, and AFHQ coverage is retained.

E2.justification: scTopoGAN is newly included in the PBMC/BM comparisons in Table 1. InfoOT remains in the relocated SNARE-seq comparison. Existing image comparators are retained; their extension to CelebA-HQ does not introduce additional comparison methods.

E3.justification: The added PBMC/BM experiments introduce 50-dimensional embeddings, k=5 cell-type/subtype evaluation, and settings including 100,000 pretraining steps, T=1000, and batch size 256. Image evaluation adds 100-step sampling alongside 50 steps and additional guidance settings. These are new protocols, not evidence that retained SNARE-seq experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's two reported guidance settings, v2 adds a focused CelebA-HQ guidance sweep from 1.5 to 7 at 50 and 100 sampling steps in Figure 8a. This examines the FID–SSIM trade-off, while Table 2 additionally tests sampling-budget sensitivity.

E5.justification: Both versions report five seeds for image results and one training run followed by five inference seeds for single-cell experiments. New mean± entries extend an existing reporting practice; no increased run count, new uncertainty estimator, or significance-testing procedure is stated.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include PBMC cell/subtype accuracies of 66.3/46.0 and CelebA-HQ FID/SSIM of 40.73/0.593 at 50 steps with guidance 2.5. Table 2 also adds 100-step results. SNARE-seq scores and existing 50-step AFHQ scores are retained up to rounding; the additions are not same-setting performance improvements between versions.

M1.justification: The cooperative two-DDPM method remains. However, Equation 11 changes the regularized denoiser's input from y=empty to y. Appendix A.3 also introduces nearest-neighbor projection within PBMC/BM training, whereas v1 describes nearest-neighbor matching for evaluation. These are limited procedural adaptations.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the single-cell experimental account, moves SNARE-seq into Appendix B.1, reorganizes Appendix A, and adds acknowledgments and a revised impact statement. The main section sequence and most introductory, methodological, and concluding prose remain intact.

Table 2 gains dataset and sampling-budget subdivisions, and the hyperparameter table gains a CelebA-HQ column. SNARE-seq displays move to the appendix with rearranged panels, while the detailed MLP table is removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations and discussion for scTopoGAN, CITE-seq, and CelebA-HQ. The central positioning relative to discrete MEC, optimal transport, and diffusion-based translation remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds Equations 12–18 deriving the conditional-model gradient swap using joint equality and exact marginal matching. v1 only asserted approximate equivalence. This supplies substantive mathematical reasoning for a central step, although it does not establish equivalence under the implemented soft constraints.

improvement.justification: The added biological populations, RNA–protein alignment, and human-face translation substantially strengthen the generality claim, which v1 supported only through SNARE-seq and AFHQ. Guidance and sampling analyses also clarify operating trade-offs, and v2 supplies a code-access pointer. The lost SNARE-seq implementation recipe and the derivation's restriction to exact matching limit the gains, but the broader and more informative empirical validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DDMEC research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains these results and reports additional PBMC, bone-marrow, and CelebA-HQ experiments, sampling-budget comparisons, and guidance sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original DDMEC results for SNARE-seq alignment and AFHQ image translation, including quantitative scores and generated examples.

results.title: Learning to Match Unpaired Data with Minimum Entropy Coupling

C1.justification: The central claims of recall-aligned joint training, stage collaboration, and improved public and industrial performance remain. The introduction changes the claimed advantage over ARF from avoiding gradient vanishing through normalization to fuller use of the soft permutation matrix.

C2.justification: Appendix E adds substantive limitations concerning gradient conflicts, mismatched training and evaluation quotas, UWL's heuristic assumptions, and quadratic computational cost. V2 also restricts compatible sorting operators and revises explanations of ARF's shortcomings and bidirectional collaboration relative to ICC.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a LCRON-specific source-code link, baseline implementation provenance, TF-Ranking adaptation details, explicit hyperparameter search grids, and A800 runtime and memory information. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's existing architecture, optimizer, and online deployment descriptions.

E1.justification: Both versions use RecFlow Period 1 and industrial advertising data. Appendix C.2 adds coverage of rerank_neg and rerank_pos samples, using rerank_pos as ground truth for three-stage evaluation. This extends the evaluated selection task within the existing dataset and domain.

E2.justification: Table 7 adds standalone NeuralSort and SoftSort training as evaluated comparators. The main and industrial comparator rosters remain unchanged. ARF-v2's documented definition also inherits the revised Lsingle objective.

E3.justification: V2 adds three-stage DSSM/MLP/DIN evaluation, sorting-operator controls, four learning-rate/batch-size configurations, and GPU profiling. It explicitly sets training quotas to 10/10, whereas v1 identifies them with stage quotas of 30/20. This changes the reported setup without establishing whether retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The existing loss-removal, weight, streaming, and temperature analyses are retained. Appendices C–E add tests of sorter dependence, three-stage scalability, learning-rate/batch-size sensitivity, quota alignment, and computational costs, substantially broadening examination of robustness and practical behavior.

E5.justification: V1 reports five-run means, standard deviations, and t-tests for the ablation table only. V2 extends this reporting to the main comparison and three-stage experiment, and reports five-run means and standard deviations for sorting comparisons. These are newly documented practices, not evidence of an explicit increase in previously performed runs.

E6.justification: Table 2 updates baseline estimates, including FS-LambdaLoss joint Recall from 0.8674 to 0.8666, while LCRON's joint 0.8732 and industrial results remain. Single-stage metric assignments change: LCRON ranking Recall/NDCG becomes 0.8729/0.7291 instead of 0.7291/0.8729, so this is not evidence of performance improvement. New results include three-stage joint Recall of 0.7390, operator and training sensitivity, resource measurements, and quota-aligned Recall of 0.8714±0.0008.

M1.justification: Equations 5, 11, and 12 add negative-label cross-entropy terms to v1's positive-only objectives. This substantially changes the documented supervision for both Le2e and Lsingle; v1 explicitly excluded negative-label supervision. Full-stage sampling, soft-sort normalization, and UWL remain.

P1.justification: The six-section main narrative and much existing prose are retained, with localized rewriting of methodological explanations, related work, and conclusions. Appendix C gains subsections, and complexity, limitations, acknowledgements, and impact sections are added; the original narrative is not extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout, substantially resizing and relocating tables and figures. Six experimental tables are added. The existing temperature table moves from Table 6 to Table 8, while several main tables become much smaller column-width displays.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused comparisons with FAA and SRCR, discusses optimal-transport sorting, revises ICC and ARF positioning, and connects future work to multi-task and meta-learning. The central positioning within joint cascade ranking remains. RecFlow's updated publication citation represents the same work.

T1.justification: Alongside the revised loss definitions, Appendix D adds asymptotic time and space analysis distinguishing O(DN) from O(DN²) costs. The central survival-probability bound and Appendix A derivation, including Equations 8 and 14–15, remain unchanged; no replacement bound proof accompanies the revised losses.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical support for its central claims: the main comparison gains uncertainty and significance reporting, and the previously asserted extension beyond two stages receives direct testing. Added robustness studies, implementation details, and explicit quota and loss-fusion limitations improve reproducibility and transparency. Some discussion remains inconsistent with the reassigned Recall/NDCG columns, and smaller tables impair readability, but these issues do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LCRON and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Corresponding content can be matched across the layout changes and expanded appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds three-stage ranking, sorting-operator comparisons, training-parameter sensitivity, and runtime and memory measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original RecFlow experiments, ablations, streaming and sensitivity evaluations, and an industrial online A/B test.

results.title: Learning Cascade Ranking as One Network

C1.justification: The abstract expands the headline empirical claim from approximately 54% success on WebArena-Lite to 57.58% there and a text-only state-of-the-art 81.36% on WebVoyager, extending claimed success to real-world web tasks. The architectural and synthetic-data contributions remain. The introduction's 53.94% contribution bullet and conclusion are not fully updated.

C2.justification: A new Limitations section identifies dependence on a capable trajectory-collection model when training data are unavailable and the efficiency cost of replanning after every action. Section 5.3.2 also interprets the smaller-model comparison as evidence for CoT's importance. Earlier interpretations concerning plan quality, overfitting and dynamic content remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.12/Figure 5 supplies previously absent training and inference specifications, including learning rate, optimizer, batch size, epochs, 8×A100 hardware, software frameworks and decoding limits. Section 5.1 identifies the CoT teacher and specifies five seed examples per ten generated examples; Section 5.5 documents WebVoyager collection and annotation models. These materially expand reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only WebArena-Lite's simulated web tasks. v3 additionally trains and evaluates on WebVoyager's dynamic, real-world websites (Section 5.5), substantially extending the represented data and environmental conditions.

E2.justification: Within WebArena-Lite, Table 1 adds GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o, AWM + GPT-4-0613 and WebPilot + GPT-4o to the retained comparisons. Tables 3–4 additionally include NNetNav, AutoWebGLM, AgentOccam variants, OpenWebVoyager, WebVoyager variants, Wilbur and Agent-E. These are reported numerical comparisons, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: v3 adds full-WebArena evaluation and 8B/32B model configurations alongside the original 70B experiments. The new WebVoyager training setup uses 1,500 synthetic trajectories and 10,000 synthetic plans. Appendix A.11 adds step-count metrics separated by success/failure. The original WebArena-Lite settings remain; newly disclosed hyperparameters do not establish changes to those settings.

E4.justification: Tables 1–2 add a focused CoT comparison and examine whether smaller CoT models approach the non-CoT 70B model. Appendix A.11 adds website-level success rates and action-length analysis by outcome. The earlier augmentation ablations, replanning examples and failure classifications are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random-seed information, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v3 continues point-estimate reporting; its additional average step counts do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All original Table 1 scores remain, including 53.94% for dynamic replanning. v3 adds 57.58% for the CoT variant, smaller-model results, and new benchmark results, including QWQ-32B's 48.15% on WebArena and 81.36% on WebVoyager. Appendix A.11 adds website and step-count results. Section 5.3.2's stated 4.36% CoT gain conflicts with Table 1's 3.64-percentage-point difference.

M1.justification: Sections 3.4 and 4.2.2 add a CoT training/inference extension, including teacher-generated action rationales and reasoning before plans/actions. The two-agent architecture, grounded-plan generation and dynamic replanning remain intact. v1 already included planner Reasoning fields in its appendix; the extension particularly changes executor reasoning and its supervision.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and Appendix A.1–A.10 remain unchanged. v3 inserts CoT subsections, additional benchmark sections, limitations and two appendix sections while preserving the original narrative sequence. Wording and cross-reference edits are limited rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adds a first-page system overview, expands Table 1 with baseline and CoT rows, and introduces Tables 2–4. Appendix figures 4–5 present website statistics and training/inference settings as tables. The original two diagrams are retained as Figures 2–3. These additions substantially expand the visual presentation beyond renumbering and pagination.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 substantially expands positioning against hierarchical planning methods, including AgentOccam, WebPilot, AdaPlanner and ADaPT, and discusses complementary trajectory-generation approaches and robotic planners. It explicitly distinguishes the work through trainable models, architectural simplicity and synthetic planning data. Additional references support the CoT extension and new benchmarks.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theoretical assumptions, theorems, proofs or mathematical derivations. The added CoT material concerns an empirical training and inference procedure.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical validation through full-WebArena and real-world WebVoyager experiments, while Appendix A.12 fills important reproducibility gaps. Expanded comparisons and explicit limitations also make the contribution easier to assess. These gains outweigh reporting problems, including the incorrect CoT-gain arithmetic and the conclusion's outdated treatment of executor CoT as future work. Sparse evaluation details for the new benchmarks and absent uncertainty estimates still limit confidence in the strongest performance claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same PLAN-AND-ACT study. Their text, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison. Appendix A.1–A.10 is retained unchanged; v3 adds A.11–A.12.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original CoT and model-size results, WebArena and WebVoyager evaluations, and website-level performance analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original WebArena-Lite experiments comparing planner/executor configurations, synthetic-data augmentation and dynamic replanning, particularly in Table 1.

results.title: Plan-and-Act: Improving Planning of Agents for Long-Horizon Tasks

C1.justification: Both versions claim that knowledge-guided visual-text alignment and forgery prompts enable generalizable, explainable detection with multi-turn dialogue. The rewritten abstract and added DF40 evidence preserve these core contributions and the broad superiority claim.

C2.justification: Appendix A.4 newly attributes detection failures to the mismatch between general VQA training and localized forgery reasoning, acknowledging that accurate localization can coexist with wrong textual judgments. Appendix A.3 also discusses increased inference cost relative to CADDM and FAK-Owl. These introduce substantive qualifications to v1's largely unqualified accuracy and explainability narrative.

V2 also specifies the localization-loss weight and low-data training budget. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's backbone, optimizer, hardware and epoch details.

Appendix A.2 also introduces six corrupted FF++ input scenarios. These substantially extend the manipulation and input-condition coverage beyond v1's retained datasets.

V1's P-Tuning row becomes Clipping with the same cited work and scores; this is a rename rather than an additional baseline.

Existing main training settings remain unchanged. The 500-step budget for low-data experiments and 32-frame LLM aggregation are newly specified; the PDFs do not establish that these disclosures represent changed earlier procedures.

E4.justification: V2 adds a direct test of reference optimization in Table 8, corruption robustness in Table 9, and failure cases where correct localization accompanies incorrect LLM judgments in Figure 6. It also supplies previously absent multi-turn conversation examples. The prompt-tuning, training-dataset and LLM-architecture ablations are retained, while the low-data analysis is revised.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The additional results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 retains the original KFD scores, but added baselines change rankings: its DFDC AUC of 79.12 is now below UDD's 81.21. FAK-Owl's CDF2 AUC changes from 73.51 to 60.85 between v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 3. The low-data table has replaced values and dataset columns, with a newly disclosed budget. DF40, robustness, reference-ablation, timing and qualitative results are also added.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 and Figure 3 revise the documented text-conditioning procedure: v1 places learnable context before the text encoder, whereas v2 concatenates learnable embeddings with encoded description features. The overall KFD–FPL–LLM pipeline and losses remain unchanged. LoRA was already used in v1's ablation experiments.

P1.justification: The abstract and introductory motivation are revised around LVLM–forensics misalignment, terminology and comparison prose are clarified, and publication details and acknowledgements are added. The placeholder appendix becomes organized subsections. The main section sequence and much of the existing method and analysis prose are retained.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the framework and KFD diagrams, removes the standalone FPL architecture diagram and detailed detector-branch schematics, enlarges the retained GradCAM display, and expands localization panels. It restructures the LVLM comparison into classifier/VQA blocks and adds experimental tables, failure illustrations and extensive dialogue screenshots.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for recent comparison methods, ImageBind, DF40 and GenFace, while removing several background citations with the revised introduction. The related-work discussion and positioning around external knowledge and fine-grained forgery prompts remain largely intact.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6 retain the same similarity calculations, losses and image-blending formulation. Renaming consistency maps from C to rho does not change the mathematics. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 adds none.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves important deficiencies in v1's evidence and reproducibility: the placeholder appendix becomes substantive implementation documentation and actual dialogue examples, while new component and robustness tests strengthen validation. Explicit failure analysis also qualifies the explainability claim. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including Table 10's CDF2 label with CDF1-matching AUC values and superiority language broader than the expanded Table 1 supports.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KFD/FPL/LVLM framework and retain identifiable equations, experiments and figures. All supplied material supports comparison, including v1's template-only appendix and v2's substantive Appendix A.

after.justification: The retained original experiments are supplemented by DF40 results, reference-optimization ablations, perturbation tests, inference timings and qualitative dialogue and failure examples.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.4 report original detection results, localization examples and experiments varying training data, prompt-tuning components and LLM architectures.

results.title: Unlocking the Capabilities of Large Vision-Language Models for Generalizable and Explainable Deepfake Detection

C1.justification: The central contributions remain identifying inefficient interactions between exploration strategies and coordinating them through KEA to improve sparse-reward learning. DeepSea supplies additional support in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion without redefining these core claims.

C2.justification: V2 Appendix A interprets its derived revisit count as explaining delayed exploration and asserts relevance to longer-horizon tasks. Section 3.4 adds interpretation of performance as DeepSea depth increases. The existing explanation of effectiveness across SAC/SQL, DQN-P, and DQN, and the off-policy-only limitation, remain.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Appendix B newly document update sequencing, network architectures, optimizer settings, learning rates, replay buffers, reward processing, and task-specific hyperparameters. Appendix D supplies navigation grid dimensions, obstacle geometry, termination conditions, and episode limits. These substantially expand reproducibility information rather than establishing changes to previously undocumented settings.

E1.justification: V2 adds DeepSea at sizes 10, 14, 20, 24, and 30, introducing sequential exploration with deceptive movement penalties and a sparse terminal reward. The existing 2D navigation task and three DeepMind Control Suite tasks remain.

E2.justification: V2 Table 3 adds comparisons against DeRL-A2C, DeRL-PPO, DeRL-DQN, SOFE-A2C, SOFE-PPO, and SOFE-DQN. These introduce two substantial baseline families. Comparator membership in the retained navigation, continuous-control, and DQN/SQL experiments is unchanged after matching renamed methods.

Separately, v1 Appendix A states 8/16/32/48 SAC updates per transition, whereas v2 Appendix C states per 32 transitions. This materially revises the reported update schedule without establishing that the retained experiments were rerun.
